metadata.title: On the Folklore set and Dirichlet spectrum for matrices

extraction_notes.note: The sketch rule asks rigor semi_formal on a proof sketch, but rigor is not allowed on proof nodes; the sketch is of a cited result with no full proof here, so no rigor and no alternative flag were set.
Remark environments retyped as open_problem: Remark 5 states that non-emptiness for n=3 remains unknown, Remark 13 asks whether Di_{m,n}=Di_{n,m}.

Sections 6 and 7 (and subsection 5.2) are proofs with no proof environment; each is one proof node with its subsections as steps. Section 5.2 ends its proof before the proof environment of the lemma it reduces to.
Theorem 3.2 has no proof of its own; Remark 9 says which theorems give each claim, so uses edges from Theorems 3.4, 3.6 and Corollary 8.2 go into Theorem 3.2.

Section 4 (outline) and the discussion paragraphs comparing results with Das et al. and Agin-Weiss are commentary and produced no nodes; the omitted dependency diagram is not reproduced in the source.

Lemma 6.1 is stated inside the proof of Theorem 2.3 and its proof uses that proof's construction (23)-(31), while the proof of Theorem 2.3 applies the lemma; the lemma is also cited from the proof of Theorem 3.6, so it is not local to one proof.
evidence: we may restrict to integer vectors of the form appearing in Lemma~\ref{wichtig!}.

nodes.name: Norms on R^n and R^m
nodes.statement: Let $n,m \in \mathbb{N}$, and let $\|\cdot\|_{1}$ be any norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\|\cdot\|_{2}$ any norm on $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.
nodes.section: 1 Uniform approximation for Systems of linear forms and arbitrary norms

nodes.name: Approximation function psi
nodes.statement: For a given real $m\times n$ matrix $\Omega \in \mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ and a parameter $t\ge 1$ define the piecewise constant approximation function \[ \psi_{\Omega}^{m\times n}(\|\cdot\|_{1},\|\cdot\|_{2}, t):= \underset{ 1 \leq \Vert \boldsymbol{\hat{b}}\Vert_{1}\leq t }{\min_{\boldsymbol{b}=(\hat{\boldsymbol{b}},\tilde{\boldsymbol{b}})\in \mathbb{Z}^{n+m}:}} \left\|\Omega \cdot \widehat{\boldsymbol{b}} + \tilde{\boldsymbol{b}} \right\|_{2} = \underset{ 1 \leq \Vert \boldsymbol{\hat{b}}\Vert_{1}\leq t }{\min_{\boldsymbol{b}=(\hat{\boldsymbol{b}},\tilde{\boldsymbol{b}})\in \mathbb{Z}^{n+m}:}} \left\|\sum_{i=1}^{n}\Omega_{i}b_{i} + \tilde{\boldsymbol{b}} \right\|_{2}, \] where $\Omega_{i}$ denotes the $i$th column of the matrix $\Omega$, and \begin{equation} \hat{\boldsymbol{b}}=(b_{1},\dots,b_{n}), \qquad \tilde{\boldsymbol{b}}=(b_{n+1},\dots,b_{n+m}),\qquad \boldsymbol{b}=(\hat{\boldsymbol{b}},\tilde{\boldsymbol{b}}) \end{equation} interpreted as column vectors.
nodes.section: 1 Uniform approximation for Systems of linear forms and arbitrary norms
nodes.statement_short: Uniform approximation function: minimum norm of Omega b-hat + b-tilde over integer vectors with 1<=|b-hat|<=t.

nodes.name: Hat/tilde notation for integer vectors (1)
nodes.statement: \hat{\boldsymbol{b}}=(b_{1},\dots,b_{n}), \qquad \tilde{\boldsymbol{b}}=(b_{n+1},\dots,b_{n+m}),\qquad \boldsymbol{b}=(\hat{\boldsymbol{b}},\tilde{\boldsymbol{b}})
nodes.section: 1 Uniform approximation for Systems of linear forms and arbitrary norms
nodes.label: eq:hatnot

nodes.name: Best approximations
nodes.statement: The column vectors $\boldsymbol{b}$ for which the minimum is attained for some $t$, are often called best approximations of $\Omega$.
nodes.section: 1 Uniform approximation for Systems of linear forms and arbitrary norms

nodes.name: Dirichlet constant
nodes.statement: Define the Dirichlet constant of a matrix as \[ \Theta^{m\times n}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1,\Vert\cdot\Vert_2,\Omega)= \limsup_{t\to\infty}\; t^{n/m} \psi_{\Omega}^{m\times n}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1,\Vert\cdot\Vert_2,t), \] and further let \[ \widetilde{\Theta}^{m\times n}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1,\Vert\cdot\Vert_2,\Omega)= \liminf_{t\to\infty}\; t^{n/m} \psi_{\Omega}^{m\times n}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1,\Vert\cdot\Vert_2,t). \]
nodes.section: 1 Uniform approximation for Systems of linear forms and arbitrary norms
nodes.statement_short: Dirichlet constant = limsup of t^{n/m} psi(t); the liminf version is the ordinary analogue.

nodes.name: Maximal Dirichlet constant D
nodes.statement: By equivalence of norms and Dirichlet's Theorem, for each pair $(m,n)$ and each pair of norms $\|\cdot\|_{1},\|\cdot\|_{2}$ we can derive the constants \begin{equation} D=D^{m\times n}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1,\Vert\cdot\Vert_2):= \sup_{\Omega\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}} \Theta^{m\times n}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1,\Vert\cdot\Vert_2,\Omega) < \infty. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 1 Uniform approximation for Systems of linear forms and arbitrary norms
nodes.statement_short: D is the supremum of the Dirichlet constant over all m x n matrices; finite by Dirichlet's theorem.

nodes.name: Definition of D (2)
nodes.statement: D=D^{m\times n}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1,\Vert\cdot\Vert_2):= \sup_{\Omega\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}} \Theta^{m\times n}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1,\Vert\cdot\Vert_2,\Omega) < \infty.
nodes.section: 1 Uniform approximation for Systems of linear forms and arbitrary norms
nodes.label: eq:obben

nodes.name: D=1 for maximum norms
nodes.statement: For $\|\cdot\|_{1}$ and $\|\cdot\|_{2}$ the standard maximum norms, we have $D=1$, with the upper estimate coming from Minkowski's Theorem for systems of linear forms.
nodes.section: 1 Uniform approximation for Systems of linear forms and arbitrary norms

nodes.name: Dirichlet Spectrum
nodes.statement: For any pair $(m,n)$ and norms $\|\cdot\|_{1},\|\cdot\|_{2}$ we follow \cite{akmo} and define the \textit{Dirichlet Spectrum} to be the set \begin{equation} \mathcal{D}_{m,n}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1,\Vert\cdot\Vert_2):= \left\{ \Theta^{m\times n}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1,\Vert\cdot\Vert_2,\Omega) : \Omega \in \mathbb{R}^{m\times n} \right\} \subseteq [0,D]\, . \end{equation}
nodes.section: 1 Uniform approximation for Systems of linear forms and arbitrary norms

nodes.name: Dirichlet spectrum (3)
nodes.statement: \mathcal{D}_{m,n}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1,\Vert\cdot\Vert_2):= \left\{ \Theta^{m\times n}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1,\Vert\cdot\Vert_2,\Omega) : \Omega \in \mathbb{R}^{m\times n} \right\} \subseteq [0,D]\, .
nodes.section: 1 Uniform approximation for Systems of linear forms and arbitrary norms
nodes.label: eq:dirspe

nodes.name: Dirichlet spectrum of one linear form is [0,1]
nodes.statement: In \cite{j2} it is proven that the spectrum is the entire unit interval in the dual setting with the max norm, i.e. $\mathcal{D}_{1,n}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_{\infty})=[0,1]$.
nodes.section: 1 Uniform approximation for Systems of linear forms and arbitrary norms

nodes.name: Dirichlet spectrum for norms on R^2 (Kleinbock-Rao; Agin)
nodes.statement: In short, it was shown in \cite[Corollary 1.2]{kleinbock} that the upper bound $D^{2\times 1}(\vert\cdot\vert,\Vert\cdot\Vert_2)$ defined in \eqref{eq:obben} is an accumulation point for any norm on $\mathbb{R}^2$, and in \cite{algo} it is proven that for any arbitrary norm the Dirichlet spectrum contains an interval starting at the origin, see \cite[Corollary 1]{algo}.
nodes.section: 1 Uniform approximation for Systems of linear forms and arbitrary norms

nodes.name: Sets Di(c) and DI(c)
nodes.statement: For $0\le c\le D$, define the following sets \begin{align*} Di_{m,n}(\|\cdot\|_{1},\|\cdot\|_{2},c)&:=\left\{ \Omega \in \mathbb{R}^{m\times n} : \Theta^{m\times n}(\|\cdot\|_{1},\|\cdot\|_{2},\Omega)\leq c \right\}, \\ DI_{m,n}(\|\cdot\|_{1},\|\cdot\|_{2},c)&:=\left\{ \Omega \in \mathbb{R}^{m\times n} : \Theta^{m\times n}(\|\cdot\|_{1},\|\cdot\|_{2},\Omega)= c \right\}. \end{align*}
nodes.section: 1 Uniform approximation for Systems of linear forms and arbitrary norms
nodes.statement_short: Di(c): matrices with Dirichlet constant at most c; DI(c): exactly c.

nodes.name: c-Dirichlet improvable matrices
nodes.statement: The set $Di_{m,n}(\|\cdot\|_{1},\|\cdot\|_{2},c)$ represents the set of $c$\textit{-Dirichlet improvable matrices with respect to norms} $\Vert\cdot\Vert_{1},\Vert\cdot\Vert_{2}$.
nodes.section: 1 Uniform approximation for Systems of linear forms and arbitrary norms

nodes.name: Dirichlet improvable matrices
nodes.statement: The more widely known set of \textit{Dirichlet improvable matrices} is denoted as \begin{equation*} Di_{m,n}(\|\cdot\|_{1},\|\cdot\|_{2}):=\left\{ \Omega \in \mathbb{R}^{m\times n} : \Theta^{m\times n}(\|\cdot\|_{1},\|\cdot\|_{2},\Omega)< D \right\}=\bigcup_{0\;<\;c\;<\;D}Di_{m,n}(\|\cdot\|_{1},\|\cdot\|_{2},c). \\ \end{equation*}
nodes.section: 1 Uniform approximation for Systems of linear forms and arbitrary norms

nodes.name: Singular and badly approximable matrices
nodes.statement: As well as the set of Dirichlet improvable matrices one can use the Dirichlet constant (the uniform and asymptotic one) to characterize the set of \textit{Singular matrices} and the set of \textit{Badly approximable matrices}. Define \begin{align*} Sing_{m,n}&:=DI_{m,n}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_{1},\Vert\cdot\Vert_{2},0)=\bigcap_{0\;<\;c\;<\;D} Di_{m,n}(\|\cdot\|_{1},\|\cdot\|_{2},c),\\ Bad_{m,n}&:=\left\{ \Omega \in \mathbb{R}^{m\times n} : \widetilde{\Theta}^{m\times n}(\|\cdot\|_{1},\|\cdot\|_{2},\Omega)> 0 \right\}. \end{align*}
nodes.section: 1 Uniform approximation for Systems of linear forms and arbitrary norms
nodes.statement_short: Singular = Dirichlet constant 0; badly approximable = positive liminf constant.

nodes.name: Mahler transference for Bad and Sing
nodes.statement: Moreover it follows from Mahler's Dual Convex Body Theory that \[ Bad_{m,n}=Bad_{n,m}, \quad \text{ and } \quad Sing_{m,n}=Sing_{n,m}. \]
nodes.section: 1 Uniform approximation for Systems of linear forms and arbitrary norms

nodes.name: Bad is contained in Di (Davenport-Schmidt)
nodes.statement: Trivially, for any $0<c<D$ we have that $Sing_{m,n} \subseteq Di_{m,n}(c)\subseteq Di_{m,n}$, and for $Bad_{m,n}$ we have the relations \begin{equation*} Bad_{m,n}\subseteq Di_{m,n} \quad \text{ and } \quad Bad_{m,n}\cap Sing_{m,n}=\emptyset\, . \end{equation*} The left was shown by Davenport and Schmidt \cite[Theorem 2]{DavenportSchmidt3} and the right is obvious.
nodes.section: 1 Uniform approximation for Systems of linear forms and arbitrary norms

nodes.name: Non-emptiness of Bad and Sing (Jarnik, Khintchine)
nodes.statement: The sets $Bad_{m,n}$ and $Sing_{m,n}$ are non-empty, as was classically shown by Jarnik and Khintchine (see \cite{Khinchin3} for the case of singular vectors).
nodes.section: 1 Uniform approximation for Systems of linear forms and arbitrary norms

nodes.name: Bad, Sing, Di are Lebesgue null
nodes.statement: Furthermore, it is well known that all of the sets highlighted above are Lebesgue nullsets.
nodes.section: 1 Uniform approximation for Systems of linear forms and arbitrary norms

nodes.name: Hausdorff dimensions of Bad, Di, Sing
nodes.statement: The following results have been proven: \begin{align*} \dim_H Bad_{m,n} &= mn\, ,\;\; \text{for $m=n=1$ in \cite{Jarnik3} and for general $m,n$ in \cite{schmidt1960,schmidtsystemoflinearforms}},\\[2ex] \dim_H Di_{m,n} &= mn\, , \text{ \cite{schmidt1960,schmidtsystemoflinearforms} combined with \cite[Theorem 2]{DavenportSchmidt3}}, \\[2ex] \dim_H Sing_{m,n} &= mn\left(1-\frac{1}{m+n}\right)\, ,\;\; \begin{array}{c}\text{for $m=2, n=1$ in \cite{Cheung}, for $m\geq 2, n=1$ in \cite{CheungChevallier},}\\ \text{and for general $m,n$ in~\cite[Theorem~1.1]{Dasetal}}. \end{array} \end{align*}
nodes.section: 1 Uniform approximation for Systems of linear forms and arbitrary norms
nodes.origin_citation: Jarnik 1929; Schmidt 1960, 1969; Davenport & Schmidt; Cheung 2011; Cheung & Chevallier 2016; Das et al. 2024
nodes.statement_short: dim Bad = dim Di = mn and dim Sing = mn(1-1/(m+n)).

nodes.name: Dimension bounds for Di_{m,1}(c) (Cheung-Chevallier)
nodes.statement: In the case of maximum norms, $m\geq 2, n=1$, and any constant $C>0$, for $c>0$ sufficiently small and for any real number $t>m$ the bounds \begin{equation*} \tfrac{m^{2}}{m+1}+c^{t}\leq \dim_H Di_{m,1}(c)\leq \tfrac{m^{2}}{m+1}+C\cdot c^{m/2} \end{equation*} were proven in \cite[Theorem 1.3]{CheungChevallier}.
nodes.section: 1 Uniform approximation for Systems of linear forms and arbitrary norms

nodes.name: Khintchine: Sing_{1,1}=Q
nodes.statement: For $m=n=1$ it was proven by Khintchine \cite{Khinchin3} that $Sing_{1,1}=\mathbb{Q}$, in fact $Di_{1,1}(c)=\mathbb{Q}$ for any $c<\frac{1}{2}$.
nodes.section: 1 Uniform approximation for Systems of linear forms and arbitrary norms

nodes.name: Di_{1,1} = Q union Bad_{1,1}
nodes.statement: By combining this with \cite[Theorem 1]{DavenportSchmidt3}, we obtain \begin{equation*} Di_{1,1}=\mathbb{Q}\cup Bad_{1,1}. \end{equation*}
nodes.section: 1 Uniform approximation for Systems of linear forms and arbitrary norms

nodes.name: Folklore set FS_{m,1} has a continuum of points (Beresnevich et al.)
nodes.statement: In higher dimensions much less was known, until the recent paper of Beresnevich et. al. \cite{BerGuaMarRamVel}, who showed that, for $n\geq 2$, the \textit{Folklore set} \begin{equation*} FS_{m,1}:=Di_{m,1}\backslash(Bad_{m,1}\cup Sing_{m,1})\, \end{equation*} has a continuum of points.
nodes.section: 1 Uniform approximation for Systems of linear forms and arbitrary norms

nodes.name: Full dimension conjecture for FS_{m,1}
nodes.statement: They mention that this question was first asked in \cite{FabianSuessThesis} (see the remark immediately following \cite[Theorem 4.6]{FabianSuessThesis}) and furthermore conjectured that, for $n\geq 2$, we should have $\dim_H FS_{m,1}=m$, see \cite[Problem 3.1]{BerGuaMarRamVel}.
nodes.section: 1 Uniform approximation for Systems of linear forms and arbitrary norms

nodes.name: Folklore set
nodes.statement: Given this setup we define the Folklore set on $m\times n$ matrices with arbitrary norms as \begin{equation*} FS_{m,n}(\|\cdot\|_{1},\|\cdot\|_{2})=Di_{m,n}(\|\cdot\|_{1},\|\cdot\|_{2})\backslash \left(Bad_{m,n} \cup Sing_{m,n} \right) \end{equation*} and, for any $0<c<D$, the smaller set \begin{equation*} FS_{m,n}(\|\cdot\|_{1},\|\cdot\|_{2},c)=DI_{m,n}(\|\cdot\|_{1},\|\cdot\|_{2},c)\backslash Bad_{m,n}. \end{equation*}
nodes.section: 1 Uniform approximation for Systems of linear forms and arbitrary norms
nodes.statement_short: Folklore set: Dirichlet improvable matrices that are neither badly approximable nor singular; FS(c) fixes the Dirichlet constant c.

nodes.name: Folklore set notation for maximum norms
nodes.statement: When the norms are the maximum norms we denote the sets by $FS_{m,n}$ and $FS_{m,n}(c)$ respectively.
nodes.section: 1 Uniform approximation for Systems of linear forms and arbitrary norms

nodes.name: Full dimension conjecture for FS_{m,n}
nodes.statement: Again, it was conjectured that the set $FS_{m,n}(\|\cdot\|_{1},\|\cdot\|_{2})$ has full Hausdorff dimension $mn$ \cite[Problem 4.1]{BerGuaMarRamVel}.
nodes.section: 1 Uniform approximation for Systems of linear forms and arbitrary norms

nodes.name: Folklore set under transposition
nodes.statement: { Given $m,n$, there exists $\delta=\delta_{m,n}>0$ so that if $\Omega \in FS_{m,n}(\|\cdot\|_{1},\|\cdot\|_{2}, c)$ for some $0<c<\delta$, then its transpose $\Omega^T$ satisfies $\Omega^{T} \in FS_{n,m}(\|\cdot\|_{2},\|\cdot\|_{1})$.}
nodes.section: 1 Uniform approximation for Systems of linear forms and arbitrary norms
nodes.statement_short: If Omega lies in FS(c) for small c, its transpose lies in the Folklore set of the transposed problem.
nodes.label: Folklore transpose

nodes.name: Das-Fishman-Simmons-Urbanski Folklore set dimension bound
nodes.statement: \dim_H FS_{m,n}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_{\infty}, \Vert\cdot\Vert_{\infty}) \geq mn\left(1-\frac{1}{m+n}\right)\, , \quad \quad \text{\cite[Theorem 3.15]{Dasetal}}.
nodes.label: eq:daset2

nodes.name: Agin-Weiss: the Dirichlet spectrum is [0,D]
nodes.statement: Precisely, in notation \eqref{eq:dirspe}, they have proven that \begin{equation*} \mathcal{D}_{m,n}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1,\Vert\cdot\Vert_2)=[0,D]\, , \quad \quad \text{\cite[Theorem 1]{AginWeiss2024}}. \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Agin-Weiss: DI(c) uncountable and dense
nodes.statement: Moreover they state that for each $c\in[0,D]$ the sets $DI_{m,n}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1,\Vert\cdot\Vert_2,c)$ are uncountable and dense in $\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$.

nodes.name: Dual-setting sets DI_n(c), FS_n(c)
nodes.statement: For ease of notation, for $c\in (0,1)$ we write $$ DI_{n}(c) :=DI_{1,n}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_{\infty},\vert\cdot\vert,c), \qquad FS_{n}(c):=DI_{n}(c)\backslash \left( Bad_{1,n} \cup Sing_{1,n} \right). $$

nodes.name: FS_n(c) non-empty for all c in (0,1)
nodes.statement: It was shown in~\cite{j2} by the second name author that the set $FS_n(c)$ is non-empty for any $c\in (0,1)$, refining the aforementioned result from~\cite{BerGuaMarRamVel} and also complementing~\cite{Dasetal}.

nodes.name: Folklore set with prescribed Dirichlet constant, dual max-norm case
nodes.statement: For any natural number $n\ge 4$, there exists explicitly computable $c_n\in~(0,1)$ such that for any $c\in (0,c_n)$ we have \begin{equation*} \dim_H FS_{n}(c)\geq n-2. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: For n>=4 and small c, the dual Folklore set with exact Dirichlet constant c has Hausdorff dimension at least n-2.
nodes.label: thm1

nodes.name: Expected n=3 case of Theorem 2.1
nodes.statement: We believe the claim holds for $n=3$ as well, probably improving on the bound that can be obtained from the methods in~\cite{j1, j2}. However, problems occur in our proof in this case stemming from auxiliary results from~\cite{ngm}, leaving this case open.

nodes.name: Comparison with earlier bounds
nodes.statement: In~\cite{j1} a lower bound of weaker order $(3/8)n+o(n)$ as $n\to\infty$ is shown for the corresponding sets with respect to simultaneous approximation for any $c\in (0,1)$. In~\cite{j2} it is shown that $FS_n(c)$ for a linear form as defined above is not empty for any $c\in (0,1)$, and reference to~\cite{j1} is given on how to obtain metrical results in a similar way. However, again these bounds will turn out considerably weaker than in Theorem~\ref{thm1} above. The bound of Theorem~\ref{thm1} can in fact be further improved a little with some effort, see Remark~\ref{rrr} in Section~\ref{proof dual case}.
nodes.label: remark4

nodes.name: Explicit value of c_n
nodes.statement: We may take \[ c_n = \frac{n-3}{8(n-2)^{3/2}}\cdot \sqrt{\pi}\cdot \frac{ \Gamma(n-\frac{1}{2})}{\Gamma(n)} \] with $\Gamma$ the Euler Gamma function.

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 2.2
nodes.statement: Using \cite[Proposition 1.1 and Lemma 4.9]{BerGuaMarRamVel} we infer the following corollary towards the original conjecture \cite[Problem 3.1]{BerGuaMarRamVel}.
nodes.statement_short: Deduce from Theorem 2.1 via Beresnevich et al.'s Proposition 1.1 and Lemma 4.9.

nodes.name: Folklore set dimension lower bound
nodes.statement: Let $n\geq 4$. Then we have \begin{equation*} \dim_H FS_{n} \geq n-2,\,\qquad \dim_H FS_{n,1}\geq n-2\, . \end{equation*}
nodes.label: Folklore set dimension lower bound

nodes.name: Simultaneous setting with fixed constant
nodes.statement: We are not able to deduce an equivalent claim for any set $ FS_{n}^{*} (c):=FS_{n,1}(c)$ with $c>0$. The reason is that the sets $FS_{n}^{*} (c)$ do not coincide with $FS_{n}(c)$ for $c>0$, indeed Lemma~\ref{Folklore transpose} is too weak. On the other hand, similar to~\cite{BerGuaMarRamVel} or~\cite[Section~11]{j2} it allows for deducing non-emptyness (Hausdorff dimension $\ge n-2$ again) for sets $Di_{n,1}(c)\backslash (Bad_{n,1} \cup Di_{n,1}(c^{\prime}))$ where suitable $c^{\prime}\in (0,c)$ can be explicitly computed as a function of $n\ge 2,c\in (0,1)$. An analogous claim, with stronger Hausdorff dimension estimate as in \eqref{eq:daset2} and a different (most likely smaller) constant $c^{\prime}$, can be obtained from the uniform version of the variational principle in~\cite{Dasetal} as well.

nodes.name: Dual-setting sets for arbitrary norms
nodes.statement: Given any norm $\Vert\cdot\Vert=\Vert\cdot\Vert_1$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$ and $c>0$, let us write \[ DI_{n}(\Vert\cdot\Vert,c) :=DI_{1,n}(\Vert\cdot\Vert,\vert\cdot\vert,c), \qquad FS_{n}(\Vert \cdot \Vert, c):=DI_{n}(\Vert\cdot\Vert,c)\backslash \left( Bad_{1,n} \cup Sing_{1,n} \right). \]

nodes.name: Folklore set with prescribed Dirichlet constant, dual case, arbitrary norm
nodes.statement: Let $n\ge 4$ and $\|\cdot\|$ be any norm on $\mathbb{R}^n$. Then there is $c_n=c_n(\Vert\cdot\Vert)>0$ such that for any $c\in[0,c_n]$ we have \[ \dim_H FS_{n}(\Vert\cdot\Vert,c) \geq n-2\, . \] In particular the Dirichlet spectrum \[ \mathcal{D}_{n}(\Vert\cdot\Vert):= \{\Theta(\Vert\cdot\Vert,\boldsymbol{\xi}): \boldsymbol{\xi}\in \mathbb{R}^n \}:= \{ \Theta^{1\times n}(\Vert\cdot\Vert, |\cdot|,\boldsymbol{\xi}): \boldsymbol{\xi}\in \mathbb{R}^n \} \subseteq [0,D], \] contains some right neighborhood of $0$, and for each $c\in [0,c_{n}]$, $\dim_H DI_{n}(\|\cdot\|,c)\geq n-2$.
assumptions: Let $n\ge 4$ and $\|\cdot\|$ be any norm on $\mathbb{R}^n$.
conclusions: contains some right neighborhood of $0$, and for each $c\in [0,c_{n}]$, $\dim_H DI_{n}(\|\cdot\|,c)\geq n-2
nodes.statement_short: For n>=4 and any norm, FS_n(norm,c) has dimension >= n-2 for small c; the spectrum contains an interval [0,c_n].
nodes.label: jia

nodes.name: Bound also applies to FS_n(norm)
nodes.statement: Since $FS_{n}(\Vert\cdot\Vert,c)\subseteq FS_{n}(\Vert\cdot\Vert)$ the lower bound on the Hausdorff dimension applies to $FS_{n}(\Vert\cdot\Vert)$ as well, which is however weaker than \eqref{eq:daset2}. \par

nodes.name: Non-emptiness of FS_3(norm,c) for general norms
nodes.statement: For $n=3$ and a general norm, even non-emptiness of the set $FS_n(\Vert\cdot\Vert,c)$ for a given $c\in(0,D)$, with $D$ as in \eqref{eq:obben}, remains unknown. In particular \cite{AginWeiss2024} tells us nothing about this. For certain norms, this can be obtained from the method in~\cite{j2}. Again we expect the Hausdorff dimension to rise as a function of $c\in[0,D]$, not reflected in the theorem.

nodes.name: Comparison with the max-norm spectrum result
nodes.statement: In \cite{j2} it is proven that the spectrum is the entire unit interval, i.e. $\mathcal{D}_n(\Vert\cdot\Vert_{\infty})=[0,1]$. Theorem~\ref{jia} tells us the weaker statement that the spectrum contains some small interval starting at the origin, however, our result holds for any norm.

nodes.name: Simultaneous analogue via transposition
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{Folklore transpose}, from Theorem~\ref{jia} we may deduce an analogous metrical result to Corollary~\ref{Folklore set dimension lower bound} on the simultaneous approximation Folklore set for an arbitrary norm and $m\ge 4$. This will be covered by the more general Theorem~\ref{tT} below.

nodes.name: Non-emptiness of the Folklore set for matrices
nodes.statement: Let $m,n$ be positive integers satisfying $\{ m,n\}\notin \left\{ \{1,1\}, \{2,3\} \right\}$. Then \[ FS_{m,n}=FS_{m,n}(\Vert \cdot\Vert_{\infty},\Vert \cdot\Vert_{\infty}) \ne \emptyset. \] In fact \[ \dim_H FS_{m,n} \geq mn-2\max\{m,n\}, \] and all claims hold when we choose the involved matrices of full $\mathbb{R}$-rank $\min\{m,n\}$.
nodes.section: 3.1 Two fundamental results for maximum norm
assumptions: Let $m,n$ be positive integers satisfying $\{ m,n\}\notin \left\{ \{1,1\}, \{2,3\} \right\}$.
conclusions: all claims hold when we choose the involved matrices of full $\mathbb{R}$-rank $\min\{m,n\}$.
nodes.label: non-empty main

nodes.name: Conjectured dimension of FS(c) as c tends to D
nodes.statement: Regarding the metrical bound appearing in Theorem~\ref{non-empty main}, we have previously mentioned that the Folklore set is conjectured to have full dimension \cite[Problem 3.1]{BerGuaMarRamVel}, and more generally that $$\dim_H FS_{m,n}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1,\Vert\cdot\Vert_2,c)=mn-o(1)$$ as $c\to D^{-}$ for $D$ from \eqref{eq:obben}, for any pair of norms. However we cannot expect the dimension of $Di_{m,n}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1,\Vert\cdot\Vert_2,c) \supseteq FS_{m,n}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1,\Vert\cdot\Vert_2,c)$ to exceed the value from \eqref{eq:daset2} as $c\to 0^{+}$.
nodes.section: 3.1 Two fundamental results for maximum norm

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3.1
nodes.statement: Our result follows from a combination of Theorems~\ref{sganz},~\ref{tT} below combined with the cases $m=1, n\ge 2$ and $m\ge 2, n=1$ already settled in~\cite{j1, j2}.
nodes.section: 3.1 Two fundamental results for maximum norm
nodes.statement_short: Combine Theorems 3.5 and 3.7 with the vector cases settled in earlier work.

nodes.name: Dimension of rank-deficient matrices
nodes.statement: Regarding the full rank claim, by considering determinants of maximum quadratic minors we see that the Hausdorff dimension of the set of rank deficient real $m\times n$ matrices equals $mn-(\max\{ m,n\}-\min\{m,n\}+1)$.
nodes.section: 3.1 Two fundamental results for maximum norm

nodes.name: Condition for the rank claim to follow from Das et al. (4)

nodes.name: Dirichlet spectrum results for maximum norms
nodes.statement: Let $k,m,n$ be positive integers. \begin{itemize} \item If $\tfrac{m}{n} \in (0,\tfrac{1}{2}]\cup (1,\infty)$, $ (m,n)\notin \{ (3,2), (5,2), (7,2),\ldots \}$, then $\mathcal{D}_{m,n}$ contains some right neighborhood $[0,c_{m,n}]$ of $0$. \item If $m\vert n$ or $n\vert m$ and $(m,n)\ne (1,1)$ we have $\mathcal{D}_{m,n}=[0,1]$. \item Moreover $\mathcal{D}_{m,n} \subseteq \mathcal{D}_{km,kn}$. \end{itemize}

nodes.name: Derivation of Theorem 3.2 and Agin-Weiss improvement
nodes.statement: The aformentioned preprint \cite{AginWeiss2024} has since improved upon these results. In particular they show that for any $m,n$ the spectrum is the full interval, even with respect to arbitrary norms. Nevertheless our results are proven via different methods, moreover they give rise to metrical estimates for the set of involved matrices. The first claim follows more generally from our results for any pair of expanding norms, see Section \ref{se3.1} for a definition. In most cases $\Vert\cdot \Vert_1$ can even be arbitrary. The first claim follows directly from a combination of Theorem~\ref{ganze} and Theorem~\ref{thm5} below, where more general norms are considered, apart from the vector cases $\min\{m,n\}=1$ which are implied by the second claim of the theorem. The last claim is Corollary \ref{multiples} below, and the second claim follows in turn via the work in \cite{j1, j2}, and since $D=1$ for maximum norms. Note that the last claim implies that we can restrict to coprime $m,n$ for the study of the Dirichlet spectrum with respect to maximum norms.
nodes.section: 3.1 Two fundamental results for maximum norm

nodes.name: Folklore set for square matrices
nodes.statement: For $m=n\ge 2$, the set $FS_{n,n}=FS_{n,n}(\Vert \cdot \Vert_{\infty},\Vert \cdot \Vert_{\infty})$ satisfies \[ \dim_H FS_{n,n} \ge (n-1)^2+1. \] Moreover, we can choose the matrices of full $\mathbb{R}$-rank $n$ (i.e. invertible).
conclusions: we can choose the matrices of full $\mathbb{R}$-rank $n$ (i.e. invertible).
nodes.label: arbn

nodes.name: Expanding norm
nodes.statement: Following~\cite{j1}, let us call a norm $\Vert\cdot\Vert$ on $\mathbb{R}^{k}$ expanding if $\Vert \textbf{x}\Vert\ge \Vert \pi_j(\textbf{x})\Vert$ for any $\textbf{x}\in \mathbb{R}^k$ and every $1\le j\le k$, where $$\pi_j: (x_1,\ldots,x_k)\to (0,\ldots,0,x_j,0,\ldots,0)$$ is the projection to the $j$-th coordinate axis.
differentia: $\Vert \textbf{x}\Vert\ge \Vert \pi_j(\textbf{x})\Vert$ for any $\textbf{x}\in \mathbb{R}^k$ and every $1\le j\le k$

nodes.name: Ceiling function
nodes.statement: Denote further by $\lceil x\rceil$ the smallest integer $\ge x$.

nodes.name: Folklore set with prescribed Dirichlet constant for m>n
nodes.statement: Assume $m,n$ are positive integers with \[ 1 < \tfrac{m}{n}, \qquad (m,n)\notin \{(3,2), (5,2), (7,2), \ldots \}. \] Let $\Vert\cdot\Vert_1$ be an arbitrary norm on $\mathbb{R}^n$ and $\Vert\cdot\Vert_2$ be any expanding norm on $\mathbb{R}^m$, unless if $n=2$ assume both norms $\Vert\cdot\Vert_1$ and $\Vert\cdot\Vert_2$ are expanding. Then there exists $c_{m,n}=c_{m,n}(\Vert\cdot \Vert_1,\Vert\cdot\Vert_2)>0$ so that for any $c\in [0,c_{m,n}]$, we have \[ FS_{m,n}(\Vert \cdot \Vert_{1},\Vert \cdot \Vert_{2},c)\ne \emptyset \] in fact unless $n=2$ or $(m,n)=(4,3)$ we have \[ \dim_H FS_{m,n}(\Vert \cdot \Vert_{1},\Vert \cdot \Vert_{2},c)\ge m\cdot (n-1)-\left\lceil\frac{m}{n}\right\rceil, \] and for $(m,n)=(4,3)$ we still have the weaker bound $ \dim_H FS_{4,3}(\Vert \cdot \Vert_{1},\Vert \cdot \Vert_{2},c)\ge 4$. In particular the Dirichlet spectrum $\mathcal{D}_{m,n}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1, \Vert\cdot\Vert_2)$ contains a right neighborhood of $0$. Moreover, in these claims we can choose the matrices of full $\mathbb{R}$-rank $n$.
assumptions: Let $\Vert\cdot\Vert_1$ be an arbitrary norm on $\mathbb{R}^n$ and $\Vert\cdot\Vert_2$ be any expanding norm on $\mathbb{R}^m$, unless if $n=2$ assume both norms $\Vert\cdot\Vert_1$ and $\Vert\cdot\Vert_2$ are expanding.
conclusions: the Dirichlet spectrum $\mathcal{D}_{m,n}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1, \Vert\cdot\Vert_2)$ contains a right neighborhood of $0$.
nodes.statement_short: For m>n (except (odd m,2)) and expanding norms, FS(c) is non-empty for small c, with dimension >= m(n-1)-ceil(m/n).
nodes.label: ganze

nodes.name: Small improvement of the dimension bound in Theorem 3.4
nodes.statement: We can improve the Hausdorff dimension formulas in Theorem~\ref{ganze} a little. For $\Vert\cdot\Vert_2$ the maximum norm, this works via applying~\cite[Theorem~3.1]{j1} to estimate from below $\dim_H FS_{\ell,1}(c)$ for $c\in [0,1]$ where $\ell=\lceil m/n\rceil$. This positive value can be added given the method of our proof below and using \eqref{eq:tric}. For general expanding $\Vert\cdot\Vert_2$ a similar argument applies see~\cite[Remark~2]{j1}. This resembles Remark~\ref{remark4}. In particular in the cases $(m,2)$ for $m\ge 4$ even, we can settle a positive Hausdorff dimension.

nodes.name: Relaxing the expanding condition
nodes.statement: The condition of $\Vert \cdot \Vert_2$ being expanding can be relaxed to asking that for some space spanned by $\ell:=\lceil m/n\rceil$ canonical base vectors $\textbf{e}_{i_1},\ldots, \textbf{e}_{i_{\ell} }$ the projected norm onto it is expanding. For example, for $n<m\le 2n$ and $i_1=1, i_2=2$ this means the norm $\Vert (x_1,x_2)\Vert_{2}^{\prime}:=\Vert (x_1,x_2,0,\ldots,0)\Vert_2$ on $\mathbb{R}^2$ is expanding.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3.5
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{Folklore transpose} we may deduce an analogous result to Theorem~\ref{ganze}, apart from notably not fixing exact Dirichlet constant $c$, in the cases $n\ge 4,\quad \tfrac{1}{2} \le \tfrac{m}{n} < 1$. Together with the case $m=n$ from Theorem~\ref{arbn}, we may summarize
nodes.statement_short: Transpose Theorem 3.4 via Lemma 1.1 and add the square case from Theorem 3.3.

nodes.name: Dimension bound (6)
nodes.statement: \dim_H FS_{m,n}(\Vert \cdot \Vert_{\infty}, \Vert \cdot \Vert_{\infty})\ge mn-2\max\{m,n\}.

nodes.name: Folklore set with prescribed Dirichlet constant for n>=2m, arbitrary norms
nodes.statement: Let $m,n$ be positive integers satisfying \begin{equation} \tfrac{m}{n}\le \tfrac{1}{2}, \qquad (m,n)\ne (1,3). \end{equation} Let $\Vert\cdot\Vert_1$ be any norm on $\mathbb{R}^n$ and $\Vert\cdot\Vert_2$ be any norm on $\mathbb{R}^m$. Then there exists $c_{m,n}=c_{m,n}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1,\Vert\cdot\Vert_2)>0$ such that for any $c\in[0,c_{m,n}]$ we have \begin{equation*} \dim_H FS_{m,n}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1,\Vert\cdot\Vert_2,c) \geq (n-2)m. \end{equation*} Analogous claims hold when we restrict to $\Omega\in FS_{m,n}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1,\Vert\cdot\Vert_2,c)$ so that \begin{itemize} \item[(i)] $\Omega$ has full $\mathbb{R}$-rank $m$ \item[(ii)] the set of all its entries $\Omega_{i,j}$ together with $1$ is linearly independent over $\mathbb{Q}$. \end{itemize}
assumptions: Let $\Vert\cdot\Vert_1$ be any norm on $\mathbb{R}^n$ and $\Vert\cdot\Vert_2$ be any norm on $\mathbb{R}^m$.
conclusions: Analogous claims hold when we restrict to $\Omega\in FS_{m,n}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1,\Vert\cdot\Vert_2,c)$ so that \begin{itemize} \item[(i)] $\Omega$ has full $\mathbb{R}$-rank $m$ \item[(ii)] the set of all its entries $\Omega_{i,j}$ together with $1$ is linearly independent over $\mathbb{Q}$.
nodes.statement_short: For m/n<=1/2 (not (1,3)) and any norms, FS(c) has dimension >= (n-2)m for small c, also with full rank and Q-independent entries.
nodes.label: thm5

nodes.name: Matrix dimension condition (7)
nodes.statement: \tfrac{m}{n}\le \tfrac{1}{2}, \qquad (m,n)\ne (1,3).
nodes.label: matrix dimension condition

nodes.name: Simplification via Agin-Weiss
nodes.statement: Similar to Theorem~\ref{ganze}, our proof below can be significantly simplified when taking into account results from the preprint \cite{AginWeiss2024}. Moreover, we may omit condition $n\ge 2m$ from \eqref{matrix dimension condition}. However, as opposed to Theorem~\ref{ganze}, it does not improve the metrical statement. See Theorem \ref{AWe}, (a) below.
nodes.label: REMA

nodes.name: Uncountability of Di_{1,3}(c) minus Bad_{1,3}
nodes.statement: In the case $(m,n)=(1,3)$ where the results of Theorem~\ref{thm5} are not applicable, avoiding results from~\cite{Dasetal}, we can still deduce that the larger set \begin{equation} Di_{1,3}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_{1},\Vert\cdot\Vert_{2},c)\setminus Bad_{1,3}\supseteq FS_{1,3}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_{1},\Vert\cdot\Vert_{2},c) \end{equation} is uncountable for arbitrarily small $c>0$, since by~\cite{j2} we have $FS_{1,3}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_{\infty},\Vert\cdot\Vert_{\infty},c)\ne \emptyset$ for any $c\in [0,1]$ and by the equivalence of norms.

nodes.name: Inclusion of FS_{1,3}(c) (8)
nodes.statement: Di_{1,3}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_{1},\Vert\cdot\Vert_{2},c)\setminus Bad_{1,3}\supseteq FS_{1,3}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_{1},\Vert\cdot\Vert_{2},c)
nodes.label: eq:FG

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3.7
nodes.statement: Similar to Section~\ref{se3.1}, using Lemma~\ref{Folklore transpose} for the reverse case $m\ge 2n$, we get the following corollary.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Lemma 1.1 (transposition) to Theorem 3.6 for the reverse case m>=2n.

nodes.name: Folklore set dimension bound for m/n outside (1/2,2)
nodes.statement: Let $m,n$ be positive integers satisfying \begin{equation} \frac{m}{n}\notin \left(\tfrac{1}{2} , 2\right) , \qquad (m,n)\notin \{ (1,3), (3,1), (2,4) , (4,2) \}. \end{equation} Let $\Vert\cdot\Vert_1$ be any norm on $\mathbb{R}^n$ and $\Vert\cdot\Vert_2$ be any norm on $\mathbb{R}^m$. Then \[ \dim_H FS_{m,n}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1,\Vert\cdot\Vert_2) \geq (\max\{m,n\}-2)\cdot \min\{m,n\}=mn-2\cdot \min\{m,n\}. \] Moreover we may again assume (i), (ii), and the Dirichlet spectrum $\mathcal{D}_{m,n}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1, \Vert\cdot\Vert_2)$ accumulates at $0$, in particular it is not finite.
assumptions: Let $\Vert\cdot\Vert_1$ be any norm on $\mathbb{R}^n$ and $\Vert\cdot\Vert_2$ be any norm on $\mathbb{R}^m$.
conclusions: Moreover we may again assume (i), (ii), and the Dirichlet spectrum $\mathcal{D}_{m,n}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1, \Vert\cdot\Vert_2)$ accumulates at $0$, in particular it is not finite.

nodes.name: Dimension condition (9)
nodes.statement: \frac{m}{n}\notin \left(\tfrac{1}{2} , 2\right) , \qquad (m,n)\notin \{ (1,3), (3,1), (2,4) , (4,2) \}.
nodes.label: eq:jjj

nodes.name: Is Di_{m,n} = Di_{n,m}?
nodes.statement: It may be true that $Di_{m,n}=Di_{n,m}$ for every pair $m,n$. If $\min\{m,n\}=1$, one inclusion of the set identity was proved by Davenport and Schmidt~\cite{dav}. Assuming this property would give a shortcut avoiding Lemma~\ref{Folklore transpose} for the proofs of Theorems~\ref{sganz},~\ref{tT}.

nodes.name: Shorthand for the dual approximation function
nodes.statement: For $\boldsymbol{\zeta} \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $t\ge 1$ for ease of notation write \begin{equation*} \psi_{\boldsymbol{\zeta}}^{1\times n}(\|\cdot\|_{1},|\cdot|,t)=\psi_{\boldsymbol{\zeta}}^{1\times n}(t). \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Linear forms in two variables with prescribed Dirichlet constant (Schleischitz)
nodes.statement: Let $n\ge 2$ and $c\in [0,1]$. Then there exist $\mathbb{Q}$-linearly independent with $1$ real vectors $\boldsymbol{\xi}=(\xi_1,\xi_2)\in\mathbb{R}^{2}$ satisfying \begin{equation} \limsup_{t\to\infty} t^n \psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{1\times 2}(t)= c, \end{equation} and moreover \begin{equation} \liminf_{t\to\infty} t^n \psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{1\times 2}(t)= 0. \end{equation}
conclusions: there exist $\mathbb{Q}$-linearly independent with $1$ real vectors $\boldsymbol{\xi}=(\xi_1,\xi_2)\in\mathbb{R}^{2}$ satisfying
nodes.label: thm2

nodes.name: limsup property (10)
nodes.statement: \limsup_{t\to\infty} t^n \psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{1\times 2}(t)= c,
nodes.label: limsup property

nodes.name: liminf property (11)
nodes.statement: \liminf_{t\to\infty} t^n \psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{1\times 2}(t)= 0.
nodes.label: liminf property

nodes.name: liminf property follows from limsup for n>=3
nodes.statement: When $n\ge 3$, the liminf statement \eqref{liminf property} follows from the limsup claim \eqref{limsup property}, for example by Marnat and Moshchevitin~\cite{mamo}. The linear independence over $\mathbb{Q}$ of $(\boldsymbol{\xi},1)$ is also implied by \eqref{limsup property}, so it is just stated for completeness.

nodes.name: Sketch of proof of Theorem 5.1
nodes.statement: We only provide a sketch of the proof since, as previously mentioned, the claim is a special case of~\cite[Theorem~1.1]{j2} for $n=2$. As the proof of this result was only sketched in~\cite{j2}, we briefly recall the construction for convenience of the reader, with $\Phi(t)=ct^{-n}$. Define an integer sequence $(a_j)_{j\ge 1}$ as follows: Take the initial two terms $a_1, a_2$ large enough with $a_1|a_2$. Now iteratively, for $k\geq 1$ having constructed the first $2k$ terms $a_1,\ldots,a_{2k}$, let the next two terms are given by the recursion \begin{equation*} a_{2k+1}= a_{2k}^{M_k} \end{equation*} and \begin{equation*} a_{2k+2}=a_{2(k+1)}= a_{2k+1}\cdot \lceil c^{-1}a_{2k+1}^{n-1}\rceil\in (a_{2k+1}^n,\infty), \end{equation*} with integers $M_k\to\infty$ that tend to be infinitely fast enough. It turns out that $\boldsymbol{\xi}=(\xi_1,\xi_2)\in \mathbb{R}^{2}$ with \[ \xi_j= \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} a_{2k+j}^{-1}, \qquad j=1,2, \] has the desired properties of Theorem~\ref{thm2}.
nodes.statement_short: Construct xi_j as sums of reciprocals of a rapidly growing integer sequence a_j with a_{2k+2} about c^{-1}a_{2k+1}^n.

nodes.name: Scope of sketch
nodes.statement: We only provide a sketch of the proof since, as previously mentioned, the claim is a special case of~\cite[Theorem~1.1]{j2} for $n=2$. As the proof of this result was only sketched in~\cite{j2}, we briefly recall the construction for convenience of the reader, with $\Phi(t)=ct^{-n}$.
nodes.statement_short: Special case n=2 of j2 Theorem 1.1; recall the construction with Phi(t)=ct^{-n}.

nodes.name: Define the sequence a_j
nodes.statement: Define an integer sequence $(a_j)_{j\ge 1}$ as follows: Take the initial two terms $a_1, a_2$ large enough with $a_1|a_2$. Now iteratively, for $k\geq 1$ having constructed the first $2k$ terms $a_1,\ldots,a_{2k}$, let the next two terms are given by the recursion \begin{equation*} a_{2k+1}= a_{2k}^{M_k} \end{equation*} and \begin{equation*} a_{2k+2}=a_{2(k+1)}= a_{2k+1}\cdot \lceil c^{-1}a_{2k+1}^{n-1}\rceil\in (a_{2k+1}^n,\infty), \end{equation*} with integers $M_k\to\infty$ that tend to be infinitely fast enough.
nodes.statement_short: Define a_j recursively by a_{2k+1}=a_{2k}^{M_k} and a_{2k+2}=a_{2k+1} ceil(c^{-1}a_{2k+1}^{n-1}).

nodes.name: Define xi
nodes.statement: It turns out that $\boldsymbol{\xi}=(\xi_1,\xi_2)\in \mathbb{R}^{2}$ with \[ \xi_j= \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} a_{2k+j}^{-1}, \qquad j=1,2, \] has the desired properties of Theorem~\ref{thm2}.
nodes.statement_short: xi_j = sum of a_{2k+j}^{-1} has the required properties.

nodes.name: Alternative constructions
nodes.statement: An alternative construction for $c$ small enough can be derived from the method in~\cite{j3}, we will need the latter for the case of arbitrary norms. Yet another proof, for arbitrary norms, can be found in the aforementioned preprint of Agin and Weiss~\cite{AginWeiss2024}.

nodes.name: Blow-up of xi lies in Di_n(c) minus Bad_n
nodes.statement: Take any $\boldsymbol{\xi}\in\mathbb{R}^2$ as in Theorem~\ref{thm2}. Any $\boldsymbol{\zeta}\in\mathbb{R}^n$ with first two coordinates $\xi_1=\zeta_1, \xi_2=\zeta_2$, that is any vector $\boldsymbol{\zeta}\in \{ \boldsymbol{\xi}\}\times \mathbb{R}^{n-2}\subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$, satisfies $\boldsymbol{\zeta}\in Di_n(c)\setminus Bad_n$.
assumptions: Any $\boldsymbol{\zeta}\in\mathbb{R}^n$ with first two coordinates $\xi_1=\zeta_1, \xi_2=\zeta_2$, that is any vector $\boldsymbol{\zeta}\in \{ \boldsymbol{\xi}\}\times \mathbb{R}^{n-2}\subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$,
nodes.label: pro

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 1
nodes.statement: Let us write $\boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}= (\xi_1, \xi_2, 1)$ and similarly $\boldsymbol{\zeta}^{\ast}=(\zeta_1,\ldots,\zeta_n,1)$. Denote $\boldsymbol{e}_i=(0,0\ldots,0,1,0,\ldots,0)$ the $i$-th canonical base vector of $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$. \par Our claim follows from the fact that \begin{equation} \psi_{\boldsymbol{\zeta}}^{1\times n}(t) \le \psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{1\times 2}(t),\qquad t>0. \end{equation} Indeed, any $t$ induces a best approximation $\boldsymbol{b}=(b_{1}, b_{2}, b_{3})\in \mathbb{Z}^3$ with respect to $\boldsymbol{\xi}$ that realizes $\psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t)$. Then the blown-up vector \[ \tilde{\boldsymbol{b}}:= b_{1} \boldsymbol{e}_1 + b_{2} \boldsymbol{e}_2+ b_{3} \boldsymbol{e}_{n+1}=(b_1, b_2, 0,\ldots,0,b_{3})\in \mathbb{Z}^{n+1} \] induces the same maximum norm and approximation quality \[ \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{b}}\Vert= \Vert \hat{\tilde{\boldsymbol{b}}}\Vert, \qquad | \tilde{\boldsymbol{b}} \cdot \boldsymbol{\zeta}^{\ast}|= | \boldsymbol{b} \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|= \psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{1\times 2}(t). \] so the minimum over all integer points defining $\psi_{\boldsymbol{\zeta}}(t)$ cannot be larger. Trivially \eqref{liminf property} and \eqref{psi decreasing} implies \begin{equation*} \liminf_{t\to \infty} t^{n}\psi_{\boldsymbol{\zeta}}^{1\times n}(t)=0\, , \end{equation*} so $\boldsymbol{\zeta} \not \in Bad_{n}$. Similarly \eqref{limsup property} and \eqref{psi decreasing} implies $\limsup_{t\to \infty} t^{n}\psi_{\boldsymbol{\zeta}}^{1\times n}(t)\leq c$, so $\boldsymbol{\zeta} \in Di_{n}(c)$.
nodes.statement_short: Embed best approximations of xi into Z^{n+1} so psi_zeta <= psi_xi, then transfer liminf and limsup.

nodes.name: psi decreasing (12)
nodes.statement: \psi_{\boldsymbol{\zeta}}^{1\times n}(t) \le \psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{1\times 2}(t),\qquad t>0.
nodes.label: psi decreasing

nodes.name: Notation
nodes.statement: Let us write $\boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}= (\xi_1, \xi_2, 1)$ and similarly $\boldsymbol{\zeta}^{\ast}=(\zeta_1,\ldots,\zeta_n,1)$. Denote $\boldsymbol{e}_i=(0,0\ldots,0,1,0,\ldots,0)$ the $i$-th canonical base vector of $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$. \par
nodes.statement_short: Introduce xi*, zeta* and canonical basis vectors.

nodes.name: Reduction
nodes.statement: Our claim follows from the fact that \begin{equation} \psi_{\boldsymbol{\zeta}}^{1\times n}(t) \le \psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{1\times 2}(t),\qquad t>0. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to the inequality psi_zeta(t) <= psi_xi(t).

nodes.name: Embedding of best approximations
nodes.statement: Indeed, any $t$ induces a best approximation $\boldsymbol{b}=(b_{1}, b_{2}, b_{3})\in \mathbb{Z}^3$ with respect to $\boldsymbol{\xi}$ that realizes $\psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t)$. Then the blown-up vector \[ \tilde{\boldsymbol{b}}:= b_{1} \boldsymbol{e}_1 + b_{2} \boldsymbol{e}_2+ b_{3} \boldsymbol{e}_{n+1}=(b_1, b_2, 0,\ldots,0,b_{3})\in \mathbb{Z}^{n+1} \] induces the same maximum norm and approximation quality \[ \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{b}}\Vert= \Vert \hat{\tilde{\boldsymbol{b}}}\Vert, \qquad | \tilde{\boldsymbol{b}} \cdot \boldsymbol{\zeta}^{\ast}|= | \boldsymbol{b} \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|= \psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{1\times 2}(t). \] so the minimum over all integer points defining $\psi_{\boldsymbol{\zeta}}(t)$ cannot be larger.
nodes.statement_short: Blown-up best approximation of xi gives the same height and quality for zeta.

nodes.name: Not badly approximable
nodes.statement: Trivially \eqref{liminf property} and \eqref{psi decreasing} implies \begin{equation*} \liminf_{t\to \infty} t^{n}\psi_{\boldsymbol{\zeta}}^{1\times n}(t)=0\, , \end{equation*} so $\boldsymbol{\zeta} \not \in Bad_{n}$.
nodes.statement_short: liminf is 0, so zeta not in Bad_n.

nodes.name: Dirichlet improvable
nodes.statement: Similarly \eqref{limsup property} and \eqref{psi decreasing} implies $\limsup_{t\to \infty} t^{n}\psi_{\boldsymbol{\zeta}}^{1\times n}(t)\leq c$, so $\boldsymbol{\zeta} \in Di_{n}(c)$.
nodes.statement_short: limsup at most c, so zeta in Di_n(c).

nodes.name: Singular blow-up example
nodes.statement: For example, if $n\ge 3$ taking $\boldsymbol{\zeta}=(\xi_{1},\xi_{2}, \xi_{1}+\xi_{2}, 0, \dots, 0)\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$ then $\boldsymbol{\zeta} \in Sing_{n}$.

nodes.name: Generic blow-up preserves the Dirichlet constant
nodes.statement: Let $n\ge 4$ be an integer. Take any $\boldsymbol{\xi}\in\mathbb{R}^2$ as in Theorem~\ref{thm2} derived from any small enough $c\in(0,c(n))$ as in Theorem~\ref{thm1}. Then for a set \[ \mathcal{Y}=\mathcal{Y}_{n,\boldsymbol{\xi}}\subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n-2} \] of positive $n-2$ dimensional Lebesgue measure consisting of $\zeta_3,\ldots,\zeta_n$, the vector $\boldsymbol{\zeta}=(\xi_1,\xi_2,\zeta_3,\ldots,\zeta_n)\in\mathbb{R}^n$ satisfies \[ \Theta^{1\times n}(\boldsymbol{\zeta})=\limsup_{t\to\infty} t^n \psi_{\boldsymbol{\zeta}}^{1\times n}(t)=\limsup_{t\to\infty} t^n \psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{1\times 2}(t)= c, \] or equivalently $\boldsymbol{\zeta}\in DI_n(c)$.
assumptions: Take any $\boldsymbol{\xi}\in\mathbb{R}^2$ as in Theorem~\ref{thm2} derived from any small enough $c\in(0,c(n))$ as in Theorem~\ref{thm1}.
conclusions: for a set \[ \mathcal{Y}=\mathcal{Y}_{n,\boldsymbol{\xi}}\subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n-2} \] of positive $n-2$ dimensional Lebesgue measure consisting of $\zeta_3,\ldots,\zeta_n$, the vector $\boldsymbol{\zeta}=(\xi_1,\xi_2,\zeta_3,\ldots,\zeta_n)\in\mathbb{R}^n$ satisfies \[ \Theta^{1\times n}(\boldsymbol{\zeta})=\limsup_{t\to\infty} t^n \psi_{\boldsymbol{\zeta}}^{1\times n}(t)=\limsup_{t\to\infty} t^n \psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{1\times 2}(t)= c,
nodes.statement_short: For n>=4, a positive-measure set of extensions zeta of xi keeps the exact Dirichlet constant c.
nodes.label: thm3

nodes.name: Measure of Y presumably full
nodes.statement: Presumably the $(n-2)$-dimensional Lebesgue measure of the set $\mathcal{Y}$ is full, however, this is not required for our purposes.
nodes.label: remarke

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2.1
nodes.statement: By combining Proposition~\ref{pro} and Theorem~\ref{thm3} it is clear that \[ \boldsymbol{\zeta}\in DI_n(c)\setminus Bad_n= FS_n(c)\, . \] Let $\mathcal{Z}_{c}$ denote the set of $\boldsymbol{\xi} \in \mathbb{R}^{2}$ satisfying Theorem~\ref{thm2}. Since $\lambda_{n}(\mathcal{Y})>0$, for any $c\in(0,c_n)$ we have that \[ \dim_H FS_n \ge \dim_H FS_n(c) \ge \dim_H \mathcal{Z}_{c}\times \mathcal{Y} \geq \dim_H(\mathcal{Z}_{c})+ \dim_H \mathcal{Y} \geq n-2\, . \] The second to last inequality follows from a standard result on the Hausdorff dimension of Cartesian products \begin{equation} \dim_H A\times B \ge \dim_H A + \dim_H B \end{equation} for $A,B$ arbitrary sets in Euclidean spaces, see~\cite{tricot}. Hence Theorem~\ref{thm1} is proven modulo Theorem ~\ref{thm3}.
nodes.statement_short: Combine Proposition 1 and Theorem 5.2, then bound dimension of Z_c x Y via the product inequality.

nodes.name: Hausdorff dimension of Cartesian products
nodes.statement: \dim_H A\times B \ge \dim_H A + \dim_H B
nodes.label: eq:tric

nodes.name: Membership in FS_n(c)
nodes.statement: By combining Proposition~\ref{pro} and Theorem~\ref{thm3} it is clear that \[ \boldsymbol{\zeta}\in DI_n(c)\setminus Bad_n= FS_n(c)\, . \]
nodes.statement_short: Proposition 1 and Theorem 5.2 give zeta in FS_n(c).

nodes.name: Dimension estimate
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{Z}_{c}$ denote the set of $\boldsymbol{\xi} \in \mathbb{R}^{2}$ satisfying Theorem~\ref{thm2}. Since $\lambda_{n}(\mathcal{Y})>0$, for any $c\in(0,c_n)$ we have that \[ \dim_H FS_n \ge \dim_H FS_n(c) \ge \dim_H \mathcal{Z}_{c}\times \mathcal{Y} \geq \dim_H(\mathcal{Z}_{c})+ \dim_H \mathcal{Y} \geq n-2\, . \]
nodes.statement_short: dim FS_n(c) >= dim Z_c + dim Y >= n-2.

nodes.name: Product inequality
nodes.statement: The second to last inequality follows from a standard result on the Hausdorff dimension of Cartesian products \begin{equation} \dim_H A\times B \ge \dim_H A + \dim_H B \end{equation} for $A,B$ arbitrary sets in Euclidean spaces, see~\cite{tricot}. Hence Theorem~\ref{thm1} is proven modulo Theorem ~\ref{thm3}.
nodes.statement_short: Use dim(AxB) >= dim A + dim B.

nodes.name: Possible improvement via dimension of Z_c
nodes.statement: Notice that in the above calculation, we simply use $\dim_H \mathcal{Z}_{c}\geq 0$. It is here where our lower bound could be improved. For $\tau>2$ a parameter, define \begin{equation*} Sing_{2}(\tau):=\left\{ \boldsymbol{\xi} \in \mathbb{R}^{2}: \limsup_{t\to \infty} t^{\tau}\psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{1\times 2}(t)=0 \right\}. \end{equation*} It can be deduced from~\cite[Theorem 1.4-1.9]{DFSU_singular} by a change of variables that for any $\tau>2+\sqrt{2}$ we have \begin{equation*} \dim_H Sing_{2}(\tau)=\frac{2}{\tau}. \end{equation*} Clearly $\mathcal{Z}_{c} \subseteq Sing_{2}(n-\varepsilon)$ for any $\varepsilon>0$, and so \[ \dim_H \mathcal{Z}_{c} \leq \frac{2}{n-\varepsilon}. \] Thus for $n\ge 4>2+\sqrt{2}$ the best we could hope for via this method is \begin{equation*} \dim_H FS_{n}(c)\geq n-2 + \frac{2}{n}\, . \end{equation*} On the other hand, a positive lower bound for $\dim_H (\mathcal{Z}_{c})$ can be obtained by a similar variational method as in~\cite[Theorem~2.1]{j3}, we do not carry it out.
nodes.label: rrr

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 5.2
nodes.statement: We have to show the Dirichlet constant of many $\boldsymbol{\zeta}$ is at least $c$, the rest is obvious. We follow ideas from the proof of Moshchevitin \cite[Theorem 12]{ngm} with some twists. Write $\boldsymbol{\zeta}=(\xi_{1},\xi_{2},\zeta_{3}, \dots , \zeta_{n})$ and restrict to $(\zeta_{3},\dots, \zeta_{n})$ in the $n-2$-dimensional unit ball $B_{n-2}(\boldsymbol{0},1)\subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n-2}$ with respect to the Euclidean norm (this will be slightly easier to handle than for the maximum norm). Denote by \[ \boldsymbol{b}_v=(b_{1,v},b_{2,v},b_{3,v})\in\mathbb{Z}^3, \qquad v\ge 1, \] the best approximations with respect to $\boldsymbol{\xi}=(\xi_1,\xi_2)$ and derive \[ M_v= \max_{j=1,2} |b_{j,v}|= \|\hat{\boldsymbol{b}}_{v}\|, \qquad v\ge 1 \] and the minimal values \[ L_v= |b_{1,v} \xi_1 + b_{2,v} \xi_2 + b_{3,v}|, \qquad v\ge 1. \] Clearly $(L_{v})_{v\geq 1}$ is a strictly decreasing sequence and $(M_{v})_{v\geq 1}$ is strictly increasing. Further, note that we have \[ \psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{1\times 2}(t)= L_v, \qquad t\in [M_v, M_{v+1}), \] hence \begin{equation} \limsup_{t\to \infty} t^{n}\psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{1\times 2}(t) = \limsup_{v\to\infty} L_v M_{v+1}^{n}. \end{equation} Denote $\boldsymbol{e}_i=(0,0\ldots,0,1,0,\ldots,0)$ the $i$-th canonical base vector of $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$. To finish the proof, it suffices to show the following: \begin{lemma} Let $n\ge 4$ an integer and $\boldsymbol{\xi}=(\xi_1,\xi_2)$ as in Theorem~\ref{thm2}. For a positive measure set $\mathcal{Y}\subseteq B_{n-2}(0,1)\subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n-2}$ consisting of $\boldsymbol{\gamma}=(\xi_3,\ldots,\xi_n)$, we can choose an infinite subsequence of integers $v_r, r\ge 1$, so that letting $T_{v}:=M_{v+1}-1/2$ for $v\ge 1$, we have \begin{equation} \lim_{r\to\infty} T_{v_r}^n\cdot \psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{1\times 2}(T_{v_{r}}) = \limsup_{v\to\infty} T_{v}^n\cdot \psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{1\times 2}(T_{v}) =c \end{equation} i.e. this subsequence realizes the limsup, and the integer best approximation for $\boldsymbol{\zeta}=(\boldsymbol{\xi}, \boldsymbol{\gamma})$ at $T_{v_{r}}$ is given as \[ b_{1,_v{r}}\boldsymbol{e}_1+ b_{2,v_r}\boldsymbol{e}_2+ b_{1,v_r}\boldsymbol{e}_{n+1}= (b_{1,v_{r}},b_{2,v_r},0,\ldots,0,b_{3,v_r})\in \mathbb{Z}^{n+1}\,, \qquad r\ge 1. \] Thus the best approximation function at values $T_{v_r}$ equals \[ \psi_{\boldsymbol{\zeta}}^{1\times n}(T_{v_{r}})=\psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{1\times 2}(T_{v_{r}})= L_{v_r},\qquad r\ge 1. \] \end{lemma} Observe that since $T_v$ is of the same order as $M_{v+1}$, for $\boldsymbol{\zeta}$ as in the lemma, \eqref{eq:tT}, \eqref{eq:igno} and the corresponding property for $\boldsymbol{\zeta}$ readily imply \[ \Theta^{1\times n}(\boldsymbol{\zeta})\ge\limsup_{v\to\infty} L_v T_{v}^{n}=\limsup_{t\to \infty} t^{n}\psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{1\times 2}(t), \] the reverse inequality is clear by Proposition~\ref{pro}. Hence, assuming the lemma is true, the claim of Theorem~\ref{thm3} follows.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce Theorem 5.2 to Lemma 5.3: best approximations of xi stay best for zeta along a subsequence, for a positive-measure set of extensions.

nodes.name: limsup via best approximations (14)
nodes.statement: \limsup_{t\to \infty} t^{n}\psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{1\times 2}(t) = \limsup_{v\to\infty} L_v M_{v+1}^{n}.
nodes.label: eq:tT

nodes.name: Best approximations of xi remain best for generic extensions
nodes.statement: Let $n\ge 4$ an integer and $\boldsymbol{\xi}=(\xi_1,\xi_2)$ as in Theorem~\ref{thm2}. For a positive measure set $\mathcal{Y}\subseteq B_{n-2}(0,1)\subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n-2}$ consisting of $\boldsymbol{\gamma}=(\xi_3,\ldots,\xi_n)$, we can choose an infinite subsequence of integers $v_r, r\ge 1$, so that letting $T_{v}:=M_{v+1}-1/2$ for $v\ge 1$, we have \begin{equation} \lim_{r\to\infty} T_{v_r}^n\cdot \psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{1\times 2}(T_{v_{r}}) = \limsup_{v\to\infty} T_{v}^n\cdot \psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{1\times 2}(T_{v}) =c \end{equation} i.e. this subsequence realizes the limsup, and the integer best approximation for $\boldsymbol{\zeta}=(\boldsymbol{\xi}, \boldsymbol{\gamma})$ at $T_{v_{r}}$ is given as \[ b_{1,_v{r}}\boldsymbol{e}_1+ b_{2,v_r}\boldsymbol{e}_2+ b_{1,v_r}\boldsymbol{e}_{n+1}= (b_{1,v_{r}},b_{2,v_r},0,\ldots,0,b_{3,v_r})\in \mathbb{Z}^{n+1}\,, \qquad r\ge 1. \] Thus the best approximation function at values $T_{v_r}$ equals \[ \psi_{\boldsymbol{\zeta}}^{1\times n}(T_{v_{r}})=\psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{1\times 2}(T_{v_{r}})= L_{v_r},\qquad r\ge 1. \]
assumptions: Let $n\ge 4$ an integer and $\boldsymbol{\xi}=(\xi_1,\xi_2)$ as in Theorem~\ref{thm2}.
conclusions: For a positive measure set $\mathcal{Y}\subseteq B_{n-2}(0,1)\subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n-2}$ consisting of $\boldsymbol{\gamma}=(\xi_3,\ldots,\xi_n)$, we can choose an infinite subsequence of integers $v_r, r\ge 1$, so that letting $T_{v}:=M_{v+1}-1/2$ for $v\ge 1$, we have \begin{equation} \lim_{r\to\infty} T_{v_r}^n\cdot \psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{1\times 2}(T_{v_{r}}) = \limsup_{v\to\infty} T_{v}^n\cdot \psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{1\times 2}(T_{v}) =c \end{equation} i.e. this subsequence realizes the limsup, and the integer best approximation for $\boldsymbol{\zeta}=(\boldsymbol{\xi}, \boldsymbol{\gamma})$ at $T_{v_{r}}$ is given as \[ b_{1,_v{r}}\boldsymbol{e}_1+ b_{2,v_r}\boldsymbol{e}_2+ b_{1,v_r}\boldsymbol{e}_{n+1}= (b_{1,v_{r}},b_{2,v_r},0,\ldots,0,b_{3,v_r})\in \mathbb{Z}^{n+1}\,, \qquad r\ge 1.
Thus the best approximation function at values $T_{v_r}$ equals \[ \psi_{\boldsymbol{\zeta}}^{1\times n}(T_{v_{r}})=\psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{1\times 2}(T_{v_{r}})= L_{v_r},\qquad r\ge 1.
nodes.statement_short: For a positive-measure set of gamma, along a limsup-realizing subsequence the best approximations of zeta=(xi,gamma) are those of xi.
nodes.label: lema

nodes.name: Subsequence realizing the limsup (15)
nodes.statement: \lim_{r\to\infty} T_{v_r}^n\cdot \psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{1\times 2}(T_{v_{r}}) = \limsup_{v\to\infty} T_{v}^n\cdot \psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{1\times 2}(T_{v}) =c
nodes.label: eq:igno

nodes.name: Reduction to lower bound
nodes.statement: We have to show the Dirichlet constant of many $\boldsymbol{\zeta}$ is at least $c$, the rest is obvious. We follow ideas from the proof of Moshchevitin \cite[Theorem 12]{ngm} with some twists.
nodes.statement_short: Only the lower bound c on the Dirichlet constant needs proof; follow Moshchevitin.

nodes.name: Best approximations of xi
nodes.statement: Write $\boldsymbol{\zeta}=(\xi_{1},\xi_{2},\zeta_{3}, \dots , \zeta_{n})$ and restrict to $(\zeta_{3},\dots, \zeta_{n})$ in the $n-2$-dimensional unit ball $B_{n-2}(\boldsymbol{0},1)\subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n-2}$ with respect to the Euclidean norm (this will be slightly easier to handle than for the maximum norm). Denote by \[ \boldsymbol{b}_v=(b_{1,v},b_{2,v},b_{3,v})\in\mathbb{Z}^3, \qquad v\ge 1, \] the best approximations with respect to $\boldsymbol{\xi}=(\xi_1,\xi_2)$ and derive \[ M_v= \max_{j=1,2} |b_{j,v}|= \|\hat{\boldsymbol{b}}_{v}\|, \qquad v\ge 1 \] and the minimal values \[ L_v= |b_{1,v} \xi_1 + b_{2,v} \xi_2 + b_{3,v}|, \qquad v\ge 1. \] Clearly $(L_{v})_{v\geq 1}$ is a strictly decreasing sequence and $(M_{v})_{v\geq 1}$ is strictly increasing.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce best approximations b_v of xi with heights M_v and values L_v.

nodes.name: limsup via L_v and M_v
nodes.statement: Further, note that we have \[ \psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{1\times 2}(t)= L_v, \qquad t\in [M_v, M_{v+1}), \] hence \begin{equation} \limsup_{t\to \infty} t^{n}\psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{1\times 2}(t) = \limsup_{v\to\infty} L_v M_{v+1}^{n}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Express the limsup as limsup L_v M_{v+1}^n.

nodes.name: Reduction to Lemma 5.3
nodes.statement: Denote $\boldsymbol{e}_i=(0,0\ldots,0,1,0,\ldots,0)$ the $i$-th canonical base vector of $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$. To finish the proof, it suffices to show the following: \begin{lemma} Let $n\ge 4$ an integer and $\boldsymbol{\xi}=(\xi_1,\xi_2)$ as in Theorem~\ref{thm2}. For a positive measure set $\mathcal{Y}\subseteq B_{n-2}(0,1)\subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n-2}$ consisting of $\boldsymbol{\gamma}=(\xi_3,\ldots,\xi_n)$, we can choose an infinite subsequence of integers $v_r, r\ge 1$, so that letting $T_{v}:=M_{v+1}-1/2$ for $v\ge 1$, we have \begin{equation} \lim_{r\to\infty} T_{v_r}^n\cdot \psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{1\times 2}(T_{v_{r}}) = \limsup_{v\to\infty} T_{v}^n\cdot \psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{1\times 2}(T_{v}) =c \end{equation} i.e. this subsequence realizes the limsup, and the integer best approximation for $\boldsymbol{\zeta}=(\boldsymbol{\xi}, \boldsymbol{\gamma})$ at $T_{v_{r}}$ is given as \[ b_{1,_v{r}}\boldsymbol{e}_1+ b_{2,v_r}\boldsymbol{e}_2+ b_{1,v_r}\boldsymbol{e}_{n+1}= (b_{1,v_{r}},b_{2,v_r},0,\ldots,0,b_{3,v_r})\in \mathbb{Z}^{n+1}\,, \qquad r\ge 1. \] Thus the best approximation function at values $T_{v_r}$ equals \[ \psi_{\boldsymbol{\zeta}}^{1\times n}(T_{v_{r}})=\psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{1\times 2}(T_{v_{r}})= L_{v_r},\qquad r\ge 1. \] \end{lemma}
nodes.statement_short: It suffices to prove Lemma 5.3.

nodes.name: Apply Lemma 5.3
nodes.statement: Observe that since $T_v$ is of the same order as $M_{v+1}$, for $\boldsymbol{\zeta}$ as in the lemma, \eqref{eq:tT}, \eqref{eq:igno} and the corresponding property for $\boldsymbol{\zeta}$ readily imply \[ \Theta^{1\times n}(\boldsymbol{\zeta})\ge\limsup_{v\to\infty} L_v T_{v}^{n}=\limsup_{t\to \infty} t^{n}\psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{1\times 2}(t), \] the reverse inequality is clear by Proposition~\ref{pro}.
nodes.statement_short: The lemma gives Theta(zeta) >= c; reverse inequality by Proposition 1.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Hence, assuming the lemma is true, the claim of Theorem~\ref{thm3} follows.
nodes.statement_short: Theorem 5.2 follows from the lemma.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.3
nodes.statement: We first note that we may assume \[ \lim_{v\to\infty} T_v^{n}\psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{1\times 2}(T_v)=c \] and hence ignore \eqref{eq:igno}. Indeed, otherwise we restrict to a subsequence satisfying \eqref{eq:igno}, which exists by definition of the limsup, and apply the argument below for this subsequence.\par We show that for a positive portion of $B_{n-2}(\boldsymbol{0},1)\subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n-2}$ of vectors $\boldsymbol{\gamma}=(\zeta_3,\ldots,\zeta_n)$, we have for infinitely many $v$ that \begin{equation} \min \left| x_{1}\xi_{1}+x_{2}\xi_{2}+ \sum_{i=3}^{n} x_i \zeta_i - y \right| \ge L_{v} \end{equation} with minimum taken over all integer points \begin{equation} \boldsymbol{z}= (x_1,\ldots,x_{n},y)\in \mathbb{Z}^{n+1}\setminus \{\boldsymbol{0}\} \quad \text{ with } \quad 0<\max_{1\le j\le n} |x_j| \le T_v\, . \end{equation} For $v\ge 1$, denote by $\mathcal{S}_v$ the set of vectors of $\mathbb{R}^{n-2}$ taken over all integer points $\boldsymbol{z}$ obeying \eqref{eq:ob}, i.e. \begin{equation*} \mathcal{S}_{v}:=\left\{ \boldsymbol{\gamma} \in B_{n-2}(\boldsymbol{0},1): \underset{0<\max_{1\leq i \leq n}|x_{j}|\leq T_{v}}{\min_{(\boldsymbol{x},y)\in\mathbb{Z}^{n+1}:}} \left| x_{1}\xi_{1}+x_{2}\xi_{2}+\sum_{i=3}^{n}x_{i}\zeta_{i} -y\right|\geq L_{v} \right\}. \end{equation*} Then our set is the limsup set of the $\mathcal{S}_v$, or its complement is the set of all vectors that lie only in finitely many $\mathcal{S}_v$, that is, \begin{equation} B_{n-2}(\boldsymbol{0},1)\setminus \mathcal{Y}\subseteq \bigcup_{i\ge 1} \bigcap_{j\ge i} \mathcal{S}_j^{c}\subseteq \bigcup_{i\ge 1} \mathcal{S}_i^{c}. \end{equation} Assume that any complement \[ \mathcal{U}_v:= \mathcal{S}_v^{c}= \left\{ \boldsymbol{\gamma} \in B_{n-2}(\boldsymbol{0},1): \underset{0<\max_{1\leq i \leq n}|x_{j}|\leq T_{v}}{\min_{(\boldsymbol{x},y)\in\mathbb{Z}^{n+1}:}} \left| x_{1}\xi_{1}+x_{2}\xi_{2}+\sum_{i=3}^{n}x_{i}\zeta_{i} -y\right|< L_{v} \right\} , \quad v\ge 1, \] has $n-2$ dimensional Lebesgue measure less than some $\delta$ strictly smaller than the volume of $B_{n-2}(\boldsymbol{0},1)$. Then this will also be true for $B_{n-2}(\boldsymbol{0},1)\setminus \mathcal{Y}$ by the following easy result. \begin{proposition} Let $\lambda$ be a measure on a space $\mathcal{T}$. Assume $H_i$ are increasing subsets of $\mathcal{T}$, i.e. $H_1\subseteq H_2 \subseteq \cdots$. Then \[ \lambda\left(\bigcup_{k=1}^{\infty} H_k\right) = \lim_{k\to\infty} \lambda(H_k). \] \end{proposition} We will require the estimate $\lambda\left(\bigcup_{k=1}^{\infty} H_k\right) \le \lim_{k\to\infty} \lambda(H_k)$ only. \begin{proof} Writing $G_j=H_j\setminus H_{j-1}$ with $H_0=\emptyset$, we see \begin{equation*} \lambda\left(\bigcup_{k=1}^{\infty} H_k\right)= \lambda\left(\bigcup_{k=1}^{\infty} G_k\right)= \lim_{N\to\infty} \sum_{k=1}^{N} \lambda(G_k)= \lim_{N\to\infty} \lambda\left(\bigcup_{k=1}^{N} H_k\right)= \lim_{N\to\infty} \lambda(H_N). \end{equation*} \end{proof} In the sequel denote by $\lambda$ the $(n-2)$-dimensional Lebesgue measure of a set $A\subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n-2}$. As indicated before, we apply Proposition~\ref{pp} to \[ H_i= \bigcap_{j\ge i} \mathcal{S}_j^{c}= \bigcap_{j\ge i} \mathcal{U}_j \subseteq \mathcal{U}_i, \qquad i\ge 1, \] to see via \eqref{eq:wia} that \[ \lambda(B_{n-2}(\boldsymbol{0},1)\setminus \mathcal{Y})\le \lim_{v\to\infty} \lambda(\mathcal{U}_v). \] Assume we have shown that for some uniform $\Delta$ we have \begin{equation} \lambda(\mathcal{U}_v)\le \Delta< \lambda(B_{n-2}(\boldsymbol{0},1)), \qquad v\ge 1. \end{equation} Then we conclude that $$\lambda(B_{n-2}(\boldsymbol{0},1)\setminus \mathcal{Y})\le \Delta<\lambda(B_{n-2}(\boldsymbol{0},1))$$ and thus \[ \lambda(\mathcal{Y}) = \lambda(B_{n-2}(\boldsymbol{0},1)) - \lambda(B_{n-2}(\boldsymbol{0},1)\setminus \mathcal{Y})\ge \lambda(B_{n-2}(\boldsymbol{0},1)) - \Delta > 0, \] as desired. To verify \eqref{eq:IND}, let us estimate $\lambda(\mathcal{U}_v)$ for fixed $v$. For any $\boldsymbol{\gamma}=(\zeta_3,\ldots,\zeta_n)\in \mathcal{U}_v$ it follows that \begin{equation*} \underset{0<\max_{1\leq i \leq n}|x_{j}|\leq T_{v}}{\min_{(\boldsymbol{x},y)\in\mathbb{Z}^{n+1}:}} \left| x_{1}\xi_{1}+x_{2}\xi_{2}+\sum_{i=3}^{n}x_{i}\zeta_{i} -y\right|< L_{v}\, . \end{equation*} Equivalently \[ x_3 \zeta_3 + \cdots+ x_n \zeta_n \in J_{v}(x_1,x_2,y) \] where $J_{v}(.)$ is given as the interval \[ J_v(x_1,x_2,y)= ( -y-x_1\xi_1-x_2\xi_2-L_v , -y-x_1\xi_1-x_2\xi_2+L_v ). \] Let \[ \Omega_v(x_1,\ldots, x_n,y)= \left\{ (\zeta_3,\ldots,\zeta_n)\in B_{n-2}(0,1)\subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n-2}: \sum_{i=3}^{n}x_{i}\zeta_{i} \in J_{v}(x_1,x_2,y) \right\}. \] Observe that $\Omega_v(x_1,\ldots,x_n,y)$ is empty if $|y|>|x_{1}\xi_{1}|+|x_{2}\xi_{2}|+\sum_{i=3}^{n} |x_i \zeta_i|+L_v$. Fix for now $\varepsilon>0$. Since $L_v\to 0$ as $v\to\infty$ and as we may take $\xi_1,\xi_2$ arbitrarily small positive numbers (the $\boldsymbol{\xi}$ from Theorem~\ref{thm2} are easily seen to be dense in $\mathbb{R}$), say smaller than $\varepsilon/8$, and $(\zeta_3,\ldots,\zeta_n)\in B_{n-2}(\boldsymbol{0},1)$, Cauchy-Schwarz inequality yields for any $\varepsilon>0$ this is true if \[ |y|> (\sqrt{n-2}+\varepsilon/2) T_v \] as then \begin{align*} |y|&> (\sqrt{n-2}+\varepsilon/2) T_v \\ &\ge (\varepsilon/4)\cdot T_v+ \left(\sum_{i=3}^{n} |x_i|^2\right)^{1/2}\left(\sum_{i=3}^{n} |\zeta_i|^2\right)^{1/2}+L_v \\ &\ge |\xi_1| |x_1| + |\xi_2| |x_2|+ \left(\sum_{i=3}^{n} |x_i|^2\right)^{1/2}\left(\sum_{i=3}^{n} |\zeta_i|^2\right)^{1/2}+L_v \\ &\ge |x_{1}\xi_{1}|+|x_{2}\xi_{2}|+ \sum_{i=1}^{n} |x_i\zeta_i|+L_v, \qquad v\ge v_0(\varepsilon). \end{align*} The above shows that if we let \begin{equation} \Omega_v= \bigcup_{x_1,\ldots,x_n} \bigcup_{y}\; \Omega_v(x_1,\ldots,x_n,y), \end{equation} with unions are taken over integers $x_1, \dots, x_{n}$ as in \eqref{eq:ob} and integers $y$ with $|y|\le (\sqrt{n-2}+\varepsilon/2)T_v$. Then \[ \mathcal{U}_v \subseteq \Omega_v, \qquad v\geq v_0(\varepsilon). \] The distance between the parallel planes defining $\Omega_v(x_1,\ldots,x_n,y)$ equals $2(x_3^2+\cdots+x_n^2)^{-1/2}$. Thus each $\Omega_v(x_1,\ldots,x_n,y)$ is contained in a cylinder of radius one and height $2L_v \cdot (x_3^2+\cdots+x_n^2)^{-1/2}$. Denoting by $\lambda^{\prime}$ the $(n-3)$-dimensional Lebesgue measure, this has volume \begin{align} \lambda(\Omega_v(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n},y))&= 2\lambda^{\prime}(B_{n-3}(\boldsymbol{0},1))\cdot L_v(x_3^2+\cdots+x_n^2)^{-1/2}\nonumber \\ &\le 2 L_v\cdot\lambda^{\prime}(B_{n-3}(\boldsymbol{0},1)) \cdot\frac{ 1}{\max_{3\le i\le n} |x_i|}. \end{align} Since, assuming $T_v\ge \varepsilon^{-1}$, there are at most $$2T_{v}(\sqrt{n-2}+\varepsilon/2)+1\le T_{v}(2\sqrt{n-2}+2\varepsilon)$$ integers $y$ in the inner union of \eqref{eq:inu}, in total we get \begin{align*} \lambda(\mathcal{U}_v) &\le \lambda(\Omega_v)\\ &\le \sum_{x_1, x_2} \sum_y \sum_{x_3,\ldots,x_n} \lambda(\Omega_v(x_1,\ldots,x_n,y))\\ &\le 2(2\sqrt{n-2}+2\varepsilon)L_vT_v \lambda^{\prime}(B_{n-3}(\boldsymbol{0},1)) \cdot \sum_{x_1, x_2} \sum_{x_3,\ldots,x_n} \frac{ 1 }{ \max_{3\le i\le n} |x_i| } \end{align*} for $v\ge v_0(\varepsilon)$. The outer sum over $x_1, x_2$ gives a factor $\lfloor T_v\rfloor^2\le T_v^2$ by \eqref{eq:ob}. We split the inner sum into sets where $\max_{3\le i\le n} |x_i|=k\in [1,\lfloor T_v\rfloor]$ is constant, which correspond to $2(n-2)=2n-4$ faces on a hypercube for each $k$ according to which variable equals $\pm k$, giving in total $(2n-4)k^{n-3}$ integer points for each $k$ to sum $1/k$ over. Hence we may further estimate \begin{align*} \lambda(\mathcal{U}_v) &\le 2(2n-4)(2\sqrt{n-2}+2\varepsilon) \lambda^{\prime}(B_{n-3}(\boldsymbol{0},1))\cdot L_v T_v^3 \cdot \sum_{k=1}^{\lfloor T_v\rfloor} k^{n-4}\\ &\le 2(2n-4)(2\sqrt{n-2}+2\varepsilon) \lambda^{\prime}(B_{n-3}(\boldsymbol{0},1)) \left(\frac{1}{n-3}+\varepsilon_2\right) L_v T_v^{n},\quad v\ge v_1(\varepsilon,\varepsilon_2). \end{align*} Here the error term $\varepsilon_2>0$ tends to $0$ as $v\to\infty$, and we used $n\ne 3$ to avoid a logarithmic term appearing in the last sum. We may assume $\varepsilon_2< \varepsilon$ for all large $v$. So if $L_v< c T_v^{-n}$ for any $c\in(0,c_n-\epsilon)$ for $\epsilon>0$ some small manipulation of $\varepsilon$ and $c_n$ satisfies \[ \lambda(B_{n-2}(\boldsymbol{0},1))> c_n\frac{ 4(2n-4)\sqrt{n-2}\lambda^{\prime}(B_{n-3}(0,1)) }{ n-3 }, \] or equivalently \[ c_n < \frac{n-3}{4(2n-4)\sqrt{n-2}}\cdot \frac{\lambda(B_{n-2}(\boldsymbol{0},1))}{\lambda^{\prime}(B_{n-3}(\boldsymbol{0},1))}= \frac{n-3}{8(n-2)^{3/2}}\cdot \sqrt{\pi}\cdot \frac{ \Gamma(n-\frac{1}{2})}{\Gamma(n)}, \] then \eqref{eq:IND} holds for some $\Delta< \lambda(B_{n-2}(\boldsymbol{0},1))$, depending on $c_n$, and all $v\ge v_0(\Delta) = v_0(c_n)$. Hence the complement contained in $\mathcal{Y}$ has positive $(n-2)$-dimensional Lebesgue measure. Since we can choose $\varepsilon>0$, and thus $\epsilon>0$, arbitrarily small we may assume that $c<c_n$ and the proof of Lemma~\ref{lema} is complete.
nodes.statement_short: Measure-theoretic counting: bound the measure of exceptional sets U_v by counting slabs. The key step is the volume bound lambda(U_v) << L_v T_v^n, below the ball volume when c<c_n.

nodes.name: Continuity of measure from below
nodes.statement: Let $\lambda$ be a measure on a space $\mathcal{T}$. Assume $H_i$ are increasing subsets of $\mathcal{T}$, i.e. $H_1\subseteq H_2 \subseteq \cdots$. Then \[ \lambda\left(\bigcup_{k=1}^{\infty} H_k\right) = \lim_{k\to\infty} \lambda(H_k). \]
assumptions: Let $\lambda$ be a measure on a space $\mathcal{T}$.
Assume $H_i$ are increasing subsets of $\mathcal{T}$, i.e. $H_1\subseteq H_2 \subseteq \cdots$.
nodes.label: pp

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2
nodes.statement: Writing $G_j=H_j\setminus H_{j-1}$ with $H_0=\emptyset$, we see \begin{equation*} \lambda\left(\bigcup_{k=1}^{\infty} H_k\right)= \lambda\left(\bigcup_{k=1}^{\infty} G_k\right)= \lim_{N\to\infty} \sum_{k=1}^{N} \lambda(G_k)= \lim_{N\to\infty} \lambda\left(\bigcup_{k=1}^{N} H_k\right)= \lim_{N\to\infty} \lambda(H_N). \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Write the union as a disjoint union of differences and use countable additivity.

nodes.name: eq:nega (16)
nodes.statement: \min \left| x_{1}\xi_{1}+x_{2}\xi_{2}+ \sum_{i=3}^{n} x_i \zeta_i - y \right| \ge L_{v}
nodes.label: eq:nega

nodes.name: eq:ob (17)
nodes.statement: \boldsymbol{z}= (x_1,\ldots,x_{n},y)\in \mathbb{Z}^{n+1}\setminus \{\boldsymbol{0}\} \quad \text{ with } \quad 0<\max_{1\le j\le n} |x_j| \le T_v\, .
nodes.label: eq:ob

nodes.name: eq:wia (18)
nodes.statement: B_{n-2}(\boldsymbol{0},1)\setminus \mathcal{Y}\subseteq \bigcup_{i\ge 1} \bigcap_{j\ge i} \mathcal{S}_j^{c}\subseteq \bigcup_{i\ge 1} \mathcal{S}_i^{c}.
nodes.label: eq:wia

nodes.name: eq:IND (19)
nodes.statement: \lambda(\mathcal{U}_v)\le \Delta< \lambda(B_{n-2}(\boldsymbol{0},1)), \qquad v\ge 1.
nodes.label: eq:IND

nodes.name: eq:inu (20)
nodes.statement: \Omega_v= \bigcup_{x_1,\ldots,x_n} \bigcup_{y}\; \Omega_v(x_1,\ldots,x_n,y),
nodes.label: eq:inu

nodes.name: Volume calculation (21)
nodes.statement: \lambda(\Omega_v(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n},y))&= 2\lambda^{\prime}(B_{n-3}(\boldsymbol{0},1))\cdot L_v(x_3^2+\cdots+x_n^2)^{-1/2}\nonumber \\ &\le 2 L_v\cdot\lambda^{\prime}(B_{n-3}(\boldsymbol{0},1)) \cdot\frac{ 1}{\max_{3\le i\le n} |x_i|}.
nodes.label: volcume calculation

nodes.name: Assume the limit exists
nodes.statement: We first note that we may assume \[ \lim_{v\to\infty} T_v^{n}\psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{1\times 2}(T_v)=c \] and hence ignore \eqref{eq:igno}. Indeed, otherwise we restrict to a subsequence satisfying \eqref{eq:igno}, which exists by definition of the limsup, and apply the argument below for this subsequence.\par
nodes.statement_short: WLOG pass to a subsequence realizing the limsup.

nodes.name: Target statement
nodes.statement: We show that for a positive portion of $B_{n-2}(\boldsymbol{0},1)\subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n-2}$ of vectors $\boldsymbol{\gamma}=(\zeta_3,\ldots,\zeta_n)$, we have for infinitely many $v$ that \begin{equation} \min \left| x_{1}\xi_{1}+x_{2}\xi_{2}+ \sum_{i=3}^{n} x_i \zeta_i - y \right| \ge L_{v} \end{equation} with minimum taken over all integer points \begin{equation} \boldsymbol{z}= (x_1,\ldots,x_{n},y)\in \mathbb{Z}^{n+1}\setminus \{\boldsymbol{0}\} \quad \text{ with } \quad 0<\max_{1\le j\le n} |x_j| \le T_v\, . \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Show that for a positive portion of gamma, the minimum over small integer points is at least L_v infinitely often.

nodes.name: Sets S_v
nodes.statement: For $v\ge 1$, denote by $\mathcal{S}_v$ the set of vectors of $\mathbb{R}^{n-2}$ taken over all integer points $\boldsymbol{z}$ obeying \eqref{eq:ob}, i.e. \begin{equation*} \mathcal{S}_{v}:=\left\{ \boldsymbol{\gamma} \in B_{n-2}(\boldsymbol{0},1): \underset{0<\max_{1\leq i \leq n}|x_{j}|\leq T_{v}}{\min_{(\boldsymbol{x},y)\in\mathbb{Z}^{n+1}:}} \left| x_{1}\xi_{1}+x_{2}\xi_{2}+\sum_{i=3}^{n}x_{i}\zeta_{i} -y\right|\geq L_{v} \right\}. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Define the good sets S_v.

nodes.name: Y as limsup set
nodes.statement: Then our set is the limsup set of the $\mathcal{S}_v$, or its complement is the set of all vectors that lie only in finitely many $\mathcal{S}_v$, that is, \begin{equation} B_{n-2}(\boldsymbol{0},1)\setminus \mathcal{Y}\subseteq \bigcup_{i\ge 1} \bigcap_{j\ge i} \mathcal{S}_j^{c}\subseteq \bigcup_{i\ge 1} \mathcal{S}_i^{c}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Complement of Y lies in the union of liminf of complements.

nodes.name: Measure bound reduction
nodes.statement: Assume that any complement \[ \mathcal{U}_v:= \mathcal{S}_v^{c}= \left\{ \boldsymbol{\gamma} \in B_{n-2}(\boldsymbol{0},1): \underset{0<\max_{1\leq i \leq n}|x_{j}|\leq T_{v}}{\min_{(\boldsymbol{x},y)\in\mathbb{Z}^{n+1}:}} \left| x_{1}\xi_{1}+x_{2}\xi_{2}+\sum_{i=3}^{n}x_{i}\zeta_{i} -y\right|< L_{v} \right\} , \quad v\ge 1, \] has $n-2$ dimensional Lebesgue measure less than some $\delta$ strictly smaller than the volume of $B_{n-2}(\boldsymbol{0},1)$. Then this will also be true for $B_{n-2}(\boldsymbol{0},1)\setminus \mathcal{Y}$ by the following easy result.
nodes.statement_short: Suppose each complement U_v has measure below delta.

nodes.name: Proposition 2
nodes.statement: \begin{proposition} Let $\lambda$ be a measure on a space $\mathcal{T}$. Assume $H_i$ are increasing subsets of $\mathcal{T}$, i.e. $H_1\subseteq H_2 \subseteq \cdots$. Then \[ \lambda\left(\bigcup_{k=1}^{\infty} H_k\right) = \lim_{k\to\infty} \lambda(H_k). \] \end{proposition} We will require the estimate $\lambda\left(\bigcup_{k=1}^{\infty} H_k\right) \le \lim_{k\to\infty} \lambda(H_k)$ only. \begin{proof} Writing $G_j=H_j\setminus H_{j-1}$ with $H_0=\emptyset$, we see \begin{equation*} \lambda\left(\bigcup_{k=1}^{\infty} H_k\right)= \lambda\left(\bigcup_{k=1}^{\infty} G_k\right)= \lim_{N\to\infty} \sum_{k=1}^{N} \lambda(G_k)= \lim_{N\to\infty} \lambda\left(\bigcup_{k=1}^{N} H_k\right)= \lim_{N\to\infty} \lambda(H_N). \end{equation*} \end{proof}
nodes.statement_short: Continuity of measure from below, with proof.

nodes.name: Apply Proposition 2
nodes.statement: In the sequel denote by $\lambda$ the $(n-2)$-dimensional Lebesgue measure of a set $A\subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n-2}$. As indicated before, we apply Proposition~\ref{pp} to \[ H_i= \bigcap_{j\ge i} \mathcal{S}_j^{c}= \bigcap_{j\ge i} \mathcal{U}_j \subseteq \mathcal{U}_i, \qquad i\ge 1, \] to see via \eqref{eq:wia} that \[ \lambda(B_{n-2}(\boldsymbol{0},1)\setminus \mathcal{Y})\le \lim_{v\to\infty} \lambda(\mathcal{U}_v). \]
nodes.statement_short: Apply Proposition 2 to H_i to bound the complement of Y.

nodes.name: Positive measure of Y
nodes.statement: Assume we have shown that for some uniform $\Delta$ we have \begin{equation} \lambda(\mathcal{U}_v)\le \Delta< \lambda(B_{n-2}(\boldsymbol{0},1)), \qquad v\ge 1. \end{equation} Then we conclude that $$\lambda(B_{n-2}(\boldsymbol{0},1)\setminus \mathcal{Y})\le \Delta<\lambda(B_{n-2}(\boldsymbol{0},1))$$ and thus \[ \lambda(\mathcal{Y}) = \lambda(B_{n-2}(\boldsymbol{0},1)) - \lambda(B_{n-2}(\boldsymbol{0},1)\setminus \mathcal{Y})\ge \lambda(B_{n-2}(\boldsymbol{0},1)) - \Delta > 0, \] as desired.
nodes.statement_short: A uniform bound Delta on lambda(U_v) gives lambda(Y)>0.

nodes.name: Slab reformulation
nodes.statement: To verify \eqref{eq:IND}, let us estimate $\lambda(\mathcal{U}_v)$ for fixed $v$. For any $\boldsymbol{\gamma}=(\zeta_3,\ldots,\zeta_n)\in \mathcal{U}_v$ it follows that \begin{equation*} \underset{0<\max_{1\leq i \leq n}|x_{j}|\leq T_{v}}{\min_{(\boldsymbol{x},y)\in\mathbb{Z}^{n+1}:}} \left| x_{1}\xi_{1}+x_{2}\xi_{2}+\sum_{i=3}^{n}x_{i}\zeta_{i} -y\right|< L_{v}\, . \end{equation*} Equivalently \[ x_3 \zeta_3 + \cdots+ x_n \zeta_n \in J_{v}(x_1,x_2,y) \] where $J_{v}(.)$ is given as the interval \[ J_v(x_1,x_2,y)= ( -y-x_1\xi_1-x_2\xi_2-L_v , -y-x_1\xi_1-x_2\xi_2+L_v ). \]
nodes.statement_short: Membership in U_v means a linear form lies in an interval J_v.

nodes.name: Sets Omega_v
nodes.statement: Let \[ \Omega_v(x_1,\ldots, x_n,y)= \left\{ (\zeta_3,\ldots,\zeta_n)\in B_{n-2}(0,1)\subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n-2}: \sum_{i=3}^{n}x_{i}\zeta_{i} \in J_{v}(x_1,x_2,y) \right\}. \] Observe that $\Omega_v(x_1,\ldots,x_n,y)$ is empty if $|y|>|x_{1}\xi_{1}|+|x_{2}\xi_{2}|+\sum_{i=3}^{n} |x_i \zeta_i|+L_v$.
nodes.statement_short: Define Omega_v(x,y); it is empty for large |y|.

nodes.name: Bound on |y|
nodes.statement: Fix for now $\varepsilon>0$. Since $L_v\to 0$ as $v\to\infty$ and as we may take $\xi_1,\xi_2$ arbitrarily small positive numbers (the $\boldsymbol{\xi}$ from Theorem~\ref{thm2} are easily seen to be dense in $\mathbb{R}$), say smaller than $\varepsilon/8$, and $(\zeta_3,\ldots,\zeta_n)\in B_{n-2}(\boldsymbol{0},1)$, Cauchy-Schwarz inequality yields for any $\varepsilon>0$ this is true if \[ |y|> (\sqrt{n-2}+\varepsilon/2) T_v \] as then \begin{align*} |y|&> (\sqrt{n-2}+\varepsilon/2) T_v \\ &\ge (\varepsilon/4)\cdot T_v+ \left(\sum_{i=3}^{n} |x_i|^2\right)^{1/2}\left(\sum_{i=3}^{n} |\zeta_i|^2\right)^{1/2}+L_v \\ &\ge |\xi_1| |x_1| + |\xi_2| |x_2|+ \left(\sum_{i=3}^{n} |x_i|^2\right)^{1/2}\left(\sum_{i=3}^{n} |\zeta_i|^2\right)^{1/2}+L_v \\ &\ge |x_{1}\xi_{1}|+|x_{2}\xi_{2}|+ \sum_{i=1}^{n} |x_i\zeta_i|+L_v, \qquad v\ge v_0(\varepsilon). \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Cauchy-Schwarz shows only |y| <= (sqrt(n-2)+eps/2)T_v matter.

nodes.name: U_v inside Omega_v
nodes.statement: The above shows that if we let \begin{equation} \Omega_v= \bigcup_{x_1,\ldots,x_n} \bigcup_{y}\; \Omega_v(x_1,\ldots,x_n,y), \end{equation} with unions are taken over integers $x_1, \dots, x_{n}$ as in \eqref{eq:ob} and integers $y$ with $|y|\le (\sqrt{n-2}+\varepsilon/2)T_v$. Then \[ \mathcal{U}_v \subseteq \Omega_v, \qquad v\geq v_0(\varepsilon). \]
nodes.statement_short: U_v is contained in the union Omega_v.

nodes.name: Volume of one slab
nodes.statement: The distance between the parallel planes defining $\Omega_v(x_1,\ldots,x_n,y)$ equals $2(x_3^2+\cdots+x_n^2)^{-1/2}$. Thus each $\Omega_v(x_1,\ldots,x_n,y)$ is contained in a cylinder of radius one and height $2L_v \cdot (x_3^2+\cdots+x_n^2)^{-1/2}$. Denoting by $\lambda^{\prime}$ the $(n-3)$-dimensional Lebesgue measure, this has volume \begin{align} \lambda(\Omega_v(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n},y))&= 2\lambda^{\prime}(B_{n-3}(\boldsymbol{0},1))\cdot L_v(x_3^2+\cdots+x_n^2)^{-1/2}\nonumber \\ &\le 2 L_v\cdot\lambda^{\prime}(B_{n-3}(\boldsymbol{0},1)) \cdot\frac{ 1}{\max_{3\le i\le n} |x_i|}. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Each slab has volume at most 2L_v vol(B_{n-3})/max|x_i|.

nodes.name: Sum over y
