nodes.statement: Since, assuming $T_v\ge \varepsilon^{-1}$, there are at most $$2T_{v}(\sqrt{n-2}+\varepsilon/2)+1\le T_{v}(2\sqrt{n-2}+2\varepsilon)$$ integers $y$ in the inner union of \eqref{eq:inu}, in total we get \begin{align*} \lambda(\mathcal{U}_v) &\le \lambda(\Omega_v)\\ &\le \sum_{x_1, x_2} \sum_y \sum_{x_3,\ldots,x_n} \lambda(\Omega_v(x_1,\ldots,x_n,y))\\ &\le 2(2\sqrt{n-2}+2\varepsilon)L_vT_v \lambda^{\prime}(B_{n-3}(\boldsymbol{0},1)) \cdot \sum_{x_1, x_2} \sum_{x_3,\ldots,x_n} \frac{ 1 }{ \max_{3\le i\le n} |x_i| } \end{align*} for $v\ge v_0(\varepsilon)$.
nodes.statement_short: Count the integers y and sum slab volumes.

nodes.name: Sum over x
nodes.statement: The outer sum over $x_1, x_2$ gives a factor $\lfloor T_v\rfloor^2\le T_v^2$ by \eqref{eq:ob}. We split the inner sum into sets where $\max_{3\le i\le n} |x_i|=k\in [1,\lfloor T_v\rfloor]$ is constant, which correspond to $2(n-2)=2n-4$ faces on a hypercube for each $k$ according to which variable equals $\pm k$, giving in total $(2n-4)k^{n-3}$ integer points for each $k$ to sum $1/k$ over. Hence we may further estimate \begin{align*} \lambda(\mathcal{U}_v) &\le 2(2n-4)(2\sqrt{n-2}+2\varepsilon) \lambda^{\prime}(B_{n-3}(\boldsymbol{0},1))\cdot L_v T_v^3 \cdot \sum_{k=1}^{\lfloor T_v\rfloor} k^{n-4}\\ &\le 2(2n-4)(2\sqrt{n-2}+2\varepsilon) \lambda^{\prime}(B_{n-3}(\boldsymbol{0},1)) \left(\frac{1}{n-3}+\varepsilon_2\right) L_v T_v^{n},\quad v\ge v_1(\varepsilon,\varepsilon_2). \end{align*} Here the error term $\varepsilon_2>0$ tends to $0$ as $v\to\infty$, and we used $n\ne 3$ to avoid a logarithmic term appearing in the last sum. We may assume $\varepsilon_2< \varepsilon$ for all large $v$.
nodes.statement_short: Summing over x gives lambda(U_v) << L_v T_v^n, using n != 3.

nodes.name: Choice of c_n
nodes.statement: So if $L_v< c T_v^{-n}$ for any $c\in(0,c_n-\epsilon)$ for $\epsilon>0$ some small manipulation of $\varepsilon$ and $c_n$ satisfies \[ \lambda(B_{n-2}(\boldsymbol{0},1))> c_n\frac{ 4(2n-4)\sqrt{n-2}\lambda^{\prime}(B_{n-3}(0,1)) }{ n-3 }, \] or equivalently \[ c_n < \frac{n-3}{4(2n-4)\sqrt{n-2}}\cdot \frac{\lambda(B_{n-2}(\boldsymbol{0},1))}{\lambda^{\prime}(B_{n-3}(\boldsymbol{0},1))}= \frac{n-3}{8(n-2)^{3/2}}\cdot \sqrt{\pi}\cdot \frac{ \Gamma(n-\frac{1}{2})}{\Gamma(n)}, \] then \eqref{eq:IND} holds for some $\Delta< \lambda(B_{n-2}(\boldsymbol{0},1))$, depending on $c_n$, and all $v\ge v_0(\Delta) = v_0(c_n)$. Hence the complement contained in $\mathcal{Y}$ has positive $(n-2)$-dimensional Lebesgue measure. Since we can choose $\varepsilon>0$, and thus $\epsilon>0$, arbitrarily small we may assume that $c<c_n$ and the proof of Lemma~\ref{lema} is complete.
nodes.statement_short: For c<c_n the bound (19) holds, so Y has positive measure.

nodes.name: Possible improvement of c_n
nodes.statement: Improvements of $c_n$ can be made by sharpening the contribution $2\sqrt{n-2}+1$ for the number of $y$. Indeed, for most $y$ the obtained intersections with the unit ball have a considerably smaller volume than $2L_v \cdot (x_3^2+\cdots+x_n^2)^{-1/2}$, so it seems we can improve by more concise estimates.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2.3
nodes.statement: \section{Proof of Theorem~\ref{jia} } \subsection{Outline} The method of proof is similar to that of Theorem~\ref{thm1}. Namely, the proof is done in two steps: \begin{enumerate} \item[Step I:] For small enough $c$, construct $\boldsymbol{\xi}=(\xi_1, \xi_2)$ such that \[ \limsup_{t\to\infty} t^n \psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{1\times 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert,t) = c. \] \item[Step II:] Show that for a positive measure set $(\xi_3,\ldots,\xi_n)$ with respect to $(n-2)$-dimensional Lebesgue measure, the extended vector $\boldsymbol{\zeta}=(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_n)$ satisfies \[ \Theta^{1\times n}(\boldsymbol{\zeta})=\limsup_{t\to\infty} t^n \psi_{\boldsymbol{\zeta}}^{1\times n}(\Vert\cdot\Vert,t) = c \] as well. \end{enumerate} Note that Step I follows immediately, for any $c\ge 0$ (and $c\in[0,D]$ if $n=2$), from the aforementioned preprint \cite[Corollary~1]{AginWeiss2024}. Note this follows from the result on $\psi$-Dirichlet Spectrum, rather than the classical Dirichlet Spectrum, since our approximation function is $t^{n}$. However, as this appeared later than the current article, we keep our original construction. Note that \cite{AginWeiss2024} does not simplify Step II of the proof. \subsection{Proof of Step I} This is the more intricate part of the proof. For this, we use a different construction than for the maximum norm where we employed the construction from~\cite{j2}. Rather we follow the proof of~\cite[Theorem~2.1]{j3} but with some notable twists. Write $\boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}=(\boldsymbol{\xi},1)\in\mathbb{R}^{3}$ and use a similar meaning of star for other quantities. Conversely denote by a hat over a vector in $\mathbb{R}^{3}$ its restriction to the first $2$ coordinates by chopping off the last coordinate, i.e. $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}}=\boldsymbol{\xi}$. We construct our real vector. Let $n<\tau<\mu$ be parameters to be chosen later related by the identity \begin{equation} \tau \mu-1=n\mu \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad \mu=\frac{1}{\tau-n}. \end{equation} Let $\alpha_j, \beta_j, \gamma_j, \delta_j$ be strictly increasing positive integer sequences and a real number $r=r(\Vert\cdot\Vert)>0$ all to be fixed later. Derive integers of the form \[ A_j= 2^{\alpha_j}3^{\gamma_j }, \qquad B_j= 5^{\beta_j }7^{\delta_j}, \] satisfying as $j\to\infty$ \begin{equation} A_{j+1}= (1+o(1))r B_j^{\tau}, \qquad B_j = (1+o(1))A_j^{\mu}. \end{equation} We first show that such choices are possible. For $A_j$, we use that $\{ \log 2, \log 3\}$ is a $\mathbb{Q}$-linearly independent set (easily seen by applying exponential map to a putative vanishing linear form and using unique prime factorization to disprove it) and the following easy Proposition~\ref{proper}. Similarly for $B_j$ we use that $\{ \log 5, \log 7\}$ is $\mathbb{Q}$-linearly independent. \begin{proposition} Let $a,b,c$ be real numbers with $a,b$ linearly independent over $\mathbb{Q}$. Then ordering the set $\{ k_1 a+k_2 b+c: k_i\in\mathbb{N} \}$ increasingly and denoting it by $(z_i)_{i\ge 1}$ we have $|z_{i+1}-z_i|\to 0$. \end{proposition} \begin{proof} Clearly, we may assume $c=0$ and suppose without loss of generality that $b<a$. We may then equivalently consider \begin{equation*} \mathcal{Z}=\{ k_1+k_2\tfrac{b}{a}: k_i\in\mathbb{N} \} \end{equation*} instead. Since $\tfrac{b}{a}$ is irrational, Kronecker's Theorem (see e.g. \cite[Section 3.5 Theorem IV]{Cassels}) shows that the set is dense in the unit interval when considering all $(k_1, k_2)\in \mathbb{Z}\times \mathbb{N}$. Let $\varepsilon=1/K>0$ with a large integer $K$ and partition $[0,1]$ into $K$ intervals \begin{equation*} I_t=[(t-1)\varepsilon,t\varepsilon], \qquad 1\le t\le K \end{equation*} of length $1/K$. Then for any $I_t$ there exist $(k_1^{\prime}(t), k_2^{\prime}(t))\in\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{N}$ so that $k_1^{\prime}(t)+k_2^{\prime}(t)\tfrac{b}{a}\in I_t$. Take $T_{\varepsilon}:= \max_t |k_1^{\prime}(t)|$ and consider the set \begin{equation*} \mathcal{Z}_{T_{\varepsilon}} = \left\{ (k_{1}(t)+N) + k_{2}(t)\tfrac{b}{a} : 1\leq t\leq K, \, N \in \mathbb{N}_{\geq T_{\varepsilon}} \right\} \subset \mathcal{Z}\, . \end{equation*} It is easy to see that for any $M\in\mathbb{N}_{\geq T_{\varepsilon}}$ the interval $M+I_{t}$ contains a point from $\mathcal{Z}_{T_{\varepsilon}}$. This shows that $\mathcal{Z}$ is $\varepsilon$ dense on some interval $[3T_{\varepsilon},\infty)$. Since $\varepsilon>0$ is arbitrary the claim is proved. \end{proof} We can now apply the proposition alternatingly to \[ a=\log 2, \, b=\log 3, \, c=\log r, \qquad\quad a=\log 5,\, b=\log 7, \, c=0 \] respectively to construct iteratively our sequences $\alpha_j, \gamma_j$, which correspond to $k_1=\alpha_{j+1}-\alpha_j\ge 0$ and $k_2=\gamma_{j+1}-\gamma_j\ge 0$, resp. $k_1=\beta_{j+1}-\beta_j\ge 0$ and $k_2=\delta_{j+1}-\delta_j\ge 0$. Thereby, having chosen all $\alpha_., \beta_., \gamma_.,\delta_.$ up to index $j$, we construct first pairs $\alpha_{j+1}, \gamma_{j+1}$ and then $\beta_{j+1}, \delta_{j+1}$, and the iterative construction is complete. So, having chosen $r$, we may assume all the above is defined. Note that \eqref{eq:accto} implies \begin{equation} A_{j+1}=(1+o(1))r A_j^{\tau \mu}, \qquad B_{j+1} =(1+o(1))r^{\mu} B_j^{\tau \mu}. \end{equation} Moreover, again by \eqref{eq:accto}, upon changing initial terms if necessary, we can assume \begin{equation} 1<A_1 < B_1 < A_2 < B_2 < \cdots. \end{equation} Finally let $\boldsymbol{\xi}=(\xi_1, \xi_2)$ with \[ \xi_1= \sum_{j\ge 1} A_j^{-1 } , \qquad \xi_2= \sum_{j\ge 1} B_j^{-1 }. \] We claim that it satisfies the assertions of the theorem upon choosing $r$ appropriately. For $j\ge 1$ put \[ \sigma_j := A_1^{-1}+\cdots+A_j^{-1}, \qquad \eta_j:= B_1^{-1}+\cdots+B_j^{-1}. \] We clearly have $\sigma_j\to \xi_1$ and $\eta_j\to \xi_2$ as $j\to \infty$, and \[ F_j= A_j\sigma_j\in \mathbb{N}, \qquad G_j=B_j \eta_j\in\mathbb{N}. \] Then since the sequences $(\alpha_j), (\beta_j), (\gamma_j), (\delta_j)$ are strictly increasing we have $F_j\equiv 1\bmod 2\cdot 3$ and $G_j\equiv 1\bmod 5\cdot 7$, which imply the coprimality assertions \begin{equation} (A_j, F_j)=(F_j,6)=1, \qquad (B_j,G_j)=(G_j,35)=1. \end{equation} Let \[ \boldsymbol{v}_j=(A_j,0,-F_j), \qquad \boldsymbol{w}_j=(0, B_j,-G_j). \] Note that $\hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_j=(A_j,0)$ and $\hat {\boldsymbol{w}}_j=(0,B_j)$. Hence their norms $\Vert\cdot\Vert$ satisfy \begin{equation} \Vert\hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_j\Vert = \Vert \boldsymbol{e}_1 \Vert A_j= d_1 A_j, \qquad d_1:=\Vert \boldsymbol{e}_1\Vert=\Vert (1,0)\Vert, \end{equation} and \begin{equation} \Vert\hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert= \Vert \boldsymbol{e}_2 \Vert B_j= d_2 B_j \overset{\eqref{eq:accto}}{=}(1+o(1))d_2 A_j^{\mu}, \qquad d_2:=\Vert \boldsymbol{e}_2\Vert=\Vert (0,1)\Vert, \end{equation} Thus by \eqref{eq:vf} clearly \begin{equation} \Vert\hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_j\Vert< \Vert\hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert< \Vert\hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_{j+1}\Vert, \qquad j\ge j_0. \end{equation} Here $j_0$ depends on $d_1, d_2$, thus on the chosen norm. Then by \eqref{eq:true} moreover \begin{align} |\boldsymbol{v}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|&= |A_j \cdot \xi_1 +0\cdot \xi_2 - F_j|= A_j(A_{j+1}^{-1}+A_{j+2}^{-1}+\cdots) \\ &= A_j A_{j+1}^{-1}(1+o(1)) \overset{\eqref{eq:true}}{=} (1+o(1))r^{-1}A_j^{-(\tau \mu-1) } \nonumber \end{align} and \begin{align} |\boldsymbol{w}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|&= |0\cdot \xi_1 + B_j \cdot \xi_2 - G_j|= B_j(B_{j+1}^{-1}+B_{j+2}^{-1}+\cdots) \\ &= (1+o(1))B_jB_{j+1}^{-1} \overset{\eqref{eq:true}}{=} (1+o(1))r^{-\mu}\cdot B_j^{-(\tau \mu-1) }, \nonumber \end{align} are small linear forms for $j\ge 1$. We next show \begin{lemma} As soon as $r$ is large enough, all best approximations for $\boldsymbol{\xi}$ of large norm have up to sign one of the following forms \[ \boldsymbol{v}_j, \quad \boldsymbol{w}_j, \quad \boldsymbol{v}_j+\boldsymbol{w}_j,\quad \boldsymbol{w}_j-\boldsymbol{v}_j, \quad \boldsymbol{w}_j+\boldsymbol{v}_{j+1}, \quad \boldsymbol{v}_{j+1}-\boldsymbol{w}_{j}. \] \end{lemma} \begin{proof} Let $\boldsymbol{b}$ be any best approximation. Then by \eqref{eq:either} there is an index $j$ such that either $\Vert\hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_j\Vert\le \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{b}}\Vert<\Vert\hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert$ or $\Vert\hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert\le \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{b}}\Vert< \Vert\hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_{j+1}\Vert$. We show that in the first case $\boldsymbol{b}=\pm \boldsymbol{v}_j$ or $\pm(\boldsymbol{v}_j\pm \boldsymbol{w}_j)$, and in the latter case $\boldsymbol{b}=\pm \boldsymbol{w}_j$ or $\pm(\boldsymbol{w}_j\pm \boldsymbol{v}_{j+1})$. Assume the first case, so \begin{equation} \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_j\Vert\le \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{b}}\Vert< \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert. \end{equation} the latter works very similarly by symmetry. First, observe that since $\boldsymbol{b}$ is the best approximation of norm at least $\Vert\hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_j\Vert$, we know that \begin{equation} |\boldsymbol{b}\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|\le |\boldsymbol{v}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|. \end{equation} We distinguish two cases. Case 1: $\boldsymbol{b}$ lies in the two-dimensonal subspace of $\mathbb{R}^3$ spanned by $\boldsymbol{v}_j, \boldsymbol{w}_j$, i.e. $\boldsymbol{b}\in \scp{\boldsymbol{v}_j, \boldsymbol{w}_j}_{\mathbb{R}}\cap \mathbb{Z}^3$. The special form of $A_j, B_j$ and \eqref{eq:witt} imply the following crucial result on integer vectors in the two-dimensional lattices $\scp{\boldsymbol{v}_j, \boldsymbol{w}_j}_{\mathbb{R}}\cap \mathbb{Z}^3$. \begin{proposition} For $\boldsymbol{v}_j, \boldsymbol{w}_j$ as above, if a linear combination $g\boldsymbol{v}_j+h\boldsymbol{w}_j$ is an integer vector, then in fact $g\in\mathbb{Z}$ and $h\in \mathbb{Z}$. In other words, $\scp{\boldsymbol{v}_j, \boldsymbol{w}_j}_{\mathbb{R}}\cap \mathbb{Z}^3=\scp{\boldsymbol{v}_j, \boldsymbol{w}_j}_{\mathbb{Z}}$. \end{proposition} \begin{proof} Clearly, we must have $g,h\in \mathbb{Q}$. If we write $(p_1/q_1)\boldsymbol{v}_j + (p_2/q_2)\boldsymbol{w}_j$ with $p_i/q_i$ in lowest terms, then it is clear that $q_1$ must consist of exclusively non-negative integer powers of $2$ and $3$ and $q_2$ of non-negative integer power of $5$ and $7$ to make the first two coordinates $(p_1/q_1)A_j=(p_1/q_1)2^{\alpha_j}3^{\gamma_j}$ resp. $(p_2/q_2)B_j=(p_2/q_2)5^{\beta_j}7^{\delta_j}$ of $g\boldsymbol{v}_j+h\boldsymbol{w}_j$ integers. But then by \eqref{eq:witt} clearly the third coordinate $(p_1/q_1)F_j+(p_2/q_2)G_j$ is not an integer unless $q_1=q_2=1$. \end{proof} We first show that any integer linear combination $\boldsymbol{b}=g\boldsymbol{v}_j+h\boldsymbol{w}_j$ representing the best approximation as above must have $|g|\le 1$. Assume $|g|\ge 2$. It is easily seen that for any norm on $\mathbb{R}^2$ there is a constant $\theta=\theta(\Vert\cdot\Vert)$ such that $\Vert \boldsymbol{w}\Vert \le W$ for $\boldsymbol{w}=(w_1,w_2)\in\mathbb{R}^2$ and $W>0$ implies $|w_i|\le \theta W$, $i=1,2$. Hence \eqref{eq:T} and the special form of $\boldsymbol{v}_j, \boldsymbol{w}_j$ imply \[ |g|\le \theta, \qquad |h|\le \theta \] for some $\theta$ independent of $j$. On the other hand, since $r,\mu$ are fixed and $A_j\to\infty$, it is clear from \eqref{eq:ti}, \eqref{eq:tz} and \eqref{eq:accto} that \[ |\boldsymbol{w}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| = o(|\boldsymbol{v}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|), \qquad j\to\infty. \] Combination implies \begin{align*} |\boldsymbol{b} \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|= | (g\boldsymbol{v}_j+h\boldsymbol{w}_j) \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| &\ge |g|\cdot |\boldsymbol{v}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| - |h|\cdot |\boldsymbol{w}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| \ge 2 |\boldsymbol{v}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| - |h|\cdot |\boldsymbol{w}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|\\ &\ge 2 |\boldsymbol{v}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| - \theta\cdot |\boldsymbol{w}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| > |\boldsymbol{v}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|, \qquad j\ge j_0, \end{align*} contradicting \eqref{eq:see}. Hence $|g|\le 1$. Now if $|h|\ge 2$ then for any $|g|\le 1$ using \eqref{eq:either} we get \[ \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{b}}\Vert= \Vert g \hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_j+h\hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert \ge |h|\cdot \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert - \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_j\Vert \ge 2 \cdot \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert - \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_j\Vert > \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert \] contradicting \eqref{eq:T}. Thus both $g,h$ are among $\{-1,0,1\}$. Hence we are left with the vectors of the lemma. Case 2: $\boldsymbol{b}$ does not lie in the space spanned by $\boldsymbol{v}_j, \boldsymbol{w}_j$. For this case, we use an easy consequence of Minkowski's Second Convex Body Theorem. \begin{lemma} There exists a constant $c>0$ such that for any $\boldsymbol{\xi}\in \mathbb{R}^2$ and any parameter $Q\ge 1$, the system \[ |b_1|\le Q,\qquad |b_2|\le Q,\qquad |b_1 \xi_1 + b_2 \xi_2+b_{3}| < cQ^{-2} \] does not have three linearly independent solutions in integer vectors $\boldsymbol{b}=(b_1,b_2,b_3)$. \end{lemma} \begin{proof} Consider the integer lattice $\mathbb{Z}^3$ and the box of $(x_1,x_2,x_3)\in \mathbb{R}^3$ with coordinates \[ |x_1|\le Q, \qquad |x_2|\le Q,\quad |\xi_1 x_1+\xi_2 x_2 + x_3|\leq cQ^{-2}. \] It has volume $8c$, independent of $Q$ and $\xi_1, \xi_2$. Hence, by Minkowski's Second Convex Body Theorem, the product of the induced successive minima is $\ll c$, hence choosing $c$ small enough the third successive minimum is smaller than $1$. This means there cannot be three linearly independent integer points within the box, which in turn is equivalent to the claim. \end{proof} We first notice that both $\boldsymbol{v}_j$ and $\boldsymbol{w}_j$ induce approximations of order greater than two. By \eqref{eq:lg2}, \eqref{eq:ti} and as our choice $(\tau \mu-1)/\mu=n>2$, we get \begin{equation} |\boldsymbol{v}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| = (1+o(1))r^{-1} A_j^{-(\tau \mu-1)} \ll r^{-1} B_j^{-n}\ll r^{-1}\Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert^{-n}< r^{-1}\Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert^{-2} \end{equation} and for $\boldsymbol{w}_j$ by \eqref{eq:tz} we have a stronger estimate that also yields \begin{equation} |\boldsymbol{w}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| = o(1)\cdot B_j^{-(\tau \mu-1)} = o(\Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert^{-n})= o(\Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert^{-2}), \quad j\to\infty. \end{equation} Combined with \eqref{eq:either}, \eqref{eq:T}, \eqref{eq:see}, we have \[ \max\{ \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{b}}\Vert, \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_j\Vert, \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert \}= \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert, \qquad \max\{|\boldsymbol{b}\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|, |\boldsymbol{v}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|,|\boldsymbol{w}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| \} \ll r^{-1}\Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert^{-2}. \] By the assumptions of Case 2, the three vectors $\boldsymbol{v}_j, \boldsymbol{w}_j, \boldsymbol{b}$ are linearly independent. So we get a contradiction to Lemma~\ref{lemur} for $r$ sufficiently large and $Q=\Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert$, as soon as $\Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert$ is sufficiently large. Hence, in total, Case 2 provides only finitely many best approximations, of small norm, so Lemma~\ref{wichtig!} is proved. \end{proof} For studying $\psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{1\times 2}$, we may restrict to integer vectors of the form appearing in Lemma~\ref{wichtig!}. Now $|\boldsymbol{w}_j \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|$ is much larger than $|\boldsymbol{v}_{j+1} \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|$, and $|\boldsymbol{v}_j \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|$ is much larger than $|\boldsymbol{w}_{j} \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|$ by \eqref{eq:accto}, \eqref{eq:ti}, \eqref{eq:tz}. Hence by the triangle inequality $\boldsymbol{v}_j\pm \boldsymbol{w}_j$ induce the same approximation quality as $\boldsymbol{v}_j$ up to a factor $1+o(1)$, and similarly, $\boldsymbol{w}_j\pm \boldsymbol{v}_{j+1}$ induce the same approximation quality up to $1+o(1)$ as $\boldsymbol{w}_j$, i.e \begin{equation} |(\boldsymbol{v}_j\pm \boldsymbol{w}_j)\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| = (1+o(1))\cdot |\boldsymbol{v}_j \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|, \quad |(\boldsymbol{v}_{j+1}\pm \boldsymbol{w}_j)\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| = (1+o(1))\cdot |\boldsymbol{w}_j \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|. \end{equation} Moreover as the norm of $\hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j$ is much larger than the norm of $\hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_j$ and the norm of $\hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_{j+1}$ is much larger than the norm of $\hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j$, by \eqref{eq:accto} and \eqref{eq:gl}, we have by the triangle inequality that \begin{equation} \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_j\pm \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert = (1+o(1)) \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert, \qquad \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_{j+1}\pm \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert = (1+o(1)) \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_{j+1}\Vert. \end{equation} By \eqref{eq:41}, \eqref{eq:51} and since we have freedom up to a factor $1+o(1)$ in our claim to be proved, we may assume that all best approximations are among $\boldsymbol{v}_j, \boldsymbol{w}_j$. Now we choose $r$ appropriately. To finish the proof we show that choosing $\tau, \mu, r$ suitably we have \begin{equation} | \boldsymbol{v}_j \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| = (1+o(1))\cdot c\Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert^{-n}, \qquad | \boldsymbol{w}_j \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| = o(1)\cdot \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_{j+1}\Vert^{-n}. \end{equation} Assume this is true. Then indeed partitioning the interval $[\Vert \boldsymbol{v}_1\Vert,\infty)$ into consecutive disjoint intervals of the form $[\Vert \boldsymbol{v}_j\Vert, \Vert \boldsymbol{w}_j\Vert)$ and $[\Vert \boldsymbol{w}_j\Vert, \Vert \boldsymbol{v}_{j+1}\Vert)$ we see \begin{equation*} t^n \psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{1\times 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert, t)\le c(1+o(1)) \qquad t\to\infty. \end{equation*} On the other hand, since there is no better approximation than the one induced by $\boldsymbol{v}_j$ for any $t<\Vert \boldsymbol{w}_j\Vert$, for $t_j:=\Vert \boldsymbol{w}_j\Vert-1$ we have the reverse inequality \begin{equation*} t_j^n \psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{1\times 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert,t_j)\ge c(1+o(1)) \qquad j\to\infty. \end{equation*} Combining proves the equality \[ \limsup_{t\to\infty} t^n \psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{1\times 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert, t) = c. \] For the left identity of \eqref{eq:frosch} equivalently by \eqref{eq:lg2}, \eqref{eq:ti} we need \[ (1+o(1))r^{-1}A_j^{-(\tau \mu-1) }= c\cdot d_2^{-n} A_j^{-n\mu}, \] so we pick \[ r= c^{-1} d_2^n A_j^{n\mu-\tau \mu+1} \overset{ \eqref{eq:IIi}}{=}c^{-1} d_2^n. \] Similarly, by \eqref{eq:gl}, \eqref{eq:tz} for the right identity of \eqref{eq:frosch} it suffices to have \[ B_j^{-(\tau \mu-1)}= o(d_1^{-n} A_{j+1}^{-n\tau}). \] Since $A_{j+1}^{-n\tau} \asymp B_{j}^{-n\tau^2}$ by \eqref{eq:accto} and $d_1$ is constant, it suffices to notice that upon \eqref{eq:IIi} we may choose $\tau<\mu$ so that $n\tau^2 < \tau \mu-1$. Indeed it suffices to choose $\tau$ just slightly larger than $n$ so that $\mu=1/(\tau-n)>\tau^2$ which is equivalent to $n\tau^2 < \tau \mu-1$. We leave the short calculation to the reader. We have completed step I. Assuming $c$ is small enough, we apply Step II below. \subsection{Proof of Step II} The proof of step II works analogously to the special case of maximum norm in Section \ref{Sect6}. Our norm $\Vert\cdot\Vert$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$ induces a projected norm $\Vert\cdot\Vert^{\prime}$ on $\mathbb{R}^2$ via \begin{equation} \Vert (x_1, x_2) \Vert^{\prime}:= \Vert (x_1,x_2,0,\ldots,0) \Vert. \end{equation} Then for this norm $\Vert\cdot\Vert^{\prime}$ we apply step I to get $\boldsymbol{\xi}=(\xi_1, \xi_2)$ with the property \[ \limsup_{t\to\infty} t^n \psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{1\times 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert^{\prime}, t) = c. \] Let $\boldsymbol{b}_v=(b_{1,v}, b_{2,v}, b_{3,v})$ be the integer vector sequence constructed in Step I. By construction of $\Vert\cdot\Vert^{\prime}$, it is again clear by the same argument as in Proposition~\ref{pro} that any vector $\boldsymbol{\zeta}=(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_n)\in \mathbb{R}^n$ extending $\boldsymbol{\xi}$ has Dirichlet constant at most $c$ with respect to $\Vert\cdot\Vert$, i.e. \[ \limsup_{t\to\infty} t^n \psi_{\boldsymbol{\zeta}}^{1\times n}(\Vert\cdot\Vert, t) \le \limsup_{t\to\infty} t^n \psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{1\times 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert^{\prime}, t) = c. \] Indeed, we can choose the embedded integer vectors $\iota(\boldsymbol{b}_v)$ via the embedding \[ \iota: (y_1, y_2,y_3)\to (y_1,y_2,0,\ldots,0,y_3) \] from $\mathbb{R}^3$ to $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$, which by \eqref{eq:pno} induce the same heights and approximation quality \[ \Vert \widehat{\iota(\boldsymbol{b}_v)}\Vert=\Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{b}}_v\Vert^{\prime}, \qquad |\iota(\boldsymbol{b}_v)\cdot \boldsymbol{\zeta}^{\ast}|=|\boldsymbol{b}_v\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast} | \] for any $\boldsymbol{b}_v$, with hat notation according to \eqref{eq:hatnot} on the respective spaces. For the non-trivial lower estimate \[ \limsup_{t\to\infty} t^n \psi_{\boldsymbol{\zeta}}^{1\times n}(\Vert\cdot\Vert, t)\ge c \] with respect to $\Vert\cdot\Vert$, define \[ L_v=|\iota(\boldsymbol{b}_v)\cdot \boldsymbol{\zeta}^{\ast}|=|\boldsymbol{b}_v\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast} |=|b_{1,v} \xi_1 + b_{2,v} \xi_2 + b_{3,v}|, \quad M_v=M_v(\Vert\cdot\Vert)=\Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{b}}_v\Vert^{\prime}=\Vert \widehat{\iota(\boldsymbol{b}_v)}\Vert \] and $T_v=M_v-1/2$ as in the proof for the maximum norm but where $M_v, T_v$ are now defined with respect to our norm $\Vert\cdot\Vert$. Then by the equivalence of norms on $\mathbb{R}^n$, for any integer vector of norm $\Vert (x_1,\ldots,x_n)\Vert\le T_v$ we still have \[ \max_{1\le i\le n} |x_i|\le C(\Vert\cdot\Vert) \cdot T_v \] for some constant $C$ depending on the norm only. We replace \eqref{eq:ob} by this modified inequality and follow the proof of the special case Lemma~\ref{lema} where the maximum norm was treated. The twist by the constant $C$ will result in some altered value of $c_n$, depending on the chosen norm, for the same conclusion. We omit its explicit calculation in dependence of~$C$.
nodes.statement_short: Step I: construct xi from integers A_j=2^a3^g, B_j=5^b7^d with exact limsup c. Step II: extend to R^n by the measure argument of Lemma 5.3.

nodes.name: Parameter relation (22)
nodes.statement: \tau \mu-1=n\mu \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad \mu=\frac{1}{\tau-n}.
nodes.label: eq:IIi

nodes.name: Norm of v_j (27)
nodes.statement: \Vert\hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_j\Vert = \Vert \boldsymbol{e}_1 \Vert A_j= d_1 A_j, \qquad d_1:=\Vert \boldsymbol{e}_1\Vert=\Vert (1,0)\Vert,
nodes.label: eq:gl

nodes.name: Norm of w_j (28)
nodes.statement: \Vert\hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert= \Vert \boldsymbol{e}_2 \Vert B_j= d_2 B_j \overset{\eqref{eq:accto}}{=}(1+o(1))d_2 A_j^{\mu}, \qquad d_2:=\Vert \boldsymbol{e}_2\Vert=\Vert (0,1)\Vert,
nodes.label: eq:lg2

nodes.name: Interlacing norms (29)
nodes.statement: \Vert\hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_j\Vert< \Vert\hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert< \Vert\hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_{j+1}\Vert, \qquad j\ge j_0.
nodes.label: eq:either

nodes.name: Linear form for v_j (30)
nodes.statement: |\boldsymbol{v}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|&= |A_j \cdot \xi_1 +0\cdot \xi_2 - F_j|= A_j(A_{j+1}^{-1}+A_{j+2}^{-1}+\cdots) \\ &= A_j A_{j+1}^{-1}(1+o(1)) \overset{\eqref{eq:true}}{=} (1+o(1))r^{-1}A_j^{-(\tau \mu-1) } \nonumber
nodes.label: eq:ti

nodes.name: Linear form for w_j (31)
nodes.statement: |\boldsymbol{w}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|&= |0\cdot \xi_1 + B_j \cdot \xi_2 - G_j|= B_j(B_{j+1}^{-1}+B_{j+2}^{-1}+\cdots) \\ &= (1+o(1))B_jB_{j+1}^{-1} \overset{\eqref{eq:true}}{=} (1+o(1))r^{-\mu}\cdot B_j^{-(\tau \mu-1) }, \nonumber
nodes.label: eq:tz

nodes.name: Gaps of k1 a + k2 b + c tend to zero
nodes.statement: Let $a,b,c$ be real numbers with $a,b$ linearly independent over $\mathbb{Q}$. Then ordering the set $\{ k_1 a+k_2 b+c: k_i\in\mathbb{N} \}$ increasingly and denoting it by $(z_i)_{i\ge 1}$ we have $|z_{i+1}-z_i|\to 0$.
assumptions: Let $a,b,c$ be real numbers with $a,b$ linearly independent over $\mathbb{Q}$.
conclusions: Then ordering the set $\{ k_1 a+k_2 b+c: k_i\in\mathbb{N} \}$ increasingly and denoting it by $(z_i)_{i\ge 1}$ we have $|z_{i+1}-z_i|\to 0$.
nodes.label: proper

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3
nodes.statement: Clearly, we may assume $c=0$ and suppose without loss of generality that $b<a$. We may then equivalently consider \begin{equation*} \mathcal{Z}=\{ k_1+k_2\tfrac{b}{a}: k_i\in\mathbb{N} \} \end{equation*} instead. Since $\tfrac{b}{a}$ is irrational, Kronecker's Theorem (see e.g. \cite[Section 3.5 Theorem IV]{Cassels}) shows that the set is dense in the unit interval when considering all $(k_1, k_2)\in \mathbb{Z}\times \mathbb{N}$. Let $\varepsilon=1/K>0$ with a large integer $K$ and partition $[0,1]$ into $K$ intervals \begin{equation*} I_t=[(t-1)\varepsilon,t\varepsilon], \qquad 1\le t\le K \end{equation*} of length $1/K$. Then for any $I_t$ there exist $(k_1^{\prime}(t), k_2^{\prime}(t))\in\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{N}$ so that $k_1^{\prime}(t)+k_2^{\prime}(t)\tfrac{b}{a}\in I_t$. Take $T_{\varepsilon}:= \max_t |k_1^{\prime}(t)|$ and consider the set \begin{equation*} \mathcal{Z}_{T_{\varepsilon}} = \left\{ (k_{1}(t)+N) + k_{2}(t)\tfrac{b}{a} : 1\leq t\leq K, \, N \in \mathbb{N}_{\geq T_{\varepsilon}} \right\} \subset \mathcal{Z}\, . \end{equation*} It is easy to see that for any $M\in\mathbb{N}_{\geq T_{\varepsilon}}$ the interval $M+I_{t}$ contains a point from $\mathcal{Z}_{T_{\varepsilon}}$. This shows that $\mathcal{Z}$ is $\varepsilon$ dense on some interval $[3T_{\varepsilon},\infty)$. Since $\varepsilon>0$ is arbitrary the claim is proved.
nodes.statement_short: Kronecker's theorem makes {k1+k2 b/a} dense mod 1; shifting by integers gives eps-density on a half-line.

nodes.name: Normalization
nodes.statement: Clearly, we may assume $c=0$ and suppose without loss of generality that $b<a$. We may then equivalently consider \begin{equation*} \mathcal{Z}=\{ k_1+k_2\tfrac{b}{a}: k_i\in\mathbb{N} \} \end{equation*} instead.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to c=0, b<a and the set k1+k2 b/a.

nodes.name: Kronecker
nodes.statement: Since $\tfrac{b}{a}$ is irrational, Kronecker's Theorem (see e.g. \cite[Section 3.5 Theorem IV]{Cassels}) shows that the set is dense in the unit interval when considering all $(k_1, k_2)\in \mathbb{Z}\times \mathbb{N}$.
nodes.statement_short: Kronecker's theorem gives density in [0,1].

nodes.name: Partition
nodes.statement: Let $\varepsilon=1/K>0$ with a large integer $K$ and partition $[0,1]$ into $K$ intervals \begin{equation*} I_t=[(t-1)\varepsilon,t\varepsilon], \qquad 1\le t\le K \end{equation*} of length $1/K$. Then for any $I_t$ there exist $(k_1^{\prime}(t), k_2^{\prime}(t))\in\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{N}$ so that $k_1^{\prime}(t)+k_2^{\prime}(t)\tfrac{b}{a}\in I_t$.
nodes.statement_short: Partition [0,1] into K intervals, each hit by some point.

nodes.name: Shifted set
nodes.statement: Take $T_{\varepsilon}:= \max_t |k_1^{\prime}(t)|$ and consider the set \begin{equation*} \mathcal{Z}_{T_{\varepsilon}} = \left\{ (k_{1}(t)+N) + k_{2}(t)\tfrac{b}{a} : 1\leq t\leq K, \, N \in \mathbb{N}_{\geq T_{\varepsilon}} \right\} \subset \mathcal{Z}\, . \end{equation*} It is easy to see that for any $M\in\mathbb{N}_{\geq T_{\varepsilon}}$ the interval $M+I_{t}$ contains a point from $\mathcal{Z}_{T_{\varepsilon}}$.
nodes.statement_short: Shifting by integers N >= T_eps hits each translate.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: This shows that $\mathcal{Z}$ is $\varepsilon$ dense on some interval $[3T_{\varepsilon},\infty)$. Since $\varepsilon>0$ is arbitrary the claim is proved.
nodes.statement_short: Z is eps-dense on a half-line for every eps.

nodes.name: Form of best approximations for the constructed xi
nodes.statement: As soon as $r$ is large enough, all best approximations for $\boldsymbol{\xi}$ of large norm have up to sign one of the following forms \[ \boldsymbol{v}_j, \quad \boldsymbol{w}_j, \quad \boldsymbol{v}_j+\boldsymbol{w}_j,\quad \boldsymbol{w}_j-\boldsymbol{v}_j, \quad \boldsymbol{w}_j+\boldsymbol{v}_{j+1}, \quad \boldsymbol{v}_{j+1}-\boldsymbol{w}_{j}. \]
assumptions: As soon as $r$ is large enough
conclusions: all best approximations for $\boldsymbol{\xi}$ of large norm have up to sign one of the following forms \[ \boldsymbol{v}_j, \quad \boldsymbol{w}_j, \quad \boldsymbol{v}_j+\boldsymbol{w}_j,\quad \boldsymbol{w}_j-\boldsymbol{v}_j, \quad \boldsymbol{w}_j+\boldsymbol{v}_{j+1}, \quad \boldsymbol{v}_{j+1}-\boldsymbol{w}_{j}.
nodes.label: wichtig!

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 6.1
nodes.statement: Let $\boldsymbol{b}$ be any best approximation. Then by \eqref{eq:either} there is an index $j$ such that either $\Vert\hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_j\Vert\le \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{b}}\Vert<\Vert\hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert$ or $\Vert\hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert\le \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{b}}\Vert< \Vert\hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_{j+1}\Vert$. We show that in the first case $\boldsymbol{b}=\pm \boldsymbol{v}_j$ or $\pm(\boldsymbol{v}_j\pm \boldsymbol{w}_j)$, and in the latter case $\boldsymbol{b}=\pm \boldsymbol{w}_j$ or $\pm(\boldsymbol{w}_j\pm \boldsymbol{v}_{j+1})$. Assume the first case, so \begin{equation} \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_j\Vert\le \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{b}}\Vert< \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert. \end{equation} the latter works very similarly by symmetry. First, observe that since $\boldsymbol{b}$ is the best approximation of norm at least $\Vert\hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_j\Vert$, we know that \begin{equation} |\boldsymbol{b}\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|\le |\boldsymbol{v}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|. \end{equation} We distinguish two cases. Case 1: $\boldsymbol{b}$ lies in the two-dimensonal subspace of $\mathbb{R}^3$ spanned by $\boldsymbol{v}_j, \boldsymbol{w}_j$, i.e. $\boldsymbol{b}\in \scp{\boldsymbol{v}_j, \boldsymbol{w}_j}_{\mathbb{R}}\cap \mathbb{Z}^3$. The special form of $A_j, B_j$ and \eqref{eq:witt} imply the following crucial result on integer vectors in the two-dimensional lattices $\scp{\boldsymbol{v}_j, \boldsymbol{w}_j}_{\mathbb{R}}\cap \mathbb{Z}^3$. \begin{proposition} For $\boldsymbol{v}_j, \boldsymbol{w}_j$ as above, if a linear combination $g\boldsymbol{v}_j+h\boldsymbol{w}_j$ is an integer vector, then in fact $g\in\mathbb{Z}$ and $h\in \mathbb{Z}$. In other words, $\scp{\boldsymbol{v}_j, \boldsymbol{w}_j}_{\mathbb{R}}\cap \mathbb{Z}^3=\scp{\boldsymbol{v}_j, \boldsymbol{w}_j}_{\mathbb{Z}}$. \end{proposition} \begin{proof} Clearly, we must have $g,h\in \mathbb{Q}$. If we write $(p_1/q_1)\boldsymbol{v}_j + (p_2/q_2)\boldsymbol{w}_j$ with $p_i/q_i$ in lowest terms, then it is clear that $q_1$ must consist of exclusively non-negative integer powers of $2$ and $3$ and $q_2$ of non-negative integer power of $5$ and $7$ to make the first two coordinates $(p_1/q_1)A_j=(p_1/q_1)2^{\alpha_j}3^{\gamma_j}$ resp. $(p_2/q_2)B_j=(p_2/q_2)5^{\beta_j}7^{\delta_j}$ of $g\boldsymbol{v}_j+h\boldsymbol{w}_j$ integers. But then by \eqref{eq:witt} clearly the third coordinate $(p_1/q_1)F_j+(p_2/q_2)G_j$ is not an integer unless $q_1=q_2=1$. \end{proof} We first show that any integer linear combination $\boldsymbol{b}=g\boldsymbol{v}_j+h\boldsymbol{w}_j$ representing the best approximation as above must have $|g|\le 1$. Assume $|g|\ge 2$. It is easily seen that for any norm on $\mathbb{R}^2$ there is a constant $\theta=\theta(\Vert\cdot\Vert)$ such that $\Vert \boldsymbol{w}\Vert \le W$ for $\boldsymbol{w}=(w_1,w_2)\in\mathbb{R}^2$ and $W>0$ implies $|w_i|\le \theta W$, $i=1,2$. Hence \eqref{eq:T} and the special form of $\boldsymbol{v}_j, \boldsymbol{w}_j$ imply \[ |g|\le \theta, \qquad |h|\le \theta \] for some $\theta$ independent of $j$. On the other hand, since $r,\mu$ are fixed and $A_j\to\infty$, it is clear from \eqref{eq:ti}, \eqref{eq:tz} and \eqref{eq:accto} that \[ |\boldsymbol{w}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| = o(|\boldsymbol{v}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|), \qquad j\to\infty. \] Combination implies \begin{align*} |\boldsymbol{b} \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|= | (g\boldsymbol{v}_j+h\boldsymbol{w}_j) \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| &\ge |g|\cdot |\boldsymbol{v}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| - |h|\cdot |\boldsymbol{w}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| \ge 2 |\boldsymbol{v}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| - |h|\cdot |\boldsymbol{w}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|\\ &\ge 2 |\boldsymbol{v}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| - \theta\cdot |\boldsymbol{w}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| > |\boldsymbol{v}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|, \qquad j\ge j_0, \end{align*} contradicting \eqref{eq:see}. Hence $|g|\le 1$. Now if $|h|\ge 2$ then for any $|g|\le 1$ using \eqref{eq:either} we get \[ \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{b}}\Vert= \Vert g \hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_j+h\hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert \ge |h|\cdot \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert - \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_j\Vert \ge 2 \cdot \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert - \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_j\Vert > \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert \] contradicting \eqref{eq:T}. Thus both $g,h$ are among $\{-1,0,1\}$. Hence we are left with the vectors of the lemma. Case 2: $\boldsymbol{b}$ does not lie in the space spanned by $\boldsymbol{v}_j, \boldsymbol{w}_j$. For this case, we use an easy consequence of Minkowski's Second Convex Body Theorem. \begin{lemma} There exists a constant $c>0$ such that for any $\boldsymbol{\xi}\in \mathbb{R}^2$ and any parameter $Q\ge 1$, the system \[ |b_1|\le Q,\qquad |b_2|\le Q,\qquad |b_1 \xi_1 + b_2 \xi_2+b_{3}| < cQ^{-2} \] does not have three linearly independent solutions in integer vectors $\boldsymbol{b}=(b_1,b_2,b_3)$. \end{lemma} \begin{proof} Consider the integer lattice $\mathbb{Z}^3$ and the box of $(x_1,x_2,x_3)\in \mathbb{R}^3$ with coordinates \[ |x_1|\le Q, \qquad |x_2|\le Q,\quad |\xi_1 x_1+\xi_2 x_2 + x_3|\leq cQ^{-2}. \] It has volume $8c$, independent of $Q$ and $\xi_1, \xi_2$. Hence, by Minkowski's Second Convex Body Theorem, the product of the induced successive minima is $\ll c$, hence choosing $c$ small enough the third successive minimum is smaller than $1$. This means there cannot be three linearly independent integer points within the box, which in turn is equivalent to the claim. \end{proof} We first notice that both $\boldsymbol{v}_j$ and $\boldsymbol{w}_j$ induce approximations of order greater than two. By \eqref{eq:lg2}, \eqref{eq:ti} and as our choice $(\tau \mu-1)/\mu=n>2$, we get \begin{equation} |\boldsymbol{v}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| = (1+o(1))r^{-1} A_j^{-(\tau \mu-1)} \ll r^{-1} B_j^{-n}\ll r^{-1}\Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert^{-n}< r^{-1}\Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert^{-2} \end{equation} and for $\boldsymbol{w}_j$ by \eqref{eq:tz} we have a stronger estimate that also yields \begin{equation} |\boldsymbol{w}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| = o(1)\cdot B_j^{-(\tau \mu-1)} = o(\Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert^{-n})= o(\Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert^{-2}), \quad j\to\infty. \end{equation} Combined with \eqref{eq:either}, \eqref{eq:T}, \eqref{eq:see}, we have \[ \max\{ \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{b}}\Vert, \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_j\Vert, \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert \}= \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert, \qquad \max\{|\boldsymbol{b}\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|, |\boldsymbol{v}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|,|\boldsymbol{w}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| \} \ll r^{-1}\Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert^{-2}. \] By the assumptions of Case 2, the three vectors $\boldsymbol{v}_j, \boldsymbol{w}_j, \boldsymbol{b}$ are linearly independent. So we get a contradiction to Lemma~\ref{lemur} for $r$ sufficiently large and $Q=\Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert$, as soon as $\Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert$ is sufficiently large. Hence, in total, Case 2 provides only finitely many best approximations, of small norm, so Lemma~\ref{wichtig!} is proved.
nodes.statement_short: Case analysis on whether b lies in the span of v_j,w_j: integrality (Prop. 4) bounds coefficients; otherwise Minkowski's second theorem (Lemma 6.2) gives a contradiction.

nodes.statement: Case 1: $\boldsymbol{b}$ lies in the two-dimensonal subspace of $\mathbb{R}^3$ spanned by $\boldsymbol{v}_j, \boldsymbol{w}_j$, i.e. $\boldsymbol{b}\in \scp{\boldsymbol{v}_j, \boldsymbol{w}_j}_{\mathbb{R}}\cap \mathbb{Z}^3$. It is easily seen that for any norm on $\mathbb{R}^2$ there is a constant $\theta=\theta(\Vert\cdot\Vert)$ such that $\Vert \boldsymbol{w}\Vert \le W$ for $\boldsymbol{w}=(w_1,w_2)\in\mathbb{R}^2$ and $W>0$ implies $|w_i|\le \theta W$, $i=1,2$. nodes.statement_short: Assume |g|>=2; coefficients are bounded and w_j is much better.

nodes.name: Contradiction for g
nodes.statement: Combination implies \begin{align*} |\boldsymbol{b} \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|= | (g\boldsymbol{v}_j+h\boldsymbol{w}_j) \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| &\ge |g|\cdot |\boldsymbol{v}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| - |h|\cdot |\boldsymbol{w}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| \ge 2 |\boldsymbol{v}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| - |h|\cdot |\boldsymbol{w}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|\\ &\ge 2 |\boldsymbol{v}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| - \theta\cdot |\boldsymbol{w}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| > |\boldsymbol{v}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|, \qquad j\ge j_0, \end{align*} contradicting \eqref{eq:see}. Hence $|g|\le 1$.
nodes.statement_short: Then b approximates worse than v_j, so |g|<=1.

nodes.name: Coefficient h
nodes.statement: Now if $|h|\ge 2$ then for any $|g|\le 1$ using \eqref{eq:either} we get \[ \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{b}}\Vert= \Vert g \hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_j+h\hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert \ge |h|\cdot \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert - \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_j\Vert \ge 2 \cdot \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert - \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_j\Vert > \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert \] contradicting \eqref{eq:T}. Thus both $g,h$ are among $\{-1,0,1\}$. Hence we are left with the vectors of the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: |h|>=2 makes the norm too large; only the listed vectors remain.

nodes.name: Case 2: b outside span
nodes.statement: Case 2: $\boldsymbol{b}$ does not lie in the space spanned by $\boldsymbol{v}_j, \boldsymbol{w}_j$. For this case, we use an easy consequence of Minkowski's Second Convex Body Theorem. \begin{lemma} There exists a constant $c>0$ such that for any $\boldsymbol{\xi}\in \mathbb{R}^2$ and any parameter $Q\ge 1$, the system \[ |b_1|\le Q,\qquad |b_2|\le Q,\qquad |b_1 \xi_1 + b_2 \xi_2+b_{3}| < cQ^{-2} \] does not have three linearly independent solutions in integer vectors $\boldsymbol{b}=(b_1,b_2,b_3)$. \end{lemma} \begin{proof} Consider the integer lattice $\mathbb{Z}^3$ and the box of $(x_1,x_2,x_3)\in \mathbb{R}^3$ with coordinates \[ |x_1|\le Q, \qquad |x_2|\le Q,\quad |\xi_1 x_1+\xi_2 x_2 + x_3|\leq cQ^{-2}. \] It has volume $8c$, independent of $Q$ and $\xi_1, \xi_2$. Hence, by Minkowski's Second Convex Body Theorem, the product of the induced successive minima is $\ll c$, hence choosing $c$ small enough the third successive minimum is smaller than $1$. This means there cannot be three linearly independent integer points within the box, which in turn is equivalent to the claim. \end{proof} We first notice that both $\boldsymbol{v}_j$ and $\boldsymbol{w}_j$ induce approximations of order greater than two. By \eqref{eq:lg2}, \eqref{eq:ti} and as our choice $(\tau \mu-1)/\mu=n>2$, we get \begin{equation} |\boldsymbol{v}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| = (1+o(1))r^{-1} A_j^{-(\tau \mu-1)} \ll r^{-1} B_j^{-n}\ll r^{-1}\Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert^{-n}< r^{-1}\Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert^{-2} \end{equation} and for $\boldsymbol{w}_j$ by \eqref{eq:tz} we have a stronger estimate that also yields \begin{equation} |\boldsymbol{w}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| = o(1)\cdot B_j^{-(\tau \mu-1)} = o(\Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert^{-n})= o(\Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert^{-2}), \quad j\to\infty. \end{equation} Combined with \eqref{eq:either}, \eqref{eq:T}, \eqref{eq:see}, we have \[ \max\{ \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{b}}\Vert, \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_j\Vert, \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert \}= \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert, \qquad \max\{|\boldsymbol{b}\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|, |\boldsymbol{v}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|,|\boldsymbol{w}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| \} \ll r^{-1}\Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert^{-2}. \] By the assumptions of Case 2, the three vectors $\boldsymbol{v}_j, \boldsymbol{w}_j, \boldsymbol{b}$ are linearly independent. So we get a contradiction to Lemma~\ref{lemur} for $r$ sufficiently large and $Q=\Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert$, as soon as $\Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert$ is sufficiently large. Hence, in total, Case 2 provides only finitely many best approximations, of small norm, so Lemma~\ref{wichtig!} is proved.
nodes.statement_short: b, v_j, w_j are linearly independent.

nodes.name: Minkowski consequence
nodes.statement: Case 2: $\boldsymbol{b}$ does not lie in the space spanned by $\boldsymbol{v}_j, \boldsymbol{w}_j$. For this case, we use an easy consequence of Minkowski's Second Convex Body Theorem.
nodes.statement_short: Use a consequence of Minkowski's second theorem.

nodes.name: Lemma 6.2
nodes.statement: \begin{lemma} There exists a constant $c>0$ such that for any $\boldsymbol{\xi}\in \mathbb{R}^2$ and any parameter $Q\ge 1$, the system \[ |b_1|\le Q,\qquad |b_2|\le Q,\qquad |b_1 \xi_1 + b_2 \xi_2+b_{3}| < cQ^{-2} \] does not have three linearly independent solutions in integer vectors $\boldsymbol{b}=(b_1,b_2,b_3)$. \end{lemma} \begin{proof} Consider the integer lattice $\mathbb{Z}^3$ and the box of $(x_1,x_2,x_3)\in \mathbb{R}^3$ with coordinates \[ |x_1|\le Q, \qquad |x_2|\le Q,\quad |\xi_1 x_1+\xi_2 x_2 + x_3|\leq cQ^{-2}. \] It has volume $8c$, independent of $Q$ and $\xi_1, \xi_2$. Hence, by Minkowski's Second Convex Body Theorem, the product of the induced successive minima is $\ll c$, hence choosing $c$ small enough the third successive minimum is smaller than $1$. This means there cannot be three linearly independent integer points within the box, which in turn is equivalent to the claim. \end{proof}
nodes.statement_short: No three independent solutions of a small system.

nodes.name: Approximation order
nodes.statement: We first notice that both $\boldsymbol{v}_j$ and $\boldsymbol{w}_j$ induce approximations of order greater than two. By \eqref{eq:lg2}, \eqref{eq:ti} and as our choice $(\tau \mu-1)/\mu=n>2$, we get \begin{equation} |\boldsymbol{v}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| = (1+o(1))r^{-1} A_j^{-(\tau \mu-1)} \ll r^{-1} B_j^{-n}\ll r^{-1}\Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert^{-n}< r^{-1}\Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert^{-2} \end{equation} and for $\boldsymbol{w}_j$ by \eqref{eq:tz} we have a stronger estimate that also yields \begin{equation} |\boldsymbol{w}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| = o(1)\cdot B_j^{-(\tau \mu-1)} = o(\Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert^{-n})= o(\Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert^{-2}), \quad j\to\infty. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: v_j and w_j approximate to order greater than two.

nodes.name: Three independent good vectors
nodes.statement: Combined with \eqref{eq:either}, \eqref{eq:T}, \eqref{eq:see}, we have \[ \max\{ \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{b}}\Vert, \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_j\Vert, \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert \}= \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert, \qquad \max\{|\boldsymbol{b}\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|, |\boldsymbol{v}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|,|\boldsymbol{w}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| \} \ll r^{-1}\Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert^{-2}. \] By the assumptions of Case 2, the three vectors $\boldsymbol{v}_j, \boldsymbol{w}_j, \boldsymbol{b}$ are linearly independent.
nodes.statement_short: b, v_j, w_j are three independent small solutions.

nodes.name: Contradiction
nodes.statement: So we get a contradiction to Lemma~\ref{lemur} for $r$ sufficiently large and $Q=\Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert$, as soon as $\Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert$ is sufficiently large. Hence, in total, Case 2 provides only finitely many best approximations, of small norm, so Lemma~\ref{wichtig!} is proved.
nodes.statement_short: Contradiction with Lemma 6.2 for large r; only finitely many exceptions.

nodes.name: eq:41 (36)
nodes.statement: |(\boldsymbol{v}_j\pm \boldsymbol{w}_j)\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| = (1+o(1))\cdot |\boldsymbol{v}_j \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|, \quad |(\boldsymbol{v}_{j+1}\pm \boldsymbol{w}_j)\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| = (1+o(1))\cdot |\boldsymbol{w}_j \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|.
nodes.label: eq:41

nodes.name: eq:51 (37)
nodes.statement: \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_j\pm \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert = (1+o(1)) \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert, \qquad \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_{j+1}\pm \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert = (1+o(1)) \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_{j+1}\Vert.
nodes.label: eq:51

nodes.name: eq:frosch (38)
nodes.statement: | \boldsymbol{v}_j \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| = (1+o(1))\cdot c\Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert^{-n}, \qquad | \boldsymbol{w}_j \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| = o(1)\cdot \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_{j+1}\Vert^{-n}.
nodes.label: eq:frosch

nodes.name: Projected norm (39)
nodes.statement: \Vert (x_1, x_2) \Vert^{\prime}:= \Vert (x_1,x_2,0,\ldots,0) \Vert.
nodes.label: eq:pno

nodes.name: Outline
nodes.statement: The method of proof is similar to that of Theorem~\ref{thm1}. Namely, the proof is done in two steps: \begin{enumerate} \item[Step I:] For small enough $c$, construct $\boldsymbol{\xi}=(\xi_1, \xi_2)$ such that \[ \limsup_{t\to\infty} t^n \psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{1\times 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert,t) = c. \] \item[Step II:] Show that for a positive measure set $(\xi_3,\ldots,\xi_n)$ with respect to $(n-2)$-dimensional Lebesgue measure, the extended vector $\boldsymbol{\zeta}=(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_n)$ satisfies \[ \Theta^{1\times n}(\boldsymbol{\zeta})=\limsup_{t\to\infty} t^n \psi_{\boldsymbol{\zeta}}^{1\times n}(\Vert\cdot\Vert,t) = c \] as well. \end{enumerate} Note that Step I follows immediately, for any $c\ge 0$ (and $c\in[0,D]$ if $n=2$), from the aforementioned preprint \cite[Corollary~1]{AginWeiss2024}. Note this follows from the result on $\psi$-Dirichlet Spectrum, rather than the classical Dirichlet Spectrum, since our approximation function is $t^{n}$. However, as this appeared later than the current article, we keep our original construction. Note that \cite{AginWeiss2024} does not simplify Step II of the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Two-step plan: construct xi in R^2, then extend generically.

nodes.name: Method
nodes.statement: The method of proof is similar to that of Theorem~\ref{thm1}. Namely, the proof is done in two steps: \begin{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Proof in two steps like Theorem 2.1.

nodes.name: Step I plan
nodes.statement: \item[Step I:] For small enough $c$, construct $\boldsymbol{\xi}=(\xi_1, \xi_2)$ such that \[ \limsup_{t\to\infty} t^n \psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{1\times 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert,t) = c. \]
nodes.statement_short: Construct xi with limsup t^n psi = c.

nodes.name: Step II plan
nodes.statement: \item[Step II:] Show that for a positive measure set $(\xi_3,\ldots,\xi_n)$ with respect to $(n-2)$-dimensional Lebesgue measure, the extended vector $\boldsymbol{\zeta}=(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_n)$ satisfies \[ \Theta^{1\times n}(\boldsymbol{\zeta})=\limsup_{t\to\infty} t^n \psi_{\boldsymbol{\zeta}}^{1\times n}(\Vert\cdot\Vert,t) = c \] as well. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Show a positive-measure set of extensions keeps constant c.

nodes.name: Agin-Weiss remark
nodes.statement: Note that Step I follows immediately, for any $c\ge 0$ (and $c\in[0,D]$ if $n=2$), from the aforementioned preprint \cite[Corollary~1]{AginWeiss2024}. Note this follows from the result on $\psi$-Dirichlet Spectrum, rather than the classical Dirichlet Spectrum, since our approximation function is $t^{n}$. However, as this appeared later than the current article, we keep our original construction. Note that \cite{AginWeiss2024} does not simplify Step II of the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Step I also follows from Agin-Weiss.

nodes.name: Proof of Step I
nodes.statement: \subsection{Proof of Step I} This is the more intricate part of the proof. For this, we use a different construction than for the maximum norm where we employed the construction from~\cite{j2}. Rather we follow the proof of~\cite[Theorem~2.1]{j3} but with some notable twists. Write $\boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}=(\boldsymbol{\xi},1)\in\mathbb{R}^{3}$ and use a similar meaning of star for other quantities. Conversely denote by a hat over a vector in $\mathbb{R}^{3}$ its restriction to the first $2$ coordinates by chopping off the last coordinate, i.e. $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}}=\boldsymbol{\xi}$. We construct our real vector. Let $n<\tau<\mu$ be parameters to be chosen later related by the identity \begin{equation} \tau \mu-1=n\mu \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad \mu=\frac{1}{\tau-n}. \end{equation} Let $\alpha_j, \beta_j, \gamma_j, \delta_j$ be strictly increasing positive integer sequences and a real number $r=r(\Vert\cdot\Vert)>0$ all to be fixed later. Derive integers of the form \[ A_j= 2^{\alpha_j}3^{\gamma_j }, \qquad B_j= 5^{\beta_j }7^{\delta_j}, \] satisfying as $j\to\infty$ \begin{equation} A_{j+1}= (1+o(1))r B_j^{\tau}, \qquad B_j = (1+o(1))A_j^{\mu}. \end{equation} We first show that such choices are possible. For $A_j$, we use that $\{ \log 2, \log 3\}$ is a $\mathbb{Q}$-linearly independent set (easily seen by applying exponential map to a putative vanishing linear form and using unique prime factorization to disprove it) and the following easy Proposition~\ref{proper}. Similarly for $B_j$ we use that $\{ \log 5, \log 7\}$ is $\mathbb{Q}$-linearly independent. \begin{proposition} Let $a,b,c$ be real numbers with $a,b$ linearly independent over $\mathbb{Q}$. Then ordering the set $\{ k_1 a+k_2 b+c: k_i\in\mathbb{N} \}$ increasingly and denoting it by $(z_i)_{i\ge 1}$ we have $|z_{i+1}-z_i|\to 0$. \end{proposition} \begin{proof} Clearly, we may assume $c=0$ and suppose without loss of generality that $b<a$. We may then equivalently consider \begin{equation*} \mathcal{Z}=\{ k_1+k_2\tfrac{b}{a}: k_i\in\mathbb{N} \} \end{equation*} instead. Since $\tfrac{b}{a}$ is irrational, Kronecker's Theorem (see e.g. \cite[Section 3.5 Theorem IV]{Cassels}) shows that the set is dense in the unit interval when considering all $(k_1, k_2)\in \mathbb{Z}\times \mathbb{N}$. Let $\varepsilon=1/K>0$ with a large integer $K$ and partition $[0,1]$ into $K$ intervals \begin{equation*} I_t=[(t-1)\varepsilon,t\varepsilon], \qquad 1\le t\le K \end{equation*} of length $1/K$. Then for any $I_t$ there exist $(k_1^{\prime}(t), k_2^{\prime}(t))\in\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{N}$ so that $k_1^{\prime}(t)+k_2^{\prime}(t)\tfrac{b}{a}\in I_t$. Take $T_{\varepsilon}:= \max_t |k_1^{\prime}(t)|$ and consider the set \begin{equation*} \mathcal{Z}_{T_{\varepsilon}} = \left\{ (k_{1}(t)+N) + k_{2}(t)\tfrac{b}{a} : 1\leq t\leq K, \, N \in \mathbb{N}_{\geq T_{\varepsilon}} \right\} \subset \mathcal{Z}\, . \end{equation*} It is easy to see that for any $M\in\mathbb{N}_{\geq T_{\varepsilon}}$ the interval $M+I_{t}$ contains a point from $\mathcal{Z}_{T_{\varepsilon}}$. This shows that $\mathcal{Z}$ is $\varepsilon$ dense on some interval $[3T_{\varepsilon},\infty)$. Since $\varepsilon>0$ is arbitrary the claim is proved. \end{proof} We can now apply the proposition alternatingly to \[ a=\log 2, \, b=\log 3, \, c=\log r, \qquad\quad a=\log 5,\, b=\log 7, \, c=0 \] respectively to construct iteratively our sequences $\alpha_j, \gamma_j$, which correspond to $k_1=\alpha_{j+1}-\alpha_j\ge 0$ and $k_2=\gamma_{j+1}-\gamma_j\ge 0$, resp. $k_1=\beta_{j+1}-\beta_j\ge 0$ and $k_2=\delta_{j+1}-\delta_j\ge 0$. Thereby, having chosen all $\alpha_., \beta_., \gamma_.,\delta_.$ up to index $j$, we construct first pairs $\alpha_{j+1}, \gamma_{j+1}$ and then $\beta_{j+1}, \delta_{j+1}$, and the iterative construction is complete. So, having chosen $r$, we may assume all the above is defined. Note that \eqref{eq:accto} implies \begin{equation} A_{j+1}=(1+o(1))r A_j^{\tau \mu}, \qquad B_{j+1} =(1+o(1))r^{\mu} B_j^{\tau \mu}. \end{equation} Moreover, again by \eqref{eq:accto}, upon changing initial terms if necessary, we can assume \begin{equation} 1<A_1 < B_1 < A_2 < B_2 < \cdots. \end{equation} Finally let $\boldsymbol{\xi}=(\xi_1, \xi_2)$ with \[ \xi_1= \sum_{j\ge 1} A_j^{-1 } , \qquad \xi_2= \sum_{j\ge 1} B_j^{-1 }. \] We claim that it satisfies the assertions of the theorem upon choosing $r$ appropriately. For $j\ge 1$ put \[ \sigma_j := A_1^{-1}+\cdots+A_j^{-1}, \qquad \eta_j:= B_1^{-1}+\cdots+B_j^{-1}. \] We clearly have $\sigma_j\to \xi_1$ and $\eta_j\to \xi_2$ as $j\to \infty$, and \[ F_j= A_j\sigma_j\in \mathbb{N}, \qquad G_j=B_j \eta_j\in\mathbb{N}. \] Then since the sequences $(\alpha_j), (\beta_j), (\gamma_j), (\delta_j)$ are strictly increasing we have $F_j\equiv 1\bmod 2\cdot 3$ and $G_j\equiv 1\bmod 5\cdot 7$, which imply the coprimality assertions \begin{equation} (A_j, F_j)=(F_j,6)=1, \qquad (B_j,G_j)=(G_j,35)=1. \end{equation} Let \[ \boldsymbol{v}_j=(A_j,0,-F_j), \qquad \boldsymbol{w}_j=(0, B_j,-G_j). \] Note that $\hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_j=(A_j,0)$ and $\hat {\boldsymbol{w}}_j=(0,B_j)$. Hence their norms $\Vert\cdot\Vert$ satisfy \begin{equation} \Vert\hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_j\Vert = \Vert \boldsymbol{e}_1 \Vert A_j= d_1 A_j, \qquad d_1:=\Vert \boldsymbol{e}_1\Vert=\Vert (1,0)\Vert, \end{equation} and \begin{equation} \Vert\hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert= \Vert \boldsymbol{e}_2 \Vert B_j= d_2 B_j \overset{\eqref{eq:accto}}{=}(1+o(1))d_2 A_j^{\mu}, \qquad d_2:=\Vert \boldsymbol{e}_2\Vert=\Vert (0,1)\Vert, \end{equation} Thus by \eqref{eq:vf} clearly \begin{equation} \Vert\hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_j\Vert< \Vert\hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert< \Vert\hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_{j+1}\Vert, \qquad j\ge j_0. \end{equation} Here $j_0$ depends on $d_1, d_2$, thus on the chosen norm. Then by \eqref{eq:true} moreover \begin{align} |\boldsymbol{v}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|&= |A_j \cdot \xi_1 +0\cdot \xi_2 - F_j|= A_j(A_{j+1}^{-1}+A_{j+2}^{-1}+\cdots) \\ &= A_j A_{j+1}^{-1}(1+o(1)) \overset{\eqref{eq:true}}{=} (1+o(1))r^{-1}A_j^{-(\tau \mu-1) } \nonumber \end{align} and \begin{align} |\boldsymbol{w}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|&= |0\cdot \xi_1 + B_j \cdot \xi_2 - G_j|= B_j(B_{j+1}^{-1}+B_{j+2}^{-1}+\cdots) \\ &= (1+o(1))B_jB_{j+1}^{-1} \overset{\eqref{eq:true}}{=} (1+o(1))r^{-\mu}\cdot B_j^{-(\tau \mu-1) }, \nonumber \end{align} are small linear forms for $j\ge 1$. We next show \begin{lemma} As soon as $r$ is large enough, all best approximations for $\boldsymbol{\xi}$ of large norm have up to sign one of the following forms \[ \boldsymbol{v}_j, \quad \boldsymbol{w}_j, \quad \boldsymbol{v}_j+\boldsymbol{w}_j,\quad \boldsymbol{w}_j-\boldsymbol{v}_j, \quad \boldsymbol{w}_j+\boldsymbol{v}_{j+1}, \quad \boldsymbol{v}_{j+1}-\boldsymbol{w}_{j}. \] \end{lemma} \begin{proof} Let $\boldsymbol{b}$ be any best approximation. Then by \eqref{eq:either} there is an index $j$ such that either $\Vert\hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_j\Vert\le \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{b}}\Vert<\Vert\hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert$ or $\Vert\hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert\le \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{b}}\Vert< \Vert\hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_{j+1}\Vert$. We show that in the first case $\boldsymbol{b}=\pm \boldsymbol{v}_j$ or $\pm(\boldsymbol{v}_j\pm \boldsymbol{w}_j)$, and in the latter case $\boldsymbol{b}=\pm \boldsymbol{w}_j$ or $\pm(\boldsymbol{w}_j\pm \boldsymbol{v}_{j+1})$. Assume the first case, so \begin{equation} \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_j\Vert\le \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{b}}\Vert< \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert. \end{equation} the latter works very similarly by symmetry. First, observe that since $\boldsymbol{b}$ is the best approximation of norm at least $\Vert\hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_j\Vert$, we know that \begin{equation} |\boldsymbol{b}\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|\le |\boldsymbol{v}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|. \end{equation} We distinguish two cases. Case 1: $\boldsymbol{b}$ lies in the two-dimensonal subspace of $\mathbb{R}^3$ spanned by $\boldsymbol{v}_j, \boldsymbol{w}_j$, i.e. $\boldsymbol{b}\in \scp{\boldsymbol{v}_j, \boldsymbol{w}_j}_{\mathbb{R}}\cap \mathbb{Z}^3$. The special form of $A_j, B_j$ and \eqref{eq:witt} imply the following crucial result on integer vectors in the two-dimensional lattices $\scp{\boldsymbol{v}_j, \boldsymbol{w}_j}_{\mathbb{R}}\cap \mathbb{Z}^3$. \begin{proposition} For $\boldsymbol{v}_j, \boldsymbol{w}_j$ as above, if a linear combination $g\boldsymbol{v}_j+h\boldsymbol{w}_j$ is an integer vector, then in fact $g\in\mathbb{Z}$ and $h\in \mathbb{Z}$. In other words, $\scp{\boldsymbol{v}_j, \boldsymbol{w}_j}_{\mathbb{R}}\cap \mathbb{Z}^3=\scp{\boldsymbol{v}_j, \boldsymbol{w}_j}_{\mathbb{Z}}$. \end{proposition} \begin{proof} Clearly, we must have $g,h\in \mathbb{Q}$. If we write $(p_1/q_1)\boldsymbol{v}_j + (p_2/q_2)\boldsymbol{w}_j$ with $p_i/q_i$ in lowest terms, then it is clear that $q_1$ must consist of exclusively non-negative integer powers of $2$ and $3$ and $q_2$ of non-negative integer power of $5$ and $7$ to make the first two coordinates $(p_1/q_1)A_j=(p_1/q_1)2^{\alpha_j}3^{\gamma_j}$ resp. $(p_2/q_2)B_j=(p_2/q_2)5^{\beta_j}7^{\delta_j}$ of $g\boldsymbol{v}_j+h\boldsymbol{w}_j$ integers. But then by \eqref{eq:witt} clearly the third coordinate $(p_1/q_1)F_j+(p_2/q_2)G_j$ is not an integer unless $q_1=q_2=1$. \end{proof} We first show that any integer linear combination $\boldsymbol{b}=g\boldsymbol{v}_j+h\boldsymbol{w}_j$ representing the best approximation as above must have $|g|\le 1$. Assume $|g|\ge 2$. It is easily seen that for any norm on $\mathbb{R}^2$ there is a constant $\theta=\theta(\Vert\cdot\Vert)$ such that $\Vert \boldsymbol{w}\Vert \le W$ for $\boldsymbol{w}=(w_1,w_2)\in\mathbb{R}^2$ and $W>0$ implies $|w_i|\le \theta W$, $i=1,2$. Hence \eqref{eq:T} and the special form of $\boldsymbol{v}_j, \boldsymbol{w}_j$ imply \[ |g|\le \theta, \qquad |h|\le \theta \] for some $\theta$ independent of $j$. On the other hand, since $r,\mu$ are fixed and $A_j\to\infty$, it is clear from \eqref{eq:ti}, \eqref{eq:tz} and \eqref{eq:accto} that \[ |\boldsymbol{w}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| = o(|\boldsymbol{v}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|), \qquad j\to\infty. \] Combination implies \begin{align*} |\boldsymbol{b} \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|= | (g\boldsymbol{v}_j+h\boldsymbol{w}_j) \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| &\ge |g|\cdot |\boldsymbol{v}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| - |h|\cdot |\boldsymbol{w}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| \ge 2 |\boldsymbol{v}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| - |h|\cdot |\boldsymbol{w}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|\\ &\ge 2 |\boldsymbol{v}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| - \theta\cdot |\boldsymbol{w}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| > |\boldsymbol{v}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|, \qquad j\ge j_0, \end{align*} contradicting \eqref{eq:see}. Hence $|g|\le 1$. Now if $|h|\ge 2$ then for any $|g|\le 1$ using \eqref{eq:either} we get \[ \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{b}}\Vert= \Vert g \hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_j+h\hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert \ge |h|\cdot \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert - \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_j\Vert \ge 2 \cdot \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert - \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_j\Vert > \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert \] contradicting \eqref{eq:T}. Thus both $g,h$ are among $\{-1,0,1\}$. Hence we are left with the vectors of the lemma. Case 2: $\boldsymbol{b}$ does not lie in the space spanned by $\boldsymbol{v}_j, \boldsymbol{w}_j$. For this case, we use an easy consequence of Minkowski's Second Convex Body Theorem. \begin{lemma} There exists a constant $c>0$ such that for any $\boldsymbol{\xi}\in \mathbb{R}^2$ and any parameter $Q\ge 1$, the system \[ |b_1|\le Q,\qquad |b_2|\le Q,\qquad |b_1 \xi_1 + b_2 \xi_2+b_{3}| < cQ^{-2} \] does not have three linearly independent solutions in integer vectors $\boldsymbol{b}=(b_1,b_2,b_3)$. \end{lemma} \begin{proof} Consider the integer lattice $\mathbb{Z}^3$ and the box of $(x_1,x_2,x_3)\in \mathbb{R}^3$ with coordinates \[ |x_1|\le Q, \qquad |x_2|\le Q,\quad |\xi_1 x_1+\xi_2 x_2 + x_3|\leq cQ^{-2}. \] It has volume $8c$, independent of $Q$ and $\xi_1, \xi_2$. Hence, by Minkowski's Second Convex Body Theorem, the product of the induced successive minima is $\ll c$, hence choosing $c$ small enough the third successive minimum is smaller than $1$. This means there cannot be three linearly independent integer points within the box, which in turn is equivalent to the claim. \end{proof} We first notice that both $\boldsymbol{v}_j$ and $\boldsymbol{w}_j$ induce approximations of order greater than two. By \eqref{eq:lg2}, \eqref{eq:ti} and as our choice $(\tau \mu-1)/\mu=n>2$, we get \begin{equation} |\boldsymbol{v}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| = (1+o(1))r^{-1} A_j^{-(\tau \mu-1)} \ll r^{-1} B_j^{-n}\ll r^{-1}\Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert^{-n}< r^{-1}\Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert^{-2} \end{equation} and for $\boldsymbol{w}_j$ by \eqref{eq:tz} we have a stronger estimate that also yields \begin{equation} |\boldsymbol{w}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| = o(1)\cdot B_j^{-(\tau \mu-1)} = o(\Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert^{-n})= o(\Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert^{-2}), \quad j\to\infty. \end{equation} Combined with \eqref{eq:either}, \eqref{eq:T}, \eqref{eq:see}, we have \[ \max\{ \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{b}}\Vert, \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_j\Vert, \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert \}= \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert, \qquad \max\{|\boldsymbol{b}\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|, |\boldsymbol{v}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|,|\boldsymbol{w}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| \} \ll r^{-1}\Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert^{-2}. \] By the assumptions of Case 2, the three vectors $\boldsymbol{v}_j, \boldsymbol{w}_j, \boldsymbol{b}$ are linearly independent. So we get a contradiction to Lemma~\ref{lemur} for $r$ sufficiently large and $Q=\Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert$, as soon as $\Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert$ is sufficiently large. Hence, in total, Case 2 provides only finitely many best approximations, of small norm, so Lemma~\ref{wichtig!} is proved. \end{proof} For studying $\psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{1\times 2}$, we may restrict to integer vectors of the form appearing in Lemma~\ref{wichtig!}. Now $|\boldsymbol{w}_j \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|$ is much larger than $|\boldsymbol{v}_{j+1} \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|$, and $|\boldsymbol{v}_j \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|$ is much larger than $|\boldsymbol{w}_{j} \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|$ by \eqref{eq:accto}, \eqref{eq:ti}, \eqref{eq:tz}. Hence by the triangle inequality $\boldsymbol{v}_j\pm \boldsymbol{w}_j$ induce the same approximation quality as $\boldsymbol{v}_j$ up to a factor $1+o(1)$, and similarly, $\boldsymbol{w}_j\pm \boldsymbol{v}_{j+1}$ induce the same approximation quality up to $1+o(1)$ as $\boldsymbol{w}_j$, i.e \begin{equation} |(\boldsymbol{v}_j\pm \boldsymbol{w}_j)\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| = (1+o(1))\cdot |\boldsymbol{v}_j \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|, \quad |(\boldsymbol{v}_{j+1}\pm \boldsymbol{w}_j)\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| = (1+o(1))\cdot |\boldsymbol{w}_j \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|. \end{equation} Moreover as the norm of $\hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j$ is much larger than the norm of $\hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_j$ and the norm of $\hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_{j+1}$ is much larger than the norm of $\hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j$, by \eqref{eq:accto} and \eqref{eq:gl}, we have by the triangle inequality that \begin{equation} \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_j\pm \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert = (1+o(1)) \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert, \qquad \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_{j+1}\pm \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert = (1+o(1)) \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_{j+1}\Vert. \end{equation} By \eqref{eq:41}, \eqref{eq:51} and since we have freedom up to a factor $1+o(1)$ in our claim to be proved, we may assume that all best approximations are among $\boldsymbol{v}_j, \boldsymbol{w}_j$. Now we choose $r$ appropriately. To finish the proof we show that choosing $\tau, \mu, r$ suitably we have \begin{equation} | \boldsymbol{v}_j \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| = (1+o(1))\cdot c\Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert^{-n}, \qquad | \boldsymbol{w}_j \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| = o(1)\cdot \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_{j+1}\Vert^{-n}. \end{equation} Assume this is true. Then indeed partitioning the interval $[\Vert \boldsymbol{v}_1\Vert,\infty)$ into consecutive disjoint intervals of the form $[\Vert \boldsymbol{v}_j\Vert, \Vert \boldsymbol{w}_j\Vert)$ and $[\Vert \boldsymbol{w}_j\Vert, \Vert \boldsymbol{v}_{j+1}\Vert)$ we see \begin{equation*} t^n \psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{1\times 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert, t)\le c(1+o(1)) \qquad t\to\infty. \end{equation*} On the other hand, since there is no better approximation than the one induced by $\boldsymbol{v}_j$ for any $t<\Vert \boldsymbol{w}_j\Vert$, for $t_j:=\Vert \boldsymbol{w}_j\Vert-1$ we have the reverse inequality \begin{equation*} t_j^n \psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{1\times 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert,t_j)\ge c(1+o(1)) \qquad j\to\infty. \end{equation*} Combining proves the equality \[ \limsup_{t\to\infty} t^n \psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{1\times 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert, t) = c. \] For the left identity of \eqref{eq:frosch} equivalently by \eqref{eq:lg2}, \eqref{eq:ti} we need \[ (1+o(1))r^{-1}A_j^{-(\tau \mu-1) }= c\cdot d_2^{-n} A_j^{-n\mu}, \] so we pick \[ r= c^{-1} d_2^n A_j^{n\mu-\tau \mu+1} \overset{ \eqref{eq:IIi}}{=}c^{-1} d_2^n. \] Similarly, by \eqref{eq:gl}, \eqref{eq:tz} for the right identity of \eqref{eq:frosch} it suffices to have \[ B_j^{-(\tau \mu-1)}= o(d_1^{-n} A_{j+1}^{-n\tau}). \] Since $A_{j+1}^{-n\tau} \asymp B_{j}^{-n\tau^2}$ by \eqref{eq:accto} and $d_1$ is constant, it suffices to notice that upon \eqref{eq:IIi} we may choose $\tau<\mu$ so that $n\tau^2 < \tau \mu-1$. Indeed it suffices to choose $\tau$ just slightly larger than $n$ so that $\mu=1/(\tau-n)>\tau^2$ which is equivalent to $n\tau^2 < \tau \mu-1$. We leave the short calculation to the reader. We have completed step I. Assuming $c$ is small enough, we apply Step II below.
nodes.statement_short: Construct xi from A_j=2^a3^g, B_j=5^b7^d and verify the exact limsup.

nodes.name: Approach
nodes.statement: This is the more intricate part of the proof. For this, we use a different construction than for the maximum norm where we employed the construction from~\cite{j2}. Rather we follow the proof of~\cite[Theorem~2.1]{j3} but with some notable twists.
nodes.statement_short: Follow j3 Theorem 2.1 with twists.

nodes.name: Star and hat notation
nodes.statement: Write $\boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}=(\boldsymbol{\xi},1)\in\mathbb{R}^{3}$ and use a similar meaning of star for other quantities. Conversely denote by a hat over a vector in $\mathbb{R}^{3}$ its restriction to the first $2$ coordinates by chopping off the last coordinate, i.e. $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}}=\boldsymbol{\xi}$.
nodes.statement_short: Notation xi* and hat.

nodes.name: Parameters and integers
nodes.statement: We construct our real vector. Let $n<\tau<\mu$ be parameters to be chosen later related by the identity \begin{equation} \tau \mu-1=n\mu \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad \mu=\frac{1}{\tau-n}. \end{equation} Let $\alpha_j, \beta_j, \gamma_j, \delta_j$ be strictly increasing positive integer sequences and a real number $r=r(\Vert\cdot\Vert)>0$ all to be fixed later. Derive integers of the form \[ A_j= 2^{\alpha_j}3^{\gamma_j }, \qquad B_j= 5^{\beta_j }7^{\delta_j}, \] satisfying as $j\to\infty$ \begin{equation} A_{j+1}= (1+o(1))r B_j^{\tau}, \qquad B_j = (1+o(1))A_j^{\mu}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Choose tau, mu with tau mu-1=n mu and integers A_j, B_j with prescribed growth.

nodes.name: Feasibility
nodes.statement: We first show that such choices are possible. For $A_j$, we use that $\{ \log 2, \log 3\}$ is a $\mathbb{Q}$-linearly independent set (easily seen by applying exponential map to a putative vanishing linear form and using unique prime factorization to disprove it) and the following easy Proposition~\ref{proper}. Similarly for $B_j$ we use that $\{ \log 5, \log 7\}$ is $\mathbb{Q}$-linearly independent.
nodes.statement_short: Use Q-independence of log 2, log 3 and log 5, log 7.

nodes.name: Proposition 3
nodes.statement: \begin{proposition} Let $a,b,c$ be real numbers with $a,b$ linearly independent over $\mathbb{Q}$. Then ordering the set $\{ k_1 a+k_2 b+c: k_i\in\mathbb{N} \}$ increasingly and denoting it by $(z_i)_{i\ge 1}$ we have $|z_{i+1}-z_i|\to 0$. \end{proposition} \begin{proof} Clearly, we may assume $c=0$ and suppose without loss of generality that $b<a$. We may then equivalently consider \begin{equation*} \mathcal{Z}=\{ k_1+k_2\tfrac{b}{a}: k_i\in\mathbb{N} \} \end{equation*} instead. Since $\tfrac{b}{a}$ is irrational, Kronecker's Theorem (see e.g. \cite[Section 3.5 Theorem IV]{Cassels}) shows that the set is dense in the unit interval when considering all $(k_1, k_2)\in \mathbb{Z}\times \mathbb{N}$. Let $\varepsilon=1/K>0$ with a large integer $K$ and partition $[0,1]$ into $K$ intervals \begin{equation*} I_t=[(t-1)\varepsilon,t\varepsilon], \qquad 1\le t\le K \end{equation*} of length $1/K$. Then for any $I_t$ there exist $(k_1^{\prime}(t), k_2^{\prime}(t))\in\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{N}$ so that $k_1^{\prime}(t)+k_2^{\prime}(t)\tfrac{b}{a}\in I_t$. Take $T_{\varepsilon}:= \max_t |k_1^{\prime}(t)|$ and consider the set \begin{equation*} \mathcal{Z}_{T_{\varepsilon}} = \left\{ (k_{1}(t)+N) + k_{2}(t)\tfrac{b}{a} : 1\leq t\leq K, \, N \in \mathbb{N}_{\geq T_{\varepsilon}} \right\} \subset \mathcal{Z}\, . \end{equation*} It is easy to see that for any $M\in\mathbb{N}_{\geq T_{\varepsilon}}$ the interval $M+I_{t}$ contains a point from $\mathcal{Z}_{T_{\varepsilon}}$. This shows that $\mathcal{Z}$ is $\varepsilon$ dense on some interval $[3T_{\varepsilon},\infty)$. Since $\varepsilon>0$ is arbitrary the claim is proved. \end{proof}
nodes.statement_short: Gaps of k1 a+k2 b+c tend to zero.

nodes.name: Iterative construction
nodes.statement: We can now apply the proposition alternatingly to \[ a=\log 2, \, b=\log 3, \, c=\log r, \qquad\quad a=\log 5,\, b=\log 7, \, c=0 \] respectively to construct iteratively our sequences $\alpha_j, \gamma_j$, which correspond to $k_1=\alpha_{j+1}-\alpha_j\ge 0$ and $k_2=\gamma_{j+1}-\gamma_j\ge 0$, resp. $k_1=\beta_{j+1}-\beta_j\ge 0$ and $k_2=\delta_{j+1}-\delta_j\ge 0$. Thereby, having chosen all $\alpha_., \beta_., \gamma_.,\delta_.$ up to index $j$, we construct first pairs $\alpha_{j+1}, \gamma_{j+1}$ and then $\beta_{j+1}, \delta_{j+1}$, and the iterative construction is complete. So, having chosen $r$, we may assume all the above is defined.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Proposition 3 alternately to choose the exponents.

nodes.name: Consequences of growth
nodes.statement: Note that \eqref{eq:accto} implies \begin{equation} A_{j+1}=(1+o(1))r A_j^{\tau \mu}, \qquad B_{j+1} =(1+o(1))r^{\mu} B_j^{\tau \mu}. \end{equation} Moreover, again by \eqref{eq:accto}, upon changing initial terms if necessary, we can assume \begin{equation} 1<A_1 < B_1 < A_2 < B_2 < \cdots. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Derive recursions (24) and ordering (25).

nodes.name: Claim: xi works
nodes.statement: Finally let $\boldsymbol{\xi}=(\xi_1, \xi_2)$ with \[ \xi_1= \sum_{j\ge 1} A_j^{-1 } , \qquad \xi_2= \sum_{j\ge 1} B_j^{-1 }. \] We claim that it satisfies the assertions of the theorem upon choosing $r$ appropriately. For $j\ge 1$ put \[ \sigma_j := A_1^{-1}+\cdots+A_j^{-1}, \qquad \eta_j:= B_1^{-1}+\cdots+B_j^{-1}. \] We clearly have $\sigma_j\to \xi_1$ and $\eta_j\to \xi_2$ as $j\to \infty$, and \[ F_j= A_j\sigma_j\in \mathbb{N}, \qquad G_j=B_j \eta_j\in\mathbb{N}. \] Then since the sequences $(\alpha_j), (\beta_j), (\gamma_j), (\delta_j)$ are strictly increasing we have $F_j\equiv 1\bmod 2\cdot 3$ and $G_j\equiv 1\bmod 5\cdot 7$, which imply the coprimality assertions \begin{equation} (A_j, F_j)=(F_j,6)=1, \qquad (B_j,G_j)=(G_j,35)=1. \end{equation} Let \[ \boldsymbol{v}_j=(A_j,0,-F_j), \qquad \boldsymbol{w}_j=(0, B_j,-G_j). \] Note that $\hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_j=(A_j,0)$ and $\hat {\boldsymbol{w}}_j=(0,B_j)$. Hence their norms $\Vert\cdot\Vert$ satisfy \begin{equation} \Vert\hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_j\Vert = \Vert \boldsymbol{e}_1 \Vert A_j= d_1 A_j, \qquad d_1:=\Vert \boldsymbol{e}_1\Vert=\Vert (1,0)\Vert, \end{equation} and \begin{equation} \Vert\hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert= \Vert \boldsymbol{e}_2 \Vert B_j= d_2 B_j \overset{\eqref{eq:accto}}{=}(1+o(1))d_2 A_j^{\mu}, \qquad d_2:=\Vert \boldsymbol{e}_2\Vert=\Vert (0,1)\Vert, \end{equation} Thus by \eqref{eq:vf} clearly \begin{equation} \Vert\hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_j\Vert< \Vert\hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert< \Vert\hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_{j+1}\Vert, \qquad j\ge j_0. \end{equation} Here $j_0$ depends on $d_1, d_2$, thus on the chosen norm. Then by \eqref{eq:true} moreover \begin{align} |\boldsymbol{v}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|&= |A_j \cdot \xi_1 +0\cdot \xi_2 - F_j|= A_j(A_{j+1}^{-1}+A_{j+2}^{-1}+\cdots) \\ &= A_j A_{j+1}^{-1}(1+o(1)) \overset{\eqref{eq:true}}{=} (1+o(1))r^{-1}A_j^{-(\tau \mu-1) } \nonumber \end{align} and \begin{align} |\boldsymbol{w}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|&= |0\cdot \xi_1 + B_j \cdot \xi_2 - G_j|= B_j(B_{j+1}^{-1}+B_{j+2}^{-1}+\cdots) \\ &= (1+o(1))B_jB_{j+1}^{-1} \overset{\eqref{eq:true}}{=} (1+o(1))r^{-\mu}\cdot B_j^{-(\tau \mu-1) }, \nonumber \end{align} are small linear forms for $j\ge 1$. We next show \begin{lemma} As soon as $r$ is large enough, all best approximations for $\boldsymbol{\xi}$ of large norm have up to sign one of the following forms \[ \boldsymbol{v}_j, \quad \boldsymbol{w}_j, \quad \boldsymbol{v}_j+\boldsymbol{w}_j,\quad \boldsymbol{w}_j-\boldsymbol{v}_j, \quad \boldsymbol{w}_j+\boldsymbol{v}_{j+1}, \quad \boldsymbol{v}_{j+1}-\boldsymbol{w}_{j}. \] \end{lemma} \begin{proof} Let $\boldsymbol{b}$ be any best approximation. Then by \eqref{eq:either} there is an index $j$ such that either $\Vert\hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_j\Vert\le \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{b}}\Vert<\Vert\hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert$ or $\Vert\hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert\le \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{b}}\Vert< \Vert\hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_{j+1}\Vert$. We show that in the first case $\boldsymbol{b}=\pm \boldsymbol{v}_j$ or $\pm(\boldsymbol{v}_j\pm \boldsymbol{w}_j)$, and in the latter case $\boldsymbol{b}=\pm \boldsymbol{w}_j$ or $\pm(\boldsymbol{w}_j\pm \boldsymbol{v}_{j+1})$. Assume the first case, so \begin{equation} \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_j\Vert\le \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{b}}\Vert< \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert. \end{equation} the latter works very similarly by symmetry. First, observe that since $\boldsymbol{b}$ is the best approximation of norm at least $\Vert\hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_j\Vert$, we know that \begin{equation} |\boldsymbol{b}\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|\le |\boldsymbol{v}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|. \end{equation} We distinguish two cases. Case 1: $\boldsymbol{b}$ lies in the two-dimensonal subspace of $\mathbb{R}^3$ spanned by $\boldsymbol{v}_j, \boldsymbol{w}_j$, i.e. $\boldsymbol{b}\in \scp{\boldsymbol{v}_j, \boldsymbol{w}_j}_{\mathbb{R}}\cap \mathbb{Z}^3$. The special form of $A_j, B_j$ and \eqref{eq:witt} imply the following crucial result on integer vectors in the two-dimensional lattices $\scp{\boldsymbol{v}_j, \boldsymbol{w}_j}_{\mathbb{R}}\cap \mathbb{Z}^3$. \begin{proposition} For $\boldsymbol{v}_j, \boldsymbol{w}_j$ as above, if a linear combination $g\boldsymbol{v}_j+h\boldsymbol{w}_j$ is an integer vector, then in fact $g\in\mathbb{Z}$ and $h\in \mathbb{Z}$. In other words, $\scp{\boldsymbol{v}_j, \boldsymbol{w}_j}_{\mathbb{R}}\cap \mathbb{Z}^3=\scp{\boldsymbol{v}_j, \boldsymbol{w}_j}_{\mathbb{Z}}$. \end{proposition} \begin{proof} Clearly, we must have $g,h\in \mathbb{Q}$. If we write $(p_1/q_1)\boldsymbol{v}_j + (p_2/q_2)\boldsymbol{w}_j$ with $p_i/q_i$ in lowest terms, then it is clear that $q_1$ must consist of exclusively non-negative integer powers of $2$ and $3$ and $q_2$ of non-negative integer power of $5$ and $7$ to make the first two coordinates $(p_1/q_1)A_j=(p_1/q_1)2^{\alpha_j}3^{\gamma_j}$ resp. $(p_2/q_2)B_j=(p_2/q_2)5^{\beta_j}7^{\delta_j}$ of $g\boldsymbol{v}_j+h\boldsymbol{w}_j$ integers. But then by \eqref{eq:witt} clearly the third coordinate $(p_1/q_1)F_j+(p_2/q_2)G_j$ is not an integer unless $q_1=q_2=1$. \end{proof} We first show that any integer linear combination $\boldsymbol{b}=g\boldsymbol{v}_j+h\boldsymbol{w}_j$ representing the best approximation as above must have $|g|\le 1$. Assume $|g|\ge 2$. It is easily seen that for any norm on $\mathbb{R}^2$ there is a constant $\theta=\theta(\Vert\cdot\Vert)$ such that $\Vert \boldsymbol{w}\Vert \le W$ for $\boldsymbol{w}=(w_1,w_2)\in\mathbb{R}^2$ and $W>0$ implies $|w_i|\le \theta W$, $i=1,2$.
