Hence \eqref{eq:T} and the special form of $\boldsymbol{v}_j, \boldsymbol{w}_j$ imply \[ |g|\le \theta, \qquad |h|\le \theta \] for some $\theta$ independent of $j$. On the other hand, since $r,\mu$ are fixed and $A_j\to\infty$, it is clear from \eqref{eq:ti}, \eqref{eq:tz} and \eqref{eq:accto} that \[ |\boldsymbol{w}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| = o(|\boldsymbol{v}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|), \qquad j\to\infty. \] Combination implies \begin{align*} |\boldsymbol{b} \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|= | (g\boldsymbol{v}_j+h\boldsymbol{w}_j) \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| &\ge |g|\cdot |\boldsymbol{v}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| - |h|\cdot |\boldsymbol{w}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| \ge 2 |\boldsymbol{v}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| - |h|\cdot |\boldsymbol{w}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|\\ &\ge 2 |\boldsymbol{v}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| - \theta\cdot |\boldsymbol{w}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| > |\boldsymbol{v}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|, \qquad j\ge j_0, \end{align*} contradicting \eqref{eq:see}. Hence $|g|\le 1$. Now if $|h|\ge 2$ then for any $|g|\le 1$ using \eqref{eq:either} we get \[ \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{b}}\Vert= \Vert g \hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_j+h\hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert \ge |h|\cdot \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert - \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_j\Vert \ge 2 \cdot \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert - \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_j\Vert > \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert \] contradicting \eqref{eq:T}. Thus both $g,h$ are among $\{-1,0,1\}$. Hence we are left with the vectors of the lemma. Case 2: $\boldsymbol{b}$ does not lie in the space spanned by $\boldsymbol{v}_j, \boldsymbol{w}_j$. For this case, we use an easy consequence of Minkowski's Second Convex Body Theorem. \begin{lemma} There exists a constant $c>0$ such that for any $\boldsymbol{\xi}\in \mathbb{R}^2$ and any parameter $Q\ge 1$, the system \[ |b_1|\le Q,\qquad |b_2|\le Q,\qquad |b_1 \xi_1 + b_2 \xi_2+b_{3}| < cQ^{-2} \] does not have three linearly independent solutions in integer vectors $\boldsymbol{b}=(b_1,b_2,b_3)$. \end{lemma} \begin{proof} Consider the integer lattice $\mathbb{Z}^3$ and the box of $(x_1,x_2,x_3)\in \mathbb{R}^3$ with coordinates \[ |x_1|\le Q, \qquad |x_2|\le Q,\quad |\xi_1 x_1+\xi_2 x_2 + x_3|\leq cQ^{-2}. \] It has volume $8c$, independent of $Q$ and $\xi_1, \xi_2$. Hence, by Minkowski's Second Convex Body Theorem, the product of the induced successive minima is $\ll c$, hence choosing $c$ small enough the third successive minimum is smaller than $1$. This means there cannot be three linearly independent integer points within the box, which in turn is equivalent to the claim. \end{proof} We first notice that both $\boldsymbol{v}_j$ and $\boldsymbol{w}_j$ induce approximations of order greater than two. By \eqref{eq:lg2}, \eqref{eq:ti} and as our choice $(\tau \mu-1)/\mu=n>2$, we get \begin{equation} |\boldsymbol{v}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| = (1+o(1))r^{-1} A_j^{-(\tau \mu-1)} \ll r^{-1} B_j^{-n}\ll r^{-1}\Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert^{-n}< r^{-1}\Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert^{-2} \end{equation} and for $\boldsymbol{w}_j$ by \eqref{eq:tz} we have a stronger estimate that also yields \begin{equation} |\boldsymbol{w}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| = o(1)\cdot B_j^{-(\tau \mu-1)} = o(\Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert^{-n})= o(\Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert^{-2}), \quad j\to\infty. \end{equation} Combined with \eqref{eq:either}, \eqref{eq:T}, \eqref{eq:see}, we have \[ \max\{ \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{b}}\Vert, \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_j\Vert, \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert \}= \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert, \qquad \max\{|\boldsymbol{b}\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|, |\boldsymbol{v}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|,|\boldsymbol{w}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| \} \ll r^{-1}\Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert^{-2}. \] By the assumptions of Case 2, the three vectors $\boldsymbol{v}_j, \boldsymbol{w}_j, \boldsymbol{b}$ are linearly independent. So we get a contradiction to Lemma~\ref{lemur} for $r$ sufficiently large and $Q=\Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert$, as soon as $\Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert$ is sufficiently large. Hence, in total, Case 2 provides only finitely many best approximations, of small norm, so Lemma~\ref{wichtig!} is proved. \end{proof} For studying $\psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{1\times 2}$, we may restrict to integer vectors of the form appearing in Lemma~\ref{wichtig!}. Now $|\boldsymbol{w}_j \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|$ is much larger than $|\boldsymbol{v}_{j+1} \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|$, and $|\boldsymbol{v}_j \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|$ is much larger than $|\boldsymbol{w}_{j} \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|$ by \eqref{eq:accto}, \eqref{eq:ti}, \eqref{eq:tz}. Hence by the triangle inequality $\boldsymbol{v}_j\pm \boldsymbol{w}_j$ induce the same approximation quality as $\boldsymbol{v}_j$ up to a factor $1+o(1)$, and similarly, $\boldsymbol{w}_j\pm \boldsymbol{v}_{j+1}$ induce the same approximation quality up to $1+o(1)$ as $\boldsymbol{w}_j$, i.e \begin{equation} |(\boldsymbol{v}_j\pm \boldsymbol{w}_j)\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| = (1+o(1))\cdot |\boldsymbol{v}_j \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|, \quad |(\boldsymbol{v}_{j+1}\pm \boldsymbol{w}_j)\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| = (1+o(1))\cdot |\boldsymbol{w}_j \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|. \end{equation} Moreover as the norm of $\hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j$ is much larger than the norm of $\hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_j$ and the norm of $\hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_{j+1}$ is much larger than the norm of $\hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j$, by \eqref{eq:accto} and \eqref{eq:gl}, we have by the triangle inequality that \begin{equation} \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_j\pm \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert = (1+o(1)) \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert, \qquad \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_{j+1}\pm \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert = (1+o(1)) \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_{j+1}\Vert. \end{equation} By \eqref{eq:41}, \eqref{eq:51} and since we have freedom up to a factor $1+o(1)$ in our claim to be proved, we may assume that all best approximations are among $\boldsymbol{v}_j, \boldsymbol{w}_j$. Now we choose $r$ appropriately. To finish the proof we show that choosing $\tau, \mu, r$ suitably we have \begin{equation} | \boldsymbol{v}_j \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| = (1+o(1))\cdot c\Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert^{-n}, \qquad | \boldsymbol{w}_j \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| = o(1)\cdot \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_{j+1}\Vert^{-n}. \end{equation} Assume this is true. Then indeed partitioning the interval $[\Vert \boldsymbol{v}_1\Vert,\infty)$ into consecutive disjoint intervals of the form $[\Vert \boldsymbol{v}_j\Vert, \Vert \boldsymbol{w}_j\Vert)$ and $[\Vert \boldsymbol{w}_j\Vert, \Vert \boldsymbol{v}_{j+1}\Vert)$ we see \begin{equation*} t^n \psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{1\times 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert, t)\le c(1+o(1)) \qquad t\to\infty. \end{equation*} On the other hand, since there is no better approximation than the one induced by $\boldsymbol{v}_j$ for any $t<\Vert \boldsymbol{w}_j\Vert$, for $t_j:=\Vert \boldsymbol{w}_j\Vert-1$ we have the reverse inequality \begin{equation*} t_j^n \psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{1\times 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert,t_j)\ge c(1+o(1)) \qquad j\to\infty. \end{equation*} Combining proves the equality \[ \limsup_{t\to\infty} t^n \psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{1\times 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert, t) = c. \] For the left identity of \eqref{eq:frosch} equivalently by \eqref{eq:lg2}, \eqref{eq:ti} we need \[ (1+o(1))r^{-1}A_j^{-(\tau \mu-1) }= c\cdot d_2^{-n} A_j^{-n\mu}, \] so we pick \[ r= c^{-1} d_2^n A_j^{n\mu-\tau \mu+1} \overset{ \eqref{eq:IIi}}{=}c^{-1} d_2^n. \] Similarly, by \eqref{eq:gl}, \eqref{eq:tz} for the right identity of \eqref{eq:frosch} it suffices to have \[ B_j^{-(\tau \mu-1)}= o(d_1^{-n} A_{j+1}^{-n\tau}). \] Since $A_{j+1}^{-n\tau} \asymp B_{j}^{-n\tau^2}$ by \eqref{eq:accto} and $d_1$ is constant, it suffices to notice that upon \eqref{eq:IIi} we may choose $\tau<\mu$ so that $n\tau^2 < \tau \mu-1$. Indeed it suffices to choose $\tau$ just slightly larger than $n$ so that $\mu=1/(\tau-n)>\tau^2$ which is equivalent to $n\tau^2 < \tau \mu-1$. We leave the short calculation to the reader. We have completed step I. Assuming $c$ is small enough, we apply Step II below.
nodes.statement_short: Define xi by reciprocal sums and verify the exact limsup.

nodes.name: Define xi
nodes.statement: Finally let $\boldsymbol{\xi}=(\xi_1, \xi_2)$ with \[ \xi_1= \sum_{j\ge 1} A_j^{-1 } , \qquad \xi_2= \sum_{j\ge 1} B_j^{-1 }. \] We claim that it satisfies the assertions of the theorem upon choosing $r$ appropriately.
nodes.statement_short: xi_1=sum 1/A_j, xi_2=sum 1/B_j; claim it works.

nodes.name: Partial sums
nodes.statement: For $j\ge 1$ put \[ \sigma_j := A_1^{-1}+\cdots+A_j^{-1}, \qquad \eta_j:= B_1^{-1}+\cdots+B_j^{-1}. \] We clearly have $\sigma_j\to \xi_1$ and $\eta_j\to \xi_2$ as $j\to \infty$, and \[ F_j= A_j\sigma_j\in \mathbb{N}, \qquad G_j=B_j \eta_j\in\mathbb{N}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Partial sums sigma_j, eta_j and integers F_j, G_j.

nodes.name: Coprimality
nodes.statement: Then since the sequences $(\alpha_j), (\beta_j), (\gamma_j), (\delta_j)$ are strictly increasing we have $F_j\equiv 1\bmod 2\cdot 3$ and $G_j\equiv 1\bmod 5\cdot 7$, which imply the coprimality assertions \begin{equation} (A_j, F_j)=(F_j,6)=1, \qquad (B_j,G_j)=(G_j,35)=1. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: F_j, G_j congruences give coprimality (26).

nodes.name: Vectors v_j, w_j
nodes.statement: Let \[ \boldsymbol{v}_j=(A_j,0,-F_j), \qquad \boldsymbol{w}_j=(0, B_j,-G_j). \] Note that $\hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_j=(A_j,0)$ and $\hat {\boldsymbol{w}}_j=(0,B_j)$. Hence their norms $\Vert\cdot\Vert$ satisfy \begin{equation} \Vert\hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_j\Vert = \Vert \boldsymbol{e}_1 \Vert A_j= d_1 A_j, \qquad d_1:=\Vert \boldsymbol{e}_1\Vert=\Vert (1,0)\Vert, \end{equation} and \begin{equation} \Vert\hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert= \Vert \boldsymbol{e}_2 \Vert B_j= d_2 B_j \overset{\eqref{eq:accto}}{=}(1+o(1))d_2 A_j^{\mu}, \qquad d_2:=\Vert \boldsymbol{e}_2\Vert=\Vert (0,1)\Vert, \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Define v_j, w_j and compute their norms.

nodes.name: Interlacing
nodes.statement: Thus by \eqref{eq:vf} clearly \begin{equation} \Vert\hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_j\Vert< \Vert\hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert< \Vert\hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_{j+1}\Vert, \qquad j\ge j_0. \end{equation} Here $j_0$ depends on $d_1, d_2$, thus on the chosen norm.
nodes.statement_short: Norms of v_j, w_j interlace.

nodes.name: Small linear forms
nodes.statement: Then by \eqref{eq:true} moreover \begin{align} |\boldsymbol{v}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|&= |A_j \cdot \xi_1 +0\cdot \xi_2 - F_j|= A_j(A_{j+1}^{-1}+A_{j+2}^{-1}+\cdots) \\ &= A_j A_{j+1}^{-1}(1+o(1)) \overset{\eqref{eq:true}}{=} (1+o(1))r^{-1}A_j^{-(\tau \mu-1) } \nonumber \end{align} and \begin{align} |\boldsymbol{w}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|&= |0\cdot \xi_1 + B_j \cdot \xi_2 - G_j|= B_j(B_{j+1}^{-1}+B_{j+2}^{-1}+\cdots) \\ &= (1+o(1))B_jB_{j+1}^{-1} \overset{\eqref{eq:true}}{=} (1+o(1))r^{-\mu}\cdot B_j^{-(\tau \mu-1) }, \nonumber \end{align} are small linear forms for $j\ge 1$.
nodes.statement_short: Compute |v_j xi*| and |w_j xi*|.

nodes.name: Lemma 6.1
nodes.statement: We next show \begin{lemma} As soon as $r$ is large enough, all best approximations for $\boldsymbol{\xi}$ of large norm have up to sign one of the following forms \[ \boldsymbol{v}_j, \quad \boldsymbol{w}_j, \quad \boldsymbol{v}_j+\boldsymbol{w}_j,\quad \boldsymbol{w}_j-\boldsymbol{v}_j, \quad \boldsymbol{w}_j+\boldsymbol{v}_{j+1}, \quad \boldsymbol{v}_{j+1}-\boldsymbol{w}_{j}. \] \end{lemma} \begin{proof} Let $\boldsymbol{b}$ be any best approximation. Then by \eqref{eq:either} there is an index $j$ such that either $\Vert\hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_j\Vert\le \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{b}}\Vert<\Vert\hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert$ or $\Vert\hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert\le \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{b}}\Vert< \Vert\hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_{j+1}\Vert$. We show that in the first case $\boldsymbol{b}=\pm \boldsymbol{v}_j$ or $\pm(\boldsymbol{v}_j\pm \boldsymbol{w}_j)$, and in the latter case $\boldsymbol{b}=\pm \boldsymbol{w}_j$ or $\pm(\boldsymbol{w}_j\pm \boldsymbol{v}_{j+1})$. Assume the first case, so \begin{equation} \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_j\Vert\le \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{b}}\Vert< \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert. \end{equation} the latter works very similarly by symmetry. First, observe that since $\boldsymbol{b}$ is the best approximation of norm at least $\Vert\hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_j\Vert$, we know that \begin{equation} |\boldsymbol{b}\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|\le |\boldsymbol{v}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|. \end{equation} We distinguish two cases. Case 1: $\boldsymbol{b}$ lies in the two-dimensonal subspace of $\mathbb{R}^3$ spanned by $\boldsymbol{v}_j, \boldsymbol{w}_j$, i.e. $\boldsymbol{b}\in \scp{\boldsymbol{v}_j, \boldsymbol{w}_j}_{\mathbb{R}}\cap \mathbb{Z}^3$. The special form of $A_j, B_j$ and \eqref{eq:witt} imply the following crucial result on integer vectors in the two-dimensional lattices $\scp{\boldsymbol{v}_j, \boldsymbol{w}_j}_{\mathbb{R}}\cap \mathbb{Z}^3$. \begin{proposition} For $\boldsymbol{v}_j, \boldsymbol{w}_j$ as above, if a linear combination $g\boldsymbol{v}_j+h\boldsymbol{w}_j$ is an integer vector, then in fact $g\in\mathbb{Z}$ and $h\in \mathbb{Z}$. In other words, $\scp{\boldsymbol{v}_j, \boldsymbol{w}_j}_{\mathbb{R}}\cap \mathbb{Z}^3=\scp{\boldsymbol{v}_j, \boldsymbol{w}_j}_{\mathbb{Z}}$. \end{proposition} \begin{proof} Clearly, we must have $g,h\in \mathbb{Q}$. If we write $(p_1/q_1)\boldsymbol{v}_j + (p_2/q_2)\boldsymbol{w}_j$ with $p_i/q_i$ in lowest terms, then it is clear that $q_1$ must consist of exclusively non-negative integer powers of $2$ and $3$ and $q_2$ of non-negative integer power of $5$ and $7$ to make the first two coordinates $(p_1/q_1)A_j=(p_1/q_1)2^{\alpha_j}3^{\gamma_j}$ resp. $(p_2/q_2)B_j=(p_2/q_2)5^{\beta_j}7^{\delta_j}$ of $g\boldsymbol{v}_j+h\boldsymbol{w}_j$ integers. But then by \eqref{eq:witt} clearly the third coordinate $(p_1/q_1)F_j+(p_2/q_2)G_j$ is not an integer unless $q_1=q_2=1$. \end{proof} We first show that any integer linear combination $\boldsymbol{b}=g\boldsymbol{v}_j+h\boldsymbol{w}_j$ representing the best approximation as above must have $|g|\le 1$. Assume $|g|\ge 2$. It is easily seen that for any norm on $\mathbb{R}^2$ there is a constant $\theta=\theta(\Vert\cdot\Vert)$ such that $\Vert \boldsymbol{w}\Vert \le W$ for $\boldsymbol{w}=(w_1,w_2)\in\mathbb{R}^2$ and $W>0$ implies $|w_i|\le \theta W$, $i=1,2$. Hence \eqref{eq:T} and the special form of $\boldsymbol{v}_j, \boldsymbol{w}_j$ imply \[ |g|\le \theta, \qquad |h|\le \theta \] for some $\theta$ independent of $j$. On the other hand, since $r,\mu$ are fixed and $A_j\to\infty$, it is clear from \eqref{eq:ti}, \eqref{eq:tz} and \eqref{eq:accto} that \[ |\boldsymbol{w}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| = o(|\boldsymbol{v}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|), \qquad j\to\infty. \] Combination implies \begin{align*} |\boldsymbol{b} \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|= | (g\boldsymbol{v}_j+h\boldsymbol{w}_j) \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| &\ge |g|\cdot |\boldsymbol{v}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| - |h|\cdot |\boldsymbol{w}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| \ge 2 |\boldsymbol{v}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| - |h|\cdot |\boldsymbol{w}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|\\ &\ge 2 |\boldsymbol{v}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| - \theta\cdot |\boldsymbol{w}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| > |\boldsymbol{v}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|, \qquad j\ge j_0, \end{align*} contradicting \eqref{eq:see}. Hence $|g|\le 1$. Now if $|h|\ge 2$ then for any $|g|\le 1$ using \eqref{eq:either} we get \[ \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{b}}\Vert= \Vert g \hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_j+h\hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert \ge |h|\cdot \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert - \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_j\Vert \ge 2 \cdot \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert - \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_j\Vert > \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert \] contradicting \eqref{eq:T}. Thus both $g,h$ are among $\{-1,0,1\}$. Hence we are left with the vectors of the lemma. Case 2: $\boldsymbol{b}$ does not lie in the space spanned by $\boldsymbol{v}_j, \boldsymbol{w}_j$. For this case, we use an easy consequence of Minkowski's Second Convex Body Theorem. \begin{lemma} There exists a constant $c>0$ such that for any $\boldsymbol{\xi}\in \mathbb{R}^2$ and any parameter $Q\ge 1$, the system \[ |b_1|\le Q,\qquad |b_2|\le Q,\qquad |b_1 \xi_1 + b_2 \xi_2+b_{3}| < cQ^{-2} \] does not have three linearly independent solutions in integer vectors $\boldsymbol{b}=(b_1,b_2,b_3)$. \end{lemma} \begin{proof} Consider the integer lattice $\mathbb{Z}^3$ and the box of $(x_1,x_2,x_3)\in \mathbb{R}^3$ with coordinates \[ |x_1|\le Q, \qquad |x_2|\le Q,\quad |\xi_1 x_1+\xi_2 x_2 + x_3|\leq cQ^{-2}. \] It has volume $8c$, independent of $Q$ and $\xi_1, \xi_2$. Hence, by Minkowski's Second Convex Body Theorem, the product of the induced successive minima is $\ll c$, hence choosing $c$ small enough the third successive minimum is smaller than $1$. This means there cannot be three linearly independent integer points within the box, which in turn is equivalent to the claim. \end{proof} We first notice that both $\boldsymbol{v}_j$ and $\boldsymbol{w}_j$ induce approximations of order greater than two. By \eqref{eq:lg2}, \eqref{eq:ti} and as our choice $(\tau \mu-1)/\mu=n>2$, we get \begin{equation} |\boldsymbol{v}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| = (1+o(1))r^{-1} A_j^{-(\tau \mu-1)} \ll r^{-1} B_j^{-n}\ll r^{-1}\Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert^{-n}< r^{-1}\Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert^{-2} \end{equation} and for $\boldsymbol{w}_j$ by \eqref{eq:tz} we have a stronger estimate that also yields \begin{equation} |\boldsymbol{w}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| = o(1)\cdot B_j^{-(\tau \mu-1)} = o(\Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert^{-n})= o(\Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert^{-2}), \quad j\to\infty. \end{equation} Combined with \eqref{eq:either}, \eqref{eq:T}, \eqref{eq:see}, we have \[ \max\{ \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{b}}\Vert, \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_j\Vert, \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert \}= \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert, \qquad \max\{|\boldsymbol{b}\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|, |\boldsymbol{v}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|,|\boldsymbol{w}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| \} \ll r^{-1}\Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert^{-2}. \] By the assumptions of Case 2, the three vectors $\boldsymbol{v}_j, \boldsymbol{w}_j, \boldsymbol{b}$ are linearly independent. So we get a contradiction to Lemma~\ref{lemur} for $r$ sufficiently large and $Q=\Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert$, as soon as $\Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert$ is sufficiently large. Hence, in total, Case 2 provides only finitely many best approximations, of small norm, so Lemma~\ref{wichtig!} is proved. \end{proof}
nodes.statement_short: Best approximations have one of six forms.

nodes.name: Reduce to v_j, w_j
nodes.statement: For studying $\psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{1\times 2}$, we may restrict to integer vectors of the form appearing in Lemma~\ref{wichtig!}. Now $|\boldsymbol{w}_j \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|$ is much larger than $|\boldsymbol{v}_{j+1} \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|$, and $|\boldsymbol{v}_j \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|$ is much larger than $|\boldsymbol{w}_{j} \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|$ by \eqref{eq:accto}, \eqref{eq:ti}, \eqref{eq:tz}. Hence by the triangle inequality $\boldsymbol{v}_j\pm \boldsymbol{w}_j$ induce the same approximation quality as $\boldsymbol{v}_j$ up to a factor $1+o(1)$, and similarly, $\boldsymbol{w}_j\pm \boldsymbol{v}_{j+1}$ induce the same approximation quality up to $1+o(1)$ as $\boldsymbol{w}_j$, i.e \begin{equation} |(\boldsymbol{v}_j\pm \boldsymbol{w}_j)\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| = (1+o(1))\cdot |\boldsymbol{v}_j \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|, \quad |(\boldsymbol{v}_{j+1}\pm \boldsymbol{w}_j)\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| = (1+o(1))\cdot |\boldsymbol{w}_j \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|. \end{equation} Moreover as the norm of $\hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j$ is much larger than the norm of $\hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_j$ and the norm of $\hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_{j+1}$ is much larger than the norm of $\hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j$, by \eqref{eq:accto} and \eqref{eq:gl}, we have by the triangle inequality that \begin{equation} \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_j\pm \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert = (1+o(1)) \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert, \qquad \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_{j+1}\pm \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert = (1+o(1)) \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_{j+1}\Vert. \end{equation} By \eqref{eq:41}, \eqref{eq:51} and since we have freedom up to a factor $1+o(1)$ in our claim to be proved, we may assume that all best approximations are among $\boldsymbol{v}_j, \boldsymbol{w}_j$.
nodes.statement_short: Mixed vectors change quality only by 1+o(1).

nodes.name: Limsup equals c
nodes.statement: Now we choose $r$ appropriately. To finish the proof we show that choosing $\tau, \mu, r$ suitably we have \begin{equation} | \boldsymbol{v}_j \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| = (1+o(1))\cdot c\Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{w}}_j\Vert^{-n}, \qquad | \boldsymbol{w}_j \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}| = o(1)\cdot \Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{v}}_{j+1}\Vert^{-n}. \end{equation} Assume this is true. Then indeed partitioning the interval $[\Vert \boldsymbol{v}_1\Vert,\infty)$ into consecutive disjoint intervals of the form $[\Vert \boldsymbol{v}_j\Vert, \Vert \boldsymbol{w}_j\Vert)$ and $[\Vert \boldsymbol{w}_j\Vert, \Vert \boldsymbol{v}_{j+1}\Vert)$ we see \begin{equation*} t^n \psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{1\times 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert, t)\le c(1+o(1)) \qquad t\to\infty. \end{equation*} On the other hand, since there is no better approximation than the one induced by $\boldsymbol{v}_j$ for any $t<\Vert \boldsymbol{w}_j\Vert$, for $t_j:=\Vert \boldsymbol{w}_j\Vert-1$ we have the reverse inequality \begin{equation*} t_j^n \psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{1\times 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert,t_j)\ge c(1+o(1)) \qquad j\to\infty. \end{equation*} Combining proves the equality \[ \limsup_{t\to\infty} t^n \psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{1\times 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert, t) = c. \]
nodes.statement_short: Given (38), upper and lower bounds give limsup c.

nodes.name: Choice of r
nodes.statement: For the left identity of \eqref{eq:frosch} equivalently by \eqref{eq:lg2}, \eqref{eq:ti} we need \[ (1+o(1))r^{-1}A_j^{-(\tau \mu-1) }= c\cdot d_2^{-n} A_j^{-n\mu}, \] so we pick \[ r= c^{-1} d_2^n A_j^{n\mu-\tau \mu+1} \overset{ \eqref{eq:IIi}}{=}c^{-1} d_2^n. \]
nodes.statement_short: Pick r=c^{-1}d_2^n.

nodes.name: Choice of tau
nodes.statement: Similarly, by \eqref{eq:gl}, \eqref{eq:tz} for the right identity of \eqref{eq:frosch} it suffices to have \[ B_j^{-(\tau \mu-1)}= o(d_1^{-n} A_{j+1}^{-n\tau}). \] Since $A_{j+1}^{-n\tau} \asymp B_{j}^{-n\tau^2}$ by \eqref{eq:accto} and $d_1$ is constant, it suffices to notice that upon \eqref{eq:IIi} we may choose $\tau<\mu$ so that $n\tau^2 < \tau \mu-1$. Indeed it suffices to choose $\tau$ just slightly larger than $n$ so that $\mu=1/(\tau-n)>\tau^2$ which is equivalent to $n\tau^2 < \tau \mu-1$. We leave the short calculation to the reader. We have completed step I. Assuming $c$ is small enough, we apply Step II below.
nodes.statement_short: Choose tau slightly above n so mu>tau^2; Step I complete.

nodes.name: Proof of Step II
nodes.statement: \subsection{Proof of Step II} The proof of step II works analogously to the special case of maximum norm in Section \ref{Sect6}. Our norm $\Vert\cdot\Vert$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$ induces a projected norm $\Vert\cdot\Vert^{\prime}$ on $\mathbb{R}^2$ via \begin{equation} \Vert (x_1, x_2) \Vert^{\prime}:= \Vert (x_1,x_2,0,\ldots,0) \Vert. \end{equation} Then for this norm $\Vert\cdot\Vert^{\prime}$ we apply step I to get $\boldsymbol{\xi}=(\xi_1, \xi_2)$ with the property \[ \limsup_{t\to\infty} t^n \psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{1\times 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert^{\prime}, t) = c. \] Let $\boldsymbol{b}_v=(b_{1,v}, b_{2,v}, b_{3,v})$ be the integer vector sequence constructed in Step I. By construction of $\Vert\cdot\Vert^{\prime}$, it is again clear by the same argument as in Proposition~\ref{pro} that any vector $\boldsymbol{\zeta}=(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_n)\in \mathbb{R}^n$ extending $\boldsymbol{\xi}$ has Dirichlet constant at most $c$ with respect to $\Vert\cdot\Vert$, i.e. \[ \limsup_{t\to\infty} t^n \psi_{\boldsymbol{\zeta}}^{1\times n}(\Vert\cdot\Vert, t) \le \limsup_{t\to\infty} t^n \psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{1\times 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert^{\prime}, t) = c. \] Indeed, we can choose the embedded integer vectors $\iota(\boldsymbol{b}_v)$ via the embedding \[ \iota: (y_1, y_2,y_3)\to (y_1,y_2,0,\ldots,0,y_3) \] from $\mathbb{R}^3$ to $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$, which by \eqref{eq:pno} induce the same heights and approximation quality \[ \Vert \widehat{\iota(\boldsymbol{b}_v)}\Vert=\Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{b}}_v\Vert^{\prime}, \qquad |\iota(\boldsymbol{b}_v)\cdot \boldsymbol{\zeta}^{\ast}|=|\boldsymbol{b}_v\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast} | \] for any $\boldsymbol{b}_v$, with hat notation according to \eqref{eq:hatnot} on the respective spaces. For the non-trivial lower estimate \[ \limsup_{t\to\infty} t^n \psi_{\boldsymbol{\zeta}}^{1\times n}(\Vert\cdot\Vert, t)\ge c \] with respect to $\Vert\cdot\Vert$, define \[ L_v=|\iota(\boldsymbol{b}_v)\cdot \boldsymbol{\zeta}^{\ast}|=|\boldsymbol{b}_v\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast} |=|b_{1,v} \xi_1 + b_{2,v} \xi_2 + b_{3,v}|, \quad M_v=M_v(\Vert\cdot\Vert)=\Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{b}}_v\Vert^{\prime}=\Vert \widehat{\iota(\boldsymbol{b}_v)}\Vert \] and $T_v=M_v-1/2$ as in the proof for the maximum norm but where $M_v, T_v$ are now defined with respect to our norm $\Vert\cdot\Vert$. Then by the equivalence of norms on $\mathbb{R}^n$, for any integer vector of norm $\Vert (x_1,\ldots,x_n)\Vert\le T_v$ we still have \[ \max_{1\le i\le n} |x_i|\le C(\Vert\cdot\Vert) \cdot T_v \] for some constant $C$ depending on the norm only. We replace \eqref{eq:ob} by this modified inequality and follow the proof of the special case Lemma~\ref{lema} where the maximum norm was treated. The twist by the constant $C$ will result in some altered value of $c_n$, depending on the chosen norm, for the same conclusion. We omit its explicit calculation in dependence of~$C$.
nodes.statement_short: Adapt the measure argument of Lemma 5.3 to an arbitrary norm.

nodes.name: Analogy
nodes.statement: The proof of step II works analogously to the special case of maximum norm in Section \ref{Sect6}.
nodes.statement_short: Analogous to the max-norm case.

nodes.name: Projected norm
nodes.statement: Our norm $\Vert\cdot\Vert$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$ induces a projected norm $\Vert\cdot\Vert^{\prime}$ on $\mathbb{R}^2$ via \begin{equation} \Vert (x_1, x_2) \Vert^{\prime}:= \Vert (x_1,x_2,0,\ldots,0) \Vert. \end{equation} Then for this norm $\Vert\cdot\Vert^{\prime}$ we apply step I to get $\boldsymbol{\xi}=(\xi_1, \xi_2)$ with the property \[ \limsup_{t\to\infty} t^n \psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{1\times 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert^{\prime}, t) = c. \] Let $\boldsymbol{b}_v=(b_{1,v}, b_{2,v}, b_{3,v})$ be the integer vector sequence constructed in Step I.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Step I to the projected norm.

nodes.name: Upper bound
nodes.statement: By construction of $\Vert\cdot\Vert^{\prime}$, it is again clear by the same argument as in Proposition~\ref{pro} that any vector $\boldsymbol{\zeta}=(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_n)\in \mathbb{R}^n$ extending $\boldsymbol{\xi}$ has Dirichlet constant at most $c$ with respect to $\Vert\cdot\Vert$, i.e. \[ \limsup_{t\to\infty} t^n \psi_{\boldsymbol{\zeta}}^{1\times n}(\Vert\cdot\Vert, t) \le \limsup_{t\to\infty} t^n \psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{1\times 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert^{\prime}, t) = c. \] Indeed, we can choose the embedded integer vectors $\iota(\boldsymbol{b}_v)$ via the embedding \[ \iota: (y_1, y_2,y_3)\to (y_1,y_2,0,\ldots,0,y_3) \] from $\mathbb{R}^3$ to $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$, which by \eqref{eq:pno} induce the same heights and approximation quality \[ \Vert \widehat{\iota(\boldsymbol{b}_v)}\Vert=\Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{b}}_v\Vert^{\prime}, \qquad |\iota(\boldsymbol{b}_v)\cdot \boldsymbol{\zeta}^{\ast}|=|\boldsymbol{b}_v\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast} | \] for any $\boldsymbol{b}_v$, with hat notation according to \eqref{eq:hatnot} on the respective spaces.
nodes.statement_short: Embedded best approximations give Dirichlet constant at most c.

nodes.name: Lower bound setup
nodes.statement: For the non-trivial lower estimate \[ \limsup_{t\to\infty} t^n \psi_{\boldsymbol{\zeta}}^{1\times n}(\Vert\cdot\Vert, t)\ge c \] with respect to $\Vert\cdot\Vert$, define \[ L_v=|\iota(\boldsymbol{b}_v)\cdot \boldsymbol{\zeta}^{\ast}|=|\boldsymbol{b}_v\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast} |=|b_{1,v} \xi_1 + b_{2,v} \xi_2 + b_{3,v}|, \quad M_v=M_v(\Vert\cdot\Vert)=\Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{b}}_v\Vert^{\prime}=\Vert \widehat{\iota(\boldsymbol{b}_v)}\Vert \] and $T_v=M_v-1/2$ as in the proof for the maximum norm but where $M_v, T_v$ are now defined with respect to our norm $\Vert\cdot\Vert$.
nodes.statement_short: Define L_v, M_v, T_v for the norm.

nodes.name: Norm equivalence
nodes.statement: Then by the equivalence of norms on $\mathbb{R}^n$, for any integer vector of norm $\Vert (x_1,\ldots,x_n)\Vert\le T_v$ we still have \[ \max_{1\le i\le n} |x_i|\le C(\Vert\cdot\Vert) \cdot T_v \] for some constant $C$ depending on the norm only. We replace \eqref{eq:ob} by this modified inequality and follow the proof of the special case Lemma~\ref{lema} where the maximum norm was treated. The twist by the constant $C$ will result in some altered value of $c_n$, depending on the chosen norm, for the same conclusion. We omit its explicit calculation in dependence of~$C$.
nodes.statement_short: Replace (17) by a constant multiple and follow Lemma 5.3.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3.6
nodes.statement:
We point out again that our proof below can be significantly shortened using the preprint~\cite[Corollary~1]{AginWeiss2024} which appeared later. We detail the parts that can be simplified in the proof below. In short, when taking into account~\cite{AginWeiss2024}, the main new substance still needed is Lemma~ef{lemme} below. \subsection{Proof excluding linear independence claims} We proceed as in~\S~ef{st1} to construct the first two elements of the first line of our matrix $\Omega$ by $ oldsymbol{\xi}=(\xi_1,\xi_2)=(\Omega_{1,1}, \Omega_{1,2})$, upon modifying the construction so that \eqref{eq:IIi} is replaced by \[ 	au \mu -1 =  rac{n}{m} \mu \overset{\eqref{matrix dimension condition}}{\ge} 2\mu. \] Define $\psi_{ oldsymbol{\xi}}^{1	imes 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}, t)$ with respect to the restriction $\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}$ of $\Vert\cdot\Vert_1$ to $\mathbb{R}^2$ in the integer vector $ oldsymbol{b}$, as in \eqref{eq:pno}. Then by the same arguments of the proof of Theorem~ef{jia} we will have  egin{equation} \limsup_{t	o\infty} t^{n/m} \psi_{ oldsymbol{\xi}}^{1	imes 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}, t)= c. \end{equation} Hereby we use our assumption $n/m\ge 2$ for Case 2, based on Minkowski's Second Convex Body Theorem, to work analogously. Now take the matrix $V\in \mathbb{R}^{m	imes 2}$ with all $m$ lines equal to $ oldsymbol{\xi}$, i.e. \[ V_{j,1}= \xi_{1}, \qquad V_{j,2}=\xi_{2}, \qquad 1\leq j\le m. \] This matrix gives rise to an approximation function $\psi_{V}^{m	imes 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}, \Vert\cdot\Vert_2, t)$ with norms defined as above. First, assume for simplicity that $\Vert\cdot\Vert_2=\Vert\cdot\Vert_{\infty}$ is the maximum norm on $\mathbb{R}^m$. We claim that  egin{equation} \psi_{V}^{m	imes 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}, \Vert\cdot\Vert_2, t)=\psi_{ oldsymbol{\xi}}^{1	imes 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}, t), \qquad t>0. \end{equation} Indeed to see  egin{equation} \psi_{V}^{m	imes 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}, \Vert\cdot\Vert_2, t)\ge \psi_{ oldsymbol{\xi}}^{1	imes 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}, t) \end{equation} for all $t$, note that for arbitrary $ oldsymbol{b}=(b_1,\ldots,b_{m+2})\in\mathbb{Z}^{m+2}$ and for $V^{\ast}\in \mathbb{R}^{m	imes (m+2)}$ obtained by glueing $V$ to the $m	imes m$ identity matrix to the right, the induced value \[ \Vert V^{\ast}\cdot  oldsymbol{b}\Vert_2= \Vert V\cdot \widehat{ oldsymbol{b}}+ 	ilde{ oldsymbol{b}}\Vert_2= \Vert V\cdot (b_1,b_{2}) + (b_{3},\ldots,b_{m+2})\Vert_2 \] with vectors interpreted as column vectors, is at least as large as the modulus of any entry, since we are considering $\|\cdot\|_{2}=\|\cdot\|_{\infty}$ for now. But for the first entry this equals $|(b_1,b_2)\cdot  oldsymbol{\xi} +b_3|=|  oldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}\cdot (b_1,b_2,b_3)|$. Taking the minimum over $ oldsymbol{b}$ as in the definition of $\psi_V^{m	imes 2}$ shows the inequality \eqref{eq:einer}. Conversely, if we extend arbitrary $ oldsymbol{b}=(b_1, b_2, b_3)\in\mathbb{Z}^3$ into $\mathbb{Z}^{m+2}$ via $\eta( oldsymbol{b}):=(b_1,b_2,b_3,\ldots,b_{3})$ with last $m$ coordinates equal to $b_3$, by choice of maximum norm, we have $\Vert V^{\ast}\cdot \eta( oldsymbol{b})\Vert_2 = | oldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast} \cdot (b_1,b_2,b_3)|$, so passing to the minimum over $ oldsymbol{b}$ again we get the reverse inequality  egin{equation} \psi_{V}^{m	imes 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}, \Vert\cdot\Vert_2, t)\le \psi_{ oldsymbol{\xi}}^{1	imes 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}, t). \end{equation} Combining \eqref{eq:fichte}, \eqref{eq:teir} we get \[ \limsup_{t	o\infty} t^{n/m} \psi_{V}^{m	imes2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}, \Vert\cdot\Vert_2, t)=\limsup_{t	o\infty} t^{n/m} \psi_{ oldsymbol{\xi}}^{1	imes 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}, t)= c. \] We note that up to this point, the claim alternatively follows directly from the aforementioned preprint~\cite[Corollary~1]{AginWeiss2024}. \par To finish the proof, we show that for a positive measure set of $B\in \mathbb{R}^{m	imes (n-2)}$ inducing $\Omega=(V,B)$ via putting it to the right of $V$, we have \[ \limsup_{t	o\infty} t^{n/m} \psi_{\Omega}^{m	imes n}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1, \Vert\cdot\Vert_2, t)=\limsup_{t	o\infty} t^{n/m} \psi_{V}^{m	imes 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}, \Vert\cdot\Vert_2, t). \] Again the inequality  egin{equation} \limsup_{t	o\infty} t^{n/m} \psi_{\Omega}^{m	imes n}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1, \Vert\cdot\Vert_2, t)\le \limsup_{t	o\infty} t^{n/m} \psi_{V}^{m	imes 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}, \Vert\cdot\Vert_2, t) \end{equation} is easy to check for arbitrary $\Vert\cdot\Vert_2$ and extensions $\Omega\in\mathbb{R}^{m	imes n}$ of $V$ by an arbitrary matrix $B\in \mathbb{R}^{m	imes (n-2)}$. Indeed, for a sufficient estimate \[ \psi_{\Omega}^{m	imes n}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1, \Vert\cdot\Vert_2, t)\le \psi_{V}^{m	imes 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}, \Vert\cdot\Vert_2, t), \qquad t>0 \] we embed the integer best approximations of $V$ by adding $0$ coordinates via \[ \sigma:\; oldsymbol{b}=(b_1, b_2, \ldots, b_{m+2})	o (b_1,b_2,0,\ldots,0,b_3,\ldots,b_{m+2})\in\mathbb{Z}^{m+n}. \] These induce the same norm $\Vert \widehat{\sigma( oldsymbol{b})} \Vert_1=\Vert \widehat{ oldsymbol{b}} \Vert_1^{\prime}$ where \[ \widehat{\sigma( oldsymbol{b})}= (b_1,b_2,\ldots,b_n)=(b_1,b_2,0,\ldots,0), \qquad \widehat{ oldsymbol{b}}= (b_1,b_2), \] with hat again as in \eqref{eq:hatnot} on the respective spaces. With $\Omega^{\ast}$ derived from $\Omega$ likewise as for $V^{\ast}$ (i.e. add the identity matrix to the right hand side of $\Omega$), they further induce the same approximation qualities $\Vert \Omega^{\ast}\cdot \sigma( oldsymbol{b}) \Vert_2=\Vert V^{\ast}\cdot  oldsymbol{b} \Vert_2$ since in fact $\Omega^{\ast}\cdot \sigma( oldsymbol{b}) =V^{\ast}\cdot  oldsymbol{b}$, proving \eqref{eq:frit}. For the reverse estimate  egin{equation} \limsup_{t	o\infty} t^{n/m} \psi_{\Omega}^{m	imes n}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1, \Vert\cdot\Vert_2, t)\ge \limsup_{t	o\infty} t^{n/m} \psi_{V}^{m	imes 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}, \Vert\cdot\Vert_2, t)=c, \end{equation} we use a generalisation of Step II from~\S~ef{st2} for $m>1$ as in Moshchevitin~\cite[Theorem~12]{ngm}. We obtain that for small enough $c$ and a positive measure set of remaining matrices $B\in \mathbb{R}^{m	imes (n-2)}$ with respect to $m(n-2)$ dimensional Lebesgue measure when added to the right of $V$ to obtain $\Omega$, we have \eqref{eq:trif}. If $m=1$ then we require the condition $n
e m+2=3$. Moreover, the assumption $n\ge 2m$ is vital for the volume estimates. See Lemma~ef{lemme} below for a generalisation. The proof for $\Vert\cdot\Vert_2$ the maximum norm is complete. Now let the norm $\Vert\cdot\Vert_2$ be arbitrary. Again we prove \eqref{eq:einer}, \eqref{eq:zweier}, \eqref{eq:frit}, \eqref{eq:trif}. The critical estimates where the norm $\Vert\cdot\Vert_2$ is relevant for the argument are \eqref{eq:einer}, \eqref{eq:zweier}. First notice that by the special form of $V$, if $ oldsymbol{b}$ is not of the form $ oldsymbol{b}=(b_1,b_2,b_3,b_3,\ldots,b_3)\in \mathbb{Z}^{m+2}$ then some entry of $V^{\ast}\cdot  oldsymbol{b}$ will be of modulus at least $1/2$, so $\Vert V^{\ast}\cdot  oldsymbol{b}\Vert_{\infty}\ge 1/2$, hence by equivalence of norms, we deduce \[ \Vert V^{\ast}\cdot  oldsymbol{b}\Vert_2 \gg 1 \] with some absolute constant depending on the norm $\Vert\cdot\Vert_2$ only. Hence we only need to take into account vectors of the form $ oldsymbol{b}=(b_1,b_2,b_3,b_3,\ldots,b_3)$ when studying $\psi_{V}^{m	imes 2}$. But then the vector $V^{\ast}\cdot  oldsymbol{b}\in \mathbb{R}^m$ lies on the line $\lambda\cdot (1,1,\ldots,1)\in \mathbb{R}^m$ and has norm $|\lambda|\cdot \Vert (1,1,\ldots,1)\Vert_2$ proportional to $|\lambda|$. Hence we have to minimize $|\lambda|$. In~\S~ef{st1}, see in particular Lemma~ef{wichtig!}, we showed that this is achieved when the subvector $(b_1,b_2,b_3)$ is essentially of the form $ oldsymbol{v}_j=(A_j,0,-F_j)$ and $ oldsymbol{w}_j=(0,B_j,-G_j)$ for $A_j, B_j, F_j, G_j$ defined in the same section (as shown in~\S~ef{st1}, for the other possible vectors of Lemma~ef{wichtig!} we may only improve the approximation quality by a negligible factor $1+o(1)$ as $j	o\infty$). These arguments show that the best integer approximations for $V$ are essentially of the form  egin{equation}  oldsymbol{c}_j:= (A_j, 0 , -F_j, \ldots , -F_j ), \qquad  oldsymbol{d}_j:= (0, B_j , -G_j, \ldots , -G_j ) \end{equation} so that for $ oldsymbol{v}_j,  oldsymbol{w}_j\in\mathbb{Z}^3$ as before, we get error vectors \[ V^{\ast}\cdot  oldsymbol{a}_j= V\cdot  egin{pmatrix} A_j \ 0 \end{pmatrix} - F_j\cdot  egin{pmatrix} 1 \ 1 \ \vdots \ 1 \end{pmatrix}= oldsymbol{v}_j\cdot  oldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}\cdot  egin{pmatrix} 1 \ 1 \ \vdots \ 1 \end{pmatrix}\in \mathbb{R}^m \] and \[ V^{\ast}\cdot  oldsymbol{b}_j= V\cdot  egin{pmatrix} 0 \ B_j \end{pmatrix}- G_j\cdot  egin{pmatrix} 1 \ 1 \ \vdots \ 1 \end{pmatrix}= oldsymbol{w}_j\cdot  oldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}\cdot  egin{pmatrix} 1 \ 1 \ \vdots \ 1 \end{pmatrix}\in \mathbb{R}^m. \] Then for $\Gamma:=\Vert(1,1,\ldots,1)\Vert_2$ they have norms \[ \left\Vert V^{\ast}\cdot  oldsymbol{c}_jight\Vert_2= \vert  oldsymbol{v}_j\cdot  oldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|\cdot \Gamma, \qquad \left\Vert V^{\ast}\cdot  oldsymbol{d}_jight\Vert_2= \vert  oldsymbol{w}_j\cdot  oldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|\cdot \Gamma. \] Thus we have to adjust the proof of the special case by the constant factor $\Gamma$ in the calculation, so that in order to finalize Step I we now need to pick \[ r=c^{-1}\Gamma^{-1} d_2^n,\qquad d_2= \Vert  oldsymbol{e}_2\Vert_1^{\prime}=\Vert (0,1)\Vert_1^{\prime} \] to get \eqref{eq:zweier}. The reverse inequality \eqref{eq:einer} holds as well as we noticed that the vectors in \eqref{eq:vecin} are (essentially) the integer best approximations. We observed that \eqref{eq:frit} holds independent of $\Vert\cdot\Vert_2$. Note that again this step follows immediately via a different proof from the preprint~\cite[Corollary~1]{AginWeiss2024}. \par Finally, Step II is to again show the reverse inequalities \eqref{eq:trif} hold. This is done analogously to Lemma~ef{lema} but in higher dimension, building up on ideas of Moshchevitin~\cite[Theorem~12]{ngm}. Again the claim is essentially irrespective of the norm $\Vert\cdot\Vert_2$. We state the according analogue of Lemma~ef{lema} that we will prove analogously but without effort to make constants effective.  egin{lemma} Let $m,n$ be positive integers with $n\ge 2$, and $(m,n)
e (1,3)$. Let $\Vert\cdot\Vert_1$ and $\Vert\cdot\Vert_2$ be any norms on $\mathbb{R}^n$ and $\mathbb{R}^m$ and $\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}$ be the restriction of $\Vert\cdot\Vert_1$ to $\mathbb{R}^2$ as in \eqref{eq:pno}. Further, let $V\in \mathbb{R}^{m	imes 2}$ be any matrix with  egin{equation} \limsup_{t	o\infty} t^{n/m} \psi_{V}^{m	imes 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}, \Vert\cdot\Vert_2, t)= c \end{equation} for small enough $c\in [0,c_0(m,n,\Vert.\Vert_1,\Vert.\Vert_2)]$, with $c_0$ depending on $m,n$ and the norms. Let $ oldsymbol{b}_v\in\mathbb{Z}^{m+2}$ be the associated sequence of best approximations, and $\hat{ oldsymbol{b}}_v= (b_{v,1}, b_{v,2})$ of norms and approximation qualities \[ M_v:=\Vert \hat{ oldsymbol{b}}_v \Vert_1^{\prime}, \qquad L_v:= \Vert V^{\ast}\cdot  oldsymbol{b}_v\Vert_2. \] Then, for a positive measure set $\mathcal{Y}\subseteq B_{m(n-2)}( oldsymbol{0},1)\subseteq \mathbb{R}^{m(n-2)}$ consisting of matrices $B\in \mathbb{R}^{m	imes (n-2)}$, we have that for an infinite subsequence of integers $(v_r)_{r\in\mathbb{N}}$, letting $T_{v}:=M_{v+1}-1/2$ for $v\ge 1$, we have  egin{equation} \lim_{r	o\infty} T_{v_r}^{n/m} \psi_V^{m	imes 2}(T_{v_r}) = \limsup_{v	o\infty} T_{v}^{n/m}\cdot \psi_{V}^{m	imes 2}(T_{v}) =c \end{equation} i.e. realising the limsup, and the integer best approximation for $\Omega=(V,B)\in \mathbb{R}^{m	imes n}$ at $T_{v_r}$ is for $r\ge 1$ given as \[ b_{1,v_r} oldsymbol{e}_1+ b_{2,v_r} oldsymbol{e}_2+ b_{3,v_r} oldsymbol{e}_{n+1}+\cdots+b_{m+2,v_r} oldsymbol{e}_{n+m}= (b_{1,v_r},b_{2,v_r},0,\ldots,0,b_{3,v_r},\ldots,b_{m+2,v_r})\in \mathbb{Z}^{n+m}. \] Thus, the best approximation function at values $T_{v_r}$ equals  egin{equation} \psi_{\Omega}^{m	imes n}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1, \Vert\cdot\Vert_2,T_{v_r})=\psi_{V}^{m	imes 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}, \Vert\cdot\Vert_2, T_{v_r})= L_{v_r},\qquad r\ge 1. \end{equation} \end{lemma}  egin{proof} First assume $n
e m+2$, this condition will be removed later in the case of $m>1$. Fix $V \in \mathbb{R}^{m	imes 2}$. For the same reason as in the proof of Lemma~ef{lema}, we may assume \[ \lim_{v	o\infty} T_v^{n/m}\psi_{V}^{m	imes 2}(T_v)=c \] and ignore \eqref{eq:ignore}. As in the proof of Lemma~ef{lema}, we construct the set $\mathcal{Y}$ to be composed of matrices $B\in \mathcal{Y}\subseteq \mathbb{R}^{m	imes(n-2)}$ such that the matrices $\Omega=(V,B)\in \mathbb{R}^{m	imes n}$ satisfy \[ \psi_{\Omega}^{m	imes n}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1, \Vert\cdot\Vert_2,T_{v})=\psi_{V}^{m	imes 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}, \Vert\cdot\Vert_2, T_{v})= L_v. \] By the equivalence of norms we have that there exists $C(\|\cdot\|_{1})>0$ dependent only on $\|\cdot\|_{1}$ such that for any $\hat{ oldsymbol{x}}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$  egin{equation*} \|\hat{ oldsymbol{x}}\|_{1}\leq T_{v} \quad \implies \quad \|\hat{ oldsymbol{x}}\|_{\infty} \leq C(\|\cdot\|_{1})T_{v}. \end{equation*} Thus if again $\Omega^{\ast}=(V,B,I)\in \mathbb{R}^{m	imes (m+n)}$ is obtained by putting the $m	imes m$ identity matrix, I, to the right of $\Omega$ and we let  egin{equation*} S_{v}:=\left\{ B \in B_{m(n-2)}( oldsymbol{0},1): \underset{0<\|\hat{ oldsymbol{x}}\|_{\infty}\leq C(\|\cdot\|_{1})T_{v}}{\min_{ oldsymbol{x} \in \mathbb{Z}^{n+m}}} \left\|(V,B,I)\cdot  oldsymbol{x} ight\|_{2} \geq L_{v} ight\}\, , \end{equation*} then $\mathcal{Y} \supseteq \limsup_{v	o \infty} S_{v}$. Hence if we can show that the set  egin{equation} \lambda_{m(n-2)}\left( \liminf_{v	o \infty} S_{v}^{c} ight) \leq \delta < \lambda_{m(n-2)}\left(B_{m(n-2)}( oldsymbol{0},1)ight) \end{equation} then clearly $\lambda_{m(n-2)}(\mathcal{Y})>0$. Furthermore, if we show that  egin{equation} \lambda_{m(n-2)}(S_{v}^{c})\leq \delta \qquad v\geq 1, \end{equation} then applying Proposition~ef{pp} we have \eqref{Y condition}, so proving \eqref{Svc size} is sufficient to verify $\lambda_{m(n-2)}(\mathcal{Y})>0$. \par Let $z=(z_{3},\dots,z_{n})$, $y=(x_{n+1},\dots, x_{n+m})$ and  egin{equation*} X_{v}(z,x_{1},x_{2},y)=\left\{  oldsymbol{\gamma} \in B_{m(n-2)}( oldsymbol{0},1) : \left(  egin{array}{c} z_{3}\gamma_{1,1} + \dots + z_{n}\gamma_{1,n-2} \ \vdots \quad \quad \vdots \ z_{3}\gamma_{m,1}+\dots + z_{n}\gamma_{m,n-2} \end{array} ight) \in J_{v}(x_{1},x_{2},y) ight\} \end{equation*} where  egin{equation*} J_{v}(x_{1},x_{2},y):=\prod_{i=1}^{m} (-x_{1}\xi_{1}-x_{2}\xi_{2} -x_{n+i}-C(\|\cdot\|_{2})L_{v}, -x_{1}\xi_{1}-x_{2}\xi_{2} -x_{n+i}+C(\|\cdot\|_{2})L_{v}). \end{equation*} Here we have again used equivalence of norms, namely that there exists $C(\|\cdot\|_{2})>0$ dependent only on $\|\cdot\|_{2}$ so that for any $X\in\mathbb{R}^{m}$  egin{equation*} C(\|\cdot\|_{2})^{-1}\|X\|_{\infty}\leq \|X\|_{2} \leq C(\|\cdot\|_{2})\|X\|_{\infty}. \end{equation*} Considering one row of $X_{v}(z,x_{1},x_{2},y)$ at a time (denoted $X_{v}^{(i)}(z,x_{1},x_{2},y)$ for $1\leq i \leq m$) we have the same calculation as in \eqref{volcume calculation}, that is  egin{equation*} \lambda_{n-2}\left(X_{v}^{(i)}(z,x_{1},x_{2},y)ight) \leq 2C(\|\cdot\|_{2})L_{v}\lambda_{n-3}(B_{n-3}( oldsymbol{0},1)) rac{1}{\|z\|_{\infty}}. \end{equation*} Hence  egin{align*} \lambda_{m(n-2)}\left(X_{v}(z,x_{1},x_{2},y)ight) &\leq 2^{m}C(\|\cdot\|_{2})^{m}L_{v}^{m}\lambda_{n-3}(B_{n-3}( oldsymbol{0},1))^{m} rac{1}{\|z\|_{\infty}^{m}}\ &=C(m,n,\|\cdot\|_{1},\|\cdot\|_{2})L_{v}^{m}  rac{1}{\|z\|_{\infty}^{m}}. \end{align*} Using similar calculations as appearing in Lemma~ef{lema} we have  egin{align*} \lambda_{m(n-2)}\left(S_{v}^{c}ight)& \leq \sum_{0< \max_{i=1,2}|x_{i}|\leq C(\|\cdot\|_{1})T_{v}}\sum_{\|y\|_{\infty}\leq C(\|\cdot\|_{1})T_{v}}\sum_{\|z\|_{\infty}\leq C(\|\cdot\|_{1})T_{v}} \lambda_{m(n-2)}\left(X_{v}(z,x_{1},x_{2},y)ight)\ &\leq C(m,n,\|\cdot\|_{1},\|\cdot\|_{2})L_{v}^{m}T_{v}^{m+2}\sum_{\|z\|_{\infty}\leq C(\|\cdot\|_{1})T_{v}} rac{1}{\|z\|_{\infty}^{m}} \ & \leq C'(m,n,\|\cdot\|_{1},\|\cdot\|_{2})L_{v}^{m}T_{v}^{m+2}\sum_{k=1}^{ \lfloor C(\|\cdot\|_{1})T_{v}floor}k^{n-3-m}\ &\overset{(n
e m+2)}{\leq} C''(m,n,\|\cdot\|_{1},\|\cdot\|_{2})L_{v}^{m}T_{v}^{m+2}T_{v}^{1+n-3-m}\ &\leq C''(m,n,\|\cdot\|_{1},\|\cdot\|_{2})L_{v}^{m}T_{v}^{n}. \end{align*} Thus, for any $0<\delta<\lambda_{m(n-2)}\left(B_{m(n-2)}( oldsymbol{0},1)ight)$, if $L_{v}<cT_{v}^{- rac{n}{m}}$ then for any $c\in(0,C'''(m,n,\|\cdot\|_{1}))$ with  egin{equation*} C'''(m,n,\|\cdot\|_{1},\|\cdot\|_{2}) < \left( rac{\delta}{C''(m,n,\|\cdot\|_{1},\|\cdot\|_{2})}ight)^{ rac{1}{m}}, \end{equation*} we have that $\lambda_{m(n-2)}\left(S_{v}^{c}ight)<\delta$ as required. Finally we explain how to avoid the condition $n
e m+2$ when $m\ge 2$. Instead of extending $V\in \mathbb{R}^{m	imes 2}$ directly to the desired $m	imes n$ matrix $\Omega$, we iteratively apply Lemma~ef{lemme}, adding a single column to $V$ at each step. Precisely, suppose $m\geq 2$ and $n=m+2$. Begin with some $V=	ilde{V}_{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{m	imes 2}$ satisfying \eqref{V property}. Apply Lemma~ef{lemme} to construct a set of $m$-dimensional positive measure matrices $\Omega_{1}\in \mathbb{R}^{m	imes 3}$ with property \eqref{eq:forti}. Define $	ilde{V}_{2}:=\Omega_{1}$ to be any of the matrices in the the constructed set. Note $	ilde{V}_{2}$ satisfies  egin{equation*} \psi_{	ilde{V}_{2}}^{m	imes 3}(\|\cdot\|^{''}_{1},\|\cdot\|_{2},T_{v_{r}})=\psi_{	ilde{V}_{1}}^{m	imes 2}(\|\cdot\|^{'}_{1},\|\cdot\|_{2},T_{v_{r}})\, , \end{equation*} with $\|\cdot\|^{''}_{1}$ now being the restriction of $\|\cdot\|_{1}$ to $\mathbb{R}^{3}$. So  egin{equation*} \limsup_{t	o\infty} t^{n/m}\psi_{	ilde{V}_{2}}^{m	imes 3}(\|\cdot\|^{''}_{1},\|\cdot\|_{2},t)=c\, , \end{equation*} Note $	ilde{V}_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{m	imes 3}$ rather than $\mathbb{R}^{m	imes 2}$, but it is readily verified that we can copy the above proof with obvious modifications. So, we construct a set of $m$-dimensional positive measure matrices $\Omega_{2}\in \mathbb{R}^{m	imes 4}$ with the desired properties of Lemma~ef{lemme}. Define $	ilde{V}_{3}:=\Omega_{2}$ for any of the matrices in the above set and repeat. The same argument follows as above. In this way we obtain a sequence of matrices  egin{equation*} \Omega_{1}=: 	ilde{V}_{2} \in \mathbb{R}^{m	imes 3}, \Omega_{2}=:	ilde{V}_{3}\in \mathbb{R}^{m	imes 4},\ldots, \Omega_{m-1}=:	ilde{V}_{m+1}\in \mathbb{R}^{m	imes(m+1)},\Omega_{m}=:\Omega\in \mathbb{R}^{m	imes (m+2)}\, . \end{equation*} For each $2< 	ilde{n} \leq m+2$ the extension from $	ilde{V}_{	ilde{n}-2} \in \mathbb{R}^{m	imes (	ilde{n}-1)}$ to an $m	imes 	ilde{n}$ matrix follows readily by copying the above proof of Lemma~ef{lemme} (with the restriction $n
eq m+2$) with obvious modifications. Note we avoid the condition $	ilde{n}= m+(	ilde{n}-1)$ since $m\geq 2$. Thus, at each step we construct a set of matrices $\Omega_{	ilde{n}-1}\in \mathbb{R}^{m	imes 	ilde{n}}$ with positive $m$-dimensional measure, each with the desired properties of \eqref{eq:forti}. It is readily checked that the required convergence estimates still work a fortiori as $n\ge 	ilde{n}$ and $m$ remains constant. Using Marstrand's slicing lemma \cite{mars} for fibered sets, we increase the Hausdorff dimension by $m$ in every step. There are $m$ steps, hence we arrive at the dimension of at least $m^{2}=m(n-2)$. \end{proof} There is nothing essential about $V$ having two columns as the last part of the proof confirms. Note that our proof above avoids the condition $n
e m+2$ as soon as $m>1$, contrasting the requirement $n\ge 4$ in Lemma~ef{lema} where $m=1$. We point out that a similar argument works to generalize the original result in~\cite{ngm}, again when $m>1$. All claims of Theorem~ef{thm5} apart from the linear independence statements are proved. \subsection{Proof of linear independence claims} The first claim (i) on linear independence of rows follows from Step II. Aside from the metrical claim, note that it suffices to prove linearly independent rows can be arranged for the submatrix $B\in \mathbb{R}^{m	imes (n-2)}$ of $\Omega=(V,B)$. Now since $n-2\ge m$ by \eqref{matrix dimension condition}, the matrix $B$ does not have fewer columns than rows, so if $B$ does not have the property it is rank deficient. However, as indicated in Section~ef{Sek3.1}, looking at minors yields that the set of rank-deficient matrices has positive codimension and thus zero Lebesgue measure. On the other hand, we showed that a positive Lebesgue measure set of matrices $B$ gives rise to $\Omega$ as in the theorem. Hence removing such rank-deficient matrices still leaves us with a set of positive $m	imes (n-2)$-dimensional Lebesgue measure from which we can choose arbitrary $B$. For the latter claim (ii) on $\mathbb{Q}$ linearly independent entries, note that in the construction of Section~ef{sec61} certain entries of $V$ (thus $\Omega$) are identical, so the condition does not hold. To fulfil this additional property, let us modify our construction by varying signs. First construct the submatrix $V\in \mathbb{R}^{m	imes 2}$ as above by taking for $A_j, B_j$ as before \[ \Omega_{k,1}=V_{k,1}= \sum_{j=1}^{\infty} \delta_{k,j} A_j^{-1}, \qquad \Omega_{k,2}=V_{k,2}= \sum_{j=1}^{\infty} \delta_{k,j}^{\ast} B_j^{-1}, \quad (1\le k\le m) \] with sequences $\delta_{k,j}\in\{-1,1\}$, $\delta_{k,j}^{\ast}\in\{-1,1\}$ to be chosen later. When $\delta_{k,j}=\delta_{k,j}^{\ast}=1$ for all $k,j$ we are in the standard case of the previous sections. When $m=1$, all arising matrices/vectors $(V_{1,1}, V_{1,2})=(\xi_1, \xi_2)$ share the properties of the standard case above. For $m>1$, we get more general error vectors than in \eqref{eq:vecin}, now of the form  egin{equation} 	ilde{ oldsymbol{c}}_j:= V\cdot  egin{pmatrix} A_j \ 0 \end{pmatrix} -  egin{pmatrix} F_{j,1} \ F_{j,2} \ \vdots \ F_{j,m} \end{pmatrix}, \qquad 	ilde{ oldsymbol{d}}_j:= V\cdot  egin{pmatrix} 0 \ B_j \end{pmatrix} -  egin{pmatrix} G_{j,1} \ G_{j,2} \ \vdots \ G_{j,m} \end{pmatrix},\qquad j\ge 1, \end{equation} where \[ F_{j,k}= A_j \sum_{u=1}^{j} \delta_{k,u} A_{u}^{-1}, \qquad G_{j,k}= B_j \sum_{u=1}^{j} \delta_{k,u}^{\ast} B_{u}^{-1}, \qquad (1\le k\le m), \] depending on the choice of $\delta_{k,j}, \delta_{k,j}^{\ast}$. They again satisfy congruence properties $$F_j\equiv \pm 1 mod 6 \quad 	ext{ and} \quad G_j\equiv \pm 1 mod 35$$ for the same reasons, sufficient for coprimality with $6$ respectively $35$. Thus the entries of the remainders $	ilde{ oldsymbol{c}}_j, 	ilde{ oldsymbol{d}}_j$ are given as \[ c_{j,k}= A_j \sum_{u=j+1}^{\infty} \delta_{k,u} A_{u}^{-1}, \qquad d_{j,k}= B_j \sum_{u=j+1}^{\infty} \delta_{k,u}^{\ast} B_{u}^{-1}, \qquad (1\le k\le m). \] However, since $A_j/A_{j+1}	o 0$ and $B_j/B_{j+1}	o 0$ we again see \[ c_{j,k}= \delta_{k,j+1} \cdot A_j A_{j+1}^{-1}(1+o(1)), \qquad d_{j,k}=\delta_{k,j+1}^{\ast} \cdot B_j B_{j+1}^{-1}(1+o(1)), \quad (1\le k\le m). \] Hence, by the equivalence of norms, it is clear that the error vectors in \eqref{eq:errt} all have $\Vert\cdot\Vert_2$ norm of order respectively  egin{equation} \Vert 	ilde{ oldsymbol{c}}_j\Vert_2= A_j A_{j+1}^{-1} \Gamma_j (1+o(1)), \qquad \Vert 	ilde{ oldsymbol{d}}_j\Vert_2=B_j B_{j+1}^{-1} 	ilde{\Gamma}_j (1+o(1)),\qquad j	o\infty, \end{equation} with $\Gamma_j, 	ilde{\Gamma}_j$ of one of the numbers \[ \Gamma_j, 	ilde{\Gamma}_j \in \{ \Vert (\pm 1,\pm 1,\ldots,\pm 1)\Vert_2\}, \qquad j\ge 1, \] for any possible sign choice. The values $	ilde{\Gamma}_j$ do not matter much as the according evaluations will be of negligible order by the analogue of \eqref{eq:frosch}. Now if we let \[ \Gamma:= \max\{ \Vert (\pm 1,\pm 1,\ldots,\pm 1)\Vert_2 \} \] with maximum overall $2^m$ sign choices, we can use the argument of Section~ef{sec61}. Hereby we may assume that the maximizing sign choice occurs for infinitely many $(\delta_{1,j}, \ldots, \delta_{m,j})$, as otherwise we redefine $\Gamma$ via the maximum among those $m$ term sign sequences occurring infinitely often. Moreover, due to \eqref{eq:fertig}, the arguments of Section~ef{st1} applied to each of the $m$ coordinates separately still apply very similarly and yield that the vectors $(A_j, 0 , -F_{j,1},\ldots,-F_{j,m})$ and $(0 , B_j, -G_{j,1},\ldots,-G_{j,m})$ essentially form the sequence of best approximations for the induced $V$. We leave the details to the reader. Then very similar arguments as in the classical case including Lemma~ef{lemme} show that the Dirichlet constant $\Theta^{m	imes n}(\Omega)$ of many such $\Omega=\Omega(\delta,\delta^{\ast})$ equals $c$, as before. Finally we show that for many choices of $\delta_{k,j}, \delta_{k,j}^{\ast}$ all entries of $\Omega\in\mathbb{R}^{m	imes n}$ are linearly independent over $\mathbb{Q}$ together with $\{1\}$. Let us first show this for the submatrix $V\in\mathbb{R}^{m	imes 2}$. Label the entries $V_{i,j}$ of $V$ by $v_1,\ldots,v_{2m}$ with $v_{2h}=V_{h,2}$ and $v_{2h-1}=V_{h,1}$, $1\le h\le m$. Now the first line of $V$ is $\mathbb{Q}$-linearly independent for any choice of $\delta_{1,j}, \delta_{1,j}^{\ast}$ sequences as otherwise the sequence of best approximations for $(V_{1,1}, V_{1,2})$ would terminate, but the proof above shows that this is not the case. Hence $\{ 1,v_1, v_2\}$ is $\mathbb{Q}$-linearly independent. Then we proceed inductively. Having constructed the first $\ell\ge 2$ elements $v_1, \ldots,v_{\ell}$, we choose the $\delta$ or $\delta^{\ast}$ sequence for $v_{\ell+1}$ so that we avoid $\mathbb{Q}$-linear dependence of $v_{\ell+1}$ with the already chosen $1,v_1, \ldots,v_{\ell}$. This is possible since the $\mathbb{Q}$-span of $\{ 1,v_1,\ldots,v_{\ell} \}$ is countable, but we have uncountably many choices of $\delta$ or $\delta^{\ast}$ sequences. These clearly induce uncountably many pairwise distinct numbers $v_{\ell+1}$, the injectivity of the corresponding maps $\varphi: \{-1,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}	o \mathbb{R}$ resp. $\varphi^{\ast}: \{-1,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}	o \mathbb{R}$ follows from the rapid increase of the sequences $A_j$ resp. $B_j$. Repeating this for $\ell=2,3,\ldots,2m-1$, finally all entries of $V$ will be independent over $\mathbb{Q}$ with $\{1\}$, as desired. Now Step II of the proof above combined with the following easy argument show that we can transition from $V$ to $\Omega$.  egin{proposition} Let $g, h$ be positive integers. Assume given real numbers $x_1, \ldots,x_g$ are $\mathbb{Q}$-linearly independent together with $1$. Then only for a set of Hausdorff dimension $h-1$ of vectors $ oldsymbol{y}=(y_1,\ldots,y_h)$ in $\mathbb{R}^h$, the joint vector $ oldsymbol{z}=(x_1,\ldots,x_g,y_1,\ldots,y_h)$ is $\mathbb{Q}$-linearly dependent with $1$. \end{proposition}  egin{proof} Since the $x_j$ are independent, if $\{ 1, oldsymbol{z}\}$ is dependent over $\mathbb{Q}$ then there are integers $M_i, N_i, N$ with \[ N+ \sum_{i=1}^{g} M_i x_i +\sum_{i=1}^{h} N_i y_i = 0 \] and not all $N_i$ are $0$. But this means that $ oldsymbol{y}$ lies in a countable union of affine hyperplanes of $\mathbb{R}^{h}$. Hence we see that the set of $ oldsymbol{y}$ inducing dependency over $\mathbb{Q}$ indeed has Hausdorff dimension at most $h-1$. \end{proof} It suffices to take $g=2m, h=(n-2)m$ and to choose $x_i$ the entries of $V$ (first two columns of $\Omega$) and $y_i$ the remaining entries of $\Omega$ (entries of $B$) in the proposition to conclude that a full dimensional set of possible matrices $B\in \mathbb{R}^{m	imes (n-2)}\cong \mathbb{R}^{m(n-2)}$ remains (in fact of positive $m(n-2)$ dimensional Hausdorff measure).

nodes.name: Generic extension of V preserves best approximations
nodes.statement: Let $m,n$ be positive integers with $n\ge 2$, and $(m,n)\ne (1,3)$. Let $\Vert\cdot\Vert_1$ and $\Vert\cdot\Vert_2$ be any norms on $\mathbb{R}^n$ and $\mathbb{R}^m$ and $\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}$ be the restriction of $\Vert\cdot\Vert_1$ to $\mathbb{R}^2$ as in \eqref{eq:pno}. Further, let $V\in \mathbb{R}^{m\times 2}$ be any matrix with \begin{equation} \limsup_{t\to\infty} t^{n/m} \psi_{V}^{m\times 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}, \Vert\cdot\Vert_2, t)= c \end{equation} for small enough $c\in [0,c_0(m,n,\Vert.\Vert_1,\Vert.\Vert_2)]$, with $c_0$ depending on $m,n$ and the norms. Let $\boldsymbol{b}_v\in\mathbb{Z}^{m+2}$ be the associated sequence of best approximations, and $\hat{\boldsymbol{b}}_v= (b_{v,1}, b_{v,2})$ of norms and approximation qualities \[ M_v:=\Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{b}}_v \Vert_1^{\prime}, \qquad L_v:= \Vert V^{\ast}\cdot \boldsymbol{b}_v\Vert_2. \] Then, for a positive measure set $\mathcal{Y}\subseteq B_{m(n-2)}(\boldsymbol{0},1)\subseteq \mathbb{R}^{m(n-2)}$ consisting of matrices $B\in \mathbb{R}^{m\times (n-2)}$, we have that for an infinite subsequence of integers $(v_r)_{r\in\mathbb{N}}$, letting $T_{v}:=M_{v+1}-1/2$ for $v\ge 1$, we have \begin{equation} \lim_{r\to\infty} T_{v_r}^{n/m} \psi_V^{m\times 2}(T_{v_r}) = \limsup_{v\to\infty} T_{v}^{n/m}\cdot \psi_{V}^{m\times 2}(T_{v}) =c \end{equation} i.e. realising the limsup, and the integer best approximation for $\Omega=(V,B)\in \mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ at $T_{v_r}$ is for $r\ge 1$ given as \[ b_{1,v_r}\boldsymbol{e}_1+ b_{2,v_r}\boldsymbol{e}_2+ b_{3,v_r}\boldsymbol{e}_{n+1}+\cdots+b_{m+2,v_r}\boldsymbol{e}_{n+m}= (b_{1,v_r},b_{2,v_r},0,\ldots,0,b_{3,v_r},\ldots,b_{m+2,v_r})\in \mathbb{Z}^{n+m}. \] Thus, the best approximation function at values $T_{v_r}$ equals \begin{equation} \psi_{\Omega}^{m\times n}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1, \Vert\cdot\Vert_2,T_{v_r})=\psi_{V}^{m\times 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}, \Vert\cdot\Vert_2, T_{v_r})= L_{v_r},\qquad r\ge 1. \end{equation}
assumptions: Let $m,n$ be positive integers with $n\ge 2$, and $(m,n)\ne (1,3)$.

Let $\Vert\cdot\Vert_1$ and $\Vert\cdot\Vert_2$ be any norms on $\mathbb{R}^n$ and $\mathbb{R}^m$ and $\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}$ be the restriction of $\Vert\cdot\Vert_1$ to $\mathbb{R}^2$ as in \eqref{eq:pno}.

Further, let $V\in \mathbb{R}^{m\times 2}$ be any matrix with \begin{equation} \limsup_{t\to\infty} t^{n/m} \psi_{V}^{m\times 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}, \Vert\cdot\Vert_2, t)= c \end{equation} for small enough $c\in [0,c_0(m,n,\Vert.\Vert_1,\Vert.\Vert_2)]$, with $c_0$ depending on $m,n$ and the norms.

Let $\boldsymbol{b}_v\in\mathbb{Z}^{m+2}$ be the associated sequence of best approximations, and $\hat{\boldsymbol{b}}_v= (b_{v,1}, b_{v,2})$ of norms and approximation qualities \[ M_v:=\Vert \hat{\boldsymbol{b}}_v \Vert_1^{\prime}, \qquad L_v:= \Vert V^{\ast}\cdot \boldsymbol{b}_v\Vert_2.
conclusions: Then, for a positive measure set $\mathcal{Y}\subseteq B_{m(n-2)}(\boldsymbol{0},1)\subseteq \mathbb{R}^{m(n-2)}$ consisting of matrices $B\in \mathbb{R}^{m\times (n-2)}$, we have that for an infinite subsequence of integers $(v_r)_{r\in\mathbb{N}}$, letting $T_{v}:=M_{v+1}-1/2$ for $v\ge 1$, we have \begin{equation} \lim_{r\to\infty} T_{v_r}^{n/m} \psi_V^{m\times 2}(T_{v_r}) = \limsup_{v\to\infty} T_{v}^{n/m}\cdot \psi_{V}^{m\times 2}(T_{v}) =c \end{equation} i.e. realising the limsup, and the integer best approximation for $\Omega=(V,B)\in \mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ at $T_{v_r}$ is for $r\ge 1$ given as \[ b_{1,v_r}\boldsymbol{e}_1+ b_{2,v_r}\boldsymbol{e}_2+ b_{3,v_r}\boldsymbol{e}_{n+1}+\cdots+b_{m+2,v_r}\boldsymbol{e}_{n+m}= (b_{1,v_r},b_{2,v_r},0,\ldots,0,b_{3,v_r},\ldots,b_{m+2,v_r})\in \mathbb{Z}^{n+m}. \] Thus, the best approximation function at values $T_{v_r}$ equals \begin{equation} \psi_{\Omega}^{m\times n}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1, \Vert\cdot\Vert_2,T_{v_r})=\psi_{V}^{m\times 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}, \Vert\cdot\Vert_2, T_{v_r})= L_{v_r},\qquad r\ge 1.
