nodes.statement:
First assume $n
e m+2$, this condition will be removed later in the case of $m>1$. Fix $V \in \mathbb{R}^{m	imes 2}$. For the same reason as in the proof of Lemma~ef{lema}, we may assume \[ \lim_{v	o\infty} T_v^{n/m}\psi_{V}^{m	imes 2}(T_v)=c \] and ignore \eqref{eq:ignore}. As in the proof of Lemma~ef{lema}, we construct the set $\mathcal{Y}$ to be composed of matrices $B\in \mathcal{Y}\subseteq \mathbb{R}^{m	imes(n-2)}$ such that the matrices $\Omega=(V,B)\in \mathbb{R}^{m	imes n}$ satisfy \[ \psi_{\Omega}^{m	imes n}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1, \Vert\cdot\Vert_2,T_{v})=\psi_{V}^{m	imes 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}, \Vert\cdot\Vert_2, T_{v})= L_v. \] By the equivalence of norms we have that there exists $C(\|\cdot\|_{1})>0$ dependent only on $\|\cdot\|_{1}$ such that for any $\hat{ oldsymbol{x}}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$  egin{equation*} \|\hat{ oldsymbol{x}}\|_{1}\leq T_{v} \quad \implies \quad \|\hat{ oldsymbol{x}}\|_{\infty} \leq C(\|\cdot\|_{1})T_{v}. \end{equation*} Thus if again $\Omega^{\ast}=(V,B,I)\in \mathbb{R}^{m	imes (m+n)}$ is obtained by putting the $m	imes m$ identity matrix, I, to the right of $\Omega$ and we let  egin{equation*} S_{v}:=\left\{ B \in B_{m(n-2)}( oldsymbol{0},1): \underset{0<\|\hat{ oldsymbol{x}}\|_{\infty}\leq C(\|\cdot\|_{1})T_{v}}{\min_{ oldsymbol{x} \in \mathbb{Z}^{n+m}}} \left\|(V,B,I)\cdot  oldsymbol{x} ight\|_{2} \geq L_{v} ight\}\, , \end{equation*} then $\mathcal{Y} \supseteq \limsup_{v	o \infty} S_{v}$. Hence if we can show that the set  egin{equation} \lambda_{m(n-2)}\left( \liminf_{v	o \infty} S_{v}^{c} ight) \leq \delta < \lambda_{m(n-2)}\left(B_{m(n-2)}( oldsymbol{0},1)ight) \end{equation} then clearly $\lambda_{m(n-2)}(\mathcal{Y})>0$. Furthermore, if we show that  egin{equation} \lambda_{m(n-2)}(S_{v}^{c})\leq \delta \qquad v\geq 1, \end{equation} then applying Proposition~ef{pp} we have \eqref{Y condition}, so proving \eqref{Svc size} is sufficient to verify $\lambda_{m(n-2)}(\mathcal{Y})>0$. \par Let $z=(z_{3},\dots,z_{n})$, $y=(x_{n+1},\dots, x_{n+m})$ and  egin{equation*} X_{v}(z,x_{1},x_{2},y)=\left\{  oldsymbol{\gamma} \in B_{m(n-2)}( oldsymbol{0},1) : \left(  egin{array}{c} z_{3}\gamma_{1,1} + \dots + z_{n}\gamma_{1,n-2} \ \vdots \quad \quad \vdots \ z_{3}\gamma_{m,1}+\dots + z_{n}\gamma_{m,n-2} \end{array} ight) \in J_{v}(x_{1},x_{2},y) ight\} \end{equation*} where  egin{equation*} J_{v}(x_{1},x_{2},y):=\prod_{i=1}^{m} (-x_{1}\xi_{1}-x_{2}\xi_{2} -x_{n+i}-C(\|\cdot\|_{2})L_{v}, -x_{1}\xi_{1}-x_{2}\xi_{2} -x_{n+i}+C(\|\cdot\|_{2})L_{v}). \end{equation*} Here we have again used equivalence of norms, namely that there exists $C(\|\cdot\|_{2})>0$ dependent only on $\|\cdot\|_{2}$ so that for any $X\in\mathbb{R}^{m}$  egin{equation*} C(\|\cdot\|_{2})^{-1}\|X\|_{\infty}\leq \|X\|_{2} \leq C(\|\cdot\|_{2})\|X\|_{\infty}. \end{equation*} Considering one row of $X_{v}(z,x_{1},x_{2},y)$ at a time (denoted $X_{v}^{(i)}(z,x_{1},x_{2},y)$ for $1\leq i \leq m$) we have the same calculation as in \eqref{volcume calculation}, that is  egin{equation*} \lambda_{n-2}\left(X_{v}^{(i)}(z,x_{1},x_{2},y)ight) \leq 2C(\|\cdot\|_{2})L_{v}\lambda_{n-3}(B_{n-3}( oldsymbol{0},1)) rac{1}{\|z\|_{\infty}}. \end{equation*} Hence  egin{align*} \lambda_{m(n-2)}\left(X_{v}(z,x_{1},x_{2},y)ight) &\leq 2^{m}C(\|\cdot\|_{2})^{m}L_{v}^{m}\lambda_{n-3}(B_{n-3}( oldsymbol{0},1))^{m} rac{1}{\|z\|_{\infty}^{m}}\ &=C(m,n,\|\cdot\|_{1},\|\cdot\|_{2})L_{v}^{m}  rac{1}{\|z\|_{\infty}^{m}}. \end{align*} Using similar calculations as appearing in Lemma~ef{lema} we have  egin{align*} \lambda_{m(n-2)}\left(S_{v}^{c}ight)& \leq \sum_{0< \max_{i=1,2}|x_{i}|\leq C(\|\cdot\|_{1})T_{v}}\sum_{\|y\|_{\infty}\leq C(\|\cdot\|_{1})T_{v}}\sum_{\|z\|_{\infty}\leq C(\|\cdot\|_{1})T_{v}} \lambda_{m(n-2)}\left(X_{v}(z,x_{1},x_{2},y)ight)\ &\leq C(m,n,\|\cdot\|_{1},\|\cdot\|_{2})L_{v}^{m}T_{v}^{m+2}\sum_{\|z\|_{\infty}\leq C(\|\cdot\|_{1})T_{v}} rac{1}{\|z\|_{\infty}^{m}} \ & \leq C'(m,n,\|\cdot\|_{1},\|\cdot\|_{2})L_{v}^{m}T_{v}^{m+2}\sum_{k=1}^{ \lfloor C(\|\cdot\|_{1})T_{v}floor}k^{n-3-m}\ &\overset{(n
e m+2)}{\leq} C''(m,n,\|\cdot\|_{1},\|\cdot\|_{2})L_{v}^{m}T_{v}^{m+2}T_{v}^{1+n-3-m}\ &\leq C''(m,n,\|\cdot\|_{1},\|\cdot\|_{2})L_{v}^{m}T_{v}^{n}. \end{align*} Thus, for any $0<\delta<\lambda_{m(n-2)}\left(B_{m(n-2)}( oldsymbol{0},1)ight)$, if $L_{v}<cT_{v}^{- rac{n}{m}}$ then for any $c\in(0,C'''(m,n,\|\cdot\|_{1}))$ with  egin{equation*} C'''(m,n,\|\cdot\|_{1},\|\cdot\|_{2}) < \left( rac{\delta}{C''(m,n,\|\cdot\|_{1},\|\cdot\|_{2})}ight)^{ rac{1}{m}}, \end{equation*} we have that $\lambda_{m(n-2)}\left(S_{v}^{c}ight)<\delta$ as required. Finally we explain how to avoid the condition $n
e m+2$ when $m\ge 2$. Instead of extending $V\in \mathbb{R}^{m	imes 2}$ directly to the desired $m	imes n$ matrix $\Omega$, we iteratively apply Lemma~ef{lemme}, adding a single column to $V$ at each step. Precisely, suppose $m\geq 2$ and $n=m+2$. Begin with some $V=	ilde{V}_{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{m	imes 2}$ satisfying \eqref{V property}. Apply Lemma~ef{lemme} to construct a set of $m$-dimensional positive measure matrices $\Omega_{1}\in \mathbb{R}^{m	imes 3}$ with property \eqref{eq:forti}. Define $	ilde{V}_{2}:=\Omega_{1}$ to be any of the matrices in the the constructed set. Note $	ilde{V}_{2}$ satisfies  egin{equation*} \psi_{	ilde{V}_{2}}^{m	imes 3}(\|\cdot\|^{''}_{1},\|\cdot\|_{2},T_{v_{r}})=\psi_{	ilde{V}_{1}}^{m	imes 2}(\|\cdot\|^{'}_{1},\|\cdot\|_{2},T_{v_{r}})\, , \end{equation*} with $\|\cdot\|^{''}_{1}$ now being the restriction of $\|\cdot\|_{1}$ to $\mathbb{R}^{3}$. So  egin{equation*} \limsup_{t	o\infty} t^{n/m}\psi_{	ilde{V}_{2}}^{m	imes 3}(\|\cdot\|^{''}_{1},\|\cdot\|_{2},t)=c\, , \end{equation*} Note $	ilde{V}_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{m	imes 3}$ rather than $\mathbb{R}^{m	imes 2}$, but it is readily verified that we can copy the above proof with obvious modifications. So, we construct a set of $m$-dimensional positive measure matrices $\Omega_{2}\in \mathbb{R}^{m	imes 4}$ with the desired properties of Lemma~ef{lemme}. Define $	ilde{V}_{3}:=\Omega_{2}$ for any of the matrices in the above set and repeat. The same argument follows as above. In this way we obtain a sequence of matrices  egin{equation*} \Omega_{1}=: 	ilde{V}_{2} \in \mathbb{R}^{m	imes 3}, \Omega_{2}=:	ilde{V}_{3}\in \mathbb{R}^{m	imes 4},\ldots, \Omega_{m-1}=:	ilde{V}_{m+1}\in \mathbb{R}^{m	imes(m+1)},\Omega_{m}=:\Omega\in \mathbb{R}^{m	imes (m+2)}\, . \end{equation*} For each $2< 	ilde{n} \leq m+2$ the extension from $	ilde{V}_{	ilde{n}-2} \in \mathbb{R}^{m	imes (	ilde{n}-1)}$ to an $m	imes 	ilde{n}$ matrix follows readily by copying the above proof of Lemma~ef{lemme} (with the restriction $n
eq m+2$) with obvious modifications. Note we avoid the condition $	ilde{n}= m+(	ilde{n}-1)$ since $m\geq 2$. Thus, at each step we construct a set of matrices $\Omega_{	ilde{n}-1}\in \mathbb{R}^{m	imes 	ilde{n}}$ with positive $m$-dimensional measure, each with the desired properties of \eqref{eq:forti}. It is readily checked that the required convergence estimates still work a fortiori as $n\ge 	ilde{n}$ and $m$ remains constant. Using Marstrand's slicing lemma \cite{mars} for fibered sets, we increase the Hausdorff dimension by $m$ in every step. There are $m$ steps, hence we arrive at the dimension of at least $m^{2}=m(n-2)$.
nodes.statement_short: Same measure counting as Lemma 5.3, row by row, giving lambda(S_v^c) << L_v^m T_v^n. For n=m+2 add one column at a time and use Marstrand's slicing lemma.

nodes.name: Y condition (50)
nodes.statement: \lambda_{m(n-2)}\left( \liminf_{v\to \infty} S_{v}^{c} \right) \leq \delta < \lambda_{m(n-2)}\left(B_{m(n-2)}(\boldsymbol{0},1)\right)
nodes.label: Y condition

nodes.name: Svc size (51)
nodes.statement: \lambda_{m(n-2)}(S_{v}^{c})\leq \delta \qquad v\geq 1,
nodes.label: Svc size

nodes.name: Restriction
nodes.statement: First assume $n\ne m+2$, this condition will be removed later in the case of $m>1$.
nodes.statement_short: First assume n != m+2.

nodes.name: Assume limit
nodes.statement: Fix $V \in \mathbb{R}^{m\times 2}$. For the same reason as in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lema}, we may assume \[ \lim_{v\to\infty} T_v^{n/m}\psi_{V}^{m\times 2}(T_v)=c \] and ignore \eqref{eq:ignore}.
nodes.statement_short: As for Lemma 5.3 assume the limit exists.

nodes.name: Set Y
nodes.statement: As in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lema}, we construct the set $\mathcal{Y}$ to be composed of matrices $B\in \mathcal{Y}\subseteq \mathbb{R}^{m\times(n-2)}$ such that the matrices $\Omega=(V,B)\in \mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ satisfy \[ \psi_{\Omega}^{m\times n}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1, \Vert\cdot\Vert_2,T_{v})=\psi_{V}^{m\times 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}, \Vert\cdot\Vert_2, T_{v})= L_v. \]
nodes.statement_short: Y consists of B keeping psi equal to L_v.

nodes.name: Norm comparison
nodes.statement: By the equivalence of norms we have that there exists $C(\|\cdot\|_{1})>0$ dependent only on $\|\cdot\|_{1}$ such that for any $\hat{\boldsymbol{x}}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$ \begin{equation*} \|\hat{\boldsymbol{x}}\|_{1}\leq T_{v} \quad \implies \quad \|\hat{\boldsymbol{x}}\|_{\infty} \leq C(\|\cdot\|_{1})T_{v}. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Compare ||.||_1 with max norm.

nodes.name: Reduction via Proposition 2
nodes.statement: Thus if again $\Omega^{\ast}=(V,B,I)\in \mathbb{R}^{m\times (m+n)}$ is obtained by putting the $m\times m$ identity matrix, I, to the right of $\Omega$ and we let \begin{equation*} S_{v}:=\left\{ B \in B_{m(n-2)}(\boldsymbol{0},1): \underset{0<\|\hat{\boldsymbol{x}}\|_{\infty}\leq C(\|\cdot\|_{1})T_{v}}{\min_{\boldsymbol{x} \in \mathbb{Z}^{n+m}}} \left\|(V,B,I)\cdot \boldsymbol{x} \right\|_{2} \geq L_{v} \right\}\, , \end{equation*} then $\mathcal{Y} \supseteq \limsup_{v\to \infty} S_{v}$. Hence if we can show that the set \begin{equation} \lambda_{m(n-2)}\left( \liminf_{v\to \infty} S_{v}^{c} \right) \leq \delta < \lambda_{m(n-2)}\left(B_{m(n-2)}(\boldsymbol{0},1)\right) \end{equation} then clearly $\lambda_{m(n-2)}(\mathcal{Y})>0$. Furthermore, if we show that \begin{equation} \lambda_{m(n-2)}(S_{v}^{c})\leq \delta \qquad v\geq 1, \end{equation} then applying Proposition~\ref{pp} we have \eqref{Y condition}, so proving \eqref{Svc size} is sufficient to verify $\lambda_{m(n-2)}(\mathcal{Y})>0$. \par
nodes.statement_short: Suffices to bound lambda(S_v^c) uniformly.

nodes.name: Sets X_v
nodes.statement: Let $z=(z_{3},\dots,z_{n})$, $y=(x_{n+1},\dots, x_{n+m})$ and \begin{equation*} X_{v}(z,x_{1},x_{2},y)=\left\{ \boldsymbol{\gamma} \in B_{m(n-2)}(\boldsymbol{0},1) : \left( \begin{array}{c} z_{3}\gamma_{1,1} + \dots + z_{n}\gamma_{1,n-2} \\ \vdots \quad \quad \vdots \\ z_{3}\gamma_{m,1}+\dots + z_{n}\gamma_{m,n-2} \end{array} \right) \in J_{v}(x_{1},x_{2},y) \right\} \end{equation*} where \begin{equation*} J_{v}(x_{1},x_{2},y):=\prod_{i=1}^{m} (-x_{1}\xi_{1}-x_{2}\xi_{2} -x_{n+i}-C(\|\cdot\|_{2})L_{v}, -x_{1}\xi_{1}-x_{2}\xi_{2} -x_{n+i}+C(\|\cdot\|_{2})L_{v}). \end{equation*} Here we have again used equivalence of norms, namely that there exists $C(\|\cdot\|_{2})>0$ dependent only on $\|\cdot\|_{2}$ so that for any $X\in\mathbb{R}^{m}$ \begin{equation*} C(\|\cdot\|_{2})^{-1}\|X\|_{\infty}\leq \|X\|_{2} \leq C(\|\cdot\|_{2})\|X\|_{\infty}. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Define slab sets X_v row-wise.

nodes.name: Row volume
nodes.statement: Considering one row of $X_{v}(z,x_{1},x_{2},y)$ at a time (denoted $X_{v}^{(i)}(z,x_{1},x_{2},y)$ for $1\leq i \leq m$) we have the same calculation as in \eqref{volcume calculation}, that is \begin{equation*} \lambda_{n-2}\left(X_{v}^{(i)}(z,x_{1},x_{2},y)\right) \leq 2C(\|\cdot\|_{2})L_{v}\lambda_{n-3}(B_{n-3}(\boldsymbol{0},1))\frac{1}{\|z\|_{\infty}}. \end{equation*} Hence \begin{align*} \lambda_{m(n-2)}\left(X_{v}(z,x_{1},x_{2},y)\right) &\leq 2^{m}C(\|\cdot\|_{2})^{m}L_{v}^{m}\lambda_{n-3}(B_{n-3}(\boldsymbol{0},1))^{m}\frac{1}{\|z\|_{\infty}^{m}}\\ &=C(m,n,\|\cdot\|_{1},\|\cdot\|_{2})L_{v}^{m} \frac{1}{\|z\|_{\infty}^{m}}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Each row contributes a factor L_v/||z||.

nodes.name: Total measure
nodes.statement: Using similar calculations as appearing in Lemma~\ref{lema} we have \begin{align*} \lambda_{m(n-2)}\left(S_{v}^{c}\right)& \leq \sum_{0< \max_{i=1,2}|x_{i}|\leq C(\|\cdot\|_{1})T_{v}}\sum_{\|y\|_{\infty}\leq C(\|\cdot\|_{1})T_{v}}\sum_{\|z\|_{\infty}\leq C(\|\cdot\|_{1})T_{v}} \lambda_{m(n-2)}\left(X_{v}(z,x_{1},x_{2},y)\right)\\ &\leq C(m,n,\|\cdot\|_{1},\|\cdot\|_{2})L_{v}^{m}T_{v}^{m+2}\sum_{\|z\|_{\infty}\leq C(\|\cdot\|_{1})T_{v}}\frac{1}{\|z\|_{\infty}^{m}} \\ & \leq C'(m,n,\|\cdot\|_{1},\|\cdot\|_{2})L_{v}^{m}T_{v}^{m+2}\sum_{k=1}^{ \lfloor C(\|\cdot\|_{1})T_{v}\rfloor}k^{n-3-m}\\ &\overset{(n\ne m+2)}{\leq} C''(m,n,\|\cdot\|_{1},\|\cdot\|_{2})L_{v}^{m}T_{v}^{m+2}T_{v}^{1+n-3-m}\\ &\leq C''(m,n,\|\cdot\|_{1},\|\cdot\|_{2})L_{v}^{m}T_{v}^{n}. \end{align*} Thus, for any $0<\delta<\lambda_{m(n-2)}\left(B_{m(n-2)}(\boldsymbol{0},1)\right)$, if $L_{v}<cT_{v}^{-\frac{n}{m}}$ then for any $c\in(0,C'''(m,n,\|\cdot\|_{1}))$ with \begin{equation*} C'''(m,n,\|\cdot\|_{1},\|\cdot\|_{2}) < \left(\frac{\delta}{C''(m,n,\|\cdot\|_{1},\|\cdot\|_{2})}\right)^{\frac{1}{m}}, \end{equation*} we have that $\lambda_{m(n-2)}\left(S_{v}^{c}\right)<\delta$ as required.
nodes.statement_short: Summing gives lambda(S_v^c) << L_v^m T_v^n < delta for small c.

nodes.name: Case n=m+2
nodes.statement: Finally we explain how to avoid the condition $n\ne m+2$ when $m\ge 2$. Instead of extending $V\in \mathbb{R}^{m\times 2}$ directly to the desired $m\times n$ matrix $\Omega$, we iteratively apply Lemma~\ref{lemme}, adding a single column to $V$ at each step. Precisely, suppose $m\geq 2$ and $n=m+2$. Begin with some $V=\tilde{V}_{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times 2}$ satisfying \eqref{V property}. Apply Lemma~\ref{lemme} to construct a set of $m$-dimensional positive measure matrices $\Omega_{1}\in \mathbb{R}^{m\times 3}$ with property \eqref{eq:forti}. Define $\tilde{V}_{2}:=\Omega_{1}$ to be any of the matrices in the the constructed set. Note $\tilde{V}_{2}$ satisfies \begin{equation*} \psi_{\tilde{V}_{2}}^{m\times 3}(\|\cdot\|^{''}_{1},\|\cdot\|_{2},T_{v_{r}})=\psi_{\tilde{V}_{1}}^{m\times 2}(\|\cdot\|^{'}_{1},\|\cdot\|_{2},T_{v_{r}})\, , \end{equation*} with $\|\cdot\|^{''}_{1}$ now being the restriction of $\|\cdot\|_{1}$ to $\mathbb{R}^{3}$. So \begin{equation*} \limsup_{t\to\infty} t^{n/m}\psi_{\tilde{V}_{2}}^{m\times 3}(\|\cdot\|^{''}_{1},\|\cdot\|_{2},t)=c\, , \end{equation*} Note $\tilde{V}_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times 3}$ rather than $\mathbb{R}^{m\times 2}$, but it is readily verified that we can copy the above proof with obvious modifications. So, we construct a set of $m$-dimensional positive measure matrices $\Omega_{2}\in \mathbb{R}^{m\times 4}$ with the desired properties of Lemma~\ref{lemme}. Define $\tilde{V}_{3}:=\Omega_{2}$ for any of the matrices in the above set and repeat. The same argument follows as above. In this way we obtain a sequence of matrices \begin{equation*} \Omega_{1}=: \tilde{V}_{2} \in \mathbb{R}^{m\times 3}, \Omega_{2}=:\tilde{V}_{3}\in \mathbb{R}^{m\times 4},\ldots, \Omega_{m-1}=:\tilde{V}_{m+1}\in \mathbb{R}^{m\times(m+1)},\Omega_{m}=:\Omega\in \mathbb{R}^{m\times (m+2)}\, . \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Add one column at a time when m>=2.

nodes.name: Dimension count
nodes.statement: For each $2< \tilde{n} \leq m+2$ the extension from $\tilde{V}_{\tilde{n}-2} \in \mathbb{R}^{m\times (\tilde{n}-1)}$ to an $m\times \tilde{n}$ matrix follows readily by copying the above proof of Lemma~\ref{lemme} (with the restriction $n\neq m+2$) with obvious modifications. Note we avoid the condition $\tilde{n}= m+(\tilde{n}-1)$ since $m\geq 2$. Thus, at each step we construct a set of matrices $\Omega_{\tilde{n}-1}\in \mathbb{R}^{m\times \tilde{n}}$ with positive $m$-dimensional measure, each with the desired properties of \eqref{eq:forti}. It is readily checked that the required convergence estimates still work a fortiori as $n\ge \tilde{n}$ and $m$ remains constant. Using Marstrand's slicing lemma \cite{mars} for fibered sets, we increase the Hausdorff dimension by $m$ in every step. There are $m$ steps, hence we arrive at the dimension of at least $m^{2}=m(n-2)$.
nodes.statement_short: Each step adds m to the dimension by Marstrand slicing.

nodes.name: Error vectors (52)
nodes.statement: \tilde{\boldsymbol{c}}_j:= V\cdot \begin{pmatrix} A_j \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} - \begin{pmatrix} F_{j,1} \\ F_{j,2} \\ \vdots \\ F_{j,m} \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \tilde{\boldsymbol{d}}_j:= V\cdot \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ B_j \end{pmatrix} - \begin{pmatrix} G_{j,1} \\ G_{j,2} \\ \vdots \\ G_{j,m} \end{pmatrix},\qquad j\ge 1,
nodes.label: eq:errt

nodes.name: Norms of error vectors (53)
nodes.statement: \Vert \tilde{\boldsymbol{c}}_j\Vert_2= A_j A_{j+1}^{-1} \Gamma_j (1+o(1)), \qquad \Vert \tilde{\boldsymbol{d}}_j\Vert_2=B_j B_{j+1}^{-1} \tilde{\Gamma}_j (1+o(1)),\qquad j\to\infty,
nodes.label: eq:fertig

nodes.name: Q-dependence occurs only on a small set
nodes.statement: Let $g, h$ be positive integers. Assume given real numbers $x_1, \ldots,x_g$ are $\mathbb{Q}$-linearly independent together with $1$. Then only for a set of Hausdorff dimension $h-1$ of vectors $\boldsymbol{y}=(y_1,\ldots,y_h)$ in $\mathbb{R}^h$, the joint vector $\boldsymbol{z}=(x_1,\ldots,x_g,y_1,\ldots,y_h)$ is $\mathbb{Q}$-linearly dependent with $1$.
assumptions: Assume given real numbers $x_1, \ldots,x_g$ are $\mathbb{Q}$-linearly independent together with $1$.
conclusions: Then only for a set of Hausdorff dimension $h-1$ of vectors $\boldsymbol{y}=(y_1,\ldots,y_h)$ in $\mathbb{R}^h$, the joint vector $\boldsymbol{z}=(x_1,\ldots,x_g,y_1,\ldots,y_h)$ is $\mathbb{Q}$-linearly dependent with $1$.
nodes.label: p

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 5
nodes.statement: Since the $x_j$ are independent, if $\{ 1,\boldsymbol{z}\}$ is dependent over $\mathbb{Q}$ then there are integers $M_i, N_i, N$ with \[ N+ \sum_{i=1}^{g} M_i x_i +\sum_{i=1}^{h} N_i y_i = 0 \] and not all $N_i$ are $0$. But this means that $\boldsymbol{y}$ lies in a countable union of affine hyperplanes of $\mathbb{R}^{h}$. Hence we see that the set of $\boldsymbol{y}$ inducing dependency over $\mathbb{Q}$ indeed has Hausdorff dimension at most $h-1$.
nodes.statement_short: A dependency places y in a countable union of affine hyperplanes, of dimension h-1.

nodes.name: Dependency relation
nodes.statement: Since the $x_j$ are independent, if $\{ 1,\boldsymbol{z}\}$ is dependent over $\mathbb{Q}$ then there are integers $M_i, N_i, N$ with \[ N+ \sum_{i=1}^{g} M_i x_i +\sum_{i=1}^{h} N_i y_i = 0 \] and not all $N_i$ are $0$.
nodes.statement_short: A dependency involves some y-coefficient.

nodes.name: Hyperplanes
nodes.statement: But this means that $\boldsymbol{y}$ lies in a countable union of affine hyperplanes of $\mathbb{R}^{h}$.
nodes.statement_short: y lies in countably many affine hyperplanes.

nodes.name: Dimension
nodes.statement: Hence we see that the set of $\boldsymbol{y}$ inducing dependency over $\mathbb{Q}$ indeed has Hausdorff dimension at most $h-1$.
nodes.statement_short: So the exceptional set has dimension at most h-1.

nodes.name: Remark on Agin-Weiss
nodes.statement: We point out again that our proof below can be significantly shortened using the preprint~\cite[Corollary~1]{AginWeiss2024} which appeared later. We detail the parts that can be simplified in the proof below. In short, when taking into account~\cite{AginWeiss2024}, the main new substance still needed is Lemma~\ref{lemme} below.
nodes.statement_short: Proof can be shortened via Agin-Weiss; main new ingredient is Lemma 7.1.

nodes.name: Main construction
nodes.statement:
\subsection{Proof excluding linear independence claims} We proceed as in~\S~ef{st1} to construct the first two elements of the first line of our matrix $\Omega$ by $ oldsymbol{\xi}=(\xi_1,\xi_2)=(\Omega_{1,1}, \Omega_{1,2})$, upon modifying the construction so that \eqref{eq:IIi} is replaced by \[ 	au \mu -1 =  rac{n}{m} \mu \overset{\eqref{matrix dimension condition}}{\ge} 2\mu. \] Define $\psi_{ oldsymbol{\xi}}^{1	imes 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}, t)$ with respect to the restriction $\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}$ of $\Vert\cdot\Vert_1$ to $\mathbb{R}^2$ in the integer vector $ oldsymbol{b}$, as in \eqref{eq:pno}. Then by the same arguments of the proof of Theorem~ef{jia} we will have  egin{equation} \limsup_{t	o\infty} t^{n/m} \psi_{ oldsymbol{\xi}}^{1	imes 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}, t)= c. \end{equation} Hereby we use our assumption $n/m\ge 2$ for Case 2, based on Minkowski's Second Convex Body Theorem, to work analogously. Now take the matrix $V\in \mathbb{R}^{m	imes 2}$ with all $m$ lines equal to $ oldsymbol{\xi}$, i.e. \[ V_{j,1}= \xi_{1}, \qquad V_{j,2}=\xi_{2}, \qquad 1\leq j\le m. \] This matrix gives rise to an approximation function $\psi_{V}^{m	imes 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}, \Vert\cdot\Vert_2, t)$ with norms defined as above. First, assume for simplicity that $\Vert\cdot\Vert_2=\Vert\cdot\Vert_{\infty}$ is the maximum norm on $\mathbb{R}^m$. We claim that  egin{equation} \psi_{V}^{m	imes 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}, \Vert\cdot\Vert_2, t)=\psi_{ oldsymbol{\xi}}^{1	imes 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}, t), \qquad t>0. \end{equation} Indeed to see  egin{equation} \psi_{V}^{m	imes 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}, \Vert\cdot\Vert_2, t)\ge \psi_{ oldsymbol{\xi}}^{1	imes 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}, t) \end{equation} for all $t$, note that for arbitrary $ oldsymbol{b}=(b_1,\ldots,b_{m+2})\in\mathbb{Z}^{m+2}$ and for $V^{\ast}\in \mathbb{R}^{m	imes (m+2)}$ obtained by glueing $V$ to the $m	imes m$ identity matrix to the right, the induced value \[ \Vert V^{\ast}\cdot  oldsymbol{b}\Vert_2= \Vert V\cdot \widehat{ oldsymbol{b}}+ 	ilde{ oldsymbol{b}}\Vert_2= \Vert V\cdot (b_1,b_{2}) + (b_{3},\ldots,b_{m+2})\Vert_2 \] with vectors interpreted as column vectors, is at least as large as the modulus of any entry, since we are considering $\|\cdot\|_{2}=\|\cdot\|_{\infty}$ for now. But for the first entry this equals $|(b_1,b_2)\cdot  oldsymbol{\xi} +b_3|=|  oldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}\cdot (b_1,b_2,b_3)|$. Taking the minimum over $ oldsymbol{b}$ as in the definition of $\psi_V^{m	imes 2}$ shows the inequality \eqref{eq:einer}. Conversely, if we extend arbitrary $ oldsymbol{b}=(b_1, b_2, b_3)\in\mathbb{Z}^3$ into $\mathbb{Z}^{m+2}$ via $\eta( oldsymbol{b}):=(b_1,b_2,b_3,\ldots,b_{3})$ with last $m$ coordinates equal to $b_3$, by choice of maximum norm, we have $\Vert V^{\ast}\cdot \eta( oldsymbol{b})\Vert_2 = | oldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast} \cdot (b_1,b_2,b_3)|$, so passing to the minimum over $ oldsymbol{b}$ again we get the reverse inequality  egin{equation} \psi_{V}^{m	imes 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}, \Vert\cdot\Vert_2, t)\le \psi_{ oldsymbol{\xi}}^{1	imes 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}, t). \end{equation} Combining \eqref{eq:fichte}, \eqref{eq:teir} we get \[ \limsup_{t	o\infty} t^{n/m} \psi_{V}^{m	imes2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}, \Vert\cdot\Vert_2, t)=\limsup_{t	o\infty} t^{n/m} \psi_{ oldsymbol{\xi}}^{1	imes 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}, t)= c. \] We note that up to this point, the claim alternatively follows directly from the aforementioned preprint~\cite[Corollary~1]{AginWeiss2024}. \par To finish the proof, we show that for a positive measure set of $B\in \mathbb{R}^{m	imes (n-2)}$ inducing $\Omega=(V,B)$ via putting it to the right of $V$, we have \[ \limsup_{t	o\infty} t^{n/m} \psi_{\Omega}^{m	imes n}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1, \Vert\cdot\Vert_2, t)=\limsup_{t	o\infty} t^{n/m} \psi_{V}^{m	imes 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}, \Vert\cdot\Vert_2, t). \] Again the inequality  egin{equation} \limsup_{t	o\infty} t^{n/m} \psi_{\Omega}^{m	imes n}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1, \Vert\cdot\Vert_2, t)\le \limsup_{t	o\infty} t^{n/m} \psi_{V}^{m	imes 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}, \Vert\cdot\Vert_2, t) \end{equation} is easy to check for arbitrary $\Vert\cdot\Vert_2$ and extensions $\Omega\in\mathbb{R}^{m	imes n}$ of $V$ by an arbitrary matrix $B\in \mathbb{R}^{m	imes (n-2)}$. Indeed, for a sufficient estimate \[ \psi_{\Omega}^{m	imes n}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1, \Vert\cdot\Vert_2, t)\le \psi_{V}^{m	imes 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}, \Vert\cdot\Vert_2, t), \qquad t>0 \] we embed the integer best approximations of $V$ by adding $0$ coordinates via \[ \sigma:\; oldsymbol{b}=(b_1, b_2, \ldots, b_{m+2})	o (b_1,b_2,0,\ldots,0,b_3,\ldots,b_{m+2})\in\mathbb{Z}^{m+n}. \] These induce the same norm $\Vert \widehat{\sigma( oldsymbol{b})} \Vert_1=\Vert \widehat{ oldsymbol{b}} \Vert_1^{\prime}$ where \[ \widehat{\sigma( oldsymbol{b})}= (b_1,b_2,\ldots,b_n)=(b_1,b_2,0,\ldots,0), \qquad \widehat{ oldsymbol{b}}= (b_1,b_2), \] with hat again as in \eqref{eq:hatnot} on the respective spaces. With $\Omega^{\ast}$ derived from $\Omega$ likewise as for $V^{\ast}$ (i.e. add the identity matrix to the right hand side of $\Omega$), they further induce the same approximation qualities $\Vert \Omega^{\ast}\cdot \sigma( oldsymbol{b}) \Vert_2=\Vert V^{\ast}\cdot  oldsymbol{b} \Vert_2$ since in fact $\Omega^{\ast}\cdot \sigma( oldsymbol{b}) =V^{\ast}\cdot  oldsymbol{b}$, proving \eqref{eq:frit}. For the reverse estimate  egin{equation} \limsup_{t	o\infty} t^{n/m} \psi_{\Omega}^{m	imes n}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1, \Vert\cdot\Vert_2, t)\ge \limsup_{t	o\infty} t^{n/m} \psi_{V}^{m	imes 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}, \Vert\cdot\Vert_2, t)=c, \end{equation} we use a generalisation of Step II from~\S~ef{st2} for $m>1$ as in Moshchevitin~\cite[Theorem~12]{ngm}. We obtain that for small enough $c$ and a positive measure set of remaining matrices $B\in \mathbb{R}^{m	imes (n-2)}$ with respect to $m(n-2)$ dimensional Lebesgue measure when added to the right of $V$ to obtain $\Omega$, we have \eqref{eq:trif}. If $m=1$ then we require the condition $n
e m+2=3$. Moreover, the assumption $n\ge 2m$ is vital for the volume estimates. See Lemma~ef{lemme} below for a generalisation. The proof for $\Vert\cdot\Vert_2$ the maximum norm is complete. Now let the norm $\Vert\cdot\Vert_2$ be arbitrary. Again we prove \eqref{eq:einer}, \eqref{eq:zweier}, \eqref{eq:frit}, \eqref{eq:trif}. The critical estimates where the norm $\Vert\cdot\Vert_2$ is relevant for the argument are \eqref{eq:einer}, \eqref{eq:zweier}. First notice that by the special form of $V$, if $ oldsymbol{b}$ is not of the form $ oldsymbol{b}=(b_1,b_2,b_3,b_3,\ldots,b_3)\in \mathbb{Z}^{m+2}$ then some entry of $V^{\ast}\cdot  oldsymbol{b}$ will be of modulus at least $1/2$, so $\Vert V^{\ast}\cdot  oldsymbol{b}\Vert_{\infty}\ge 1/2$, hence by equivalence of norms, we deduce \[ \Vert V^{\ast}\cdot  oldsymbol{b}\Vert_2 \gg 1 \] with some absolute constant depending on the norm $\Vert\cdot\Vert_2$ only. Hence we only need to take into account vectors of the form $ oldsymbol{b}=(b_1,b_2,b_3,b_3,\ldots,b_3)$ when studying $\psi_{V}^{m	imes 2}$. But then the vector $V^{\ast}\cdot  oldsymbol{b}\in \mathbb{R}^m$ lies on the line $\lambda\cdot (1,1,\ldots,1)\in \mathbb{R}^m$ and has norm $|\lambda|\cdot \Vert (1,1,\ldots,1)\Vert_2$ proportional to $|\lambda|$. Hence we have to minimize $|\lambda|$. In~\S~ef{st1}, see in particular Lemma~ef{wichtig!}, we showed that this is achieved when the subvector $(b_1,b_2,b_3)$ is essentially of the form $ oldsymbol{v}_j=(A_j,0,-F_j)$ and $ oldsymbol{w}_j=(0,B_j,-G_j)$ for $A_j, B_j, F_j, G_j$ defined in the same section (as shown in~\S~ef{st1}, for the other possible vectors of Lemma~ef{wichtig!} we may only improve the approximation quality by a negligible factor $1+o(1)$ as $j	o\infty$). These arguments show that the best integer approximations for $V$ are essentially of the form  egin{equation}  oldsymbol{c}_j:= (A_j, 0 , -F_j, \ldots , -F_j ), \qquad  oldsymbol{d}_j:= (0, B_j , -G_j, \ldots , -G_j ) \end{equation} so that for $ oldsymbol{v}_j,  oldsymbol{w}_j\in\mathbb{Z}^3$ as before, we get error vectors \[ V^{\ast}\cdot  oldsymbol{a}_j= V\cdot  egin{pmatrix} A_j \ 0 \end{pmatrix} - F_j\cdot  egin{pmatrix} 1 \ 1 \ \vdots \ 1 \end{pmatrix}= oldsymbol{v}_j\cdot  oldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}\cdot  egin{pmatrix} 1 \ 1 \ \vdots \ 1 \end{pmatrix}\in \mathbb{R}^m \] and \[ V^{\ast}\cdot  oldsymbol{b}_j= V\cdot  egin{pmatrix} 0 \ B_j \end{pmatrix}- G_j\cdot  egin{pmatrix} 1 \ 1 \ \vdots \ 1 \end{pmatrix}= oldsymbol{w}_j\cdot  oldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}\cdot  egin{pmatrix} 1 \ 1 \ \vdots \ 1 \end{pmatrix}\in \mathbb{R}^m. \] Then for $\Gamma:=\Vert(1,1,\ldots,1)\Vert_2$ they have norms \[ \left\Vert V^{\ast}\cdot  oldsymbol{c}_jight\Vert_2= \vert  oldsymbol{v}_j\cdot  oldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|\cdot \Gamma, \qquad \left\Vert V^{\ast}\cdot  oldsymbol{d}_jight\Vert_2= \vert  oldsymbol{w}_j\cdot  oldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|\cdot \Gamma. \] Thus we have to adjust the proof of the special case by the constant factor $\Gamma$ in the calculation, so that in order to finalize Step I we now need to pick \[ r=c^{-1}\Gamma^{-1} d_2^n,\qquad d_2= \Vert  oldsymbol{e}_2\Vert_1^{\prime}=\Vert (0,1)\Vert_1^{\prime} \] to get \eqref{eq:zweier}. The reverse inequality \eqref{eq:einer} holds as well as we noticed that the vectors in \eqref{eq:vecin} are (essentially) the integer best approximations. We observed that \eqref{eq:frit} holds independent of $\Vert\cdot\Vert_2$. Note that again this step follows immediately via a different proof from the preprint~\cite[Corollary~1]{AginWeiss2024}. \par Finally, Step II is to again show the reverse inequalities \eqref{eq:trif} hold. This is done analogously to Lemma~ef{lema} but in higher dimension, building up on ideas of Moshchevitin~\cite[Theorem~12]{ngm}. Again the claim is essentially irrespective of the norm $\Vert\cdot\Vert_2$. We state the according analogue of Lemma~ef{lema} that we will prove analogously but without effort to make constants effective.  egin{lemma} Let $m,n$ be positive integers with $n\ge 2$, and $(m,n)
e (1,3)$. Let $\Vert\cdot\Vert_1$ and $\Vert\cdot\Vert_2$ be any norms on $\mathbb{R}^n$ and $\mathbb{R}^m$ and $\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}$ be the restriction of $\Vert\cdot\Vert_1$ to $\mathbb{R}^2$ as in \eqref{eq:pno}. Further, let $V\in \mathbb{R}^{m	imes 2}$ be any matrix with  egin{equation} \limsup_{t	o\infty} t^{n/m} \psi_{V}^{m	imes 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}, \Vert\cdot\Vert_2, t)= c \end{equation} for small enough $c\in [0,c_0(m,n,\Vert.\Vert_1,\Vert.\Vert_2)]$, with $c_0$ depending on $m,n$ and the norms. Let $ oldsymbol{b}_v\in\mathbb{Z}^{m+2}$ be the associated sequence of best approximations, and $\hat{ oldsymbol{b}}_v= (b_{v,1}, b_{v,2})$ of norms and approximation qualities \[ M_v:=\Vert \hat{ oldsymbol{b}}_v \Vert_1^{\prime}, \qquad L_v:= \Vert V^{\ast}\cdot  oldsymbol{b}_v\Vert_2. \] Then, for a positive measure set $\mathcal{Y}\subseteq B_{m(n-2)}( oldsymbol{0},1)\subseteq \mathbb{R}^{m(n-2)}$ consisting of matrices $B\in \mathbb{R}^{m	imes (n-2)}$, we have that for an infinite subsequence of integers $(v_r)_{r\in\mathbb{N}}$, letting $T_{v}:=M_{v+1}-1/2$ for $v\ge 1$, we have  egin{equation} \lim_{r	o\infty} T_{v_r}^{n/m} \psi_V^{m	imes 2}(T_{v_r}) = \limsup_{v	o\infty} T_{v}^{n/m}\cdot \psi_{V}^{m	imes 2}(T_{v}) =c \end{equation} i.e. realising the limsup, and the integer best approximation for $\Omega=(V,B)\in \mathbb{R}^{m	imes n}$ at $T_{v_r}$ is for $r\ge 1$ given as \[ b_{1,v_r} oldsymbol{e}_1+ b_{2,v_r} oldsymbol{e}_2+ b_{3,v_r} oldsymbol{e}_{n+1}+\cdots+b_{m+2,v_r} oldsymbol{e}_{n+m}= (b_{1,v_r},b_{2,v_r},0,\ldots,0,b_{3,v_r},\ldots,b_{m+2,v_r})\in \mathbb{Z}^{n+m}. \] Thus, the best approximation function at values $T_{v_r}$ equals  egin{equation} \psi_{\Omega}^{m	imes n}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1, \Vert\cdot\Vert_2,T_{v_r})=\psi_{V}^{m	imes 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}, \Vert\cdot\Vert_2, T_{v_r})= L_{v_r},\qquad r\ge 1. \end{equation} \end{lemma}  egin{proof} First assume $n
e m+2$, this condition will be removed later in the case of $m>1$. Fix $V \in \mathbb{R}^{m	imes 2}$. For the same reason as in the proof of Lemma~ef{lema}, we may assume \[ \lim_{v	o\infty} T_v^{n/m}\psi_{V}^{m	imes 2}(T_v)=c \] and ignore \eqref{eq:ignore}. As in the proof of Lemma~ef{lema}, we construct the set $\mathcal{Y}$ to be composed of matrices $B\in \mathcal{Y}\subseteq \mathbb{R}^{m	imes(n-2)}$ such that the matrices $\Omega=(V,B)\in \mathbb{R}^{m	imes n}$ satisfy \[ \psi_{\Omega}^{m	imes n}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1, \Vert\cdot\Vert_2,T_{v})=\psi_{V}^{m	imes 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}, \Vert\cdot\Vert_2, T_{v})= L_v. \] By the equivalence of norms we have that there exists $C(\|\cdot\|_{1})>0$ dependent only on $\|\cdot\|_{1}$ such that for any $\hat{ oldsymbol{x}}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$  egin{equation*} \|\hat{ oldsymbol{x}}\|_{1}\leq T_{v} \quad \implies \quad \|\hat{ oldsymbol{x}}\|_{\infty} \leq C(\|\cdot\|_{1})T_{v}. \end{equation*} Thus if again $\Omega^{\ast}=(V,B,I)\in \mathbb{R}^{m	imes (m+n)}$ is obtained by putting the $m	imes m$ identity matrix, I, to the right of $\Omega$ and we let  egin{equation*} S_{v}:=\left\{ B \in B_{m(n-2)}( oldsymbol{0},1): \underset{0<\|\hat{ oldsymbol{x}}\|_{\infty}\leq C(\|\cdot\|_{1})T_{v}}{\min_{ oldsymbol{x} \in \mathbb{Z}^{n+m}}} \left\|(V,B,I)\cdot  oldsymbol{x} ight\|_{2} \geq L_{v} ight\}\, , \end{equation*} then $\mathcal{Y} \supseteq \limsup_{v	o \infty} S_{v}$. Hence if we can show that the set  egin{equation} \lambda_{m(n-2)}\left( \liminf_{v	o \infty} S_{v}^{c} ight) \leq \delta < \lambda_{m(n-2)}\left(B_{m(n-2)}( oldsymbol{0},1)ight) \end{equation} then clearly $\lambda_{m(n-2)}(\mathcal{Y})>0$. Furthermore, if we show that  egin{equation} \lambda_{m(n-2)}(S_{v}^{c})\leq \delta \qquad v\geq 1, \end{equation} then applying Proposition~ef{pp} we have \eqref{Y condition}, so proving \eqref{Svc size} is sufficient to verify $\lambda_{m(n-2)}(\mathcal{Y})>0$. \par Let $z=(z_{3},\dots,z_{n})$, $y=(x_{n+1},\dots, x_{n+m})$ and  egin{equation*} X_{v}(z,x_{1},x_{2},y)=\left\{  oldsymbol{\gamma} \in B_{m(n-2)}( oldsymbol{0},1) : \left(  egin{array}{c} z_{3}\gamma_{1,1} + \dots + z_{n}\gamma_{1,n-2} \ \vdots \quad \quad \vdots \ z_{3}\gamma_{m,1}+\dots + z_{n}\gamma_{m,n-2} \end{array} ight) \in J_{v}(x_{1},x_{2},y) ight\} \end{equation*} where  egin{equation*} J_{v}(x_{1},x_{2},y):=\prod_{i=1}^{m} (-x_{1}\xi_{1}-x_{2}\xi_{2} -x_{n+i}-C(\|\cdot\|_{2})L_{v}, -x_{1}\xi_{1}-x_{2}\xi_{2} -x_{n+i}+C(\|\cdot\|_{2})L_{v}). \end{equation*} Here we have again used equivalence of norms, namely that there exists $C(\|\cdot\|_{2})>0$ dependent only on $\|\cdot\|_{2}$ so that for any $X\in\mathbb{R}^{m}$  egin{equation*} C(\|\cdot\|_{2})^{-1}\|X\|_{\infty}\leq \|X\|_{2} \leq C(\|\cdot\|_{2})\|X\|_{\infty}. \end{equation*} Considering one row of $X_{v}(z,x_{1},x_{2},y)$ at a time (denoted $X_{v}^{(i)}(z,x_{1},x_{2},y)$ for $1\leq i \leq m$) we have the same calculation as in \eqref{volcume calculation}, that is  egin{equation*} \lambda_{n-2}\left(X_{v}^{(i)}(z,x_{1},x_{2},y)ight) \leq 2C(\|\cdot\|_{2})L_{v}\lambda_{n-3}(B_{n-3}( oldsymbol{0},1)) rac{1}{\|z\|_{\infty}}. \end{equation*} Hence  egin{align*} \lambda_{m(n-2)}\left(X_{v}(z,x_{1},x_{2},y)ight) &\leq 2^{m}C(\|\cdot\|_{2})^{m}L_{v}^{m}\lambda_{n-3}(B_{n-3}( oldsymbol{0},1))^{m} rac{1}{\|z\|_{\infty}^{m}}\ &=C(m,n,\|\cdot\|_{1},\|\cdot\|_{2})L_{v}^{m}  rac{1}{\|z\|_{\infty}^{m}}. \end{align*} Using similar calculations as appearing in Lemma~ef{lema} we have  egin{align*} \lambda_{m(n-2)}\left(S_{v}^{c}ight)& \leq \sum_{0< \max_{i=1,2}|x_{i}|\leq C(\|\cdot\|_{1})T_{v}}\sum_{\|y\|_{\infty}\leq C(\|\cdot\|_{1})T_{v}}\sum_{\|z\|_{\infty}\leq C(\|\cdot\|_{1})T_{v}} \lambda_{m(n-2)}\left(X_{v}(z,x_{1},x_{2},y)ight)\ &\leq C(m,n,\|\cdot\|_{1},\|\cdot\|_{2})L_{v}^{m}T_{v}^{m+2}\sum_{\|z\|_{\infty}\leq C(\|\cdot\|_{1})T_{v}} rac{1}{\|z\|_{\infty}^{m}} \ & \leq C'(m,n,\|\cdot\|_{1},\|\cdot\|_{2})L_{v}^{m}T_{v}^{m+2}\sum_{k=1}^{ \lfloor C(\|\cdot\|_{1})T_{v}floor}k^{n-3-m}\ &\overset{(n
e m+2)}{\leq} C''(m,n,\|\cdot\|_{1},\|\cdot\|_{2})L_{v}^{m}T_{v}^{m+2}T_{v}^{1+n-3-m}\ &\leq C''(m,n,\|\cdot\|_{1},\|\cdot\|_{2})L_{v}^{m}T_{v}^{n}. \end{align*} Thus, for any $0<\delta<\lambda_{m(n-2)}\left(B_{m(n-2)}( oldsymbol{0},1)ight)$, if $L_{v}<cT_{v}^{- rac{n}{m}}$ then for any $c\in(0,C'''(m,n,\|\cdot\|_{1}))$ with  egin{equation*} C'''(m,n,\|\cdot\|_{1},\|\cdot\|_{2}) < \left( rac{\delta}{C''(m,n,\|\cdot\|_{1},\|\cdot\|_{2})}ight)^{ rac{1}{m}}, \end{equation*} we have that $\lambda_{m(n-2)}\left(S_{v}^{c}ight)<\delta$ as required. Finally we explain how to avoid the condition $n
e m+2$ when $m\ge 2$. Instead of extending $V\in \mathbb{R}^{m	imes 2}$ directly to the desired $m	imes n$ matrix $\Omega$, we iteratively apply Lemma~ef{lemme}, adding a single column to $V$ at each step. Precisely, suppose $m\geq 2$ and $n=m+2$. Begin with some $V=	ilde{V}_{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{m	imes 2}$ satisfying \eqref{V property}. Apply Lemma~ef{lemme} to construct a set of $m$-dimensional positive measure matrices $\Omega_{1}\in \mathbb{R}^{m	imes 3}$ with property \eqref{eq:forti}. Define $	ilde{V}_{2}:=\Omega_{1}$ to be any of the matrices in the the constructed set. Note $	ilde{V}_{2}$ satisfies  egin{equation*} \psi_{	ilde{V}_{2}}^{m	imes 3}(\|\cdot\|^{''}_{1},\|\cdot\|_{2},T_{v_{r}})=\psi_{	ilde{V}_{1}}^{m	imes 2}(\|\cdot\|^{'}_{1},\|\cdot\|_{2},T_{v_{r}})\, , \end{equation*} with $\|\cdot\|^{''}_{1}$ now being the restriction of $\|\cdot\|_{1}$ to $\mathbb{R}^{3}$. So  egin{equation*} \limsup_{t	o\infty} t^{n/m}\psi_{	ilde{V}_{2}}^{m	imes 3}(\|\cdot\|^{''}_{1},\|\cdot\|_{2},t)=c\, , \end{equation*} Note $	ilde{V}_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{m	imes 3}$ rather than $\mathbb{R}^{m	imes 2}$, but it is readily verified that we can copy the above proof with obvious modifications. So, we construct a set of $m$-dimensional positive measure matrices $\Omega_{2}\in \mathbb{R}^{m	imes 4}$ with the desired properties of Lemma~ef{lemme}. Define $	ilde{V}_{3}:=\Omega_{2}$ for any of the matrices in the above set and repeat. The same argument follows as above. In this way we obtain a sequence of matrices  egin{equation*} \Omega_{1}=: 	ilde{V}_{2} \in \mathbb{R}^{m	imes 3}, \Omega_{2}=:	ilde{V}_{3}\in \mathbb{R}^{m	imes 4},\ldots, \Omega_{m-1}=:	ilde{V}_{m+1}\in \mathbb{R}^{m	imes(m+1)},\Omega_{m}=:\Omega\in \mathbb{R}^{m	imes (m+2)}\, . \end{equation*} For each $2< 	ilde{n} \leq m+2$ the extension from $	ilde{V}_{	ilde{n}-2} \in \mathbb{R}^{m	imes (	ilde{n}-1)}$ to an $m	imes 	ilde{n}$ matrix follows readily by copying the above proof of Lemma~ef{lemme} (with the restriction $n
eq m+2$) with obvious modifications. Note we avoid the condition $	ilde{n}= m+(	ilde{n}-1)$ since $m\geq 2$. Thus, at each step we construct a set of matrices $\Omega_{	ilde{n}-1}\in \mathbb{R}^{m	imes 	ilde{n}}$ with positive $m$-dimensional measure, each with the desired properties of \eqref{eq:forti}. It is readily checked that the required convergence estimates still work a fortiori as $n\ge 	ilde{n}$ and $m$ remains constant. Using Marstrand's slicing lemma \cite{mars} for fibered sets, we increase the Hausdorff dimension by $m$ in every step. There are $m$ steps, hence we arrive at the dimension of at least $m^{2}=m(n-2)$. \end{proof} There is nothing essential about $V$ having two columns as the last part of the proof confirms. Note that our proof above avoids the condition $n
e m+2$ as soon as $m>1$, contrasting the requirement $n\ge 4$ in Lemma~ef{lema} where $m=1$. We point out that a similar argument works to generalize the original result in~\cite{ngm}, again when $m>1$. All claims of Theorem~ef{thm5} apart from the linear independence statements are proved.
nodes.statement_short: Construct V and extend to Omega with exact constant c.

nodes.name: First row
nodes.statement: We proceed as in~\S~\ref{st1} to construct the first two elements of the first line of our matrix $\Omega$ by $\boldsymbol{\xi}=(\xi_1,\xi_2)=(\Omega_{1,1}, \Omega_{1,2})$, upon modifying the construction so that \eqref{eq:IIi} is replaced by \[ \tau \mu -1 = \frac{n}{m} \mu \overset{\eqref{matrix dimension condition}}{\ge} 2\mu. \] Define $\psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{1\times 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}, t)$ with respect to the restriction $\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}$ of $\Vert\cdot\Vert_1$ to $\mathbb{R}^2$ in the integer vector $\boldsymbol{b}$, as in \eqref{eq:pno}. Then by the same arguments of the proof of Theorem~\ref{jia} we will have \begin{equation} \limsup_{t\to\infty} t^{n/m} \psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{1\times 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}, t)= c. \end{equation} Hereby we use our assumption $n/m\ge 2$ for Case 2, based on Minkowski's Second Convex Body Theorem, to work analogously.
nodes.statement_short: Construct xi as in Step I with exponent n/m.

nodes.name: Matrix V
nodes.statement: Now take the matrix $V\in \mathbb{R}^{m\times 2}$ with all $m$ lines equal to $\boldsymbol{\xi}$, i.e. \[ V_{j,1}= \xi_{1}, \qquad V_{j,2}=\xi_{2}, \qquad 1\leq j\le m. \] This matrix gives rise to an approximation function $\psi_{V}^{m\times 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}, \Vert\cdot\Vert_2, t)$ with norms defined as above. First, assume for simplicity that $\Vert\cdot\Vert_2=\Vert\cdot\Vert_{\infty}$ is the maximum norm on $\mathbb{R}^m$.
nodes.statement_short: V has all rows equal to xi; first assume max norm.

nodes.name: Claim psi_V = psi_xi
nodes.statement: We claim that \begin{equation} \psi_{V}^{m\times 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}, \Vert\cdot\Vert_2, t)=\psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{1\times 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}, t), \qquad t>0. \end{equation} Indeed to see \begin{equation} \psi_{V}^{m\times 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}, \Vert\cdot\Vert_2, t)\ge \psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{1\times 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}, t) \end{equation} for all $t$, note that for arbitrary $\boldsymbol{b}=(b_1,\ldots,b_{m+2})\in\mathbb{Z}^{m+2}$ and for $V^{\ast}\in \mathbb{R}^{m\times (m+2)}$ obtained by glueing $V$ to the $m\times m$ identity matrix to the right, the induced value \[ \Vert V^{\ast}\cdot \boldsymbol{b}\Vert_2= \Vert V\cdot \widehat{\boldsymbol{b}}+ \tilde{\boldsymbol{b}}\Vert_2= \Vert V\cdot (b_1,b_{2}) + (b_{3},\ldots,b_{m+2})\Vert_2 \] with vectors interpreted as column vectors, is at least as large as the modulus of any entry, since we are considering $\|\cdot\|_{2}=\|\cdot\|_{\infty}$ for now. But for the first entry this equals $|(b_1,b_2)\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi} +b_3|=| \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}\cdot (b_1,b_2,b_3)|$. Taking the minimum over $\boldsymbol{b}$ as in the definition of $\psi_V^{m\times 2}$ shows the inequality \eqref{eq:einer}. Conversely, if we extend arbitrary $\boldsymbol{b}=(b_1, b_2, b_3)\in\mathbb{Z}^3$ into $\mathbb{Z}^{m+2}$ via $\eta(\boldsymbol{b}):=(b_1,b_2,b_3,\ldots,b_{3})$ with last $m$ coordinates equal to $b_3$, by choice of maximum norm, we have $\Vert V^{\ast}\cdot \eta(\boldsymbol{b})\Vert_2 = |\boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast} \cdot (b_1,b_2,b_3)|$, so passing to the minimum over $\boldsymbol{b}$ again we get the reverse inequality \begin{equation} \psi_{V}^{m\times 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}, \Vert\cdot\Vert_2, t)\le \psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{1\times 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}, t). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: psi_V equals psi_xi.

nodes.name: Statement
nodes.statement: We claim that \begin{equation} \psi_{V}^{m\times 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}, \Vert\cdot\Vert_2, t)=\psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{1\times 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}, t), \qquad t>0. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: State (41).

nodes.name: Lower bound
nodes.statement: Indeed to see \begin{equation} \psi_{V}^{m\times 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}, \Vert\cdot\Vert_2, t)\ge \psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{1\times 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}, t) \end{equation} for all $t$, note that for arbitrary $\boldsymbol{b}=(b_1,\ldots,b_{m+2})\in\mathbb{Z}^{m+2}$ and for $V^{\ast}\in \mathbb{R}^{m\times (m+2)}$ obtained by glueing $V$ to the $m\times m$ identity matrix to the right, the induced value \[ \Vert V^{\ast}\cdot \boldsymbol{b}\Vert_2= \Vert V\cdot \widehat{\boldsymbol{b}}+ \tilde{\boldsymbol{b}}\Vert_2= \Vert V\cdot (b_1,b_{2}) + (b_{3},\ldots,b_{m+2})\Vert_2 \] with vectors interpreted as column vectors, is at least as large as the modulus of any entry, since we are considering $\|\cdot\|_{2}=\|\cdot\|_{\infty}$ for now. But for the first entry this equals $|(b_1,b_2)\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi} +b_3|=| \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}\cdot (b_1,b_2,b_3)|$. Taking the minimum over $\boldsymbol{b}$ as in the definition of $\psi_V^{m\times 2}$ shows the inequality \eqref{eq:einer}.
nodes.statement_short: Max norm dominates the first entry.

nodes.name: Upper bound
nodes.statement: Conversely, if we extend arbitrary $\boldsymbol{b}=(b_1, b_2, b_3)\in\mathbb{Z}^3$ into $\mathbb{Z}^{m+2}$ via $\eta(\boldsymbol{b}):=(b_1,b_2,b_3,\ldots,b_{3})$ with last $m$ coordinates equal to $b_3$, by choice of maximum norm, we have $\Vert V^{\ast}\cdot \eta(\boldsymbol{b})\Vert_2 = |\boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast} \cdot (b_1,b_2,b_3)|$, so passing to the minimum over $\boldsymbol{b}$ again we get the reverse inequality \begin{equation} \psi_{V}^{m\times 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}, \Vert\cdot\Vert_2, t)\le \psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{1\times 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}, t). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Repeat b_3 in all last coordinates.

nodes.name: limsup for V
nodes.statement: Combining \eqref{eq:fichte}, \eqref{eq:teir} we get \[ \limsup_{t\to\infty} t^{n/m} \psi_{V}^{m\times2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}, \Vert\cdot\Vert_2, t)=\limsup_{t\to\infty} t^{n/m} \psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{1\times 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}, t)= c. \] We note that up to this point, the claim alternatively follows directly from the aforementioned preprint~\cite[Corollary~1]{AginWeiss2024}. \par
nodes.statement_short: V has Dirichlet constant c.

nodes.name: Remaining claim
nodes.statement: To finish the proof, we show that for a positive measure set of $B\in \mathbb{R}^{m\times (n-2)}$ inducing $\Omega=(V,B)$ via putting it to the right of $V$, we have \[ \limsup_{t\to\infty} t^{n/m} \psi_{\Omega}^{m\times n}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1, \Vert\cdot\Vert_2, t)=\limsup_{t\to\infty} t^{n/m} \psi_{V}^{m\times 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}, \Vert\cdot\Vert_2, t). \]
nodes.statement_short: Need a positive-measure set of B preserving the limsup.

nodes.name: Easy inequality
nodes.statement: Again the inequality \begin{equation} \limsup_{t\to\infty} t^{n/m} \psi_{\Omega}^{m\times n}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1, \Vert\cdot\Vert_2, t)\le \limsup_{t\to\infty} t^{n/m} \psi_{V}^{m\times 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}, \Vert\cdot\Vert_2, t) \end{equation} is easy to check for arbitrary $\Vert\cdot\Vert_2$ and extensions $\Omega\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ of $V$ by an arbitrary matrix $B\in \mathbb{R}^{m\times (n-2)}$. Indeed, for a sufficient estimate \[ \psi_{\Omega}^{m\times n}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1, \Vert\cdot\Vert_2, t)\le \psi_{V}^{m\times 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}, \Vert\cdot\Vert_2, t), \qquad t>0 \] we embed the integer best approximations of $V$ by adding $0$ coordinates via \[ \sigma:\;\boldsymbol{b}=(b_1, b_2, \ldots, b_{m+2})\to (b_1,b_2,0,\ldots,0,b_3,\ldots,b_{m+2})\in\mathbb{Z}^{m+n}. \] These induce the same norm $\Vert \widehat{\sigma(\boldsymbol{b})} \Vert_1=\Vert \widehat{\boldsymbol{b}} \Vert_1^{\prime}$ where \[ \widehat{\sigma(\boldsymbol{b})}= (b_1,b_2,\ldots,b_n)=(b_1,b_2,0,\ldots,0), \qquad \widehat{\boldsymbol{b}}= (b_1,b_2), \] with hat again as in \eqref{eq:hatnot} on the respective spaces. With $\Omega^{\ast}$ derived from $\Omega$ likewise as for $V^{\ast}$ (i.e. add the identity matrix to the right hand side of $\Omega$), they further induce the same approximation qualities $\Vert \Omega^{\ast}\cdot \sigma(\boldsymbol{b}) \Vert_2=\Vert V^{\ast}\cdot \boldsymbol{b} \Vert_2$ since in fact $\Omega^{\ast}\cdot \sigma(\boldsymbol{b}) =V^{\ast}\cdot \boldsymbol{b}$, proving \eqref{eq:frit}.
nodes.statement_short: Embedding gives psi_Omega <= psi_V.

nodes.name: Reverse via Step II
nodes.statement: For the reverse estimate \begin{equation} \limsup_{t\to\infty} t^{n/m} \psi_{\Omega}^{m\times n}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1, \Vert\cdot\Vert_2, t)\ge \limsup_{t\to\infty} t^{n/m} \psi_{V}^{m\times 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}, \Vert\cdot\Vert_2, t)=c, \end{equation} we use a generalisation of Step II from~\S~\ref{st2} for $m>1$ as in Moshchevitin~\cite[Theorem~12]{ngm}. We obtain that for small enough $c$ and a positive measure set of remaining matrices $B\in \mathbb{R}^{m\times (n-2)}$ with respect to $m(n-2)$ dimensional Lebesgue measure when added to the right of $V$ to obtain $\Omega$, we have \eqref{eq:trif}. If $m=1$ then we require the condition $n\ne m+2=3$. Moreover, the assumption $n\ge 2m$ is vital for the volume estimates. See Lemma~\ref{lemme} below for a generalisation. The proof for $\Vert\cdot\Vert_2$ the maximum norm is complete.
nodes.statement_short: Generalized Step II (Moshchevitin) gives the reverse inequality.

nodes.name: Arbitrary norm
nodes.statement: Now let the norm $\Vert\cdot\Vert_2$ be arbitrary. Again we prove \eqref{eq:einer}, \eqref{eq:zweier}, \eqref{eq:frit}, \eqref{eq:trif}. The critical estimates where the norm $\Vert\cdot\Vert_2$ is relevant for the argument are \eqref{eq:einer}, \eqref{eq:zweier}. First notice that by the special form of $V$, if $\boldsymbol{b}$ is not of the form $\boldsymbol{b}=(b_1,b_2,b_3,b_3,\ldots,b_3)\in \mathbb{Z}^{m+2}$ then some entry of $V^{\ast}\cdot \boldsymbol{b}$ will be of modulus at least $1/2$, so $\Vert V^{\ast}\cdot \boldsymbol{b}\Vert_{\infty}\ge 1/2$, hence by equivalence of norms, we deduce \[ \Vert V^{\ast}\cdot \boldsymbol{b}\Vert_2 \gg 1 \] with some absolute constant depending on the norm $\Vert\cdot\Vert_2$ only. Hence we only need to take into account vectors of the form $\boldsymbol{b}=(b_1,b_2,b_3,b_3,\ldots,b_3)$ when studying $\psi_{V}^{m\times 2}$. But then the vector $V^{\ast}\cdot \boldsymbol{b}\in \mathbb{R}^m$ lies on the line $\lambda\cdot (1,1,\ldots,1)\in \mathbb{R}^m$ and has norm $|\lambda|\cdot \Vert (1,1,\ldots,1)\Vert_2$ proportional to $|\lambda|$. Hence we have to minimize $|\lambda|$. In~\S~\ref{st1}, see in particular Lemma~\ref{wichtig!}, we showed that this is achieved when the subvector $(b_1,b_2,b_3)$ is essentially of the form $\boldsymbol{v}_j=(A_j,0,-F_j)$ and $\boldsymbol{w}_j=(0,B_j,-G_j)$ for $A_j, B_j, F_j, G_j$ defined in the same section (as shown in~\S~\ref{st1}, for the other possible vectors of Lemma~\ref{wichtig!} we may only improve the approximation quality by a negligible factor $1+o(1)$ as $j\to\infty$). These arguments show that the best integer approximations for $V$ are essentially of the form \begin{equation} \boldsymbol{c}_j:= (A_j, 0 , -F_j, \ldots , -F_j ), \qquad \boldsymbol{d}_j:= (0, B_j , -G_j, \ldots , -G_j ) \end{equation} so that for $\boldsymbol{v}_j, \boldsymbol{w}_j\in\mathbb{Z}^3$ as before, we get error vectors \[ V^{\ast}\cdot \boldsymbol{a}_j= V\cdot \begin{pmatrix} A_j \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} - F_j\cdot \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ \vdots \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}=\boldsymbol{v}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}\cdot \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ \vdots \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}\in \mathbb{R}^m \] and \[ V^{\ast}\cdot \boldsymbol{b}_j= V\cdot \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ B_j \end{pmatrix}- G_j\cdot \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ \vdots \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}=\boldsymbol{w}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}\cdot \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ \vdots \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}\in \mathbb{R}^m. \] Then for $\Gamma:=\Vert(1,1,\ldots,1)\Vert_2$ they have norms \[ \left\Vert V^{\ast}\cdot \boldsymbol{c}_j\right\Vert_2= \vert \boldsymbol{v}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|\cdot \Gamma, \qquad \left\Vert V^{\ast}\cdot \boldsymbol{d}_j\right\Vert_2= \vert \boldsymbol{w}_j\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}^{\ast}|\cdot \Gamma. \]
nodes.statement_short: Best approximations of V are essentially c_j, d_j with errors scaled by Gamma.

nodes.name: Adjust r
nodes.statement: Thus we have to adjust the proof of the special case by the constant factor $\Gamma$ in the calculation, so that in order to finalize Step I we now need to pick \[ r=c^{-1}\Gamma^{-1} d_2^n,\qquad d_2= \Vert \boldsymbol{e}_2\Vert_1^{\prime}=\Vert (0,1)\Vert_1^{\prime} \] to get \eqref{eq:zweier}. The reverse inequality \eqref{eq:einer} holds as well as we noticed that the vectors in \eqref{eq:vecin} are (essentially) the integer best approximations. We observed that \eqref{eq:frit} holds independent of $\Vert\cdot\Vert_2$. Note that again this step follows immediately via a different proof from the preprint~\cite[Corollary~1]{AginWeiss2024}. \par
nodes.statement_short: Pick r=c^{-1}Gamma^{-1}d_2^n.

nodes.name: Step II statement
nodes.statement: Finally, Step II is to again show the reverse inequalities \eqref{eq:trif} hold. This is done analogously to Lemma~\ref{lema} but in higher dimension, building up on ideas of Moshchevitin~\cite[Theorem~12]{ngm}. Again the claim is essentially irrespective of the norm $\Vert\cdot\Vert_2$. We state the according analogue of Lemma~\ref{lema} that we will prove analogously but without effort to make constants effective.
nodes.statement_short: State Lemma 7.1, the analogue of Lemma 5.3.

nodes.name: Lemma 7.1

nodes.statement_short: Lemma 7.1 with proof.

nodes.name: Generality
nodes.statement: There is nothing essential about $V$ having two columns as the last part of the proof confirms. Note that our proof above avoids the condition $n\ne m+2$ as soon as $m>1$, contrasting the requirement $n\ge 4$ in Lemma~\ref{lema} where $m=1$. We point out that a similar argument works to generalize the original result in~\cite{ngm}, again when $m>1$.
nodes.statement_short: V need not have two columns.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: All claims of Theorem~\ref{thm5} apart from the linear independence statements are proved.
nodes.statement_short: All claims except linear independence are proved.

nodes.name: Linear independence claims
nodes.statement: \subsection{Proof of linear independence claims} The first claim (i) on linear independence of rows follows from Step II. Aside from the metrical claim, note that it suffices to prove linearly independent rows can be arranged for the submatrix $B\in \mathbb{R}^{m\times (n-2)}$ of $\Omega=(V,B)$. Now since $n-2\ge m$ by \eqref{matrix dimension condition}, the matrix $B$ does not have fewer columns than rows, so if $B$ does not have the property it is rank deficient. However, as indicated in Section~\ref{Sek3.1}, looking at minors yields that the set of rank-deficient matrices has positive codimension and thus zero Lebesgue measure. On the other hand, we showed that a positive Lebesgue measure set of matrices $B$ gives rise to $\Omega$ as in the theorem. Hence removing such rank-deficient matrices still leaves us with a set of positive $m\times (n-2)$-dimensional Lebesgue measure from which we can choose arbitrary $B$. For the latter claim (ii) on $\mathbb{Q}$ linearly independent entries, note that in the construction of Section~\ref{sec61} certain entries of $V$ (thus $\Omega$) are identical, so the condition does not hold. To fulfil this additional property, let us modify our construction by varying signs. First construct the submatrix $V\in \mathbb{R}^{m\times 2}$ as above by taking for $A_j, B_j$ as before \[ \Omega_{k,1}=V_{k,1}= \sum_{j=1}^{\infty} \delta_{k,j} A_j^{-1}, \qquad \Omega_{k,2}=V_{k,2}= \sum_{j=1}^{\infty} \delta_{k,j}^{\ast} B_j^{-1}, \quad (1\le k\le m) \] with sequences $\delta_{k,j}\in\{-1,1\}$, $\delta_{k,j}^{\ast}\in\{-1,1\}$ to be chosen later. When $\delta_{k,j}=\delta_{k,j}^{\ast}=1$ for all $k,j$ we are in the standard case of the previous sections. When $m=1$, all arising matrices/vectors $(V_{1,1}, V_{1,2})=(\xi_1, \xi_2)$ share the properties of the standard case above. For $m>1$, we get more general error vectors than in \eqref{eq:vecin}, now of the form \begin{equation} \tilde{\boldsymbol{c}}_j:= V\cdot \begin{pmatrix} A_j \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} - \begin{pmatrix} F_{j,1} \\ F_{j,2} \\ \vdots \\ F_{j,m} \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \tilde{\boldsymbol{d}}_j:= V\cdot \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ B_j \end{pmatrix} - \begin{pmatrix} G_{j,1} \\ G_{j,2} \\ \vdots \\ G_{j,m} \end{pmatrix},\qquad j\ge 1, \end{equation} where \[ F_{j,k}= A_j \sum_{u=1}^{j} \delta_{k,u} A_{u}^{-1}, \qquad G_{j,k}= B_j \sum_{u=1}^{j} \delta_{k,u}^{\ast} B_{u}^{-1}, \qquad (1\le k\le m), \] depending on the choice of $\delta_{k,j}, \delta_{k,j}^{\ast}$. They again satisfy congruence properties $$F_j\equiv \pm 1\bmod 6 \quad \text{ and} \quad G_j\equiv \pm 1\bmod 35$$ for the same reasons, sufficient for coprimality with $6$ respectively $35$. Thus the entries of the remainders $\tilde{\boldsymbol{c}}_j, \tilde{\boldsymbol{d}}_j$ are given as \[ c_{j,k}= A_j \sum_{u=j+1}^{\infty} \delta_{k,u} A_{u}^{-1}, \qquad d_{j,k}= B_j \sum_{u=j+1}^{\infty} \delta_{k,u}^{\ast} B_{u}^{-1}, \qquad (1\le k\le m). \] However, since $A_j/A_{j+1}\to 0$ and $B_j/B_{j+1}\to 0$ we again see \[ c_{j,k}= \delta_{k,j+1} \cdot A_j A_{j+1}^{-1}(1+o(1)), \qquad d_{j,k}=\delta_{k,j+1}^{\ast} \cdot B_j B_{j+1}^{-1}(1+o(1)), \quad (1\le k\le m). \] Hence, by the equivalence of norms, it is clear that the error vectors in \eqref{eq:errt} all have $\Vert\cdot\Vert_2$ norm of order respectively \begin{equation} \Vert \tilde{\boldsymbol{c}}_j\Vert_2= A_j A_{j+1}^{-1} \Gamma_j (1+o(1)), \qquad \Vert \tilde{\boldsymbol{d}}_j\Vert_2=B_j B_{j+1}^{-1} \tilde{\Gamma}_j (1+o(1)),\qquad j\to\infty, \end{equation} with $\Gamma_j, \tilde{\Gamma}_j$ of one of the numbers \[ \Gamma_j, \tilde{\Gamma}_j \in \{ \Vert (\pm 1,\pm 1,\ldots,\pm 1)\Vert_2\}, \qquad j\ge 1, \] for any possible sign choice. The values $\tilde{\Gamma}_j$ do not matter much as the according evaluations will be of negligible order by the analogue of \eqref{eq:frosch}. Now if we let \[ \Gamma:= \max\{ \Vert (\pm 1,\pm 1,\ldots,\pm 1)\Vert_2 \} \] with maximum overall $2^m$ sign choices, we can use the argument of Section~\ref{sec61}. Hereby we may assume that the maximizing sign choice occurs for infinitely many $(\delta_{1,j}, \ldots, \delta_{m,j})$, as otherwise we redefine $\Gamma$ via the maximum among those $m$ term sign sequences occurring infinitely often. Moreover, due to \eqref{eq:fertig}, the arguments of Section~\ref{st1} applied to each of the $m$ coordinates separately still apply very similarly and yield that the vectors $(A_j, 0 , -F_{j,1},\ldots,-F_{j,m})$ and $(0 , B_j, -G_{j,1},\ldots,-G_{j,m})$ essentially form the sequence of best approximations for the induced $V$. We leave the details to the reader. Then very similar arguments as in the classical case including Lemma~\ref{lemme} show that the Dirichlet constant $\Theta^{m\times n}(\Omega)$ of many such $\Omega=\Omega(\delta,\delta^{\ast})$ equals $c$, as before. Finally we show that for many choices of $\delta_{k,j}, \delta_{k,j}^{\ast}$ all entries of $\Omega\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ are linearly independent over $\mathbb{Q}$ together with $\{1\}$. Let us first show this for the submatrix $V\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times 2}$. Label the entries $V_{i,j}$ of $V$ by $v_1,\ldots,v_{2m}$ with $v_{2h}=V_{h,2}$ and $v_{2h-1}=V_{h,1}$, $1\le h\le m$. Now the first line of $V$ is $\mathbb{Q}$-linearly independent for any choice of $\delta_{1,j}, \delta_{1,j}^{\ast}$ sequences as otherwise the sequence of best approximations for $(V_{1,1}, V_{1,2})$ would terminate, but the proof above shows that this is not the case. Hence $\{ 1,v_1, v_2\}$ is $\mathbb{Q}$-linearly independent. Then we proceed inductively. Having constructed the first $\ell\ge 2$ elements $v_1, \ldots,v_{\ell}$, we choose the $\delta$ or $\delta^{\ast}$ sequence for $v_{\ell+1}$ so that we avoid $\mathbb{Q}$-linear dependence of $v_{\ell+1}$ with the already chosen $1,v_1, \ldots,v_{\ell}$. This is possible since the $\mathbb{Q}$-span of $\{ 1,v_1,\ldots,v_{\ell} \}$ is countable, but we have uncountably many choices of $\delta$ or $\delta^{\ast}$ sequences. These clearly induce uncountably many pairwise distinct numbers $v_{\ell+1}$, the injectivity of the corresponding maps $\varphi: \{-1,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}\to \mathbb{R}$ resp. $\varphi^{\ast}: \{-1,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}\to \mathbb{R}$ follows from the rapid increase of the sequences $A_j$ resp. $B_j$. Repeating this for $\ell=2,3,\ldots,2m-1$, finally all entries of $V$ will be independent over $\mathbb{Q}$ with $\{1\}$, as desired. Now Step II of the proof above combined with the following easy argument show that we can transition from $V$ to $\Omega$. \begin{proposition} Let $g, h$ be positive integers. Assume given real numbers $x_1, \ldots,x_g$ are $\mathbb{Q}$-linearly independent together with $1$. Then only for a set of Hausdorff dimension $h-1$ of vectors $\boldsymbol{y}=(y_1,\ldots,y_h)$ in $\mathbb{R}^h$, the joint vector $\boldsymbol{z}=(x_1,\ldots,x_g,y_1,\ldots,y_h)$ is $\mathbb{Q}$-linearly dependent with $1$. \end{proposition} \begin{proof} Since the $x_j$ are independent, if $\{ 1,\boldsymbol{z}\}$ is dependent over $\mathbb{Q}$ then there are integers $M_i, N_i, N$ with \[ N+ \sum_{i=1}^{g} M_i x_i +\sum_{i=1}^{h} N_i y_i = 0 \] and not all $N_i$ are $0$. But this means that $\boldsymbol{y}$ lies in a countable union of affine hyperplanes of $\mathbb{R}^{h}$. Hence we see that the set of $\boldsymbol{y}$ inducing dependency over $\mathbb{Q}$ indeed has Hausdorff dimension at most $h-1$. \end{proof} It suffices to take $g=2m, h=(n-2)m$ and to choose $x_i$ the entries of $V$ (first two columns of $\Omega$) and $y_i$ the remaining entries of $\Omega$ (entries of $B$) in the proposition to conclude that a full dimensional set of possible matrices $B\in \mathbb{R}^{m\times (n-2)}\cong \mathbb{R}^{m(n-2)}$ remains (in fact of positive $m(n-2)$ dimensional Hausdorff measure).
nodes.statement_short: Prove the rank and Q-independence claims.

nodes.name: Rank claim
nodes.statement: The first claim (i) on linear independence of rows follows from Step II. Aside from the metrical claim, note that it suffices to prove linearly independent rows can be arranged for the submatrix $B\in \mathbb{R}^{m\times (n-2)}$ of $\Omega=(V,B)$. Now since $n-2\ge m$ by \eqref{matrix dimension condition}, the matrix $B$ does not have fewer columns than rows, so if $B$ does not have the property it is rank deficient. However, as indicated in Section~\ref{Sek3.1}, looking at minors yields that the set of rank-deficient matrices has positive codimension and thus zero Lebesgue measure.
nodes.statement_short: Rank-deficient B form a null set.

nodes.name: Rank conclusion
nodes.statement: On the other hand, we showed that a positive Lebesgue measure set of matrices $B$ gives rise to $\Omega$ as in the theorem. Hence removing such rank-deficient matrices still leaves us with a set of positive $m\times (n-2)$-dimensional Lebesgue measure from which we can choose arbitrary $B$.
nodes.statement_short: Removing them leaves positive measure.

nodes.name: Problem with equal rows
nodes.statement: For the latter claim (ii) on $\mathbb{Q}$ linearly independent entries, note that in the construction of Section~\ref{sec61} certain entries of $V$ (thus $\Omega$) are identical, so the condition does not hold.
nodes.statement_short: Equal entries violate (ii).

nodes.name: Sign variation
nodes.statement: To fulfil this additional property, let us modify our construction by varying signs. First construct the submatrix $V\in \mathbb{R}^{m\times 2}$ as above by taking for $A_j, B_j$ as before \[ \Omega_{k,1}=V_{k,1}= \sum_{j=1}^{\infty} \delta_{k,j} A_j^{-1}, \qquad \Omega_{k,2}=V_{k,2}= \sum_{j=1}^{\infty} \delta_{k,j}^{\ast} B_j^{-1}, \quad (1\le k\le m) \] with sequences $\delta_{k,j}\in\{-1,1\}$, $\delta_{k,j}^{\ast}\in\{-1,1\}$ to be chosen later. When $\delta_{k,j}=\delta_{k,j}^{\ast}=1$ for all $k,j$ we are in the standard case of the previous sections.
nodes.statement_short: Vary signs delta_{k,j} in the series.

nodes.name: Error vectors
nodes.statement: When $m=1$, all arising matrices/vectors $(V_{1,1}, V_{1,2})=(\xi_1, \xi_2)$ share the properties of the standard case above. For $m>1$, we get more general error vectors than in \eqref{eq:vecin}, now of the form \begin{equation} \tilde{\boldsymbol{c}}_j:= V\cdot \begin{pmatrix} A_j \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} - \begin{pmatrix} F_{j,1} \\ F_{j,2} \\ \vdots \\ F_{j,m} \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \tilde{\boldsymbol{d}}_j:= V\cdot \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ B_j \end{pmatrix} - \begin{pmatrix} G_{j,1} \\ G_{j,2} \\ \vdots \\ G_{j,m} \end{pmatrix},\qquad j\ge 1, \end{equation} where \[ F_{j,k}= A_j \sum_{u=1}^{j} \delta_{k,u} A_{u}^{-1}, \qquad G_{j,k}= B_j \sum_{u=1}^{j} \delta_{k,u}^{\ast} B_{u}^{-1}, \qquad (1\le k\le m), \] depending on the choice of $\delta_{k,j}, \delta_{k,j}^{\ast}$. They again satisfy congruence properties $$F_j\equiv \pm 1\bmod 6 \quad \text{ and} \quad G_j\equiv \pm 1\bmod 35$$ for the same reasons, sufficient for coprimality with $6$ respectively $35$. Thus the entries of the remainders $\tilde{\boldsymbol{c}}_j, \tilde{\boldsymbol{d}}_j$ are given as \[ c_{j,k}= A_j \sum_{u=j+1}^{\infty} \delta_{k,u} A_{u}^{-1}, \qquad d_{j,k}= B_j \sum_{u=j+1}^{\infty} \delta_{k,u}^{\ast} B_{u}^{-1}, \qquad (1\le k\le m). \] However, since $A_j/A_{j+1}\to 0$ and $B_j/B_{j+1}\to 0$ we again see \[ c_{j,k}= \delta_{k,j+1} \cdot A_j A_{j+1}^{-1}(1+o(1)), \qquad d_{j,k}=\delta_{k,j+1}^{\ast} \cdot B_j B_{j+1}^{-1}(1+o(1)), \quad (1\le k\le m). \]
nodes.statement_short: Error vectors keep size A_j/A_{j+1}.

nodes.name: Norms of errors
nodes.statement: Hence, by the equivalence of norms, it is clear that the error vectors in \eqref{eq:errt} all have $\Vert\cdot\Vert_2$ norm of order respectively \begin{equation} \Vert \tilde{\boldsymbol{c}}_j\Vert_2= A_j A_{j+1}^{-1} \Gamma_j (1+o(1)), \qquad \Vert \tilde{\boldsymbol{d}}_j\Vert_2=B_j B_{j+1}^{-1} \tilde{\Gamma}_j (1+o(1)),\qquad j\to\infty, \end{equation} with $\Gamma_j, \tilde{\Gamma}_j$ of one of the numbers \[ \Gamma_j, \tilde{\Gamma}_j \in \{ \Vert (\pm 1,\pm 1,\ldots,\pm 1)\Vert_2\}, \qquad j\ge 1, \] for any possible sign choice. The values $\tilde{\Gamma}_j$ do not matter much as the according evaluations will be of negligible order by the analogue of \eqref{eq:frosch}. Now if we let \[ \Gamma:= \max\{ \Vert (\pm 1,\pm 1,\ldots,\pm 1)\Vert_2 \} \] with maximum overall $2^m$ sign choices, we can use the argument of Section~\ref{sec61}. Hereby we may assume that the maximizing sign choice occurs for infinitely many $(\delta_{1,j}, \ldots, \delta_{m,j})$, as otherwise we redefine $\Gamma$ via the maximum among those $m$ term sign sequences occurring infinitely often. Moreover, due to \eqref{eq:fertig}, the arguments of Section~\ref{st1} applied to each of the $m$ coordinates separately still apply very similarly and yield that the vectors $(A_j, 0 , -F_{j,1},\ldots,-F_{j,m})$ and $(0 , B_j, -G_{j,1},\ldots,-G_{j,m})$ essentially form the sequence of best approximations for the induced $V$. We leave the details to the reader. Then very similar arguments as in the classical case including Lemma~\ref{lemme} show that the Dirichlet constant $\Theta^{m\times n}(\Omega)$ of many such $\Omega=\Omega(\delta,\delta^{\ast})$ equals $c$, as before.
nodes.statement_short: Error norms scale with Gamma_j; argument of 7.1 applies.

nodes.name: Q-independence of V
nodes.statement: Finally we show that for many choices of $\delta_{k,j}, \delta_{k,j}^{\ast}$ all entries of $\Omega\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ are linearly independent over $\mathbb{Q}$ together with $\{1\}$. Let us first show this for the submatrix $V\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times 2}$. Label the entries $V_{i,j}$ of $V$ by $v_1,\ldots,v_{2m}$ with $v_{2h}=V_{h,2}$ and $v_{2h-1}=V_{h,1}$, $1\le h\le m$. Now the first line of $V$ is $\mathbb{Q}$-linearly independent for any choice of $\delta_{1,j}, \delta_{1,j}^{\ast}$ sequences as otherwise the sequence of best approximations for $(V_{1,1}, V_{1,2})$ would terminate, but the proof above shows that this is not the case. Hence $\{ 1,v_1, v_2\}$ is $\mathbb{Q}$-linearly independent. Then we proceed inductively. Having constructed the first $\ell\ge 2$ elements $v_1, \ldots,v_{\ell}$, we choose the $\delta$ or $\delta^{\ast}$ sequence for $v_{\ell+1}$ so that we avoid $\mathbb{Q}$-linear dependence of $v_{\ell+1}$ with the already chosen $1,v_1, \ldots,v_{\ell}$. This is possible since the $\mathbb{Q}$-span of $\{ 1,v_1,\ldots,v_{\ell} \}$ is countable, but we have uncountably many choices of $\delta$ or $\delta^{\ast}$ sequences. These clearly induce uncountably many pairwise distinct numbers $v_{\ell+1}$, the injectivity of the corresponding maps $\varphi: \{-1,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}\to \mathbb{R}$ resp. $\varphi^{\ast}: \{-1,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}\to \mathbb{R}$ follows from the rapid increase of the sequences $A_j$ resp. $B_j$. Repeating this for $\ell=2,3,\ldots,2m-1$, finally all entries of $V$ will be independent over $\mathbb{Q}$ with $\{1\}$, as desired.
nodes.statement_short: Choose sign sequences inductively avoiding countable spans.

nodes.name: Proposition 5
nodes.statement: Now Step II of the proof above combined with the following easy argument show that we can transition from $V$ to $\Omega$. \begin{proposition} Let $g, h$ be positive integers. Assume given real numbers $x_1, \ldots,x_g$ are $\mathbb{Q}$-linearly independent together with $1$. Then only for a set of Hausdorff dimension $h-1$ of vectors $\boldsymbol{y}=(y_1,\ldots,y_h)$ in $\mathbb{R}^h$, the joint vector $\boldsymbol{z}=(x_1,\ldots,x_g,y_1,\ldots,y_h)$ is $\mathbb{Q}$-linearly dependent with $1$. \end{proposition} \begin{proof} Since the $x_j$ are independent, if $\{ 1,\boldsymbol{z}\}$ is dependent over $\mathbb{Q}$ then there are integers $M_i, N_i, N$ with \[ N+ \sum_{i=1}^{g} M_i x_i +\sum_{i=1}^{h} N_i y_i = 0 \] and not all $N_i$ are $0$. But this means that $\boldsymbol{y}$ lies in a countable union of affine hyperplanes of $\mathbb{R}^{h}$. Hence we see that the set of $\boldsymbol{y}$ inducing dependency over $\mathbb{Q}$ indeed has Hausdorff dimension at most $h-1$. \end{proof}
nodes.statement_short: Transition from V to Omega.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: It suffices to take $g=2m, h=(n-2)m$ and to choose $x_i$ the entries of $V$ (first two columns of $\Omega$) and $y_i$ the remaining entries of $\Omega$ (entries of $B$) in the proposition to conclude that a full dimensional set of possible matrices $B\in \mathbb{R}^{m\times (n-2)}\cong \mathbb{R}^{m(n-2)}$ remains (in fact of positive $m(n-2)$ dimensional Hausdorff measure).
nodes.statement_short: Apply Proposition 5 with g=2m, h=(n-2)m.

nodes.name: Approximation function of block-diagonal matrices
nodes.statement: Let $\Omega\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ be a block matrix consisting of rectangular blocks $\Omega_1,\ldots,\Omega_k$ of sizes $(m_j,n_j), 1\le j\le k$ along the diagonal, $m=\sum m_j$, $n=\sum n_j$. Then \[ \psi_{\Omega}^{m\times n}(t)= \min_{1\leq j \leq k} \psi_{\Omega_j}^{m_j\times n_j}(t), \qquad t>0. \]
assumptions: Let $\Omega\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ be a block matrix consisting of rectangular blocks $\Omega_1,\ldots,\Omega_k$ of sizes $(m_j,n_j), 1\le j\le k$ along the diagonal, $m=\sum m_j$, $n=\sum n_j$.
nodes.label: llemma

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 8.1
nodes.statement: First observe that by the form of $\Omega$, the problem decomposes into $k$ decoupled linear form approximation problems. Fix $t$ and let $\boldsymbol{b}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{b}_k$ in $\mathbb{Z}^{m_j+n_j}$ be the best approximation integer vectors inducing $\psi_{\Omega_j}^{m_{j}\times n_{j}}(t)$ for $1\le j\le k$, i.e. $\boldsymbol{b}=\boldsymbol{b}_j$ minimizes $\Vert\Omega_j^{\ast} \boldsymbol{b}\Vert_{\infty}=\Vert\Omega_j \hat{\boldsymbol{b}}-\tilde{\boldsymbol{b}}\Vert_{\infty}$ among integer vectors $\boldsymbol{b}$ with $0<\Vert \boldsymbol{b}\Vert_{\infty}\le t$. The inequality \[ \psi_{\Omega}^{m\times n}(t) \le \min_{1\le j\le k} \psi_{\Omega_j}^{m_j\times n_j}(t) \] follows by taking the integer vector $\boldsymbol{b}\in \mathbb{Z}^{m+n}$ with entries of $\boldsymbol{b}_{j_0}$ at the according places, with $j_0$ inducing the minimum of $\Vert\Omega_j^{\ast} \boldsymbol{b}_j\Vert_{\infty}$ over $j$, and $0$ entries at all other places. By choice of the maximum norm, this will have the same norm \[ \Vert \Omega^{\ast}\cdot \boldsymbol{b}\Vert_{\infty} = \Vert\Omega_{j_0}^{\ast}\cdot \boldsymbol{b}_{j_{0}}\Vert_{\infty} =\psi_{\Omega_{j_0}}^{m_{j_0}\times n_{j_0}}(t) = \min_{1\le j\le k} \psi_{\Omega_j}^{m_j\times n_j}(t). \] Conversely, since some coordinate of the best approximation vector for given $t$ is not $0$ and the system is decoupled and we use maximum norm, we must have \[ \psi_{\Omega}^{m\times n}(t) \ge \min_{1\le j\le k} \psi_{\Omega_j}^{m_j\times n_j}(t). \]
nodes.statement_short: The problem decouples into blocks; with max norm the minimum over blocks is attained by padding with zeros.

nodes.name: Decoupling
nodes.statement: First observe that by the form of $\Omega$, the problem decomposes into $k$ decoupled linear form approximation problems. Fix $t$ and let $\boldsymbol{b}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{b}_k$ in $\mathbb{Z}^{m_j+n_j}$ be the best approximation integer vectors inducing $\psi_{\Omega_j}^{m_{j}\times n_{j}}(t)$ for $1\le j\le k$, i.e. $\boldsymbol{b}=\boldsymbol{b}_j$ minimizes $\Vert\Omega_j^{\ast} \boldsymbol{b}\Vert_{\infty}=\Vert\Omega_j \hat{\boldsymbol{b}}-\tilde{\boldsymbol{b}}\Vert_{\infty}$ among integer vectors $\boldsymbol{b}$ with $0<\Vert \boldsymbol{b}\Vert_{\infty}\le t$.
nodes.statement_short: Blocks decouple; take best approximations per block.

nodes.name: Upper bound
nodes.statement: The inequality \[ \psi_{\Omega}^{m\times n}(t) \le \min_{1\le j\le k} \psi_{\Omega_j}^{m_j\times n_j}(t) \] follows by taking the integer vector $\boldsymbol{b}\in \mathbb{Z}^{m+n}$ with entries of $\boldsymbol{b}_{j_0}$ at the according places, with $j_0$ inducing the minimum of $\Vert\Omega_j^{\ast} \boldsymbol{b}_j\Vert_{\infty}$ over $j$, and $0$ entries at all other places. By choice of the maximum norm, this will have the same norm \[ \Vert \Omega^{\ast}\cdot \boldsymbol{b}\Vert_{\infty} = \Vert\Omega_{j_0}^{\ast}\cdot \boldsymbol{b}_{j_{0}}\Vert_{\infty} =\psi_{\Omega_{j_0}}^{m_{j_0}\times n_{j_0}}(t) = \min_{1\le j\le k} \psi_{\Omega_j}^{m_j\times n_j}(t). \]
nodes.statement_short: Padding the best block vector with zeros.

nodes.name: Lower bound
nodes.statement: Conversely, since some coordinate of the best approximation vector for given $t$ is not $0$ and the system is decoupled and we use maximum norm, we must have \[ \psi_{\Omega}^{m\times n}(t) \ge \min_{1\le j\le k} \psi_{\Omega_j}^{m_j\times n_j}(t). \]
nodes.statement_short: Some nonzero block gives the reverse inequality.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3.3
nodes.statement:
As in Lemma~ef{llemma}, take a matrix of the form $\Omega=m{diag}(\Omega_1, \Omega_2)$ with diagonal blocks $\Omega_1\in Bad_{n-1,n-1}$ and $\Omega_2=\{\eta\}
otin Bad_{1,1}\cup \mathbb{Q}$ are arbitrary. Keep in mind that as $n/n=(n-1)/(n-1)=1/1=1$, the Dirichlet exponent (remark: not constant) is $1$ for all $\Omega_1$, $\eta$ and $\Omega$, for all arguments below. By Lemma~ef{llemma} we have  egin{equation} \Theta^{n	imes n}(\Omega) = \limsup_{t	o\infty} t \cdot \psi_{\Omega}^{n	imes n}(t) = \limsup_{t	o\infty} t \cdot \min \{ \psi_{\Omega_1}^{(n-1)	imes (n-1)}(t), \psi_{\eta}^{1	imes 1}(t)\}. \end{equation} Now since $\Omega_1\in Bad_{n-1,n-1}\subseteq Di_{n-1,n-1}$ we have \[ \Theta^{(n-1)	imes (n-1)}(\Omega_1)= \limsup_{t	o\infty} t^{ rac{n-1}{n-1}} \cdot \psi_{\Omega_1}^{(n-1)	imes (n-1)}(t)=\limsup_{t	o\infty} t \cdot \psi_{\Omega_1}^{(n-1)	imes (n-1)}(t) < 1 \] so $\Omega\in Di_{n,n}$ as well by \eqref{eq:ABC}. Moreover since \[ \limsup_{t	o\infty} t\psi^{1	imes 1}_{\eta}(t)\ge 1/2>0 \] for any irrational $\eta$ by Khintchine~\cite{Khinchin3} and \[ \liminf_{t	o\infty} t\psi_{\Omega_1}^{(n-1)	imes (n-1)}(t) >0 \] since $\Omega_1\in Bad_{n-1,n-1}$, again by \eqref{eq:ABC} we have $\Theta^{n	imes n}(\Omega)>0$ and thus $\Omega
otin Sing_{n,n}$. Finally again by Lemma~ef{llemma} \[ 	ilde{\Theta}^{n	imes n}(\Omega)=\liminf_{t	o\infty} t^{n/n} \psi_{\Omega}(t) \le \liminf_{t	o\infty} t^{1/1} \psi_{\eta}(t) = 0 \] since $\eta
otin Bad_{1,1}$, so $\Omega
otin Bad_{n,n}$. Hence $\Omega\in FS_{n,n}$. It is well-known that $Bad_{n-1,n-1}$ has full Hausdorff dimension $(n-1)^2$ and that the complement of $Bad_{1,1}$ has full $1$-dimensional Lebesgue measure, see Section~ef{s12}. Removing the countable set $\mathbb{Q}$ clearly has no effect on the Lebesgue measure. In particular, we can choose regular (full $\mathbb{R}$-rank) matrices $B$ as the complementary set has strictly lower Hausdorff dimension, and by the diagonal form and $\eta
e 0$ the same will be true for any arising $\Omega$. This argument together with \eqref{eq:tric} also shows that the dimension of the set of matrices $\Omega$ constructed above is at least $(n-1)^2+1$.
nodes.statement_short: Take diag(Omega_1, eta) with Omega_1 badly approximable and eta irrational non-badly approximable; Lemma 8.1 gives membership in FS_{n,n}.

nodes.name: eq:ABC (54)
nodes.statement: \Theta^{n\times n}(\Omega) = \limsup_{t\to\infty} t \cdot \psi_{\Omega}^{n\times n}(t) = \limsup_{t\to\infty} t \cdot \min \{ \psi_{\Omega_1}^{(n-1)\times (n-1)}(t), \psi_{\eta}^{1\times 1}(t)\}.
nodes.label: eq:ABC

nodes.name: Block construction
nodes.statement: As in Lemma~\ref{llemma}, take a matrix of the form $\Omega=\rm{diag}(\Omega_1, \Omega_2)$ with diagonal blocks $\Omega_1\in Bad_{n-1,n-1}$ and $\Omega_2=\{\eta\}\notin Bad_{1,1}\cup \mathbb{Q}$ are arbitrary. Keep in mind that as $n/n=(n-1)/(n-1)=1/1=1$, the Dirichlet exponent (remark: not constant) is $1$ for all $\Omega_1$, $\eta$ and $\Omega$, for all arguments below.
nodes.statement_short: Omega=diag(Omega_1,eta).

nodes.name: Apply Lemma 8.1
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{llemma} we have \begin{equation} \Theta^{n\times n}(\Omega) = \limsup_{t\to\infty} t \cdot \psi_{\Omega}^{n\times n}(t) = \limsup_{t\to\infty} t \cdot \min \{ \psi_{\Omega_1}^{(n-1)\times (n-1)}(t), \psi_{\eta}^{1\times 1}(t)\}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Theta of Omega via min of block functions.

nodes.name: Dirichlet improvable
nodes.statement: Now since $\Omega_1\in Bad_{n-1,n-1}\subseteq Di_{n-1,n-1}$ we have \[ \Theta^{(n-1)\times (n-1)}(\Omega_1)= \limsup_{t\to\infty} t^{\frac{n-1}{n-1}} \cdot \psi_{\Omega_1}^{(n-1)\times (n-1)}(t)=\limsup_{t\to\infty} t \cdot \psi_{\Omega_1}^{(n-1)\times (n-1)}(t) < 1 \] so $\Omega\in Di_{n,n}$ as well by \eqref{eq:ABC}.
nodes.statement_short: Omega_1 in Di gives Omega in Di.

nodes.name: Not singular
nodes.statement: Moreover since \[ \limsup_{t\to\infty} t\psi^{1\times 1}_{\eta}(t)\ge 1/2>0 \] for any irrational $\eta$ by Khintchine~\cite{Khinchin3} and \[ \liminf_{t\to\infty} t\psi_{\Omega_1}^{(n-1)\times (n-1)}(t) >0 \] since $\Omega_1\in Bad_{n-1,n-1}$, again by \eqref{eq:ABC} we have $\Theta^{n\times n}(\Omega)>0$ and thus $\Omega\notin Sing_{n,n}$.
nodes.statement_short: Khintchine and Bad give Theta>0.

nodes.name: Not badly approximable
nodes.statement: Finally again by Lemma~\ref{llemma} \[ \tilde{\Theta}^{n\times n}(\Omega)=\liminf_{t\to\infty} t^{n/n} \psi_{\Omega}(t) \le \liminf_{t\to\infty} t^{1/1} \psi_{\eta}(t) = 0 \] since $\eta\notin Bad_{1,1}$, so $\Omega\notin Bad_{n,n}$. Hence $\Omega\in FS_{n,n}$.
nodes.statement_short: eta not in Bad gives liminf 0.

nodes.name: Dimension and rank
nodes.statement: It is well-known that $Bad_{n-1,n-1}$ has full Hausdorff dimension $(n-1)^2$ and that the complement of $Bad_{1,1}$ has full $1$-dimensional Lebesgue measure, see Section~\ref{s12}. Removing the countable set $\mathbb{Q}$ clearly has no effect on the Lebesgue measure. In particular, we can choose regular (full $\mathbb{R}$-rank) matrices $B$ as the complementary set has strictly lower Hausdorff dimension, and by the diagonal form and $\eta\ne 0$ the same will be true for any arising $\Omega$. This argument together with \eqref{eq:tric} also shows that the dimension of the set of matrices $\Omega$ constructed above is at least $(n-1)^2+1$.
