nodes.statement_short: Full dimension of Bad and the product inequality give (n-1)^2+1.

nodes.name: Spectrum inclusion for multiples
nodes.statement: With $\mathcal{D}_{m,n}$ as in \eqref{eq:dirspe}, for any positive integers $m,n,k$ and $c>0$ we have \[ \mathcal{D}_{m,n} \subseteq \mathcal{D}_{km,kn}, \] and \[ \dim_H FS_{m,n} \le \dim_H FS_{km,kn} \;, \qquad \dim_H FS_{m,n}(c) \le \dim_H FS_{km,kn}(c). \]
nodes.label: multiples

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 8.2
nodes.statement: For any $m\times n$ matrix $\Omega$, by Lemma \ref{llemma} the $km\times kn$-matrix $\Omega^{\prime}:=\rm{diag}(\Omega,\ldots,\Omega)$ with $k$ diagonal blocks $\Omega$ induces the same approximation function \[ \psi_{\Omega}^{m\times n}(t)= \psi_{\Omega^{\prime} }^{km\times kn}(t), \qquad t>0. \] Since the Dirichlet exponents coincide via $(kn)/(km)=n/m$, the claims follow directly.
nodes.statement_short: Repeat Omega k times on the diagonal; Lemma 8.1 gives the same approximation function.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3.4
nodes.statement:
Let us introduce $\ell:= \left\lceil  rac{m}{n}ightceil \ge 2$, so that  egin{equation} (\ell-1)n< m \le \ell n. \end{equation} For simplicity, first we treat the case $\ell=2$ (that suffices for the sake of Theorem ef{non-empty main}). {\em Case $\ell=2$:} Then  egin{equation}  rac{1}{2}\le  rac{n}{m} < 1. \end{equation} Moreover we can assume $m\ge 4$ and $n\ge 2$, as the otherwise our exclusion of $(m,n)=(3,2)$ forces $n=1$, and this case is a trivial consequence of \cite{j1}. Let us first consider maximum norms  egin{equation} \Vert\cdot\Vert_1=\Vert\cdot\Vert_2=\Vert\cdot\Vert_{\infty}. \end{equation} Then~\cite[Theorem~2.2]{j1} in the case of simultaneous approximation to two numbers can be applied to $\Phi(t)=ct^{-n/m}$ for any $c\in (0,1)$, as the conditions (d1)-(d3) of \cite{j1} are satisfied by our choice of $\Phi$ and \eqref{nm bound}. This yields $ oldsymbol{\xi}\in \mathbb{R}^{2	imes 1}$ with \[ \limsup_{t	o\infty} t^{n/m} \psi^{2	imes 1}_{ oldsymbol{\xi}}(t) = c, \quad 	ext{and} \quad \liminf_{t	o\infty} t^{n/m} \psi^{2	imes 1}_{ oldsymbol{\xi}}(t) = 0. \] Now let $ oldsymbol{\zeta}\in Bad_{m-2,1}$ arbitrary unless if $m=4$ then $ oldsymbol{\zeta}= oldsymbol{\xi}$. Since $m-2\ge 2$ by assumption, it is easily seen that in either case \[ \psi_{ oldsymbol{\xi}}^{2	imes 1}(t) \le \psi_{ oldsymbol{\zeta}}^{(m-2)	imes 1}(t), \qquad t\ge t_0. \] Hence by Lemma~ef{llemma} the matrix $U=m{diag}( oldsymbol{\xi}, oldsymbol{\zeta})\in \mathbb{R}^{ m 	imes 2}$ satisfies  egin{equation} \limsup_{t	o\infty} t^{n/m} \psi^{m	imes 2}_{U}(t) = c, \qquad \liminf_{t	o\infty} t^{n/m} \psi^{m	imes 2}_{U}(t) = 0, \end{equation} as well. \par If $n=2$ then we must have $m=4$ due to our assumptions $	frac{n}{m}\geq  rac{1}{2}$ and $m\ge 4$, and then we can just take $\Omega=U$. Note also that in this case our claimed bound for Hausdorff dimension becomes zero, so there is nothing more to prove.\par If $n\geq 3$, then in Lemma~ef{lemme} take $V=U\in \mathbb{R}^{m	imes2}$. Note that the problematic case $n=m+2$ of the lemma is excluded here via \eqref{nm bound}. Notice further $V$ satisfies \eqref{V property} by \eqref{Vt property}. Hence, assuming $c>0$ is small enough, there exists a set of positive $m(n-2)$-dimensional Lebesgue measure $\mathcal{Y}\subseteq \mathbb{R}^{m	imes(n-2)}$ of matrices so that for any $B\in\mathcal{Y}$, the $\mathbb{R}^{m	imes n}$ matrix $\Omega=(B,U)$ satisfies  egin{equation*} \limsup_{t	o\infty}t^{n/m}\psi_{\Omega}^{m	imes n}(t)=c\, . \end{equation*} Finally, we show $\Omega$ is not badly approximable. By \eqref{Vt property} there exists a sequence of best approximations such that on the sequence $(t_{j})_{j\geq 1}$ we have  egin{equation*} \lim_{j	o \infty} t_{j}^{n/m}\psi_{U}^{m	imes 2}(t_{j})=0. \end{equation*} Considering $\Omega$, take the same sequence of the best approximations and place a zero in all entries not related to $U$ (that is starting from the third) to obtain the same statement, i.e.  egin{equation*} \lim_{j	o \infty} t_{j}^{n/m}\psi_{\Omega}^{m	imes n}(t_{j})=0. \end{equation*} Combining these two claims we infer $\Omega \in FS_{m,n}(c)$. Using \eqref{eq:tric} the dimension statement follows since we have shown that (when $m\geq 5$)  egin{equation*} \dim_H FS_{m,n}(c) \geq \dim_H \mathcal{Y} + \dim_H Bad_{m-2,1} = m(n-2) + m-2, \end{equation*} where we used that $Bad_{m-2,1}$ has full Hausdorff dimension and $\mathcal{Y}$ has positive Lebesgue measure. In the case $(m,n)=(4,3)$ we obtain  egin{equation*} \dim_H FS_{4,3}(c) \geq \dim_H \mathcal{Y} = m(n-2)=4. \end{equation*} We remark that for $(m,n)=(4,2)$ the according estimate holds as well, but the right hand side vanishes. This completes the proofs for the maximum norm, i.e. \eqref{eq:maxno}. Now let $\Vert \cdot\Vert_1$ be arbitrary and still $\Vert\cdot\Vert_2=\Vert \cdot\Vert_{\infty}$. Let $\Vert\cdot \Vert_1^{\prime}$ be the projected norm \[ \Vert (x_1,x_2)\Vert_1^{\prime} := \Vert (x_1,x_2,0,\ldots,0)\Vert_1. \] Let $\gamma= \Vert oldsymbol{e}_1\Vert_1^{\prime}$ be the norm of the first base vector of $\mathbb{R}^2$. By \cite[Theorem 2.2]{j1} and again \eqref{nm bound}, for small enough $c>0$ we may pick $ oldsymbol{\xi}\in\mathbb{R}^{2	imes 1}$ such that  egin{equation} \limsup_{t	o\infty} t^{n/m} \psi^{ 2	imes1}_{ oldsymbol{\xi}}(t) = c_1:=c \gamma^{n/m}, \qquad \liminf_{t	o\infty} t^{n/m} \psi^{2	imes1}_{ oldsymbol{\xi}}(t) = 0. \end{equation} Suppose we can show that, for any $U= m{diag}( oldsymbol{\xi}, oldsymbol{\zeta})\in \mathbb{R}^{m	imes 2}$ as above, which we can identify with elements in $\{  oldsymbol{\xi}\}	imes Bad_{m-2,1}\subseteq \mathbb{R}^{m}$, we have that  egin{equation} \psi_U^{m	imes 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}, \Vert\cdot\Vert_2,t) = \psi_{ oldsymbol{\xi}}^{2	imes 1}(|\cdot |,\Vert \cdot\Vert_{\infty},\gamma^{-1} t),\qquad t\ge t_0 \, . \end{equation} If \eqref{claim} holds, then indeed \[ \limsup_{t	o\infty} t^{n/m} \psi_U^{m	imes 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_{1}',\Vert\cdot\Vert_{2},t) =\gamma^{-n/m} \limsup_{t	o\infty} t^{n/m} \psi_{ oldsymbol{\xi}}^{2	imes 1}(|\cdot |,\Vert \cdot\Vert_{\infty},\gamma^{-1} t)= \gamma^{-n/m} c_1=c, \] and \[ \liminf_{t	o\infty} t^{n/m}\psi_U^{m	imes 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_{1}',\Vert\cdot\Vert_{2},t) = \gamma^{-n/m} \liminf_{t	o\infty}t^{n/m}\psi_{ oldsymbol{\xi}}^{2	imes 1}(|\cdot |,\Vert \cdot\Vert_{\infty},\gamma^{-1} t)= 0. \] Hence for $c$ small enough we again we may again apply Lemma~ef{lemme}, to find some set $\mathcal{Y}\subseteq \mathbb{R}^{m	imes (n-2)}$ of positive Lebesgue measure such that for any $B\in \mathcal{Y}$ we have  egin{equation*} \limsup_{t	o\infty} t^{n/m}\psi^{m	imes n}_{(U,B)}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_{1},\Vert\cdot\Vert_{2},t)=c \, ,\qquad \liminf_{t	o\infty} t^{n/m}\psi^{m	imes n}_{(U,B)}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_{1},\Vert\cdot\Vert_{2},t)=0\, . \end{equation*} So $(U,B)\in FS_{m,n}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_{1},\Vert\cdot\Vert_{2},c)$, and analogously to the maximum norm by \eqref{eq:tric} we conclude  egin{equation*} \dim_H FS_{m,n}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_{1},\Vert\cdot\Vert_{2},c) \geq \dim_H \mathcal{Y} + \dim_H Bad_{m-2,1} = m(n-2) + m-2, \end{equation*} for $m\ge 5$, and accordingly for $(m,n)=(4,3)$ we get the bound \[ \dim_H FS_{4,3}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_{1},\Vert\cdot\Vert_{2},c) \geq m(n-2)=4. \] Since $\lceil m/nceil=2$ by \eqref{nm bound}, we indeed recognize these as special cases of our claim. Thus to complete the proof for $\ell=2$ we need to show \eqref{claim} holds. For the inequality  egin{equation} \psi_U^{m	imes 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}, \Vert\cdot\Vert_2,t) \le \psi_{ oldsymbol{\xi}}^{2	imes 1}(|\cdot |,\Vert \cdot\Vert_{\infty},\gamma^{-1} t), \qquad t\geq t_{0} \end{equation} observe that any $(x, oldsymbol{w})\in \mathbb{Z}	imes \mathbb{Z}^2$ with $| x\vert\le \gamma^{-1} t$ gives rise to $ oldsymbol{z}=(x,0)=x  oldsymbol{e}_1\in \mathbb{Z}^2$ of norm $\Vert  oldsymbol{z} \Vert_1^{\prime}= |x|\gamma\le t$. Moreover since  egin{equation} U\cdot  oldsymbol{z}-( oldsymbol{w},0,\ldots,0)= ( oldsymbol{\xi}\cdot x -  oldsymbol{w} , 0, \ldots,0)\in\mathbb{R}^m, \end{equation} with the same first two coordinates followed by $m-2$ zeros, we have the identity  egin{equation} \Vert U\cdot  oldsymbol{z}-( oldsymbol{w},0,\ldots,0)\Vert_{\infty}= \Vert oldsymbol{\xi}\cdot x- oldsymbol{w}\Vert_{\infty}\, , \end{equation} where we used $\Vert\cdot\Vert_2$ being the maximum norm. As $t$ is arbitrary \eqref{eq:unn} is implied. Now consider the reverse inequality  egin{equation} \psi_U^{m	imes 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}, \Vert\cdot\Vert_2,t) \ge \psi_{ oldsymbol{\xi}}^{2	imes 1}(|\cdot |,\Vert \cdot\Vert_{\infty},\gamma^{-1} t), \qquad t\geq t_{0}. \end{equation} Begin with $(m,n)
e (4,2)$. Note that if $ oldsymbol{z}=(z_1,z_2)\in \mathbb{Z}^2$ with $\Vert  oldsymbol{z}\Vert_{1}^{\prime} \le t$ does not lie in the space $z_2=0$, then by equivalence of norms for any $	extbf{y}\in\mathbb{Z}^m$  egin{equation} \Vert U\cdot  oldsymbol{z}-  oldsymbol{y} \Vert_{\infty} \gg \Vert oldsymbol{z}\Vert_{\infty}^{-1/(m-2)}\gg \Vert oldsymbol{z}\Vert_{1}^{\prime -1/(m-2)}\ge t^{-1/(m-2)} \end{equation} where the most left estimate holds since the system is decoupled and $ oldsymbol{\zeta}\in Bad_{m-2,1}$. As we noticed above that $m\ge 4$ and $1/2\le n/m$, in our case $(m,n)
e (4,2)$ we have the strict inequality $1/(m-2)< n/m$. Then, in view of \eqref{eq:invo}, approximation quality \eqref{eq:impco} is beaten by $\psi_{ oldsymbol{\xi}}^{2	imes 1}(|\cdot |,\Vert \cdot\Vert_{\infty},\gamma^{-1} t)$, so extending accordingly the involved integer best approximation approximations to $\mathbb{Z}^n$ by adding $0$ entries leads to the same smaller value. So we can exclude such vectors. But for vectors $ oldsymbol{z}$ in the linear space $z_2=0$, the integer vector $	extbf{y}$ minimizing $\Vert U\cdot 	extbf{z}-	extbf{y}\Vert_{\infty}$ for given $	extbf{z}$ is easily seen to be of the form $	extbf{y}=(	extbf{w},0,\ldots,0)$ with $	extbf{w}\in\mathbb{Z}^2$, as otherwise some entry of $U\cdot 	extbf{z}-	extbf{y}$ is of modulus at least $1$. Then the output $U\cdot 	extbf{z}-	extbf{y}\in \mathbb{R}^m$ again satisfies \eqref{eq:noon} and hence \eqref{eq:spet}, settling \eqref{eq:rever} via a short calculation. For $m=4, n=2$ a very similar argument applies using $ oldsymbol{\zeta}= oldsymbol{\xi}$, however we need $\Vert\cdot\Vert_1$ to be expanding to exclude better approximations outside the space $z_2=0$. If the expanding property is assumed, then it is again easy to see that we may restrict $	extbf{z}$ to this space and the claims follows easily. We leave the details to the reader. Finally, let $\Vert\cdot\Vert_2$ be any expanding norm on $\mathbb{R}^m$ and consider again the induced projected norm $\Vert\cdot\Vert_2^{\prime}$ on $\mathbb{R}^2$ by \[ \Vert (x_1,x_2)\Vert_2^{\prime}:= \Vert (x_1,x_2,0,\ldots,0)\Vert_2. \] It is easy to see that $\Vert\cdot\Vert_2^{\prime}$ is an expanding norm on $\mathbb{R}^2$. A minor adaption of~\cite[Corollary~2]{j1} to more general $\Phi$ satisfying (d1)-(d3) of \cite{j1} can be proved analogously. When applied with respect to simultaneous approximation of two reals, and as (d1)-(d3) hold for our $\Phi(t)=ct^{-n/m}$ in view of \eqref{nm bound} and $c\le 1$, it yields the following: For any small enough $c>0$, we can similarly arrange some $ oldsymbol{\xi}\in\mathbb{R}^{2	imes 1}$ to satisfy \[ \limsup_{t	o\infty} t^{n/m} \psi^{ 2	imes1}_{ oldsymbol{\xi}}(|\cdot|,\Vert\cdot\Vert_2^{\prime},t) = c_1:=c \gamma^{n/m},\quad 	ext{ and } \quad \liminf_{t	o\infty} t^{n/m} \psi^{2	imes1}_{ oldsymbol{\xi}}(|\cdot|,\Vert\cdot\Vert_2^{\prime},t) = 0.\] We can then copy the proof above replacing $\Vert\cdot \Vert_{\infty}$ by $\Vert\cdot\Vert_2^{\prime}$ whenever considering $\psi^{2	imes 1}_{ oldsymbol{\xi}}$. Again by the same argument, it suffices to show the accordingly altered variant of \eqref{claim}. For the estimate \eqref{eq:unn}, the only place where we needed $\Vert\cdot\Vert_2$ to be the maximum norm is to deduce that the projected vectors satisfy \eqref{eq:spet}. However, in view of \eqref{eq:noon}, the defining property of $\Vert\cdot\Vert_2^{\prime}$ means that the according equality still holds. The proof of the reverse inequality \eqref{eq:rever} is analogous to the above, only with different implied constants in \eqref{eq:impco}. The case $\ell=2$ is done up to the full rank claim. For the rank claim, consider first the $n	imes 2$ matrix obtained from any $n$ lines of $V$ containing its first and last line, and complete it to an $n	imes n$ matrix $H$ by adding to the right an $n	imes (n-2)$ matrix of free variable entries $x_{i,j}$, $1\le i\le n$, $3\le j\le n$. Then writing $ oldsymbol{\xi}=(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_{\ell})$, $ oldsymbol{\zeta}=(\zeta_1,\ldots,\zeta_{m-\ell})$, the first and last line of $H$ are of the form $(\xi_1, 0, x_{1,3}, \ldots, x_{1,n})$ resp. $(0, \zeta_{m-\ell}, x_{n,3}, \ldots, x_{n,n})$. Since $\xi_i
e 0$ and $\zeta_j
e 0$ for all $1\le i\le \ell, 1\le j\le m-\ell$ is easy to see (otherwise $ oldsymbol{\xi}$ or $ oldsymbol{\zeta}$ would be singular, contradicting $ oldsymbol{\xi}\in DI_{\ell}(c)$ resp. $ oldsymbol{\zeta}\in Bad_{m-\ell,1}$), it is further readily checked that the determinant of $H$ is not the constant $0$ polynomial in the $x_{i,j}$. Hence only a Lebesgue nullset of $G:=(x_{i,j})\in \mathbb{R}^{n	imes (n-2)}$ will induce non invertible $H$. Now as $G\in \mathbb{R}^{n	imes (n-2)}$ can be considered a submatrix of $B\in \mathbb{R}^{m	imes (n-2)}$ above, by considering the Cartesian product $G	imes \mathbb{R}^{(m-n)	imes (n-2)}$ only a nullset of $B$ will lead to $\Omega$ of deficient rank. On the other hand, we are equipped with a positive measure set $B$ by Lemma~ef{lemme}. Hence indeed we can restrict to full rank matrices without affecting the metrical claim. {\em Case $\ell\ge 3$:} Then by \eqref{eq:ojsi} similarly to \eqref{nm bound} we have  egin{equation}  rac{1}{\ell}\le  rac{n}{m} <  rac{1}{\ell-1}. \end{equation} Now again~\cite[Theorem~2.2]{j1} can be applied, with respect to simultaneous approximation to $\ell$ numbers, to $\Phi(t)=ct^{-n/m}$ for any $c\in (0,1)$, as its conditions (d1)-(d3) are satisfied by \eqref{eq:Dd}. This yields $ oldsymbol{\xi}\in \mathbb{R}^{\ell 	imes 1}$ so that \[ \limsup_{t	o\infty} t^{n/m} \psi^{\ell 	imes 1}_{ oldsymbol{\xi}}(t) = c, \quad 	ext{and} \quad \liminf_{t	o\infty} t^{n/m} \psi^{\ell 	imes 1}_{ oldsymbol{\xi}}(t) = 0. \] Now let $ oldsymbol{\zeta}\in Bad_{m-\ell ,1}$ arbitrary unless if $m=2\ell$ then $ oldsymbol{\zeta}= oldsymbol{\xi}$. We again consider $U=m{diag}( oldsymbol{\xi},  oldsymbol{\zeta})\in \mathbb{R}^{m	imes 2}$ as above. As soon as strict inequality  egin{equation} m> 2\ell \end{equation} holds, we have $1/(m-\ell)< n/m$ so that the analogue of \eqref{eq:impco} similarly implies that we can restrict to the space $z_2=0$. It can be checked that the analogous arguments of the case $\ell=2$ above apply. Notably when transitioning to any expanding norm $\Vert\cdot\Vert_2$, here we consider the restriction \[ \Vert (x_1,\ldots,x_{\ell})\Vert_2^{\prime}:= \Vert (x_1,\ldots,x_{\ell},0,\ldots,0)\Vert_2, \] and apply an analogous variant of~\cite[Corollary~2]{j1} with respect to simultaneous approximation to $\ell$ numbers. Finally we need to discuss the separate cases when \eqref{eq:mpso} is satisfied, and evaluate the Hausdorff dimensions. Recall we have assumed $\ell\ge 3$, moreover we can assume $n\ge 2$ as $n=1$ was done in \cite{j2}. Via \eqref{eq:ojsi}, condition \eqref{eq:mpso} is readily checked to be satisfied if $n\ge 3$. Thus we are left with the subset of cases $n=2$. The cases $n=2, m\ge 4$ even, leading to $m=2\ell$, can be dealt with similarly to the case $(m,n)=(4,2)$ for $\ell=2$ above. This indeed leaves open only the cases $n=2$, and $m$ odd, as excluded in the theorem. By construction, and the repeatedly used observation that $Bad_{m-\ell ,1}$ has full Hausdorff dimension $m-\ell$, we obtain the Hausdorff dimension bound \[ \dim_H FS_{m,n}(c) \ge m\cdot (n-2)+(m-\ell)=m(n-1)-\left\lceil rac{m}{n}ightceil, \qquad m\ge 2\ell+1, \] of the theorem. The remaining case $m=2\ell=2\lceil m/nceil$ is readily checked to lead precisely to the cases $n=2$ and $m$ even or $(m,n)=(4,3)$. When $(m,n)=(4,3)$ we have $\ell=2$, which is already treated above. It should be remarked that for $n=2$ our Hausdorff dimension bound is just $m(n-2)=0$, thus of no interest. The full rank claim is also proved analogously to the case $\ell=2$.
nodes.statement_short: Block-diagonal U=diag(xi,zeta) with xi from j1 and zeta badly approximable, extended by Lemma 7.1. The key step is identity (60) reducing psi_U to psi_xi.

nodes.name: Range of ell (55)
nodes.statement: (\ell-1)n< m \le \ell n.
nodes.label: eq:ojsi

nodes.name: nm bound (56)
nodes.statement: \frac{1}{2}\le \frac{n}{m} < 1.
nodes.label: nm bound

nodes.name: Maximum norms (57)
nodes.statement: \Vert\cdot\Vert_1=\Vert\cdot\Vert_2=\Vert\cdot\Vert_{\infty}.
nodes.label: eq:maxno

nodes.name: Vt property (58)
nodes.statement: \limsup_{t\to\infty} t^{n/m} \psi^{m\times 2}_{U}(t) = c, \qquad \liminf_{t\to\infty} t^{n/m} \psi^{m\times 2}_{U}(t) = 0,
nodes.label: Vt property

nodes.name: eq:invo (59)
nodes.statement: \limsup_{t\to\infty} t^{n/m} \psi^{ 2\times1}_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t) = c_1:=c \gamma^{n/m}, \qquad \liminf_{t\to\infty} t^{n/m} \psi^{2\times1}_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t) = 0.
nodes.label: eq:invo

nodes.name: Key identity (60)
nodes.statement: \psi_U^{m\times 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}, \Vert\cdot\Vert_2,t) = \psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{2\times 1}(|\cdot |,\Vert \cdot\Vert_{\infty},\gamma^{-1} t),\qquad t\ge t_0 \, .
nodes.label: claim

nodes.name: eq:unn (61)
nodes.statement: \psi_U^{m\times 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}, \Vert\cdot\Vert_2,t) \le \psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{2\times 1}(|\cdot |,\Vert \cdot\Vert_{\infty},\gamma^{-1} t), \qquad t\geq t_{0}
nodes.label: eq:unn

nodes.name: eq:noon (62)
nodes.statement: U\cdot \boldsymbol{z}-(\boldsymbol{w},0,\ldots,0)= (\boldsymbol{\xi}\cdot x - \boldsymbol{w} , 0, \ldots,0)\in\mathbb{R}^m,
nodes.label: eq:noon

nodes.name: eq:spet (63)
nodes.statement: \Vert U\cdot \boldsymbol{z}-(\boldsymbol{w},0,\ldots,0)\Vert_{\infty}= \Vert\boldsymbol{\xi}\cdot x-\boldsymbol{w}\Vert_{\infty}\, ,
nodes.label: eq:spet

nodes.name: eq:rever (64)
nodes.statement: \psi_U^{m\times 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}, \Vert\cdot\Vert_2,t) \ge \psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{2\times 1}(|\cdot |,\Vert \cdot\Vert_{\infty},\gamma^{-1} t), \qquad t\geq t_{0}.
nodes.label: eq:rever

nodes.name: eq:impco (65)
nodes.statement: \Vert U\cdot \boldsymbol{z}- \boldsymbol{y} \Vert_{\infty} \gg \Vert\boldsymbol{z}\Vert_{\infty}^{-1/(m-2)}\gg \Vert\boldsymbol{z}\Vert_{1}^{\prime -1/(m-2)}\ge t^{-1/(m-2)}
nodes.label: eq:impco

nodes.name: eq:Dd (66)
nodes.statement: \frac{1}{\ell}\le \frac{n}{m} < \frac{1}{\ell-1}.
nodes.label: eq:Dd

nodes.name: eq:mpso (67)
nodes.statement: m> 2\ell

nodes.name: Parameter ell
nodes.statement: Let us introduce $\ell:= \left\lceil \frac{m}{n}\right\rceil \ge 2$, so that \begin{equation} (\ell-1)n< m \le \ell n. \end{equation} For simplicity, first we treat the case $\ell=2$ (that suffices for the sake of Theorem \ref{non-empty main}).
nodes.statement_short: Introduce ell=ceil(m/n); treat ell=2 first.

nodes.name: Case ell=2
nodes.statement:
{\em Case $\ell=2$:} Then  egin{equation}  rac{1}{2}\le  rac{n}{m} < 1. \end{equation} Moreover we can assume $m\ge 4$ and $n\ge 2$, as the otherwise our exclusion of $(m,n)=(3,2)$ forces $n=1$, and this case is a trivial consequence of \cite{j1}. Let us first consider maximum norms  egin{equation} \Vert\cdot\Vert_1=\Vert\cdot\Vert_2=\Vert\cdot\Vert_{\infty}. \end{equation} Then~\cite[Theorem~2.2]{j1} in the case of simultaneous approximation to two numbers can be applied to $\Phi(t)=ct^{-n/m}$ for any $c\in (0,1)$, as the conditions (d1)-(d3) of \cite{j1} are satisfied by our choice of $\Phi$ and \eqref{nm bound}. This yields $ oldsymbol{\xi}\in \mathbb{R}^{2	imes 1}$ with \[ \limsup_{t	o\infty} t^{n/m} \psi^{2	imes 1}_{ oldsymbol{\xi}}(t) = c, \quad 	ext{and} \quad \liminf_{t	o\infty} t^{n/m} \psi^{2	imes 1}_{ oldsymbol{\xi}}(t) = 0. \] Now let $ oldsymbol{\zeta}\in Bad_{m-2,1}$ arbitrary unless if $m=4$ then $ oldsymbol{\zeta}= oldsymbol{\xi}$. Since $m-2\ge 2$ by assumption, it is easily seen that in either case \[ \psi_{ oldsymbol{\xi}}^{2	imes 1}(t) \le \psi_{ oldsymbol{\zeta}}^{(m-2)	imes 1}(t), \qquad t\ge t_0. \] Hence by Lemma~ef{llemma} the matrix $U=m{diag}( oldsymbol{\xi}, oldsymbol{\zeta})\in \mathbb{R}^{ m 	imes 2}$ satisfies  egin{equation} \limsup_{t	o\infty} t^{n/m} \psi^{m	imes 2}_{U}(t) = c, \qquad \liminf_{t	o\infty} t^{n/m} \psi^{m	imes 2}_{U}(t) = 0, \end{equation} as well. \par If $n=2$ then we must have $m=4$ due to our assumptions $	frac{n}{m}\geq  rac{1}{2}$ and $m\ge 4$, and then we can just take $\Omega=U$. Note also that in this case our claimed bound for Hausdorff dimension becomes zero, so there is nothing more to prove.\par If $n\geq 3$, then in Lemma~ef{lemme} take $V=U\in \mathbb{R}^{m	imes2}$. Note that the problematic case $n=m+2$ of the lemma is excluded here via \eqref{nm bound}. Notice further $V$ satisfies \eqref{V property} by \eqref{Vt property}. Hence, assuming $c>0$ is small enough, there exists a set of positive $m(n-2)$-dimensional Lebesgue measure $\mathcal{Y}\subseteq \mathbb{R}^{m	imes(n-2)}$ of matrices so that for any $B\in\mathcal{Y}$, the $\mathbb{R}^{m	imes n}$ matrix $\Omega=(B,U)$ satisfies  egin{equation*} \limsup_{t	o\infty}t^{n/m}\psi_{\Omega}^{m	imes n}(t)=c\, . \end{equation*} Finally, we show $\Omega$ is not badly approximable. By \eqref{Vt property} there exists a sequence of best approximations such that on the sequence $(t_{j})_{j\geq 1}$ we have  egin{equation*} \lim_{j	o \infty} t_{j}^{n/m}\psi_{U}^{m	imes 2}(t_{j})=0. \end{equation*} Considering $\Omega$, take the same sequence of the best approximations and place a zero in all entries not related to $U$ (that is starting from the third) to obtain the same statement, i.e.  egin{equation*} \lim_{j	o \infty} t_{j}^{n/m}\psi_{\Omega}^{m	imes n}(t_{j})=0. \end{equation*} Combining these two claims we infer $\Omega \in FS_{m,n}(c)$. Using \eqref{eq:tric} the dimension statement follows since we have shown that (when $m\geq 5$)  egin{equation*} \dim_H FS_{m,n}(c) \geq \dim_H \mathcal{Y} + \dim_H Bad_{m-2,1} = m(n-2) + m-2, \end{equation*} where we used that $Bad_{m-2,1}$ has full Hausdorff dimension and $\mathcal{Y}$ has positive Lebesgue measure. In the case $(m,n)=(4,3)$ we obtain  egin{equation*} \dim_H FS_{4,3}(c) \geq \dim_H \mathcal{Y} = m(n-2)=4. \end{equation*} We remark that for $(m,n)=(4,2)$ the according estimate holds as well, but the right hand side vanishes. This completes the proofs for the maximum norm, i.e. \eqref{eq:maxno}. Now let $\Vert \cdot\Vert_1$ be arbitrary and still $\Vert\cdot\Vert_2=\Vert \cdot\Vert_{\infty}$. Let $\Vert\cdot \Vert_1^{\prime}$ be the projected norm \[ \Vert (x_1,x_2)\Vert_1^{\prime} := \Vert (x_1,x_2,0,\ldots,0)\Vert_1. \] Let $\gamma= \Vert oldsymbol{e}_1\Vert_1^{\prime}$ be the norm of the first base vector of $\mathbb{R}^2$. By \cite[Theorem 2.2]{j1} and again \eqref{nm bound}, for small enough $c>0$ we may pick $ oldsymbol{\xi}\in\mathbb{R}^{2	imes 1}$ such that  egin{equation} \limsup_{t	o\infty} t^{n/m} \psi^{ 2	imes1}_{ oldsymbol{\xi}}(t) = c_1:=c \gamma^{n/m}, \qquad \liminf_{t	o\infty} t^{n/m} \psi^{2	imes1}_{ oldsymbol{\xi}}(t) = 0. \end{equation} Suppose we can show that, for any $U= m{diag}( oldsymbol{\xi}, oldsymbol{\zeta})\in \mathbb{R}^{m	imes 2}$ as above, which we can identify with elements in $\{  oldsymbol{\xi}\}	imes Bad_{m-2,1}\subseteq \mathbb{R}^{m}$, we have that  egin{equation} \psi_U^{m	imes 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}, \Vert\cdot\Vert_2,t) = \psi_{ oldsymbol{\xi}}^{2	imes 1}(|\cdot |,\Vert \cdot\Vert_{\infty},\gamma^{-1} t),\qquad t\ge t_0 \, . \end{equation} If \eqref{claim} holds, then indeed \[ \limsup_{t	o\infty} t^{n/m} \psi_U^{m	imes 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_{1}',\Vert\cdot\Vert_{2},t) =\gamma^{-n/m} \limsup_{t	o\infty} t^{n/m} \psi_{ oldsymbol{\xi}}^{2	imes 1}(|\cdot |,\Vert \cdot\Vert_{\infty},\gamma^{-1} t)= \gamma^{-n/m} c_1=c, \] and \[ \liminf_{t	o\infty} t^{n/m}\psi_U^{m	imes 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_{1}',\Vert\cdot\Vert_{2},t) = \gamma^{-n/m} \liminf_{t	o\infty}t^{n/m}\psi_{ oldsymbol{\xi}}^{2	imes 1}(|\cdot |,\Vert \cdot\Vert_{\infty},\gamma^{-1} t)= 0. \] Hence for $c$ small enough we again we may again apply Lemma~ef{lemme}, to find some set $\mathcal{Y}\subseteq \mathbb{R}^{m	imes (n-2)}$ of positive Lebesgue measure such that for any $B\in \mathcal{Y}$ we have  egin{equation*} \limsup_{t	o\infty} t^{n/m}\psi^{m	imes n}_{(U,B)}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_{1},\Vert\cdot\Vert_{2},t)=c \, ,\qquad \liminf_{t	o\infty} t^{n/m}\psi^{m	imes n}_{(U,B)}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_{1},\Vert\cdot\Vert_{2},t)=0\, . \end{equation*} So $(U,B)\in FS_{m,n}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_{1},\Vert\cdot\Vert_{2},c)$, and analogously to the maximum norm by \eqref{eq:tric} we conclude  egin{equation*} \dim_H FS_{m,n}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_{1},\Vert\cdot\Vert_{2},c) \geq \dim_H \mathcal{Y} + \dim_H Bad_{m-2,1} = m(n-2) + m-2, \end{equation*} for $m\ge 5$, and accordingly for $(m,n)=(4,3)$ we get the bound \[ \dim_H FS_{4,3}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_{1},\Vert\cdot\Vert_{2},c) \geq m(n-2)=4. \] Since $\lceil m/nceil=2$ by \eqref{nm bound}, we indeed recognize these as special cases of our claim. Thus to complete the proof for $\ell=2$ we need to show \eqref{claim} holds. For the inequality  egin{equation} \psi_U^{m	imes 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}, \Vert\cdot\Vert_2,t) \le \psi_{ oldsymbol{\xi}}^{2	imes 1}(|\cdot |,\Vert \cdot\Vert_{\infty},\gamma^{-1} t), \qquad t\geq t_{0} \end{equation} observe that any $(x, oldsymbol{w})\in \mathbb{Z}	imes \mathbb{Z}^2$ with $| x\vert\le \gamma^{-1} t$ gives rise to $ oldsymbol{z}=(x,0)=x  oldsymbol{e}_1\in \mathbb{Z}^2$ of norm $\Vert  oldsymbol{z} \Vert_1^{\prime}= |x|\gamma\le t$. Moreover since  egin{equation} U\cdot  oldsymbol{z}-( oldsymbol{w},0,\ldots,0)= ( oldsymbol{\xi}\cdot x -  oldsymbol{w} , 0, \ldots,0)\in\mathbb{R}^m, \end{equation} with the same first two coordinates followed by $m-2$ zeros, we have the identity  egin{equation} \Vert U\cdot  oldsymbol{z}-( oldsymbol{w},0,\ldots,0)\Vert_{\infty}= \Vert oldsymbol{\xi}\cdot x- oldsymbol{w}\Vert_{\infty}\, , \end{equation} where we used $\Vert\cdot\Vert_2$ being the maximum norm. As $t$ is arbitrary \eqref{eq:unn} is implied. Now consider the reverse inequality  egin{equation} \psi_U^{m	imes 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}, \Vert\cdot\Vert_2,t) \ge \psi_{ oldsymbol{\xi}}^{2	imes 1}(|\cdot |,\Vert \cdot\Vert_{\infty},\gamma^{-1} t), \qquad t\geq t_{0}. \end{equation} Begin with $(m,n)
e (4,2)$. Note that if $ oldsymbol{z}=(z_1,z_2)\in \mathbb{Z}^2$ with $\Vert  oldsymbol{z}\Vert_{1}^{\prime} \le t$ does not lie in the space $z_2=0$, then by equivalence of norms for any $	extbf{y}\in\mathbb{Z}^m$  egin{equation} \Vert U\cdot  oldsymbol{z}-  oldsymbol{y} \Vert_{\infty} \gg \Vert oldsymbol{z}\Vert_{\infty}^{-1/(m-2)}\gg \Vert oldsymbol{z}\Vert_{1}^{\prime -1/(m-2)}\ge t^{-1/(m-2)} \end{equation} where the most left estimate holds since the system is decoupled and $ oldsymbol{\zeta}\in Bad_{m-2,1}$. As we noticed above that $m\ge 4$ and $1/2\le n/m$, in our case $(m,n)
e (4,2)$ we have the strict inequality $1/(m-2)< n/m$. Then, in view of \eqref{eq:invo}, approximation quality \eqref{eq:impco} is beaten by $\psi_{ oldsymbol{\xi}}^{2	imes 1}(|\cdot |,\Vert \cdot\Vert_{\infty},\gamma^{-1} t)$, so extending accordingly the involved integer best approximation approximations to $\mathbb{Z}^n$ by adding $0$ entries leads to the same smaller value. So we can exclude such vectors. But for vectors $ oldsymbol{z}$ in the linear space $z_2=0$, the integer vector $	extbf{y}$ minimizing $\Vert U\cdot 	extbf{z}-	extbf{y}\Vert_{\infty}$ for given $	extbf{z}$ is easily seen to be of the form $	extbf{y}=(	extbf{w},0,\ldots,0)$ with $	extbf{w}\in\mathbb{Z}^2$, as otherwise some entry of $U\cdot 	extbf{z}-	extbf{y}$ is of modulus at least $1$. Then the output $U\cdot 	extbf{z}-	extbf{y}\in \mathbb{R}^m$ again satisfies \eqref{eq:noon} and hence \eqref{eq:spet}, settling \eqref{eq:rever} via a short calculation. For $m=4, n=2$ a very similar argument applies using $ oldsymbol{\zeta}= oldsymbol{\xi}$, however we need $\Vert\cdot\Vert_1$ to be expanding to exclude better approximations outside the space $z_2=0$. If the expanding property is assumed, then it is again easy to see that we may restrict $	extbf{z}$ to this space and the claims follows easily. We leave the details to the reader. Finally, let $\Vert\cdot\Vert_2$ be any expanding norm on $\mathbb{R}^m$ and consider again the induced projected norm $\Vert\cdot\Vert_2^{\prime}$ on $\mathbb{R}^2$ by \[ \Vert (x_1,x_2)\Vert_2^{\prime}:= \Vert (x_1,x_2,0,\ldots,0)\Vert_2. \] It is easy to see that $\Vert\cdot\Vert_2^{\prime}$ is an expanding norm on $\mathbb{R}^2$. A minor adaption of~\cite[Corollary~2]{j1} to more general $\Phi$ satisfying (d1)-(d3) of \cite{j1} can be proved analogously. When applied with respect to simultaneous approximation of two reals, and as (d1)-(d3) hold for our $\Phi(t)=ct^{-n/m}$ in view of \eqref{nm bound} and $c\le 1$, it yields the following: For any small enough $c>0$, we can similarly arrange some $ oldsymbol{\xi}\in\mathbb{R}^{2	imes 1}$ to satisfy \[ \limsup_{t	o\infty} t^{n/m} \psi^{ 2	imes1}_{ oldsymbol{\xi}}(|\cdot|,\Vert\cdot\Vert_2^{\prime},t) = c_1:=c \gamma^{n/m},\quad 	ext{ and } \quad \liminf_{t	o\infty} t^{n/m} \psi^{2	imes1}_{ oldsymbol{\xi}}(|\cdot|,\Vert\cdot\Vert_2^{\prime},t) = 0.\] We can then copy the proof above replacing $\Vert\cdot \Vert_{\infty}$ by $\Vert\cdot\Vert_2^{\prime}$ whenever considering $\psi^{2	imes 1}_{ oldsymbol{\xi}}$. Again by the same argument, it suffices to show the accordingly altered variant of \eqref{claim}. For the estimate \eqref{eq:unn}, the only place where we needed $\Vert\cdot\Vert_2$ to be the maximum norm is to deduce that the projected vectors satisfy \eqref{eq:spet}. However, in view of \eqref{eq:noon}, the defining property of $\Vert\cdot\Vert_2^{\prime}$ means that the according equality still holds. The proof of the reverse inequality \eqref{eq:rever} is analogous to the above, only with different implied constants in \eqref{eq:impco}. The case $\ell=2$ is done up to the full rank claim. For the rank claim, consider first the $n	imes 2$ matrix obtained from any $n$ lines of $V$ containing its first and last line, and complete it to an $n	imes n$ matrix $H$ by adding to the right an $n	imes (n-2)$ matrix of free variable entries $x_{i,j}$, $1\le i\le n$, $3\le j\le n$. Then writing $ oldsymbol{\xi}=(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_{\ell})$, $ oldsymbol{\zeta}=(\zeta_1,\ldots,\zeta_{m-\ell})$, the first and last line of $H$ are of the form $(\xi_1, 0, x_{1,3}, \ldots, x_{1,n})$ resp. $(0, \zeta_{m-\ell}, x_{n,3}, \ldots, x_{n,n})$. Since $\xi_i
e 0$ and $\zeta_j
e 0$ for all $1\le i\le \ell, 1\le j\le m-\ell$ is easy to see (otherwise $ oldsymbol{\xi}$ or $ oldsymbol{\zeta}$ would be singular, contradicting $ oldsymbol{\xi}\in DI_{\ell}(c)$ resp. $ oldsymbol{\zeta}\in Bad_{m-\ell,1}$), it is further readily checked that the determinant of $H$ is not the constant $0$ polynomial in the $x_{i,j}$. Hence only a Lebesgue nullset of $G:=(x_{i,j})\in \mathbb{R}^{n	imes (n-2)}$ will induce non invertible $H$. Now as $G\in \mathbb{R}^{n	imes (n-2)}$ can be considered a submatrix of $B\in \mathbb{R}^{m	imes (n-2)}$ above, by considering the Cartesian product $G	imes \mathbb{R}^{(m-n)	imes (n-2)}$ only a nullset of $B$ will lead to $\Omega$ of deficient rank. On the other hand, we are equipped with a positive measure set $B$ by Lemma~ef{lemme}. Hence indeed we can restrict to full rank matrices without affecting the metrical claim.
nodes.statement_short: Case ell=2.

nodes.name: Reductions
nodes.statement: {\em Case $\ell=2$:} Then \begin{equation} \frac{1}{2}\le \frac{n}{m} < 1. \end{equation} Moreover we can assume $m\ge 4$ and $n\ge 2$, as the otherwise our exclusion of $(m,n)=(3,2)$ forces $n=1$, and this case is a trivial consequence of \cite{j1}.

nodes.name: Apply j1 Theorem 2.2
nodes.statement: Let us first consider maximum norms \begin{equation} \Vert\cdot\Vert_1=\Vert\cdot\Vert_2=\Vert\cdot\Vert_{\infty}. \end{equation} Then~\cite[Theorem~2.2]{j1} in the case of simultaneous approximation to two numbers can be applied to $\Phi(t)=ct^{-n/m}$ for any $c\in (0,1)$, as the conditions (d1)-(d3) of \cite{j1} are satisfied by our choice of $\Phi$ and \eqref{nm bound}. This yields $\boldsymbol{\xi}\in \mathbb{R}^{2\times 1}$ with \[ \limsup_{t\to\infty} t^{n/m} \psi^{2\times 1}_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t) = c, \quad \text{and} \quad \liminf_{t\to\infty} t^{n/m} \psi^{2\times 1}_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t) = 0. \]
nodes.statement_short: Get xi in R^{2x1} with limsup c and liminf 0.

nodes.name: Block matrix U
nodes.statement: Now let $\boldsymbol{\zeta}\in Bad_{m-2,1}$ arbitrary unless if $m=4$ then $\boldsymbol{\zeta}=\boldsymbol{\xi}$. Since $m-2\ge 2$ by assumption, it is easily seen that in either case \[ \psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{2\times 1}(t) \le \psi_{\boldsymbol{\zeta}}^{(m-2)\times 1}(t), \qquad t\ge t_0. \] Hence by Lemma~\ref{llemma} the matrix $U=\rm{diag}(\boldsymbol{\xi},\boldsymbol{\zeta})\in \mathbb{R}^{ m \times 2}$ satisfies \begin{equation} \limsup_{t\to\infty} t^{n/m} \psi^{m\times 2}_{U}(t) = c, \qquad \liminf_{t\to\infty} t^{n/m} \psi^{m\times 2}_{U}(t) = 0, \end{equation} as well. \par
nodes.statement_short: U=diag(xi,zeta) satisfies (58) by Lemma 8.1.

nodes.name: n=2
nodes.statement: If $n=2$ then we must have $m=4$ due to our assumptions $\tfrac{n}{m}\geq \frac{1}{2}$ and $m\ge 4$, and then we can just take $\Omega=U$. Note also that in this case our claimed bound for Hausdorff dimension becomes zero, so there is nothing more to prove.\par
nodes.statement_short: Take Omega=U.

nodes.name: n>=3
nodes.statement: If $n\geq 3$, then in Lemma~\ref{lemme} take $V=U\in \mathbb{R}^{m\times2}$. Note that the problematic case $n=m+2$ of the lemma is excluded here via \eqref{nm bound}. Notice further $V$ satisfies \eqref{V property} by \eqref{Vt property}. Hence, assuming $c>0$ is small enough, there exists a set of positive $m(n-2)$-dimensional Lebesgue measure $\mathcal{Y}\subseteq \mathbb{R}^{m\times(n-2)}$ of matrices so that for any $B\in\mathcal{Y}$, the $\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ matrix $\Omega=(B,U)$ satisfies \begin{equation*} \limsup_{t\to\infty}t^{n/m}\psi_{\Omega}^{m\times n}(t)=c\, . \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Apply Lemma 7.1 with V=U.

nodes.name: Not badly approximable
nodes.statement: Finally, we show $\Omega$ is not badly approximable. By \eqref{Vt property} there exists a sequence of best approximations such that on the sequence $(t_{j})_{j\geq 1}$ we have \begin{equation*} \lim_{j\to \infty} t_{j}^{n/m}\psi_{U}^{m\times 2}(t_{j})=0. \end{equation*} Considering $\Omega$, take the same sequence of the best approximations and place a zero in all entries not related to $U$ (that is starting from the third) to obtain the same statement, i.e. \begin{equation*} \lim_{j\to \infty} t_{j}^{n/m}\psi_{\Omega}^{m\times n}(t_{j})=0. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Liminf 0 transfers to Omega.

nodes.name: Dimension for max norm
nodes.statement: Combining these two claims we infer $\Omega \in FS_{m,n}(c)$. Using \eqref{eq:tric} the dimension statement follows since we have shown that (when $m\geq 5$) \begin{equation*} \dim_H FS_{m,n}(c) \geq \dim_H \mathcal{Y} + \dim_H Bad_{m-2,1} = m(n-2) + m-2, \end{equation*} where we used that $Bad_{m-2,1}$ has full Hausdorff dimension and $\mathcal{Y}$ has positive Lebesgue measure. In the case $(m,n)=(4,3)$ we obtain \begin{equation*} \dim_H FS_{4,3}(c) \geq \dim_H \mathcal{Y} = m(n-2)=4. \end{equation*} We remark that for $(m,n)=(4,2)$ the according estimate holds as well, but the right hand side vanishes. This completes the proofs for the maximum norm, i.e. \eqref{eq:maxno}.
nodes.statement_short: dim >= m(n-2)+m-2 by the product inequality.

nodes.name: Arbitrary first norm
nodes.statement: Now let $\Vert \cdot\Vert_1$ be arbitrary and still $\Vert\cdot\Vert_2=\Vert \cdot\Vert_{\infty}$. Let $\Vert\cdot \Vert_1^{\prime}$ be the projected norm \[ \Vert (x_1,x_2)\Vert_1^{\prime} := \Vert (x_1,x_2,0,\ldots,0)\Vert_1. \] Let $\gamma= \Vert\boldsymbol{e}_1\Vert_1^{\prime}$ be the norm of the first base vector of $\mathbb{R}^2$. By \cite[Theorem 2.2]{j1} and again \eqref{nm bound}, for small enough $c>0$ we may pick $\boldsymbol{\xi}\in\mathbb{R}^{2\times 1}$ such that \begin{equation} \limsup_{t\to\infty} t^{n/m} \psi^{ 2\times1}_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t) = c_1:=c \gamma^{n/m}, \qquad \liminf_{t\to\infty} t^{n/m} \psi^{2\times1}_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t) = 0. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Use projected norm and rescaled constant c_1.

nodes.name: Reduction to (60)
nodes.statement: Suppose we can show that, for any $U= \rm{diag}(\boldsymbol{\xi},\boldsymbol{\zeta})\in \mathbb{R}^{m\times 2}$ as above, which we can identify with elements in $\{ \boldsymbol{\xi}\}\times Bad_{m-2,1}\subseteq \mathbb{R}^{m}$, we have that \begin{equation} \psi_U^{m\times 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}, \Vert\cdot\Vert_2,t) = \psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{2\times 1}(|\cdot |,\Vert \cdot\Vert_{\infty},\gamma^{-1} t),\qquad t\ge t_0 \, . \end{equation} If \eqref{claim} holds, then indeed \[ \limsup_{t\to\infty} t^{n/m} \psi_U^{m\times 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_{1}',\Vert\cdot\Vert_{2},t) =\gamma^{-n/m} \limsup_{t\to\infty} t^{n/m} \psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{2\times 1}(|\cdot |,\Vert \cdot\Vert_{\infty},\gamma^{-1} t)= \gamma^{-n/m} c_1=c, \] and \[ \liminf_{t\to\infty} t^{n/m}\psi_U^{m\times 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_{1}',\Vert\cdot\Vert_{2},t) = \gamma^{-n/m} \liminf_{t\to\infty}t^{n/m}\psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{2\times 1}(|\cdot |,\Vert \cdot\Vert_{\infty},\gamma^{-1} t)= 0. \] Hence for $c$ small enough we again we may again apply Lemma~\ref{lemme}, to find some set $\mathcal{Y}\subseteq \mathbb{R}^{m\times (n-2)}$ of positive Lebesgue measure such that for any $B\in \mathcal{Y}$ we have \begin{equation*} \limsup_{t\to\infty} t^{n/m}\psi^{m\times n}_{(U,B)}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_{1},\Vert\cdot\Vert_{2},t)=c \, ,\qquad \liminf_{t\to\infty} t^{n/m}\psi^{m\times n}_{(U,B)}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_{1},\Vert\cdot\Vert_{2},t)=0\, . \end{equation*} So $(U,B)\in FS_{m,n}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_{1},\Vert\cdot\Vert_{2},c)$, and analogously to the maximum norm by \eqref{eq:tric} we conclude \begin{equation*} \dim_H FS_{m,n}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_{1},\Vert\cdot\Vert_{2},c) \geq \dim_H \mathcal{Y} + \dim_H Bad_{m-2,1} = m(n-2) + m-2, \end{equation*} for $m\ge 5$, and accordingly for $(m,n)=(4,3)$ we get the bound \[ \dim_H FS_{4,3}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_{1},\Vert\cdot\Vert_{2},c) \geq m(n-2)=4. \] Since $\lceil m/n\rceil=2$ by \eqref{nm bound}, we indeed recognize these as special cases of our claim. Thus to complete the proof for $\ell=2$ we need to show \eqref{claim} holds.
nodes.statement_short: If (60) holds the conclusion follows via Lemma 7.1.

nodes.name: Inequality (61)
nodes.statement: For the inequality \begin{equation} \psi_U^{m\times 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}, \Vert\cdot\Vert_2,t) \le \psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{2\times 1}(|\cdot |,\Vert \cdot\Vert_{\infty},\gamma^{-1} t), \qquad t\geq t_{0} \end{equation} observe that any $(x,\boldsymbol{w})\in \mathbb{Z}\times \mathbb{Z}^2$ with $| x\vert\le \gamma^{-1} t$ gives rise to $\boldsymbol{z}=(x,0)=x \boldsymbol{e}_1\in \mathbb{Z}^2$ of norm $\Vert \boldsymbol{z} \Vert_1^{\prime}= |x|\gamma\le t$. Moreover since \begin{equation} U\cdot \boldsymbol{z}-(\boldsymbol{w},0,\ldots,0)= (\boldsymbol{\xi}\cdot x - \boldsymbol{w} , 0, \ldots,0)\in\mathbb{R}^m, \end{equation} with the same first two coordinates followed by $m-2$ zeros, we have the identity \begin{equation} \Vert U\cdot \boldsymbol{z}-(\boldsymbol{w},0,\ldots,0)\Vert_{\infty}= \Vert\boldsymbol{\xi}\cdot x-\boldsymbol{w}\Vert_{\infty}\, , \end{equation} where we used $\Vert\cdot\Vert_2$ being the maximum norm. As $t$ is arbitrary \eqref{eq:unn} is implied.
nodes.statement_short: Vectors z=x e_1 give the upper bound.

nodes.name: Inequality (64)
nodes.statement: Now consider the reverse inequality \begin{equation} \psi_U^{m\times 2}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1^{\prime}, \Vert\cdot\Vert_2,t) \ge \psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{2\times 1}(|\cdot |,\Vert \cdot\Vert_{\infty},\gamma^{-1} t), \qquad t\geq t_{0}. \end{equation} Begin with $(m,n)\ne (4,2)$. Note that if $\boldsymbol{z}=(z_1,z_2)\in \mathbb{Z}^2$ with $\Vert \boldsymbol{z}\Vert_{1}^{\prime} \le t$ does not lie in the space $z_2=0$, then by equivalence of norms for any $\textbf{y}\in\mathbb{Z}^m$ \begin{equation} \Vert U\cdot \boldsymbol{z}- \boldsymbol{y} \Vert_{\infty} \gg \Vert\boldsymbol{z}\Vert_{\infty}^{-1/(m-2)}\gg \Vert\boldsymbol{z}\Vert_{1}^{\prime -1/(m-2)}\ge t^{-1/(m-2)} \end{equation} where the most left estimate holds since the system is decoupled and $\boldsymbol{\zeta}\in Bad_{m-2,1}$. As we noticed above that $m\ge 4$ and $1/2\le n/m$, in our case $(m,n)\ne (4,2)$ we have the strict inequality $1/(m-2)< n/m$. Then, in view of \eqref{eq:invo}, approximation quality \eqref{eq:impco} is beaten by $\psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{2\times 1}(|\cdot |,\Vert \cdot\Vert_{\infty},\gamma^{-1} t)$, so extending accordingly the involved integer best approximation approximations to $\mathbb{Z}^n$ by adding $0$ entries leads to the same smaller value. So we can exclude such vectors. But for vectors $\boldsymbol{z}$ in the linear space $z_2=0$, the integer vector $\textbf{y}$ minimizing $\Vert U\cdot \textbf{z}-\textbf{y}\Vert_{\infty}$ for given $\textbf{z}$ is easily seen to be of the form $\textbf{y}=(\textbf{w},0,\ldots,0)$ with $\textbf{w}\in\mathbb{Z}^2$, as otherwise some entry of $U\cdot \textbf{z}-\textbf{y}$ is of modulus at least $1$. Then the output $U\cdot \textbf{z}-\textbf{y}\in \mathbb{R}^m$ again satisfies \eqref{eq:noon} and hence \eqref{eq:spet}, settling \eqref{eq:rever} via a short calculation. For $m=4, n=2$ a very similar argument applies using $\boldsymbol{\zeta}=\boldsymbol{\xi}$, however we need $\Vert\cdot\Vert_1$ to be expanding to exclude better approximations outside the space $z_2=0$. If the expanding property is assumed, then it is again easy to see that we may restrict $\textbf{z}$ to this space and the claims follows easily. We leave the details to the reader.
nodes.statement_short: Vectors outside z_2=0 are beaten since zeta is badly approximable.

nodes.name: Expanding second norm
nodes.statement: Finally, let $\Vert\cdot\Vert_2$ be any expanding norm on $\mathbb{R}^m$ and consider again the induced projected norm $\Vert\cdot\Vert_2^{\prime}$ on $\mathbb{R}^2$ by \[ \Vert (x_1,x_2)\Vert_2^{\prime}:= \Vert (x_1,x_2,0,\ldots,0)\Vert_2. \] It is easy to see that $\Vert\cdot\Vert_2^{\prime}$ is an expanding norm on $\mathbb{R}^2$.
nodes.statement_short: Projected norm is expanding.

nodes.name: Adapt j1 Corollary 2
nodes.statement: A minor adaption of~\cite[Corollary~2]{j1} to more general $\Phi$ satisfying (d1)-(d3) of \cite{j1} can be proved analogously. When applied with respect to simultaneous approximation of two reals, and as (d1)-(d3) hold for our $\Phi(t)=ct^{-n/m}$ in view of \eqref{nm bound} and $c\le 1$, it yields the following: For any small enough $c>0$, we can similarly arrange some $\boldsymbol{\xi}\in\mathbb{R}^{2\times 1}$ to satisfy \[ \limsup_{t\to\infty} t^{n/m} \psi^{ 2\times1}_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(|\cdot|,\Vert\cdot\Vert_2^{\prime},t) = c_1:=c \gamma^{n/m},\quad \text{ and } \quad \liminf_{t\to\infty} t^{n/m} \psi^{2\times1}_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(|\cdot|,\Vert\cdot\Vert_2^{\prime},t) = 0.\] We can then copy the proof above replacing $\Vert\cdot \Vert_{\infty}$ by $\Vert\cdot\Vert_2^{\prime}$ whenever considering $\psi^{2\times 1}_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}$. Again by the same argument, it suffices to show the accordingly altered variant of \eqref{claim}. For the estimate \eqref{eq:unn}, the only place where we needed $\Vert\cdot\Vert_2$ to be the maximum norm is to deduce that the projected vectors satisfy \eqref{eq:spet}. However, in view of \eqref{eq:noon}, the defining property of $\Vert\cdot\Vert_2^{\prime}$ means that the according equality still holds. The proof of the reverse inequality \eqref{eq:rever} is analogous to the above, only with different implied constants in \eqref{eq:impco}. The case $\ell=2$ is done up to the full rank claim.
nodes.statement_short: Repeat the argument with the projected norm.

nodes.name: Rank claim
nodes.statement: For the rank claim, consider first the $n\times 2$ matrix obtained from any $n$ lines of $V$ containing its first and last line, and complete it to an $n\times n$ matrix $H$ by adding to the right an $n\times (n-2)$ matrix of free variable entries $x_{i,j}$, $1\le i\le n$, $3\le j\le n$. Then writing $\boldsymbol{\xi}=(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_{\ell})$, $\boldsymbol{\zeta}=(\zeta_1,\ldots,\zeta_{m-\ell})$, the first and last line of $H$ are of the form $(\xi_1, 0, x_{1,3}, \ldots, x_{1,n})$ resp. $(0, \zeta_{m-\ell}, x_{n,3}, \ldots, x_{n,n})$. Since $\xi_i\ne 0$ and $\zeta_j\ne 0$ for all $1\le i\le \ell, 1\le j\le m-\ell$ is easy to see (otherwise $\boldsymbol{\xi}$ or $\boldsymbol{\zeta}$ would be singular, contradicting $\boldsymbol{\xi}\in DI_{\ell}(c)$ resp. $\boldsymbol{\zeta}\in Bad_{m-\ell,1}$), it is further readily checked that the determinant of $H$ is not the constant $0$ polynomial in the $x_{i,j}$. Hence only a Lebesgue nullset of $G:=(x_{i,j})\in \mathbb{R}^{n\times (n-2)}$ will induce non invertible $H$. Now as $G\in \mathbb{R}^{n\times (n-2)}$ can be considered a submatrix of $B\in \mathbb{R}^{m\times (n-2)}$ above, by considering the Cartesian product $G\times \mathbb{R}^{(m-n)\times (n-2)}$ only a nullset of $B$ will lead to $\Omega$ of deficient rank. On the other hand, we are equipped with a positive measure set $B$ by Lemma~\ref{lemme}. Hence indeed we can restrict to full rank matrices without affecting the metrical claim.
nodes.statement_short: Determinant is a nonzero polynomial, so full rank generically.

nodes.name: Case ell>=3
nodes.statement: {\em Case $\ell\ge 3$:} Then by \eqref{eq:ojsi} similarly to \eqref{nm bound} we have \begin{equation} \frac{1}{\ell}\le \frac{n}{m} < \frac{1}{\ell-1}. \end{equation} Now again~\cite[Theorem~2.2]{j1} can be applied, with respect to simultaneous approximation to $\ell$ numbers, to $\Phi(t)=ct^{-n/m}$ for any $c\in (0,1)$, as its conditions (d1)-(d3) are satisfied by \eqref{eq:Dd}. This yields $\boldsymbol{\xi}\in \mathbb{R}^{\ell \times 1}$ so that \[ \limsup_{t\to\infty} t^{n/m} \psi^{\ell \times 1}_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t) = c, \quad \text{and} \quad \liminf_{t\to\infty} t^{n/m} \psi^{\ell \times 1}_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t) = 0. \] Now let $\boldsymbol{\zeta}\in Bad_{m-\ell ,1}$ arbitrary unless if $m=2\ell$ then $\boldsymbol{\zeta}=\boldsymbol{\xi}$. We again consider $U=\rm{diag}(\boldsymbol{\xi}, \boldsymbol{\zeta})\in \mathbb{R}^{m\times 2}$ as above. As soon as strict inequality \begin{equation} m> 2\ell \end{equation} holds, we have $1/(m-\ell)< n/m$ so that the analogue of \eqref{eq:impco} similarly implies that we can restrict to the space $z_2=0$. It can be checked that the analogous arguments of the case $\ell=2$ above apply. Notably when transitioning to any expanding norm $\Vert\cdot\Vert_2$, here we consider the restriction \[ \Vert (x_1,\ldots,x_{\ell})\Vert_2^{\prime}:= \Vert (x_1,\ldots,x_{\ell},0,\ldots,0)\Vert_2, \] and apply an analogous variant of~\cite[Corollary~2]{j1} with respect to simultaneous approximation to $\ell$ numbers. Finally we need to discuss the separate cases when \eqref{eq:mpso} is satisfied, and evaluate the Hausdorff dimensions. Recall we have assumed $\ell\ge 3$, moreover we can assume $n\ge 2$ as $n=1$ was done in \cite{j2}. Via \eqref{eq:ojsi}, condition \eqref{eq:mpso} is readily checked to be satisfied if $n\ge 3$. Thus we are left with the subset of cases $n=2$. The cases $n=2, m\ge 4$ even, leading to $m=2\ell$, can be dealt with similarly to the case $(m,n)=(4,2)$ for $\ell=2$ above. This indeed leaves open only the cases $n=2$, and $m$ odd, as excluded in the theorem. By construction, and the repeatedly used observation that $Bad_{m-\ell ,1}$ has full Hausdorff dimension $m-\ell$, we obtain the Hausdorff dimension bound \[ \dim_H FS_{m,n}(c) \ge m\cdot (n-2)+(m-\ell)=m(n-1)-\left\lceil\frac{m}{n}\right\rceil, \qquad m\ge 2\ell+1, \] of the theorem. The remaining case $m=2\ell=2\lceil m/n\rceil$ is readily checked to lead precisely to the cases $n=2$ and $m$ even or $(m,n)=(4,3)$. When $(m,n)=(4,3)$ we have $\ell=2$, which is already treated above. It should be remarked that for $n=2$ our Hausdorff dimension bound is just $m(n-2)=0$, thus of no interest. The full rank claim is also proved analogously to the case $\ell=2$.
nodes.statement_short: Case ell>=3.

nodes.name: Apply j1 Theorem 2.2
nodes.statement: {\em Case $\ell\ge 3$:} Then by \eqref{eq:ojsi} similarly to \eqref{nm bound} we have \begin{equation} \frac{1}{\ell}\le \frac{n}{m} < \frac{1}{\ell-1}. \end{equation} Now again~\cite[Theorem~2.2]{j1} can be applied, with respect to simultaneous approximation to $\ell$ numbers, to $\Phi(t)=ct^{-n/m}$ for any $c\in (0,1)$, as its conditions (d1)-(d3) are satisfied by \eqref{eq:Dd}. This yields $\boldsymbol{\xi}\in \mathbb{R}^{\ell \times 1}$ so that \[ \limsup_{t\to\infty} t^{n/m} \psi^{\ell \times 1}_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t) = c, \quad \text{and} \quad \liminf_{t\to\infty} t^{n/m} \psi^{\ell \times 1}_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t) = 0. \]
nodes.statement_short: Get xi in R^{ell x 1}.

nodes.name: Block matrix
nodes.statement: Now let $\boldsymbol{\zeta}\in Bad_{m-\ell ,1}$ arbitrary unless if $m=2\ell$ then $\boldsymbol{\zeta}=\boldsymbol{\xi}$. We again consider $U=\rm{diag}(\boldsymbol{\xi}, \boldsymbol{\zeta})\in \mathbb{R}^{m\times 2}$ as above. As soon as strict inequality \begin{equation} m> 2\ell \end{equation} holds, we have $1/(m-\ell)< n/m$ so that the analogue of \eqref{eq:impco} similarly implies that we can restrict to the space $z_2=0$. It can be checked that the analogous arguments of the case $\ell=2$ above apply. Notably when transitioning to any expanding norm $\Vert\cdot\Vert_2$, here we consider the restriction \[ \Vert (x_1,\ldots,x_{\ell})\Vert_2^{\prime}:= \Vert (x_1,\ldots,x_{\ell},0,\ldots,0)\Vert_2, \] and apply an analogous variant of~\cite[Corollary~2]{j1} with respect to simultaneous approximation to $\ell$ numbers.
nodes.statement_short: U=diag(xi,zeta); restrict to z_2=0 when m>2 ell.

nodes.name: Remaining cases
nodes.statement: Finally we need to discuss the separate cases when \eqref{eq:mpso} is satisfied, and evaluate the Hausdorff dimensions. Recall we have assumed $\ell\ge 3$, moreover we can assume $n\ge 2$ as $n=1$ was done in \cite{j2}. Via \eqref{eq:ojsi}, condition \eqref{eq:mpso} is readily checked to be satisfied if $n\ge 3$. Thus we are left with the subset of cases $n=2$. The cases $n=2, m\ge 4$ even, leading to $m=2\ell$, can be dealt with similarly to the case $(m,n)=(4,2)$ for $\ell=2$ above. This indeed leaves open only the cases $n=2$, and $m$ odd, as excluded in the theorem.
nodes.statement_short: Only n=2, m odd remain open.

nodes.name: Dimension bound
nodes.statement: By construction, and the repeatedly used observation that $Bad_{m-\ell ,1}$ has full Hausdorff dimension $m-\ell$, we obtain the Hausdorff dimension bound \[ \dim_H FS_{m,n}(c) \ge m\cdot (n-2)+(m-\ell)=m(n-1)-\left\lceil\frac{m}{n}\right\rceil, \qquad m\ge 2\ell+1, \] of the theorem. The remaining case $m=2\ell=2\lceil m/n\rceil$ is readily checked to lead precisely to the cases $n=2$ and $m$ even or $(m,n)=(4,3)$. When $(m,n)=(4,3)$ we have $\ell=2$, which is already treated above. It should be remarked that for $n=2$ our Hausdorff dimension bound is just $m(n-2)=0$, thus of no interest. The full rank claim is also proved analogously to the case $\ell=2$.
nodes.statement_short: dim >= m(n-1)-ceil(m/n).

nodes.name: Convex bodies M_{A,B} and dual bodies
nodes.statement: For matrix $\Omega \in \mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ and real numbers $A,B\in\mathbb{R}_{+}$ define the convex bodies \begin{align*} M_{A,B}(\Omega)&:=\left\{ \boldsymbol{z}\in \mathbb{R}^{n+m}: \max_{1\leq j\leq m} \left| \sum_{i=1}^{n}\Omega_{j,i}z_{i}+z_{n+j}\right|\leq A, \quad \max_{1\leq i \leq n }|z_{i}|\leq B \right\}, \\ \widehat{M}_{A,B}(\Omega)&:=\left\{ \boldsymbol{z}\in \mathbb{R}^{n+m}: \max_{1\leq i \leq n} \left|z_{i}-\sum_{j=1}^{m}\Omega_{i,j}z_{n+j}\right|\leq B, \quad \max_{1\leq j \leq m} |z_{n+j}|\leq A \right\}. \end{align*}

nodes.name: German's transference theorem
nodes.statement: {\cite[Theorem 7]{german}} Let $\Omega \in \mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ and $A,B\in\mathbb{R}_{+}$. If \begin{equation*} M_{A,B}(\Omega)\cap \mathbb{Z}^{n+m}\backslash\{ \boldsymbol{0} \} \neq \emptyset \, , \end{equation*} then \begin{equation*} \widehat{M}_{A^{*},B^{*}}(\Omega)\cap \mathbb{Z}^{n+m}\backslash \{ \boldsymbol{0} \} \neq \emptyset \end{equation*} for \begin{equation*} A^{*}=C(A^{n}B^{1-n})^{\frac{1}{n+m-1}} \quad \text{ and } \quad B^{*}=C(A^{1-m}B^{m})^{\frac{1}{n+m-1}}, \end{equation*} with $C>0$ constant dependent only on $n$ and $m$.
nodes.label: transference

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 1.1
nodes.statement: Since $\Omega \in FS_{m,n}(\|\cdot\|_{1},\|\cdot\|_{2},c)\subseteq \mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ we have $\Theta^{m\times n}(\|\cdot\|_{1},\|\cdot\|_{2},\Omega)=c$. By the equivalence of norms we have that the same is true up to some constant, and so \begin{equation*} \Theta^{m\times n}(\|\cdot\|_{\infty},\|\cdot\|_{\infty},\Omega)\asymp c\, . \end{equation*} Hence, for all sufficiently large $t\in\mathbb{R}$ and some $\rho>0$ there is an integer \begin{equation*} \boldsymbol{b} \in M_{\rho t^{-n/m},t}(\Omega)\cap\mathbb{Z}^{n+m}\backslash \{\textbf{0}\}\, . \end{equation*} By Theorem~\ref{transference}, for all sufficiently large $u\in\mathbb{R}$ there exists integer \begin{equation*} \boldsymbol{b} \in \widehat{M}_{u,\delta u^{-m/n}}(\Omega)\cap\mathbb{Z}^{n+m}\backslash \{\textbf{0}\}\, , \quad \text{ for } \quad \delta=C^{\tfrac{m+n}{n}}\rho^{\tfrac{m}{n(n+m-1)}}. \end{equation*} Hence $\Omega^{T} \in Di_{n,m}(\delta)$, and by equivalence of norms there exists some $\delta^{*}>0$ such that $\Omega^{T}\in Di_{n,m}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_{2},\Vert\cdot\Vert_{1},\delta^{*})$. If $D^{*}=D^{n\times m}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1,\Vert\cdot\Vert_2)$ is the Dirichlet constant from \eqref{eq:obben} for the transpose problem, for small enough $\delta$ and thus $\delta^{*}<D^{*}$ this will induce a Dirichlet improvable matrix $\Omega^{T}$. Conversely, for any $0<\gamma<c$ there exists an unbounded sequence of $t\in\mathbb{R}$ for which \begin{equation*} \widehat{M}_{t,\gamma t^{-n/m}}(\Omega^{T})\cap \mathbb{Z}^{n+m}\backslash\{\textbf{0}\} = \emptyset\, , \end{equation*} otherwise $\Omega \in Di_{m,n}(\gamma)$, which is clearly false since $\Omega \in DI_{m,n}(c)$. Applying the contrapositive of Theorem~\ref{transference} we obtain that there exist certain arbitrarily large $u\in\mathbb{R}$ and a constant $C^{*}>0$ for which \begin{equation*} M_{C^{*}u^{-n/m},u}(\Omega^{T})\cap\mathbb{Z}^{n+m}\backslash\{\textbf{0}\} = \emptyset\, . \end{equation*} Hence $\Omega^{T} \not\in Sing_{n,m}$. Furthermore, one can similarly show that $\Omega^{T} \not \in Bad_{n,m}$, and so $$\Omega^{T} \in Di_{n,m}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_{2},\Vert\cdot\Vert_{1},\delta^{*})\backslash (Sing_{n,m}\cup Bad_{n,m})\subseteq FS_{n,m}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_{2},\Vert\cdot\Vert_{1}).$$
nodes.statement_short: Apply German's transference (Theorem 9.1) in both directions to transfer Dirichlet improvability and non-singularity to the transpose.

nodes.name: Constant up to norms
nodes.statement: Since $\Omega \in FS_{m,n}(\|\cdot\|_{1},\|\cdot\|_{2},c)\subseteq \mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ we have $\Theta^{m\times n}(\|\cdot\|_{1},\|\cdot\|_{2},\Omega)=c$. By the equivalence of norms we have that the same is true up to some constant, and so \begin{equation*} \Theta^{m\times n}(\|\cdot\|_{\infty},\|\cdot\|_{\infty},\Omega)\asymp c\, . \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Theta in max norms is comparable to c.

nodes.name: Integer points
nodes.statement: Hence, for all sufficiently large $t\in\mathbb{R}$ and some $\rho>0$ there is an integer \begin{equation*} \boldsymbol{b} \in M_{\rho t^{-n/m},t}(\Omega)\cap\mathbb{Z}^{n+m}\backslash \{\textbf{0}\}\, . \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Integer points in M_{rho t^{-n/m},t}.

nodes.name: Transfer Dirichlet improvability
nodes.statement: By Theorem~\ref{transference}, for all sufficiently large $u\in\mathbb{R}$ there exists integer \begin{equation*} \boldsymbol{b} \in \widehat{M}_{u,\delta u^{-m/n}}(\Omega)\cap\mathbb{Z}^{n+m}\backslash \{\textbf{0}\}\, , \quad \text{ for } \quad \delta=C^{\tfrac{m+n}{n}}\rho^{\tfrac{m}{n(n+m-1)}}. \end{equation*} Hence $\Omega^{T} \in Di_{n,m}(\delta)$, and by equivalence of norms there exists some $\delta^{*}>0$ such that $\Omega^{T}\in Di_{n,m}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_{2},\Vert\cdot\Vert_{1},\delta^{*})$. If $D^{*}=D^{n\times m}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1,\Vert\cdot\Vert_2)$ is the Dirichlet constant from \eqref{eq:obben} for the transpose problem, for small enough $\delta$ and thus $\delta^{*}<D^{*}$ this will induce a Dirichlet improvable matrix $\Omega^{T}$.
nodes.statement_short: Transference gives Omega^T in Di.

nodes.name: Not singular
nodes.statement: Conversely, for any $0<\gamma<c$ there exists an unbounded sequence of $t\in\mathbb{R}$ for which \begin{equation*} \widehat{M}_{t,\gamma t^{-n/m}}(\Omega^{T})\cap \mathbb{Z}^{n+m}\backslash\{\textbf{0}\} = \emptyset\, , \end{equation*} otherwise $\Omega \in Di_{m,n}(\gamma)$, which is clearly false since $\Omega \in DI_{m,n}(c)$. Applying the contrapositive of Theorem~\ref{transference} we obtain that there exist certain arbitrarily large $u\in\mathbb{R}$ and a constant $C^{*}>0$ for which \begin{equation*} M_{C^{*}u^{-n/m},u}(\Omega^{T})\cap\mathbb{Z}^{n+m}\backslash\{\textbf{0}\} = \emptyset\, . \end{equation*} Hence $\Omega^{T} \not\in Sing_{n,m}$.
nodes.statement_short: Contrapositive of transference gives Omega^T not singular.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Furthermore, one can similarly show that $\Omega^{T} \not \in Bad_{n,m}$, and so $$\Omega^{T} \in Di_{n,m}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_{2},\Vert\cdot\Vert_{1},\delta^{*})\backslash (Sing_{n,m}\cup Bad_{n,m})\subseteq FS_{n,m}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_{2},\Vert\cdot\Vert_{1}).$$
nodes.statement_short: Similarly not badly approximable; so Omega^T in FS.

nodes.name: Improvements using Agin-Weiss
nodes.statement: Let $m,n$ be positive integers and $\Vert.\Vert_1$ and $\Vert.\Vert_2$ be arbitrary norms on $\mathbb{R}^n$ and $\mathbb{R}^m$ respectively. Then there exists $c_0=c_0(m,n,\Vert.\Vert_1,\Vert.\Vert_2)>0$ so that for any $c\in [0,c_0]$ we have the following: \begin{itemize} \item[(a)] As soon as $m\ne n$ and $(m,n)\ne (1,3)$ we have \[ \dim_H FS_{m,n}(\Vert \cdot \Vert_{1},\Vert \cdot \Vert_{2},c)\ge m\cdot (n-2). \] For $m=n$ we still have \[ \dim_H DI_{n,n}(\Vert \cdot \Vert_{1},\Vert \cdot \Vert_{2},c)\ge n\cdot (n-2). \] \item[(b)] If $m>n$ we have the stronger bound \[ \dim_H FS_{m,n}(\Vert \cdot \Vert_{1},\Vert \cdot \Vert_{2},c)\ge m\cdot (n-1). \] \end{itemize}
nodes.section: 10 Appendix: Improvements using subsequent work by Agin and Weiss
assumptions: Let $m,n$ be positive integers and $\Vert.\Vert_1$ and $\Vert.\Vert_2$ be arbitrary norms on $\mathbb{R}^n$ and $\mathbb{R}^m$ respectively.
nodes.statement_short: Using Agin-Weiss: dim FS(c) >= m(n-2) for m != n (not (1,3)) and >= m(n-1) for m>n, for small c and any norms.
nodes.label: AWe

nodes.name: The square case m=n
nodes.statement: In part (a), for $m=n$ we cannot exclude that the matrices in $DI_{n,n}(\Vert \cdot \Vert_{1},\Vert \cdot \Vert_{2},c)$ we obtain are badly approximable and thus outside our sets $FS_{n,n}(\Vert \cdot \Vert_{1},\Vert \cdot \Vert_{2},c)$. In private communication with the authors of \cite{AginWeiss2024}, they were optimistic that some refinement of their method may close the gap, however it is by no means immediate from their work. We can prove unconditionally a weaker positive lower bound for $\dim_H FS_{n,n}(\Vert \cdot \Vert_{1},\Vert \cdot \Vert_{2},c)$ when $n\ge 3$, by combining the diagonal block method from Theorem \ref{arbn} with the case $m=n=2$ of \cite{AginWeiss2024}, however we prefer to omit it.
nodes.section: 10 Appendix: Improvements using subsequent work by Agin and Weiss

nodes.name: Folklore set non-empty for all (m,n) other than (1,1)
nodes.statement: Combining Theorem~\ref{AWe} with Lemma \ref{Folklore transpose} and Theorem \ref{arbn} we may infer that the Folklore set is not empty for any $(m,n)\ne (1,1)$, and obtain reasonably good metrical bounds, however still weaker than \cite[Theorem~3.15]{Dasetal} (for max norms) recalled in Section~\ref{recentadvances}.
nodes.section: 10 Appendix: Improvements using subsequent work by Agin and Weiss

As in the notation in~\cite[Corollary~1]{AginWeiss2024} set $\gamma=	frac{n}{m}$ and consider the matrices $M_{m,1}$. Then, since we assume $	frac{n}{m}<1$, by \cite[Corollary~1]{AginWeiss2024} we have that for any given $c\ge 0$, there are uncountably many $ oldsymbol{\xi}\in \mathbb{R}^{m	imes 1}$ such that \[ \limsup_{t	o\infty} t^{n/m}\psi_{ oldsymbol{\xi}}^{m	imes 1}(\Vert \cdot \Vert_{1}^{\prime},\Vert \cdot \Vert_{2},t)=c\, . \] Now, a variant of Lemma~ef{lemme}, with $V= oldsymbol{\xi}\in \mathbb{R}^{m	imes 1}$ a column vector (proved analogously, see the last part of its proof and the comment below Lemma~ef{lemme}), combined with the argument in Section~ef{st2} reads as follows: If $c$ was chosen small enough, then for a positive $m(n-1)$-Lebesgue measure set of matrices $B\in \mathbb{R}^{m	imes (n-1)}$, the extension of $V= oldsymbol{\xi}$ to a matrix $\Omega=(V,B)\in \mathbb{R}^{m	imes n}$ via adding $B$ to the right of $ oldsymbol{\xi}$ has the property \[ \Theta^{m	imes n}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1,\Vert\cdot\Vert_2,\Omega)=\limsup_{t	o\infty} t^{n/m}\psi_{\Omega}^{m	imes n}(\Vert \cdot \Vert_{1},\Vert \cdot \Vert_{2},t)= \limsup_{t	o\infty} t^{n/m}\psi_{ oldsymbol{\xi}}^{m	imes 1}(\Vert \cdot \Vert_{1}^{\prime},\Vert \cdot \Vert_{2},t)=c\, . \] The obtained condition $n
e m+1$ is irrelevant since $m>n$. nodes.statement: Proof part (b): Similar to \eqref{eq:pno}, by abuse of notation let now $\Vert.\Vert_1^{\prime}$ be the restriction of $\Vert.\Vert_1$ to the first coordinate, that is \[ \Vert x_1 \Vert_1^{\prime}:= \Vert (x_1,0,\ldots,0)\Vert_1. \] Clearly this is a multiple of the absolute value. As in the notation in~\cite[Corollary~1]{AginWeiss2024} set $\gamma=\tfrac{n}{m}$ and consider the matrices $M_{m,1}$. Then, since we assume $\tfrac{n}{m}<1$, by \cite[Corollary~1]{AginWeiss2024} we have that for any given $c\ge 0$, there are uncountably many $\boldsymbol{\xi}\in \mathbb{R}^{m\times 1}$ such that \[ \limsup_{t\to\infty} t^{n/m}\psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{m\times 1}(\Vert \cdot \Vert_{1}^{\prime},\Vert \cdot \Vert_{2},t)=c\, . \] Now, a variant of Lemma~\ref{lemme}, with $V=\boldsymbol{\xi}\in \mathbb{R}^{m\times 1}$ a column vector (proved analogously, see the last part of its proof and the comment below Lemma~\ref{lemme}), combined with the argument in Section~\ref{st2} reads as follows: If $c$ was chosen small enough, then for a positive $m(n-1)$-Lebesgue measure set of matrices $B\in \mathbb{R}^{m\times (n-1)}$, the extension of $V=\boldsymbol{\xi}$ to a matrix $\Omega=(V,B)\in \mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ via adding $B$ to the right of $\boldsymbol{\xi}$ has the property \[ \Theta^{m\times n}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1,\Vert\cdot\Vert_2,\Omega)=\limsup_{t\to\infty} t^{n/m}\psi_{\Omega}^{m\times n}(\Vert \cdot \Vert_{1},\Vert \cdot \Vert_{2},t)= \limsup_{t\to\infty} t^{n/m}\psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{m\times 1}(\Vert \cdot \Vert_{1}^{\prime},\Vert \cdot \Vert_{2},t)=c\, . \] The obtained condition $n\ne m+1$ is irrelevant since $m>n$. Now notice that we can assume $n \ge 2$ (otherwise our statement is trivial) and thus $n/m>1/m$ exceeds the trivial Dirichlet exponent for an $m\times 1$ column vector. It then follows from non-trivial estimates relating uniform versus ordinary exponents of approximation for simultaneous approximation (see~\cite{mamo} for optimal estimates, weaker bounds from~\cite{SchmidtSummerer} suffice as well) that for some explicit $\beta>n/m$ \[ \liminf_{t\to\infty} t^{\beta}\psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{m\times 1}(\Vert \cdot \Vert_{1}^{\prime},\Vert \cdot \Vert_{2},t)=0 \] and thus similarly as in part (a) further \[ \tilde{\Theta}^{m\times n}(\Vert\cdot\Vert_1,\Vert\cdot\Vert_2,\Omega)=\liminf_{t\to\infty} t^{n/m}\psi_{\Omega}^{m\times n}(\Vert \cdot \Vert_{1},\Vert \cdot \Vert_{2},t)\le \liminf_{t\to\infty} t^{n/m}\psi_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{m\times 1}(\Vert \cdot \Vert_{1}^{\prime},\Vert \cdot \Vert_{2},t)=0. \] Hence again any such $B$ induces $\Omega\in FS_{m,n}(\Vert.\Vert_1, \Vert.\Vert_2,c)$ and we conclude as in part (a).
